purpose:
As part of a planning permission granted to
Sheffield University it was agreed that an Experimental Traffic
Order (ETO) should be introduced on Northumberland Road between
Marlborough Road (Goodwin Sports Centre) and Whitham Road. The
purpose of the ETO is to trial a revised traffic arrangement
incorporating improved infrastructure for cyclists, one-way
operation for motor vehicles including contraflow cycle lane (with
segregation), pedestrian safety improvements, and the removal of
on-street parking. The scheme was implemented in April of 2025.
The scheme has generated a total of 107
objections and 27 expressions of support. A considerable proportion
of objections were submitted at the initial stages of
implementation or prior to the scheme
becoming fully operational.  Engagement
has reduced significantly over time, with very few representations
received during the latter stages of the experimental period.
The principal concerns raised relate to
perceived traffic displacement onto surrounding streets, the
removal of on-street parking, and changes to local traffic
operation. These objections have been considered alongside
monitoring data collected throughout the experimental period, which
indicates the measures are operating as intended with no evidence
of significant adverse operational impacts.
Approval has now been sought to make the ETO
permanent as currently implemented.
content:
As part of a planning permission granted to
Sheffield University it was agreed that an Experimental Traffic
Order (ETO) should be introduced on Northumberland Road between
Marlborough Road (Goodwin Sports Centre) and Whitham Road. The
purpose of the ETO is to trial a revised traffic arrangement
incorporating improved infrastructure for cyclists, one-way
operation for motor vehicles including contraflow cycle lane (with
segregation), pedestrian safety improvements, and the removal of
on-street parking. The scheme was implemented in April of 2025.
The scheme has generated a total of 107
objections and 27 expressions of support. A considerable proportion
of objections were submitted at the initial stages of
implementation or prior to the scheme
becoming fully operational.  Engagement
has reduced significantly over time, with very few representations
received during the latter stages of the experimental period.
The principal concerns raised relate to
perceived traffic displacement onto surrounding streets, the
removal of on-street parking, and changes to local traffic
operation. These objections have been considered alongside
monitoring data collected throughout the experimental period, which
indicates the measures are operating as intended with no evidence
of significant adverse operational impacts.
Approval has now been sought to make the ETO
permanent as currently implemented.
 


Consider the
objections to the proposed Experimental Traffic Order together with
responses provided by officers of City Transport.
Make permanent the ETO, as currently
implemented, in accordance with the Road Traffic Regulation Act
1984
Inform all objectors
of this decision.

 
 

The Northumberland Road ETO has been
introduced to trial changes to how traffic uses the road, in
particular cyclists and pedestrians. The temporary measures have
created an environment where cyclists can feel comfortable to use
the route and pedestrians can also feel comfortable crossing the
road. According to traffic flow data collected during the
experimental period there has been some minor reallocation of
motorised traffic on roads adjacent to Northumberland Road but not
at a level to cause concern.
 
The scheme has been subject to statutory
consultation and monitoring throughout the experimental period. In
total, 107 objections and 27 expressions of support have been
received. A considerable proportion of objections were submitted at
the initial stages of implementation or prior to the scheme
becoming fully operational. Correspondence in the latter stages of
the experimental period has been limited, with very few
representations received in the last 10 months.
 
Having regard to the monitoring evidence, the
objectives of the scheme, and the statutory duties of the Council,
the measures are considered to be
operating satisfactorily and delivering the intended outcomes in
relation to active travel provision and traffic management within
the corridor. On balance, it is considered that the benefits of the
scheme outweigh the unwithdrawn objections received.
 
The Order is therefore required to be made
permanent to retain the measures currently in operation and provide
long-term certainty for users of the route.
 


1)   
A ‘do nothing’ option was considered, whereby the
existing two-way operation and on-street parking arrangements on
Northumberland Road would have been retained. However, this would
not safely address the identified issues relating to pedestrian
safety, cycle provision, and traffic conflict within a constrained
corridor with prominent levels of pedestrian activity.
 

2)   
An option to introduce limited or partial measures, such as
retaining two-way traffic operation while introducing advisory
cycle provision or reduced parking restrictions, was also
considered. This approach was discounted as it would not provide
sufficient space to safely accommodate cycling infrastructure or
meaningfully reduce conflict between road users.
 

3)   
Consideration was also given to implementing the scheme without
physical segregation for the contraflow cycle lane. This option was
not progressed, as it would offer a lower level of protection for
cyclists and would be less likely to achieve the intended safety
and mode shift objectives.
topline: The Assistant Director City Transport has decided to make the Experimental Traffic Order on Northumberland Road permanent, despite objections raised by stakeholders.

purpose:

cloud-based telephony system that supports the Council’s
contact centre, phone services and call routing for several
critical services. This telephony system also connects with Council
systems to deliver automated self-service and webchat
functionality.
 
The managed service contract commenced on 1
August 2023 and was expected to end on 31 July 2026.
 
Approval was sought to commission a new
three-year contract for the cloud-hosted telephony system, with the
option to extend for one further year, at a total estimated value
of £3,431,073 excluding VAT.
content:

Guru under a managed service contract for the provision of
cloud-based telephony system that supports the Council’s
contact centre, phone services and call routing for several
critical services. This telephony system also connects with Council
systems to deliver automated self-service and webchat
functionality.
 
The managed service contract commenced on 1
August 2023 and was expected to end on 31 July 2026.
 
Approval was sought to commission a new
three-year contract for the cloud-hosted telephony system, with the
option to extend for one further year, at a total estimated value
of £3,431,073 excluding VAT.
 

The commission of a contract for the
cloud-based telephony system service for the duration of 3 years,
with the option to extend for one year at the total estimated value
of £3,431,073 excluding VAT.

The current contract for the cloud-based
telephony system is coming to an end.
 

Alternative Option 1: Allow the existing
contract to expire without commissioning a replacement
provider.
This is not an option; the Council requires a
cloud-hosted telephony System to support and underpin its critical
services and other routine daily activities; this option would have
a significant and adverse impact on the range of Council services
described in this report as reliant on the cloud- hosted telephony
system.
 
Alternative Option 2: Extend the current
contract
Whilst the current contract includes a
12-month extension option, this would only provide a short-term
continuation and defer the need for a longer-term commissioning
decision.
 
 A new three-year
contract, with a one-year extension option, provides greater
service stability, commercial certainty and continuity for a
platform that supports critical Council services, the Future
Sheffield Programme, the Council’s Digital Strategy and the
development of the Core Customer Hub.
 
Using the CCS G-Cloud 14 framework provides a
compliant route to market and enables the Council to retain the
incumbent provider, avoiding the additional cost, resource
commitment, operational disruption and technical migration risk
associated with moving platform.
 
Alternative Option 3: Insourcing the
service
This is not a viable option as it is not
practical for the Council to host and maintain telephony
infrastructure, and it does not align with the Council's
cloud-first IT strategy.

purpose:
A secondary financial support package for Moor
Market traders has been recommended following the temporary closure
of the market, in response to evidence of pest activity and the
associated public health, food hygiene, health and safety and
reputational risks.
 
The Council has already developed a targeted
one-month rent and service charge relief package for Moor Market
traders affected by the closure and recovery response. That package
was designed as a one-off recovery support measure linked to the
exceptional circumstances of the incident.
 
Further representations have been received
from traders and stakeholders about the ongoing financial impact of
the closure and recovery period, including lost trading
opportunities, disruption to business continuity, additional
cleaning and reopening costs, stock-related impacts, the need to
restore customer confidence and footfall.
 
The recommended proposal provides a further
one-month rent and service charge relief package together with a
£500 discretionary payment to each trader. The proposal is
designed to provide immediate and equitable financial support, is
capable of rapid implementation, and can be funded within the
current Environmental Services and Regulation budget forecast
position.
content:
A secondary financial support package for Moor
Market traders has been recommended following the temporary closure
of the market, in response to evidence of pest activity and the
associated public health, food hygiene, health and safety and
reputational risks.
 
The Council has already developed a targeted
one-month rent and service charge relief package for Moor Market
traders affected by the closure and recovery response. That package
was designed as a one-off recovery support measure linked to the
exceptional circumstances of the incident.
 
Further representations have been received
from traders and stakeholders about the ongoing financial impact of
the closure and recovery period, including lost trading
opportunities, disruption to business continuity, additional
cleaning and reopening costs, stock-related impacts, the need to
restore customer confidence and footfall.
 
The recommended proposal provides a further
one-month rent and service charge relief package together with a
£500 discretionary payment to each trader. The proposal is
designed to provide immediate and equitable financial support, is
capable of rapid implementation, and can be funded within the
current Environmental Services and Regulation budget forecast
position.
 

1.   
The temporary closure of Moor Market and the impact this has had on
traders, customers and the wider market recovery was noted.
2.   
The existing targeted one-month rent and service charge relief
package for Moor Market traders was noted.
3.   
The fact that the existing support package was designed as a
one-off recovery support measure and not as compensation for loss
of income, loss of profits, stock losses, staff costs or wider
business interruption was noted.
4.   
The proposal, comprising a further one month's rent and service
charge relief together with a one-off discretionary recovery
payment of £500 for each eligible Moor Market trader, was
approved, subject to all necessary legal, financial and subsidy
control requirements.
 

The Council has responsibility for ensuring
that Moor Market is managed safely and that appropriate action is
taken where conditions present a risk to public health, food
safety, staff, traders or visitors.
 
The temporary closure was necessary and
proportionate to protect public health, enable effective pest
control and deep cleaning, support Environmental Health assurance,
reduce the risk of further spread, and maintain public
confidence.
 
The recovery communications approach is
necessary to rebuild confidence, support traders, counter
misinformation, and encourage customers to return to Moor
Market.
 
The trader support package has been proposed
to help traders recover from the exceptional disruption caused by
the closure and recovery response, while making clear that the
package is not compensation for wider business interruption.
 
The proposal provides the most balanced
response to the exceptional circumstances affecting Moor Market
traders. It delivers meaningful and immediate financial assistance,
can be implemented quickly, avoids the complexity and delay
associated with assessing individual losses, and remains affordable
within the current budget forecast position. It therefore offers
the most proportionate and deliverable means of supporting trader
recovery while maintaining appropriate financial governance.


1)   
No further financial support beyond the existing
month relief
 

2)

budget forecast position, which will require a referral to Strategy

topline: The Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services has decided to provide financial support to Moor Market traders following its temporary closure due to pest activity.

purpose:
It is proposed that
a) the contract for supported accommodation
for young women (and their children) affected by domestic and
sexual abuse is recommissioned with a start date of 1st April 2027
for a contract duration of 5 years plus two.
b) the contract for support for children
affected by domestic abuse, delivered by Haven, is extended from
the current end date of 30th September 2027 to the 31st March 2028
for reasons of commissioning capacity.
content:
It is proposed that
a) the contract for supported accommodation
for young women (and their children) affected by domestic and
sexual abuse is recommissioned with a start date of 1st April 2027
for a contract duration of 5 years plus two.
b) the contract for support for children
affected by domestic abuse, delivered by Haven, is extended from
the current end date of 30th September 2027 to the 31st March 2028
for reasons of commissioning capacity.





a)  


The contract for
supported accommodation for young women (and their children)
affected by domestic and sexual abuse is recommissioned with a
start date of 1st April 2027 for a contract duration of 5 years
plus two. 




b)  


The contract for
support for children affected by domestic abuse, delivered by
Haven, is extended from the current end date of 30th September 2027
to the 31st March 2028 for reasons of
commissioning capacity. 




 

Recommissioning the young women’s safe
supported accommodation is necessary as it provides a vital
resource for the city that is highly valued internally and by
partners, and supports vulnerable young
women to address several key needs: healthy relationships, good
parenting, employment and training and independent living skills
for rehousing.  
 
Extending the Support for Children Affected by
Domestic Abuse contract will give staff sufficient time and
resources to effectively recommission both this and the Domestic
Abuse Safe Accommodation Contract, ensuring optimal outcomes for
customers. 
 
Taken together these proposals will enable the
council to continue to support its commitments to tackle domestic
abuse and support victims, effectively utilise its commissioning
and procurement capacity and meet its legal obligations regarding
fair and transparent commissioning and contracting
processes. 
 

Alternative Option 1: 
Not to recommission the contract for supported
accommodation for young women (and their children) affected by
domestic and sexual abuse.  
This option was rejected due to the high
impact of the support provided which is partly funded through a
government grant and is a cost-effective way to support vulnerable
young women, around half of whom are mothers, to recover from
abuse. Without this trauma informed support these young women would
be less likely to be in education employment or training, more
likely to stay in or enter into new unhealthy relationships, and
some of the children would likely be removed from their
mother’s care and looked after with costs for this falling to
the Council.  
 
Alternative Option 2: 
Recommission two contracts: Domestic Abuse
Safe Accommodation (Adults) Contact and Domestic Abuse Children and
Young People’s Support contracts, at the same time. 
This option was rejected due to capacity
issues as outlined above. Risk of consultation work needing to be
reduced, process being less thorough and timescales slipping in
relation to other work including statutory Domestic Abuse Related
Death Reviews.  
 
Alternative Option 3:  
Extend Safe Accommodation contract instead of
Children’s Support contract.  
This option was rejected as it will be less
risky to extend the lower value contract.
topline: The Strategic Director of Public Health and Integrated Commissioning has decided to recommission supported accommodation for young women affected by domestic and sexual abuse, and extend support for children affected by domestic abuse.

9.1


The Committee
considered a report which set out the required
re-structuring of the current lease arrangements at the Springs
Academy in order that the new leisure centre redevelopment may proceed.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance
and Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the current position and endorse the surrender of the existing
underlease and taking of a new
underlease on the revised terms as set out in this
report.
b)   
Authorise the Chief Property Officer
and Head of Legal Services to finalise
terms and complete the necessary documentation.




 


 




9.3


Reasons
for Decision




 


 




9.3.1


Recommendations were made to enable the Council to surrender the
existing underlease and enter into a new
underlease with revised boundaries, which is required to facilitate
the construction of the new Springs Leisure Centre on adjacent
land. The revised leasing arrangements were necessary to align the
property interests with the approved redevelopment proposals,
secure the Council’s position, and allow the project to
progress within the planned programme.




 


 




9.3.2


Approval was recommended because the proposal supports delivery
of a modern, accessible and sustainable leisure facility for the
local community while allowing existing leisure services to remain
operational during construction. The new centre will help address identified health
inequalities, respond to community feedback, improve the quality
and accessibility of local sport and leisure provision, and ensure
that the associated land and remediation arrangements are properly
documented and implemented.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Deliver a new leisure centre on
the site of the old leisure centre,
with no need for lease boundary changes.
 
This
option was rejected as it does not allow the additional space
requirements to house a teaching pool and additional facilities
that the community has asked for and that are needed to meet
demand. It would also mean closure of the leisure centre for the 20-month construction period, which
would impact customers and access to
health and wellbeing services in an area of health
inequalities.




 


 




9.4.2


Do
not deliver a new leisure centre, with
no need for boundary changes.
 
This
option was rejected as Springs Leisure Centre was recommended for
rebuild because it is an ageing facility nearing the end of its
life. It is no longer fit for purpose,
is unable to meet modern accessibility standards or climate net
zero targets and has limited opportunity to expand membership and
usage. Its size is a limiting factor, and it is
not able to meet demand from the demographic population it
serves due to capacity issues in areas such as the swimming pool,
lack of studio space and a small fitness suite.




 


 




9.4.3


Deliver the new leisure centre
with boundary changes with alternative facilities provided on the
demolition site.
 
Alternative facilities were considered for the demolition site
(Plan 4), which moves into the Academy’s lease following the
proposed lease changes. These were discounted following a sport
needs assessment, which identified the need for hardstanding court provision.
topline: The Council has decided to re-structure lease arrangements at Springs Academy to facilitate the construction of a new leisure centre.

10.1


The Committee
considered a report which provided a detailed overview of
the Concord Sports Centre new build proposal to support the
proposed additions and variations to the Capital
Programme.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance
and Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the current position and approve the proposed additions and
variations to the Capital Programme listed in Appendix
1.




 


 




10.3


Reasons
for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The
recommendation was made to enable the Concord Sports Centre
investment to progress through the Council’s capital
approvals process and move into the next stage of design,
procurement and delivery. Concord Sports Centre has been identified
through the Leisure and Entertainment Facilities Review and
subsequent feasibility work as an ageing facility requiring
significant investment. Approval of the proposed budget will
support delivery of a modern, accessible and sustainable
replacement facility that better meets community need, improves the
quality of sport and leisure provision, and contributes to the
Council’s health, wellbeing, equality and climate
objectives.




 


 




10.3.2


The
preferred option has been developed following feasibility work,
option appraisal and public and stakeholder engagement. It is
recommended because it provides the best opportunity to maintain
leisure provision during construction, deliver the required
facility mix, improve integration with Concord Park and wider
outdoor activity provision, and support a more financially and
environmentally sustainable leisure estate. The proposal also
aligns with the Council Plan, Sheffield’s Sport and Leisure
Strategy, the emerging Built Sport and Leisure Strategy, and the
wider objectives of the Leisure Investment Programme.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do nothing Under this option, no capital
investment would be made in Concord Sports Centre.
 
This
option was rejected because the existing facility is deteriorating
and is no longer considered fit for purpose. Taking no action would
leave the Council with ongoing maintenance pressures, a poorer
quality facility for public use, reduced ability to support local
health and wellbeing outcomes, and increased reputational risk. It
would also fail to deliver the previously approved priorities from
the Leisure and Entertainment Facilities Review and would not
support the recommendations of Sheffield’s Built Sporting
Facilities Strategy.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Refurbishment of the existing leisure
centre
 
This
option would involve refurbishing the existing Concord Sports
Centre rather than replacing it with a new build
facility.
 
This
option was rejected because the existing building envelope is in
poor condition and refurbishment would not provide the same
long-term benefit as a new build facility. It would retain
significant constraints associated with the age, layout and
condition of the current building, would not provide the same
opportunity to increase accessibility, sustainability and service
quality, and would not deliver the same level of integration with
Concord Park and wider site improvements. The option would also
carry ongoing maintenance and operational risks.




 


 




10.4.3


Alternative Option 3: Demolition of the existing facility and
new build on the current Concord Sports Centre location This option
would involve demolishing the existing centre and constructing a
new facility on the current building footprint.
 
This
option was rejected because it would require the existing leisure
centre to close during construction, resulting in a loss of access
to services and facilities for the local community and existing
users for a significant period (2 years +) in an area of high
health inequalities. It would also reduce the ability to deliver
the proposed facility mix and wider benefits. The option would have
greater service disruption and income/revenue implications during
the construction period.




 


 




 


Preferred Option:
Demolition of the existing facility and new build within the red
line boundary adjacent to the existing leisure centre.
 
The preferred option
is to construct the new facility adjacent to the existing leisure
centre before demolishing the current building and completing the
external pitches and landscaping.
 
This option is
preferred because it enables the existing centre to remain
operational during construction, provides a larger site area to
deliver an improved facility offer, allows stronger integration
with Concord Park and wider outdoor activity provision, and
supports the delivery of a more sustainable building designed to
BREEAM Excellent standards. It also provides the best opportunity
to deliver the intended community, health, accessibility and
sustainability benefits.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the construction of a new Concord Sports Centre to meet community needs and improve sport and leisure provision.

leasehold customers, aimed at recovering some costs associated with
maintaining shared external spaces around flats and maisonette
properties. This measure will prevent tenants rent from being used

content:
To introduce a new service charge for
leasehold customers, aimed at recovering some costs associated with
maintaining shared external spaces around flats and maisonette
properties. This measure will prevent tenants rent from being used
to fund this service, which is currently provided by the Parks and
Countryside team, and will align with the principles of full cost
recovery as outlined in the Leasehold Management Policy, which was
approved in December 2025.
 


a)   
To approve the
introduction of a new service charge for leaseholders to recover
the costs associated with external space maintenance.
 

b)   
To implement a
consistent and transparent charging model for external space
maintenance in line with lease agreements and the Leasehold
Management Policy (December 2025).
 
c)   
To introduce the new
charge from March 2027, supported by a programme of communication and engagement with
leaseholders.
 

The decision provides a fair, consistent and legally robust
framework for the recovery of costs associated with maintaining
external spaces linked to leasehold properties. It addresses a
long-standing inconsistency in current arrangements, where costs
are incurred but not fully recovered, resulting in financial
pressure on the Housing Revenue Account and an inequitable subsidy
from tenants.
 
The introduction of a structured and transparent charging
model ensures that leaseholders contribute appropriately to
services from which they benefit. It also supports the
Council’s wider strategic objectives by enabling the
sustainable maintenance of external environments, contributing to
safer, more green and better managed neighbourhoods, while improving transparency and
reducing the risk of dispute.
 

The option to continue absorbing costs within the Housing
Revenue Account without recovering them from leaseholders was
considered but rejected due to its financial unsustainability and
the inequity it creates between tenants and
leaseholders.
 
The option to introduce partial or inconsistent charging
was also rejected, as it would not address existing
inconsistencies, could increase confusion and challenge, and would
fail to deliver a fair and transparent approach across all
estates.
 
A
full, consistent and transparent charging model was therefore
identified as the preferred option.
topline: The Director of Housing has decided to introduce a new service charge for leasehold customers to recover costs associated with maintaining shared external spaces.

The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director Neighbourhood Services providing an update on
the actions being taken to maintain burial provision in the short
term while progressing the delivery of new cemetery
sites.
 
A programme of interim measures is being
implemented to increase and manage capacity within existing
cemeteries. At the same time, work is progressing to bring forward
new sites in line with the Citywide Cemetery Plan, with a proposed
approach to prioritising site development, including the
progression of feasibility at the Beaver Hill
site.
 
The report also introduces the proposed
exploration of partnership approaches to the delivery of burial
provision, following engagement with
stakeholders.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED: That Strategy and Resources Policy
Committee:-




 


 




 


(a) notes the
contents of the report, including the current position on burial
capacity and the need for interim measures;
 
(b) notes and
support the programme of interim measures being implemented to
maintain burial capacity across the city;
 
(c) notes the
progress being made to secure new cemetery land, including legal,
technical and feasibility work;
 
(d) supports the
proposed approach to prioritising the progression of work and
allocation of resources across identified sites, including
progressing feasibility at the Beaver Hill site, recognising the
significant burial capacity pressures within the southeast of the
city and the need to bring forward potential solutions in a timely
manner;
 
(e) agrees that
the Council continues to engage with stakeholders to explore
potential partnership models for the delivery of burial provision,
including the potential for a community organisation to acquire and
operate burial land at one or more sites, with a further report to
Committee setting out options and recommendations;
and
 
(f) confirms
that the Strategy and Resources Policy Committee will retain
strategic oversight of this programme and requests a further
update.




 


 




 


(NOTE: The result of the vote on the resolution was For –
16 Against – 0, 
Abstentions 3).




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The Council is
facing increasing pressure on burial capacity across the city, with
limited remaining provision in some areas. The approach set out in
this report provides a coordinated programme of interim measures to
maintain capacity in the short term while progressing the
development of new cemetery sites in line with the Citywide
Cemetery Plan.




 


 




10.3.2


The recommendations enable continued progress in securing new
burial land, prioritising resources to areas of greatest need, and
exploring potential partnership approaches where appropriate. The
Committee is asked to note the progress made, support the proposed
approach to delivery, and agree that further work is undertaken,
while retaining oversight of this programme to ensure that burial
provision is maintained for residents of all faiths and
none.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do nothing / rely on existing
provision
 
This option would involve continuing to operate within existing
cemetery provision without implementing the interim measures or
progressing new sites at pace.
 
This option has been rejected as it would not address the
identified shortfall in burial capacity. Evidence set out in this
report demonstrates that existing provision is limited, with
capacity expected to be exhausted within the next few years, and
significantly sooner for some types of
burial.
 
Taking no action would lead to a loss of local burial provision,
reduced ability to meet the needs of residents of all faiths and
none, and increased reputational and operational risk for the
Council. It would also be inconsistent with the Council’s
responsibility to plan for future demand and maintain essential
services.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Rely solely on interim measures within
existing cemeteries
 
This option would focus on extending capacity only through
interim measures, such as reconfiguring existing sites and managing
demand, without progressing new cemetery
provision.
 
This option has been rejected as it would only provide a
short-term solution and would not address the long-term requirement
for additional burial land identified in the Citywide Cemetery
Plan. While interim measures are necessary to maintain provision in
the short term, there is insufficient land within existing
cemeteries to meet future demand over the medium to long
term.
 
Relying solely on this approach would increase the risk of
repeated shortfalls in capacity and would not provide a sustainable
solution for the city.




 


 




10.4.3


Alternative Option 3: Commission burial provision entirely
through external providers
 
This option would involve the Council not directly delivering
new cemetery provision, instead relying on private or external
providers to meet future burial needs.
 
This option has been considered but is not viable as a full
delivery model. There is currently very limited private provision
in this sector. Cemeteries are large areas of green space requiring
significant infrastructure and ongoing maintenance, and as a result
are costly to operate with limited commercial return. This makes
them generally unattractive to the wider commercial market, except
in specific circumstances where targeted services can be
delivered.
 
In addition, the availability of suitable land would remain a
key constraint and would likely continue to require the Council to
identify and bring forward sites. This option would therefore not
remove the need for the Council to lead the development of new
cemetery provision.
 
There would also be operational, legal and governance challenges
in transferring responsibility in this way. Where the Council acts
as a burial authority it takes on statutory responsibilities in
relation to how those services are provided and managed. The
Council currently delivers a comprehensive cemetery service across
16 sites, including second interments and the ongoing management of
existing graves. Moving to a fully externally delivered model would
introduce complexity in how these responsibilities are discharged,
and in maintaining consistent standards, access and oversight
across the service.
 
This option has therefore been discounted as a full approach, as
it would be unlikely to be deliverable at the scale required, would
not provide a timely or cost-effective solution, and would not
address the underlying need to bring forward new cemetery
sites.
 
However, elements of this option have been incorporated within
the current proposals through the exploration of partnership
approaches. This reflects specific interest from parts of the
community in supporting or contributing to service delivery in
defined areas, where this can be developed in a way that is lawful,
viable and aligned with the Council’s wider
responsibilities.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Policy Committee has decided to support measures to maintain burial capacity and progress new cemetery sites.

12.1



The
Committee considered a report of the Chief Executive outlining that
the Council is seeking approval to secure the continued hosting of
the World Snooker Championship in Sheffield following the expiry of
the current arrangements in 2027.  It
was noted that an additional appendix 6 and revised covering
report, containing an additional recommendation in respect of
compliance with the Subsidy Control Act, had been published and
circulated.

The
proposed arrangements would provide for an initial term of 15
years, with the option to extend for a further five years by mutual
agreement, subject to the future redevelopment of the Crucible
Theatre.

The
proposed arrangements would require the Council to enter into a new
Staging Agreement with World Snooker Limited (WSL). This has been
developed following detailed commercial, financial and legal due
diligence and seeks to balance the Council’s financial
commitment with opportunities for future commercial growth and
wider economic benefit and we are now at the stage to be able to
ask the Committee to agree that we should continue to host the
World Snooker Championships.




 


 




.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Strategy and
Resources Policy Committee:-




 


 




 


(a) endorses the
continued hosting of the World Snooker Championship in Sheffield in
2028 and for 15 years following completion of the refurbishment of
the Crucible with an option to extend for a further 5
years;
 
(b) approves the
Council proceeding on proposed commercial, financial and
operational terms for the future hosting of the Championship, as
outlined in this report and the exempt
appendices;
 
(c) notes that
the Chief Executive, in consultation with the Director of Finance
and Commercial and the General Counsel will:
 
(i)   Finalise
negotiations with World Snooker Limited;
(ii)  Agree the final
terms of the Staging Agreement and associated contractual
documentation;
(iii)  Agree the final
terms of the Venue Hire Agreement between SCC and STT and
associated documentation;
(iv)Agree any ancillary agreements arising from
SCC’s obligations in the new Staging
Agreement;
(v)  Agree any
necessary amendments to the commercial model, financial
arrangements and governance provisions, provided such amendments
remain within the overall policy and financial framework approved
by Committee;
 
(d) notes and
accepts the evidence and assessment contained in Closed Appendix 6
and this forms the evidential basis upon which it has been
concluded that the proposed arrangements comply with section 3(2)
of the Subsidy Control Act 2022 and do not constitute a subsidy
because they do not confer an economic advantage on World Snooker
Limited;
 
(e) delegates
authority to the Chief Executive, in consultation with the Director
of Finance and Commercial and the General Counsel, to take all
necessary steps to implement the Committee’s decision, that
are not already delegated, including the execution of all legal
agreements and associated documentation required to give effect to
the recommendations;
 
(f) notes that
the Council will enter into a direct contractual arrangement with
World Snooker Limited, as the holder of the exclusive commercial
and intellectual property rights required to stage the World
Snooker Championship and the implications, as set out in the
report; and
 
(g) notes that
any future decisions relating to the proposed redevelopment of the
Crucible Theatre, associated capital funding arrangements or
material changes to the approved financial framework will be
subject to separate governance and approval processes as
required.




 


 




12.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




12.3.1


The World
Snooker Championship is one of Sheffield's most significant
sporting and cultural assets and has been hosted at the Crucible
Theatre since 1977. The Championship contributes substantially to
Sheffield's economy, international reputation, visitor economy and
cultural identity and has become synonymous with the city over
almost five decades.




 


 




12.3.2


Without a new agreement there is a significant risk that the
Championship could relocate from Sheffield following the expiry of
the current arrangements in 2027, resulting in the loss of
substantial economic, social, cultural and reputational benefits.
The loss of the Championship would also undermine Sheffield's
long-established position as the home of snooker and weaken a major
contributor to the city's visitor economy and international
profile.




 


 




12.3.3


The recommendations provide a framework to secure the continued
hosting of the World Snooker Championship in Sheffield for up to 20
years, creating long-term certainty for the Council, World Snooker
Limited, Sheffield Theatres Trust and other stakeholders. This
certainty will support future investment decisions, enable venue
improvements to be aligned with event requirements and facilitate
the development of longer-term visitor economy, cultural and city
centre activation initiatives linked to the
Championship.




 


 




12.3.4


The proposal aligns with existing Council priorities and
represents the delivery of established Council policy, including
ambitions set out through the Council Plan and Major Events
Strategy. It will help ensure that Sheffield continues to benefit
from a globally recognised event that delivers economic growth,
enhances the city's reputation and supports wider cultural and
community outcomes.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




12.4.1



Alternative Option 1;
Do nothing: Not recommended.

The Council could
choose not to enter into a new Staging Agreement following the
expiry of the current arrangements in 2027. This option was not
recommended because it would create a significant risk that the
World Snooker Championship would relocate from Sheffield. The loss
of the Championship would result in the loss of substantial
economic, cultural and reputational benefits for the city and would
undermine Sheffield's long-established position as the home of
snooker. In addition, Sheffield Theatres Trust would lose an
important income stream associated with hosting the Championship,
potentially increasing financial pressures on the Trust and
creating a greater risk of future financial support being required
from the Council.




 


 




12.4.2


5.2.    Alternative Option
2; Secure a shorter-term agreement: Not
recommended.
 
A
shorter-term agreement was considered as an alternative to the
proposed long-term arrangements. This option was not recommended
because the scale of investment and partnership required to secure
the future of the Championship and support the future development
of the Crucible Theatre requires longer-term certainty. A
shorter-term arrangement would reduce confidence for all parties,
limit opportunities for future investment and restrict the ability
to maximise long-term economic, commercial and visitor economy
benefits.




 


 




12.4.3


Alternative Option 3; Undertake a competitive procurement
process: Not recommended.
 
The Council considered whether a competitive procurement process
could be undertaken. This option was not recommended because World
Snooker Limited holds the exclusive commercial and intellectual
property rights necessary to stage the World Snooker Championship
and is the only organisation able to grant the rights required for
Sheffield to continue hosting the event. A competitive procurement
process would therefore not be capable of securing the same event
and an alternative snooker event would not be capable of delivering
the same outcomes.




 


 




12.4.4


5.4.   
Alternative Option 4; Seek to replace the Championship with
alternative major events: Not recommended.
 
The Council could choose to focus on
attracting alternative major events rather than seeking to retain
the World Snooker Championship. This option was not recommended
because no alternative event offers the same combination of
heritage, international profile, established association with
Sheffield and long-term economic impact as the World Snooker
Championship. Whilst the Council will continue to pursue
opportunities to develop its wider major events portfolio,
alternative events would not provide an equivalent replacement for
the economic, cultural and reputational benefits generated by the
Championship.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Policy Committee has decided to secure the hosting of the World Snooker Championship in Sheffield for up to 20 years.

Alternatives Considered and
Rejected

and an approach to use some additional City Regional Sustainable
Transport Settlement (CRSTS) – revenue - funding to develop
and/or deliver some additional smaller scale projects.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY:- That the
Transport, Regeneration and Climate Policy Committee:
 

(a) 
notes the progress on the Local and Neighbourhood Transport
Complimentary (LaNTCP - formally known as the Local Transport Plan
Integrated Transport Block); and

‘smaller schemes’ as set out in section 2.18, noting
projects would still need to go through the Councils capital
process – i.e. to be considered for approval by the Finance
and Performance Policy Committee.




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision

The proposed LaNTCP programme balances the
availability of funding sources with local and national policy to
give a clear focus for the 2025/27 financial year, with an
opportunity for changes to be considered by Committee that could be
made over the remainder of the programme. The proposed programme is
extensive and ambitious which comes with its own challenges. The
programme utilises internal and external funding sources and staff
resources to deliver change to the transport system, considering
environmental, economic and societal needs.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


‘Do nothing’ has been considered
but is not considered appropriate as this would result in projects
not being delivered.  The LaNTCP
programme would not be introduced and the opportunity for economic,
environmental and societal benefits will be missed.




 


 




9.4.2


It would also be possible to consider a
different balance between types of schemes as part of the
programme.  However, it is felt that the
proposed programme achieves a good balance of economic,
environmental and societal benefits to the communities and
businesses in Sheffield.

content:
Sheffield does not currently have a Built
Facilities Strategy for Sport and Leisure. The BFS will provide a
key strategic document to support future planning and investment
and is a requirement to bid for Sport England capital funding.





9.1


The Committee considered a
report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services seeking
approval to adopt Sheffield's Sport and Leisure Built Facilities
Strategy 2026-2039. The Strategy provides the city's evidence-based
framework for future investment, planning and partnership working
across indoor and outdoor sport and leisure facilities. It
identifies priorities to address ageing facilities, improve access,
reduce inequalities and support population growth, whilst
strengthening Sheffield's ability to secure external funding and
align future development with the needs of residents.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee:-

(a) 
Approves the adoption of the Sport and Leisure Built Facilities
Strategy for Sheffield 2026-2039 as set out in this report.

(b) 
Notes the content of the strategy and report.




 


 




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The recommendation to adopt the Built Sport
and Leisure Facilities Strategy is made because it provides
Sheffield with a robust, up-to-date and citywide evidence base to
guide future decisions about sport and leisure facilities to 2039.
The strategy has been developed through assessment, consultation
and partnership working, and responds to the key issues identified
in the report, including ageing facilities, peak-time capacity
pressures, uneven access across the city and the need to reduce
barriers to participation. Adopting the strategy will give the
Council and its partners a clear framework for prioritising
investment, protecting and improving important facilities, and
directing resources to the communities where need and inequality
are greatest.




 


 




9.3.2


Adoption is also recommended because the
strategy supports wider Council objectives and strengthens the
Council’s ability to plan effectively for future growth. It
will help ensure that planning decisions are informed by current
evidence, support the use of Section 106 and Community
Infrastructure Levy funding, and provide a key foundation for
securing external investment from partners such as Sport England
and National Governing Bodies. The strategy also promotes an
inclusive and sustainable approach to future provision by
prioritising access, health improvement, environmental performance
and long-term resilience, making it the most effective basis for
future decision-making in this area.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do not have a BSLFS
 
The option to not have a BSLFS was discounted
for the following reasons:
 
• There is a risk that without an adopted
strategy Sport England and the
Sport’s Governing Bodies will not
consider applications for external
funding from the council or from any sports
club within the city and it
would both the council and partners would miss
out on opportunities to
secure external funding.
• The National Planning Policy Framework
requires planning polices to
be based on robust and up to date assessments
of the need for open
space, sport, and recreation facilities
(including quantitative or
qualitative deficits or surpluses) and
opportunities for new provision.
Without the BSLFS there would be no up to date
evidence base to
inform planning decisions.
• Without an adopted strategy the council
may not be able to collect
developer contributions for key strategic
sites.




 


 




9.4.2


Alternative Option 2: BSLFS only includes
indoor facilities
 
The option to only include indoor built sport
and leisure facilities in the strategy was discounted for the
following reasons:
• The strategy would only provide an
evidence base for indoor facilities and there would be no strategic
evidence base guiding planning and investment into outdoor built
sport and leisure facilities, which we know from our consultation
are as important to people in supporting their ability to be
physically active.
topline: The Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to adopt Sheffield's Sport and Leisure Built Facilities Strategy 2026-2039 to guide future planning and investment in sport and leisure facilities.

providing an update on the actions to date in the review of the
Sheffield Green & Open Spaces Strategy. It includes the work of
the Task and Finish Group held in 2025/26 with Committee members,
Council officers, and partners from around the city. There was also
consideration of the Sheffield Waterways Strategy, as it was felt
important to broaden the scope of a refreshed strategy to include
green and blue spaces.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Communities, Parks
and Leisure Policy Committee:-

(a) 
Notes the contents of the report.

(b) 
Thanks the elected members, and partners who participated in and
supported the Task and Finish Group.

(c) 
Supports the outcomes and recommendations of the Task and Finish
Group.

(d) 
Approves the Task and Finish Group’s recommendation to
deliver a refresh of this strategy and as part of this broaden its
remit to become a Green and Blue Spaces Strategy for Sheffield
2040.

(e) 
Instructs officers to explore the resourcing options to undertake
the development of the Green and Blue Spaces Strategy renewal




 


 




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The Sheffield Green & Open Spaces Strategy
2010-2030 (GOSS) is a comprehensive plan aimed at enhancing and
protecting the city's green spaces over two decades. It remains the
key strategy setting out the goals and objectives for green spaces
across the city and is the backdrop of decision-making and
identifying priorities. With several years of the strategy
remaining, this is the right time to undertake the work required to
establish a new strategy for Sheffield’s green and blue
spaces for the time beyond 2030.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
nothing
 
The Green and Open Spaces
Strategy 2010 – 2030 has 3.5 years left and there is an
option to not carry out a review at this stage and not begin work
on a new strategy beyond 2030. Doing nothing could mean that
Sheffield falls short of the objectives set out in the strategy,
does not adequately consider current and future challenges for the
city’s green and blue infrastructure, and potentially lose
out on opportunities to attract external investment. These would
impact our ability to contribute to priorities in the Council Plan
and City Goals.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Review and Refresh the
strategy in 2030.
 
The changes to the external environment set
out in section 1 of this report, mean that Sheffield must review
its strategic approach to managing its green and blue
infrastructure and ensure that this key policy is fit for purpose
both now and beyond 2030. As this is a significant strategy, it
requires early consideration, to develop an evidenced based
strategic approach to managing, developing and protecting
Sheffield’s blue and green infrastructure. Delaying this work
until 2030 would mean that Sheffield is left without a strategic
response to the external environment, where a clear strategic
framework is increasingly required to secure external funding and
maximise partnership potential.
topline: The Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to refresh the Sheffield Green & Open Spaces Strategy to include green and blue spaces for Sheffield 2040.

11.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services providing an overview
of the Sport England Place Investment secured by Sheffield for the
period April 2026 to March 2028. The investment will support
delivery of the Move More Sheffield programme, with Sheffield City
Council (SCC) providing operational management and delivery of the
Community Development and Move Well work programmes.
 
The report sought approval for SCC to enter
into a subcontract with Sheffield Hallam University Services
Limited for delivery of the agreed work programmes.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Communities, Parks, and Leisure Policy Committee approves the
Council entering into a subcontract with Sheffield Hallam
University Services Limited for the delivery of the Community
Development and Move Well work programmes as part of the Sport
England Place Investment programme with a total contract value of
£1,053,927.24 (including VAT), subject to the terms not being
materially different from those outlined in this report.




 


 




 


 




11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


Approval of the proposed subcontract with
Sheffield Hallam University Services Limited will enable Sheffield
City Council to deliver the Community Development & Services
and Move Well work programmes as part of the Sport England Place
Investment programme, maintaining its strong position within local,
regional and national physical activity and health
partnerships.




 


 




11.3.2


The investment will support community-based
services within five priority neighbourhoods, increasing
opportunities for residents to improve their health and wellbeing
whilst strengthening the capacity of VCSE organisations and
community-led provision.




 


 




11.3.3


The expansion of the Move Well service will
enable more residents living with long-term health conditions to
access support to improve their health and wellbeing, whilst
strengthening links between healthcare pathways and community-based
physical activity opportunities.




 


 




11.3.4


Whilst there are contractual obligations
associated with delivery of the work programmes, the anticipated
benefits to residents, communities and the wider health and
wellbeing system are considered to significantly outweigh the
associated risks.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Do not enter into the proposed subcontract
with Sheffield Hallam University Services Limited for delivery of
the Community Development & Services and Move Well work
programmes.
 
Advantages
 

·      
The Council would avoid any financial, operational or contractual
risks associated with delivering the work programmes and meeting
the associated performance, monitoring and reporting
requirements.

·      
No additional management, governance or contract management
responsibilities would fall to the Council.
 
Disadvantages
 

·      
SCC was identified by NCSEM and partner organisations as the
preferred delivery body for the Community Development &
Services and Move Well work programmes due to its established
governance arrangements, existing service provision and experience
in delivering physical activity, health and wellbeing programmes.
Declining this role would present a reputational risk with
national, regional and local partners.

·      
It is unlikely that an alternative organisation could assume
delivery of these work programmes within the required timescales,
creating a significant risk to programme delivery and the
associated Sport England investment.

·      
Failure to enter into the subcontract would result in a missed
opportunity to invest in priority neighbourhoods, expand the Move
Well service and strengthen community-led and VCSE delivery,
reducing the city's ability to address physical inactivity and
health inequalities.

·      
Declining the opportunity would weaken SCC's strategic role within
the city's physical activity and health system and could reduce
future opportunities to secure external investment and influence
programme development.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to approve a subcontract with Sheffield Hallam University Services Limited for the delivery of community development and Move Well work programmes.

9.1


The Centre in the Park (CITP) building in
Norfolk Park includes a café that is currently occupied
under a Tenancy at Will (TAW) pending the completion of a
lease previously approved by the Charity
Trustee (Sub) Committee on 26th January 2023. The operators of the
cafe have advised the Council that they wish to dissolve their
existing partnership. The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services proposing to safeguard
the future of this cafe by agreeing terms with a new operator at
the earliest opportunity.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-
 

a)   
Notes the contents of this report.

b)   
Considered whether the proposal within the report and the
suggested
recommendations were in the best interest of
the Norfolk Heritage Park Charity
c) Authorises the
Chief Property Officer to: - 

     
i.        
engage with the two individuals named under the current tenancy
to
establish their individual
proposals and determine what represents
the best outcome for the
charity. 

    
ii.        
select an operator and negotiate the best terms on behalf of
the
Charity for a tenancy at will
and instruct the Head of Legal Services
to complete any required
formal documentation.

   
iii.        
ensure that the terms negotiated meet a minimum requirement of
maintaining quality of
service and (or improving on if possible)
established income levels to
the Charity.




 


 




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The proposal safeguards the continued
provision of the café facility at Norfolk Park while
maintaining an income stream through rent and contributions towards
the running costs of the CITP. It supports continuity of service
and avoids the risk of vacancy or disruption associated with re
tendering, while also enhancing the attractiveness of the park as a
community asset. In addition, it ensures that the demised property
continues to be occupied in a way that supports the charitable
objects of the Charity.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Do nothing: reason for
rejection
 
Doing nothing is not a
realistic option given the partnership situation. Action is
required to safeguard the cafe provision and ensure that the
quality of the visitor experience is not impacted and the rental
income to the Charity is maintained.




 


 




9.4.2


Offer the cafe to the open
market
 
The case against undertaking a
further marketing exercise only three years since the last
competitive process is based on the café’s strong
recent performance and wider community value at Norfolk Park. The
café has thrived under its current operators, and
re-tendering at this stage would introduce a risk of disruption to
established community benefits and undermining the goodwill the
business has built.
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to engage with new operators to safeguard the future of a cafe in Norfolk Park.

11.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services seeking approval for
Graves Park Charity to undertake a procurement exercise for the
supply of toys and gifts to be sold through the Graves Park Animal
Farm shop.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-
(a) 
Confirms that the commencement of a procurement exercise for a gift
shop toy supplier is in the best interest of the Graves Park
Charity.
(b) 
Subject to (1) approve commissioning of a contract for a gift shop
toy supplier for Graves Park Animal Farm shop, for a period up to 3
years with an estimated value of £300,000, as set out in this
report.
(c) 
Give delegated authority to officers to appoint a supplier based on
assessment of quality and price.




 


 




 


 




11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The provision of toys and gifts at the Animal
Farm shop contributes to the objects of the charity by supporting
the overall visitor experience at Graves Park Animal Farm, which is
a valued recreational facility within Graves Park. The shop has
become an established and expected part of a visit to the farm and
contributes to the attractiveness of the site as a family
destination.




 


 




11.3.2


In addition, the income generated through the
shop supports the operation, management and maintenance of the park
and farm, helping the charity to sustain and improve facilities for
public benefit. Given the increased scale of sales and the
anticipated contract value, a committee decision is required to
authorise the procurement of a new contract and ensure that the
Council, acting as sole corporate trustee, secures best value for
the charity through a transparent and competitive process.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option 1 – Do nothing:
Reasons for rejection
 
There is the option not to tender the contract
and to allow the current contract to end on 31 March 2027. This
would mean there would be no planned provision for toys and gifts
at the Animal Farm shop. This would reduce income to the charity
and could affect the resources available to support the operation,
management and maintenance of the park and farm. It would also
remove an established part of the visitor offer and would be likely
to have a detrimental impact on the quality of the visitor
experience. This option has therefore been rejected.




 


 




11.4.2


Alternative Option 2 – Purchase toys in
batches via quotation: Reasons for rejection
 
It would be possible not to procure a
longer-term contract and instead to obtain quotes for each restock
of the shop. This could potentially provide some flexibility in
using different providers, but it is not a practical or efficient
method of purchasing. It would require repeated quotation processes
for each restock, which could result in empty shelves, delays in
replenishing stock and loss of income while the process is
completed. It could also create a risk of over-ordering,
insufficient storage capacity or purchasing stock that does not
meet visitor demand. This option would not provide the continuity
or certainty needed to maintain a high-quality retail offer for
visitors and could reduce the income available to support the
charity’s objectives. This option has therefore been
rejected.
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to approve a procurement exercise for toys and gifts to be sold at the Graves Park Animal Farm shop.

12.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services requesting
confirmation that Weston Park Trust acknowledges and accepts that a
legacy referenced in the latest Will of a deceased individual was
not intended for the Trust and agrees that the intended beneficiary
is Weston Park Cancer Hospital.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Sub-Committee Committee:-
(a) 
Confirms that Weston Park Trust acknowledges and accepts that the
legacy referred to in the Will of the deceased was not intended for
Weston Park Trust;
(b) 
Agrees that the intended beneficiary of the legacy is Weston Park
Cancer Hospital, as set out in the solicitor’s
correspondence;
(c) 
Delegates authority to the General Counsel to provide written
confirmation to the estate’s solicitors (as per CLOSED
Appendix B) and to execute any associated documentation required to
give effect to this position, where necessary.




 


 




 


 




12.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




12.3.1


Approving this proposal ensures that Weston
Park Trust acts transparently, lawfully and in accordance with the
clearly evidenced wishes of the donor. It also provides a clear
audit trail linking this report to the previous report considered
by the Charity Trustee Committee on 8 April 2026 under item 71,
where the matter was discussed and a decision was taken. The
proposed approach avoids the Trust benefiting from a legacy that
was not intended for it, thereby protecting the integrity of the
charity and supporting proper administration of the estate in line
with charity law principles and trustee responsibilities.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Contact solicitors to
suggest the legacy may have been intended for the Weston Park
Charity
 
An alternative option would be to not respond
to the request from the solicitors. However, this would potentially
lead to the Trust benefiting from a legacy that was not intended
for it and therefore compromise the integrity of the charity. For
these reasons, this option has been rejected.
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to confirm that a legacy in a deceased individual's will was not intended for Weston Park Trust, but for Weston Park Cancer Hospital.

13.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services seeking a decision on
whether the proposal to withdraw interest accrued on the Annie
Frances Styring Fund to support improvements to the basketball
court in Chelsea Park is in the best interest of the charity.




 


 




13.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-
(a) 
Notes the contents of this report
(b) 
Considered whether the proposed use of funds is in the best
interests of the charity, taking into account the purpose of the
Anne Frances Styring Memorial Fund and the benefits to Chelsea Park
and its users.
(c) 
Approves the release of accrued interest from the Anne Frances
Styring Memorial Fund to fund improvement works to the basketball
area at Chelsea Park, including cleaning, graffiti removal and
repainting.
(d) 
Notes that the expenditure constitutes a one-off capital
improvement, consistent with the conditions of the fund that
interest may be used for non recurring purposes.
(e) 
Delegates authority to the Director Finance and Commercial Services
and the General Counsel, to:
• Confirm the
total interest available for drawdown
• Finalise the
value to be released
• Ensure the
appropriate financial mechanism is applied to draw funds from the
balance sheet to revenue




 


 




 


 




13.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




13.3.1


The proposed use of accrued interest from the
Annie Frances Styring Memorial Fund contributes to the objects of
the charity, which are for Chelsea Park to be used for the
recreation of the public as public walks or pleasure grounds or as
an open space.




 


 




13.3.2


Releasing interest from the fund for a one-off
improvement to the basketball area allows the Council, as sole
trustee, to support the maintenance and improvement of recreational
facilities within the park, while retaining the capital value of
the endowment.




 


 




13.3.3


The proposal is considered to be in the best
interests of the charity because it will provide direct public
benefit through improving the condition, appearance and usability
of an open-access recreational facility within Chelsea Park.




 


 




13.3.4


In addition:
• The works will help address
deterioration in the basketball area and reduce the risk of the
facility becoming less attractive or usable for park visitors.
• Improved recreational provision will
support informal physical activity, community use and enjoyment of
the park.
• The proposal makes appropriate use of
available accrued interest for non-recurring expenditure, in line
with the purpose of the fund.
• Supporting these works will complement
external funding already secured by the Friends of Chelsea Park for
nearby playground improvements, helping to deliver a more coherent
improvement to this part of the park.
• Undertaking the works now will reduce
the likelihood of further decline and support the long-term
maintenance of the park environment.




 


 




13.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




13.4.1


Alternative Option 1 – Do nothing
 
Under this option, no funding would be
released from the memorial fund.
 
Implications include:
• Continued deterioration of the
basketball area
• Missed opportunity to utilise available
interest for a one-off improvement
• Potential negative impact on community
perception and park usage
 
This option would not align with the intention
to use accrued interest for appropriate improvement projects within
the park. This option has therefore been discounted.




 


 




13.4.2


Alternative Option 2 – Wait until
specific costs are available
 
Under this option, the decision to release the
funded would be delayed until exact costs are known for the
proposed works.
 
Implications include:
• Continued deterioration of the
basketball area
• Potential missed opportunity to utilise
available interest for a one-off improvement
• Delay to undertaking any works due to
existing committee schedules
 
This option delays the decision until
specifics are known however as an upper limit of interest is known,
this is not considered necessary. This option has therefore been
discounted.
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to approve the release of accrued interest from the Annie Frances Styring Memorial Fund for improvement works to the basketball area at Chelsea Park.

14.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services seeking approval, in
the Council’s capacity as sole corporate trustee of the
Hillsborough Park Charity, to increase the pay and display parking
tariff at Hillsborough Park from £1.00 to £1.10 per
hour.




 


 




14.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-
(a) 
Notes the contents of the report, including the wider city-wide
decision to increase parking tariffs in line with inflation as set
out in the Officer Decision Report on Parking Fees and Charges.
(b) 
Considered whether it is in the best interests of the Hillsborough
Park Charity to approve an increase in parking tariffs within the
Hillsborough Park car park, specifically an increase of £0.10
per hour (from £1.00 to £1.10).
(c) 
Approves an increase in the hourly parking tariff at Hillsborough
Park from £1.00 to £1.10, to be implemented in line
with the wider parking tariff changes.
(d) 
Approves a delegation to the Executive Director of Neighbourhoods
Services to make future changes to the parking fees and charges for
Hillsborough Park in line with changes to Pay and Display tariffs
in the parking zones outside the city centre.




 


 




 


 




14.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




14.3.1


The recommended decision enables the Charity
Trustee Committee to consider the parking tariff within
Hillsborough Park separately from the wider city-wide parking fees
decision, recognising the Council’s distinct role as sole
corporate trustee of the Hillsborough Park Charity. The wider city
parking review provides relevant context, but the central question
for the Committee is whether the increase is in the best interests
of the Hillsborough Park Charity and supports the charitable object
of the provision and maintenance of a public park and recreation
ground in Sheffield for the use of members of the public resorting
thereto with the object of improving their conditions of life.




 


 




14.3.2


The increase from £1.00 to £1.10
per hour is modest and reflects inflationary pressures since the
last review, while avoiding a greater increase that may be
disproportionate for park users. The proposal supports the
charitable object of provision and maintenance of a public park and
recreation ground in Sheffield for the use of members of the public
by helping to manage demand for limited parking spaces, reducing
congestion, and contributing to the quality and accessibility of
the park environment.




 


 




14.3.3


Any additional income generated from the
tariff increase will be retained within the Hillsborough Park
charitable account and used only in accordance with the
charity’s purposes. This will help support the ongoing
maintenance, management and improvement of the park, and is
therefore considered to be in the best interests of the
charity.




 


 




14.3.4


The proposed delegation for future changes
would allow parking charges at Hillsborough Park to be kept under
review and adjusted in line with the wider parking tariff
framework, where this remains consistent with trustee duties and
the best interests of the charity. This would avoid unnecessary
delay in implementing future changes, help prevent the
charity’s parking income falling behind inflation or wider
tariff changes, and support timely income generation for the
maintenance and management of the park. The delegation would
therefore serve the charity’s interests as well as reducing
administrative duplication.




 


 




14.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




14.4.1


Alternative Option 1 – Do nothing
 
Maintaining the current tariff at Hillsborough
Park would mean that charges are not aligned with the wider city
approach or inflation. As set out in the Officer Decision Report
seeking to increase other (non-charitable site) parking fees,
failure to increase tariffs would reduce the effectiveness of
parking as a demand management tool and may lead to increased
congestion and reduced availability of spaces.
 
It would also reduce the real-terms income
available to support the maintenance and improvement of the
park.
 
This option has therefore been discounted




 


 




14.4.2


Alternative Option 2 – Increase tariffs
by a greater amount
 
Whilst higher increases have the potential to
generate additional income for the Hillsborough Park Charity, they
may also reduce income if cheaper alternatives are sought out by
park users.
 
A higher increase is not considered
proportionate and would go beyond the CPI-based approach adopted
across the wider parking estate.
 
This option has therefore been discounted
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to approve an increase in the parking tariff at Hillsborough Park to £1.10 per hour.
