failure to increase tariffs would reduce the effectiveness of
parking as a demand management tool and may lead to increased
congestion and reduced availability of spaces.
 
It would also reduce the real-terms income
available to support the maintenance and improvement of the
park.
 
This option has therefore been discounted




 


 




15.4.2


Alternative Option 2 – Increase tariffs
by a greater amount
 
Whilst higher increases have the potential to
generate additional income for the Graves Park Charity, they may
also reduce income if cheaper alternatives are sought out by park
users.
 
A higher increase is not considered
proportionate and would go beyond the CPI-based approach adopted
across the wider parking estate.
 
This option has therefore been discounted
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to approve an increase in the parking tariff at Graves Park from £1.00 to £1.10 per hour.

content:
16.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services seeking approval, in
the Council’s capacity as sole corporate trustee of the
Endcliffe Park Charity, to increase the
pay and display parking tariff at Endcliffe Park from £1.00 to £1.10 per
hour.




 


 




16.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-
(a) 
Notes the contents of the report, including the wider city-wide
decision to increase parking tariffs in line with inflation as set
out in the Officer Decision Report on Parking Fees and Charges.
(b) 
Considered whether it is in the best interests of the Endcliffe Park Charity to approve an increase in
parking tariffs within the Endcliffe
Park car park, specifically an increase of £0.10 per hour
(from £1.00 to £1.10).
(c) 
Approves an increase in the hourly parking tariff at Endcliffe Park from £1.00 to £1.10, to
be implemented in line with the wider parking tariff changes.
(d) 
Approves a delegation to the Executive Director of Neighbourhoods
Services to make future changes to the parking fees and charges for
Endcliffe Park in line with changes to
Pay and Display tariffs in the parking zones outside the city
centre.




 


 




 


 




16.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




16.3.1


The recommended decision enables the Charity
Trustee Committee to consider the parking tariff within
Endcliffe Park separately from the
wider city-wide parking fees decision, recognising the
Council’s distinct role as sole corporate trustee of the
Endcliffe Park Charity. The wider city
parking review provides relevant context, but the central question
for the Committee is whether the increase is in the best interests
of the Endcliffe Park Charity and
supports the charitable object of the provision and maintenance of
a public park and recreation ground in Sheffield for the use of
members of the public resorting thereto with the object of
improving their conditions of life.




 


 




16.3.2


The increase from £1.00 to £1.10
per hour is modest and reflects inflationary pressures since the
last review, while avoiding a greater increase that may be
disproportionate for park users. The proposal supports the
charitable object of provision and maintenance of a public park and
recreation ground in Sheffield for the use of members of the public
by helping to manage demand for limited parking spaces, reducing
congestion, and contributing to the quality and accessibility of
the park environment.




 


 




16.3.3


Any additional income generated from the
tariff increase will be retained within the Endcliffe Park charitable account and used only in
accordance with the charity’s purposes. This will help
support the ongoing maintenance, management and improvement of the
park, and is therefore considered to be in the best interests of
the charity.




 


 




16.3.4


The proposed delegation for future changes
would allow parking charges at Endcliffe Park to be kept under review and adjusted
in line with the wider parking tariff framework, where this remains
consistent with trustee duties and the best interests of the
charity. This would avoid unnecessary delay in implementing future
changes, help prevent the charity’s parking income falling
behind inflation or wider tariff changes, and support timely income
generation for the maintenance and management of the park. The
delegation would therefore serve the charity’s interests as
well as reducing administrative duplication.




 


 




16.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




16.4.1


Alternative Option 1 – Do nothing
 
Maintaining the current tariff at Endcliffe Park would mean that charges are not
aligned with the wider city approach or inflation. As set out in
the Officer Decision Report seeking to increase other
(non-charitable site) parking fees, failure to increase tariffs
would reduce the effectiveness of parking as a demand management
tool and may lead to increased congestion and reduced availability
of spaces.
 
It would also reduce the real-terms income
available to support the maintenance and improvement of the
park.
 
This option has therefore been discounted




 


 




16.4.2


Alternative Option 2 – Increase tariffs
by a greater amount
 
Whilst higher increases have the potential to
generate additional income for the Endcliffe Park Charity, they may also reduce income
if cheaper alternatives are sought out by park users.
 
A higher increase is not considered
proportionate and would go beyond the CPI-based approach adopted
across the wider parking estate.
 
This option has therefore been discounted
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to approve an increase in the parking tariff at Endcliffe Park to £1.10 per hour.

The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services requesting that it
notes the Charity Commission’s correspondence regarding
Norton Nurseries and approve progression of the arrangements
previously agreed by the Trustee, including completion of the
licence documentation and associated legal and property
processes.




 


 




17.2


RESOLVED: That the Charity
Trustee Committee:-
(a) 
Notes the correspondence from the Charity Commission regarding
Norton Nurseries and the Commission's conclusion that the Trustee's
previous decision was taken in the best interests of the
charity.
(b) 
Approves that the Council as trustee now progress the
implementation of the approved arrangements, including completion
of the longer-term licence documentation and any associated legal
and property processes.




 


 




 


 




17.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




17.3.1


The Charity Trustee Committee is asked to note
the Charity Commission’s correspondence because it confirms
that the Trustee’s previous decision in relation to Norton
Nurseries was taken in the best interests of Graves Park Charity.
The Commission has indicated that it is satisfied that a case has
been made that it is expedient in the interests of the Charity for
the Council, acting as trustee, to enter into a five-year licence
for the Norton Nurseries land with the Council in its capacity as
local authority.




 


 




17.3.2


Noting the correspondence enables the Trustee
to demonstrate that it has considered the Charity
Commission’s advice, including the need to act in the
Charity’s best interests, manage conflicts of interest,
account properly for the Charity’s funds and assets, and
ensure that the terms of the licence are enforced and monitored.
This is important because the advice has been provided under
section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011 and failure to have regard
to it may expose the Charity and Trustee to further regulatory
scrutiny.




 


 




17.3.3


The decision also provides a clear basis for
officers to progress implementation of the approved arrangements,
including completion of the longer-term licence documentation and
any associated legal and property processes. This will support
proper governance of the charitable asset, ensure the depot
arrangements are regularised, and maintain the ongoing maintenance
and upkeep functions which support Graves Park and other sites.

Considered and Rejected




 


 




17.4.1


Option 1: Do nothing (do not respond to the

In the event that the Trustee ceases to engage
with the CC this may be construed as a breach of the
Trustee’s duties that could ultimately lead to the CC
instigating a Statutory Inquiry and cause reputational damage to
the charity. This option has therefore been discounted.

The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services seeking approval for a
short-term licence to allow Weston Park's existing mobile catering
operator, Motore Café, to
continue trading within the park on revised terms.




 


 




18.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-
(a) 
Notes the contents of this report.
(b) 
Considered whether granting a short-term mobile catering licence
within the park is?in the best interest of the?Weston Park
Charity.
(c) 
Subject to being satisfied that the proposal supports the
Charity’s objects and represents the best outcome for the
Charity, approves the licence agreement with Motore Café as described in closed appendix
2.
(d) 
Delegates authority to officers to finalise the terms of the
agreement.




 


 




 


 




18.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




18.3.1


The proposed decision enables the Charity
Trustee Committee to regularise and approve a short-term mobile
catering licence within Weston Park, having considered whether the
arrangement is in the best interests of the Weston Park Charity and
supports its charitable objects.




 


 




18.3.2


The continuation of the mobile catering
provision supports the use and enjoyment of the park by providing
an accessible refreshment offer for visitors, enhancing the overall
visitor experience and contributing to the recreational purpose of
the charity.




 


 




18.3.3


Approving the revised short-term licence
provides continuity of service, reduces the risk of vacancy or
interruption to the visitor offer, and protects an income stream
for the charity while allowing time for any longer-term options to
be considered in a planned and transparent way.




 


 




18.3.4


The Committee has considered the operator's
track record, the role the concession plays in supporting the
visitor experience and the commercial terms proposed. Officers are
satisfied that the revised terms represent an appropriate
arrangement for the charity and that continuing with the existing
operator on a short-term basis represents the best outcome
reasonably available at this time.




 


 




18.3.5


The proposed arrangement reflects the current
commercial context and seeks to balance the need to secure
appropriate value for the charity with the practical need to
maintain a viable on-site provision. The alternative options were
not recommended because they would create a higher risk of vacancy,
loss of income and reduced benefit to park users.




 


 




18.3.6


For these reasons, and subject to the
Committee being satisfied that the proposed terms represent the
best outcome reasonably available for the charity at this time, the
approval of the short-term licence is
considered to be a proportionate and appropriate
decision.




 


 




18.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




18.4.1


Alternative Option – Terminate agreement
and undertake an immediate market exercise
 
The Council could seek to terminate or not
continue the current arrangement and undertake an open market
exercise at this stage. Whilst this may identify alternative
operators, there is no certainty that a better commercial or
operational outcome would be achieved for the charity. The existing
operator has an established track record at the site, has
demonstrated reliability and has developed a service which is well
used by visitors.
 
An immediate market exercise would also create
a risk of interruption to service provision and associated loss of
income whilst any procurement and mobilisation process is
undertaken. The recommended short-term arrangement allows the
charity to retain a proven operator and maintain continuity of
service and income whilst providing time to consider longer term
arrangements in a planned and transparent manner.
 
This option has therefore not been
recommended.
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to approve a short-term mobile catering licence for Motore Café to continue trading within Weston Park.

content:
10.1


Rose Garden Cafe lies within Graves Park and
is occupied under a Tenancy at
Will (TAW). The operators of the cafe have
advised the Council that they wish
to dissolve their existing partnership and
therefore a decision is required on the
future provision of this facility. The
Committee considered a report of the Executive Director of
Neighbourhood Services proposing to safeguard the future of this
cafe by agreeing terms with a new operator at the earliest
opportunity, based upon a Tenancy at Will, as per the current
arrangement.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Charity Trustee Committee:-

a)   
Notes the contents of this report.

b)   
Considered whether the proposal within the report and the suggested
recommendations are in the best interest of the Graves Park
Charity

c)   
and authorises the Chief Property Officer to: -
i)              
engage with the two individuals named under the current tenancy to
establish their individual proposals and determine what represents
the best outcome for the charity.
ii)             
select an operator and negotiate the best terms on behalf of the
Charity for a tenancy at will and instruct the Head of Legal
Services to complete any required formal documentation.
iii)           
ensure that the terms negotiated meet a minimum requirement of
maintaining quality of service and (or improving on if possible)
established income levels to the Charity.




 


 




 


 




10.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The proposed tenancy will safeguard the
continued operation of the café at Graves Park while the
wider restoration strategy is developed and implemented. It will
maintain a valuable income stream for the Charity through rental
payments and contributions towards the running costs of the park,
while ensuring continuity of service and avoiding the risks
associated with a vacant property or disruption during the interim
period. Continued occupation of the café will also enhance
the attractiveness of Graves Park as a well-used community asset
and ensure that the property continues to be used in furtherance of
the Charity's charitable objects.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Do nothing: reason for
rejection
 
Doing nothing is not considered
a viable option given the current partnership situation. Action is
required to safeguard cafe provision, protect the quality of the
visitor experience, and maintain rental income to the Charity. This
option is therefore not recommended.




 


 




10.4.2


Offer the café to the
open market
 
The cafe is subject to an
ongoing restoration strategy being delivered by Sheffield City
Council in partnership with key stakeholders. In this context, it
is not considered appropriate to test the market at this stage, as
this may limit flexibility during the restoration period. A
competitive process would be more appropriate once the restoration
works are complete. This option is therefore not
recommended.
topline: The Charity Trustee Committee has decided to engage with new operators and negotiate terms for a tenancy at will to safeguard the future provision of the Rose Garden Cafe in Graves Park.

purpose:
To seek a decision regarding the
implementation of the double yellow line parking restrictions and
the removal of a section of 40mph speed limit, replaced with 30mph
Restricted Road speed limit, on Abbey Lane.
content:
To seek a decision regarding the
implementation of the double yellow line parking restrictions and
the removal of a section of 40mph speed limit, replaced with 30mph
Restricted Road speed limit, on Abbey Lane.
 

Authorise the implementation of the double
yellow line parking restrictions and the removal of a section of
40mph speed limit, replaced with 30mph Restricted Road speed limit
on Abbey Lane.

The wider pedestrian Accessibiiity scheme is
designed to provide crossings and safer walking facilities on Abbey
Lane and Ecclesall Woods. This in
turn promotes healthier lifestyles whilst encouraging vibrancy in
local areas and supports access to public transport. 
 
The proposed double yellow lines will
formalise parking, reduce obstructive parking and protect the grass
verges. The reduction in speed limit for a short section of Abbey
Lane is to protect the new proposed Pegasus Crossing and slow
traffic on the approach, making it safer for pedestrians to
cross.

The only alternative is to not introduce any
parking restrictions to support the new pedestrian crossing
facilities within the full scheme. This is not considered to be an
acceptable option for this location as the proposed crossings alone
on Abbey Lane would not provide the required amount of safety
measures, including sufficient visibility and space for both
pedestrians and drivers. The measures proposed will contribute to
pedestrian safety by improving visibility at crossing points and
the disabled parking bays and prevent obstructive parking. The
proposed parking restrictions will also protect both the upper and
lower Abbey Lane/Whirlowdale Road
junctions.
 
Without the introduction of the parking
restrictions, outlined in this report, all road safety and
accessibility issues, for both pedestrians and vehicles, will
remain.
topline: The Assistant Director City Transport has decided to implement double yellow line parking restrictions and change a section of 40mph speed limit to 30mph on Abbey Lane to improve pedestrian safety and access to public transport.

accordingly.

local residents, and it would limit the potential safety and
environmental benefits associated with the proposal.

12.1


The Chief Social Work Officer brought a report
to Committee which asked for the approval of the Fairer Support
Planning and Choice Policy for Adult Care and Wellbeing.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Adult
Health and Social Care Policy Committee:
 

a.   
Approve the Fairer Support Planning and Choice Policy for
implementation across Adult Care and Wellbeing

b.   
Note that the policy provides a consistent framework for fair,
transparent and legally compliant support planning, review and
decision-making

c.    
Note that implementation will be supported through communications,
workforce briefings, guidance, management oversight and quality
assurance arrangements




 


 




12.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




12.3.1


The recommendations are being made because the
Council requires a clear, consistent and legally robust policy
framework for fairer support planning and choice in Adult Care and
Wellbeing. The proposed policy supports person-centred,
strengths-based and proportionate practice while also clarifying
how the Council will meet its duties to use public funds fairly and
transparently. Approving the policy will help improve consistency
in support planning, reviews, direct payments, top ups and
recording of decisions. It will also provide clearer guidance for
staff and managers, improve transparency for people and carers, and
support defensible decision-making where support arrangements are
challenged or need to change.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do not introduce
a new policy at this time. This option
was rejected because it would leave Adult Care and Wellbeing
without a single clear and current framework for fairer support
planning and choice. That would risk continued inconsistency in
practice, variation in decision-making, weaker organisational
support for staff, and reduced clarity for people and carers.




 


 




12.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Rely only on
existing guidance and local practice materials without an
overarching policy. This option was rejected because existing
guidance does not provide the same level of clarity, authority or
coherence as a formally approved policy. A policy is needed to set
a clear framework across services and to support lawful,
proportionate and transparent decision-making in a consistent
way.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the Fairer Support Planning and Choice Policy for Adult Care and Wellbeing.

understand and respond to the funding constraints that are applied
to services.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


To issue an ITT based on the current model.
This would offer continuity of the current provision but not allow
us the ability to work with the market to develop a wider breadth,
or to evaluate alternative delivery models.
topline: The Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee has decided to approve the extension of contracts for Dementia Day activities.

content:
8.1


The Strategic Director of Adult Care and
Wellbeing was in attendance to present the DASS Overview. The
Director stated that this DASS report would cover a significant
period of time as the Committee’s
last meeting had been held in March. The DASS overview
included:
 

-      
The latest performance data and reports to Members going
forward

-      
Statutory adherence and compliance

-      
Progress in delivery the business plan/strategy

-      
Summary of key risks and issues, including mitigation

-      
Key achievements during the period

-      
Horizon scan

-      
ACW Improvement Plan and CQC update




 


 




8.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Adult
Health and Social Care Policy Committee:
 

a.   
Notes progress in delivery upon the Adult Care Strategy Living the
Life You Want to Live

b.   
Notes the performance update areas for prioritisation and focus,
including performance dashboard at Appendix A.

c.    
Notes the strategy delivery updates and achievements for this
period

d.   
Notes the progress of our preparation for CQC following the site
visit in September, and next steps. (Separate Committee Report)




 


 




8.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




8.3.1


Asking for regular updates on the Strategy
Delivery, our Performance and CQC will enable the Committee, wider
stakeholders, and the public to hold the Council to account for
progress and impact and will provide an additional mechanism to
input to future development.




 


 




8.3.2


Endorsing the Strategy Delivery Programme and
Assurance Programme enables Committee to continue to undertake
scrutiny of the service and strategy delivery plan in an informed
and meaningful way.




 


 




8.3.3


Asking for regular updates and refreshes of
the CQC self-assessment, including wider assessment preparations
and communications will enable Committee to have oversight and
assurance that Adult Care know themselves and are able to drive
forward service improvements, alongside the assurance that we are
well prepared for the CQC assessment process.




 


 




8.3.4


Noting the performance update, enables
Committee to undertake scrutiny of Adult Care performance including
strengths and areas for prioritisation, including the development
of our Performance Management framework / cycle of Assurance,
alongside our improvement plans in this area.




 


 




8.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




8.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do Not Provide an
Update on The Strategy Delivery Plan Progress – When the
Strategy Delivery Plan was approved by Committee in June 2022 the
was a commitment to review the plan regularly and by not reviewing,
we would not be meeting that commitment. Due to the significant
amount that has been delivered on the plan, leaving it as it would
make it harder to identify the priorities going forward.




 


 




8.4.2


Alternative Option 2: A different delivery
plan - The real options for the delivery plan are around the
individual elements, which will be worked through as part of the
constituent pieces of work. These will be worked through in
different ways, with many of them resulting in their own future
reports to the Committee.




 


 




8.4.3


Alternative Option 3: Do not Review Our
Strategy. The strategy for Adult Care and wellbeing is nearly 3
years ago. Although co-produced the portfolio is in a very
different position now compared to the time when the strategy was
originally written. Undertaking a mid-term review enables us to
refresh our strategy and priority outcomes to ensure that it is fit
for purpose and maintains its relevance. ?




 


 




8.4.4


Alternative Option 4: Do not work in
partnership / collaboratively. It is a statutory requirement to
work in partnership with colleagues across the health, care, and
wellbeing system, as set out in the 2021 White Paper. The Statutory
Duty to Involve also requires us to engage and involve people who
use services, and unpaid carers in the design and delivery of care
and wellbeing. We would not be meeting these requirements if we did
not work in meaningful partnership across, they system, and with
all stakeholders.




 


 




8.4.5


Alternative Option 5: Do not Prepare for
the CQC Assessment. The CQC assessment of Adult Social Care
Services is not optional. The outcomes of the assessment are
published on the CQC website and have ramifications wider than
Adult Care and Wellbeing. A negative Outcome would mean that we are
not delivering our duties under the Care Act. In addition, a
negative outcome would impact on the reputation of the Council, the
confidence of our customers and partners, recruitment and
retention, staff morale, and potential funding opportunities.




 


 




8.4.6


Alternative Option 6. Do not share the ACW
CQC Self-Assessment with partners and in the public domain
To not share the self assessment and ask for comment would go
against the approach and principles we are embedding as business as
usual in Adult Care. To have both credibility and relevance, it is
vital that this is a report which provides an honest and
transparent narrative for adult social care informed by the voices
and experiences of staff, partners, commissioned providers, VCSE,
and the people who access our services, their families, carers, and
those with lived experience.
topline: The Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee has decided to approve progress updates on the Adult Care Strategy and preparation for a CQC assessment.

content:
10.1


The Assistant Director of Mental Health and
Wellbeing was in attendance to present a report on Adult Mental
Health services in Sheffield. The report was set in the context of
sustained demand, increased complexity and financial pressure. The
report stated that a key focus during 2025/26 and 2026/27 had been
on effectively using investment from Future Sheffield and the
Integrated Care Board (ICB) through the Better Care Fund (BCF) to
support review activity, improving value for money and ensuring
that care and support arrangements remain proportionate to need. It
was stated that this included a focus on annual reviews, targeted
reviews, enablement activity and the development of alternative
provision for people with multiple disadvantages and support for a
hospital social work discharge team.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Adult
Health and Social Care Policy Committee:
 

a.   
Notes the progress and continued focus on increasing adult mental
health review, enablement, and placement activity

b.   
Note the systemic challenges related to hospital discharge and
maintaining services delivering duties in relation to the 1983
Mental Health Act

c.    
Acknowledge the ongoing delivery risks associated with demand
pressures, system wide challenges, workforce capacity and
recruitment issues




 


 




10.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




10.3.1


This report is relevant for Committee
consideration as it provides oversight of a high-risk statutory
service area under increasing demand and complexity. It sets out
progress in delivering improvement activity, including review and
enablement programmes, alongside clear evidence of system
pressures, workforce constraints, and hospital discharge
challenges. The report enables Members to scrutinise performance,
assess financial sustainability and value for money, and seek
assurance that statutory duties are being met. It also highlights
key risks and dependencies across the wider health and care system,
supporting informed governance and decision-making.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


The report is an update on progress as such no
specific options are considered nor any alternatives.

content:
9.1


The Head of Lifelong Learning and Skills was
in attendance to present a paper which sought approval for
Sheffield City Council to accept, and act as the accountable body
for, the 2026/27 Adult Skills Fund (ASF) grant of £2.27m from
SYMCA. The report set out how the Lifelong Learning and Skills
Service, through FACES, would manage and administer the funding to
deliver adult education and skills provision across the city,
including commissioning around £650k of activity through
external providers using an established procurement framework.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Economic
Development, Skills and Culture Policy Committee:
 

a)   
The Economic Development, Skills and Culture Policy Committee
approve and accept the Adult Skills Fund allocation from SYMCA and
allow the Council to become the accountable body for the grant




 


 




 



b)   
The Economic Development, Skills and Culture Policy Committee note
the commissioning and procurement of 19+ adult learning and skills
activities in community setting across Sheffield, from external
providers for a period of one year from 1st August 2026
to 31st July 2027 with an estimated value of
£650,000 under the 4-year procurement framework agreement
made by this Committee in January 2023.




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The recommended outcome is for the Economic
Development, Skills and Culture Policy Committee to make a formal
decision to allow the Council to become the accountable body for
the Adult Skills Fund grant allocation of £2.27m for the
2026/27 academic year.




 


 




9.3.2


This decision will also enable FACES to move
to procurement of £650k of subcontracted provision so that
the service can deliver the necessary niche or high demand Adult
Skills activities from partners and training providers to meet the
regional skills priorities. We ask that the Committee note the
service’s intention to do so, under the 4-year adult skills
procurement framework agreed by Committee members in January
2023.




 


 




9.3.3


The recommended outcome will also enable the
service to continue to reach to some of the most disadvantaged
communities and those furthest from the labour market and offer
those communities learning opportunities to begin a pathway towards
employment and active citizenship.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Do Nothing – This is not an option as
the Council has proposed a delivery plan with SYMCA which requires
the Adult Skills grant to be agreed to enable delivery. This plan
includes sub-contracting a proportion of the ASF towards its
overall targets and needs to proceed with delivery to ensure the
contract for 2026/27 is met.




 


 




9.4.2


Self-Deliver only –The service does not
have the capacity to deliver the necessary skills activities where
demand is high or where niche activity is required, or to reach all
communities in the same way that local, trusted community
organisations often can do.




 


 




9.4.3


Working with appropriately qualified and
capable partners / training providers will therefore enable FACES
to:
 
• Help widen participation amongst niche
groups that would otherwise be hard to reach, but only where this
enriches the strategic curriculum intent learning offer
• Address high demand in a specific
curriculum that the service does not have the capacity to meet
learner need through our direct delivery • Add diversity in
the types of curricula we can offer to meet employment and skills
priorities for the region
• Secure expertise and skills that
address key policy issues such as climate change and sustainability
and increase skills within learning cultures to solve local
issues
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to accept a £2.27m Adult Skills Fund grant to provide adult education and skills provision in the city.

content:
11.1


The Committee considered a report which
provided an update on pupil outcomes and wider educational
performance in Sheffield, using the most recent nationally
published performance data.
 
The report
summarised headline trends across
inspection outcomes, pupil characteristics, attendance, exclusions
and attainment from Early Years through to secondary
education.
 
It was noted that,
while Sheffield continued to perform strongly in relation to
inspection outcomes, challenges remained in attendance, exclusions
and secondary attainment, particularly for vulnerable groups.
Members heard that addressing these challenges would require
sustained, system-wide collaboration and a clear focus on
inclusion, attendance and the quality of
education.
 
The report
highlighted the need to establish a clearer citywide Education
Strategy. The Committee was asked to endorse the Local Authority
taking a leadership role in developing this strategy, working in
partnership with Trust Chief Executive Officers, school leaders and
wider civic leaders. It was noted that the strategy would set out
shared priorities, strengthen collective accountability and provide
a coherent framework for improving outcomes for all children and
young people in Sheffield.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the current position on pupil outcomes and system trends
across Sheffield
b)   
Acknowledge the areas of strength and the key challenges
identified, particularly in attendance, exclusions and secondary
attainment
c)   
Endorse the continued system-wide focus on improving outcomes for
vulnerable learners
d)   
Request a further report setting out progress against these
priorities, including attendance, exclusions and attainment, within
the next reporting cycle
e)   
Agree the development with Education Leaders across the system an
Education Strategy that will drive improved attainment and
inclusion.




 


 




11.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




11.3.1


For members to understand the educational
landscape of pupil outcomes in Sheffield.




 


 




11.3.2


To agree the development with
Education Leaders across the system an Education Strategy that will
drive improved attainment and inclusion




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


There were no other alternatives
to consider.
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to endorse the development of a citywide Education Strategy in Sheffield to improve outcomes for vulnerable learners.

content:
13.1


The Committee considered a report which
provided an overview of the Youth Voice and Influence
function and its contribution to Sheffield’s strategic
priorities.
 
The report outlined
how youth voice was embedded across
Council services, highlighted participation activity and its
impact, and emphasised the importance
of continued engagement with children and young people. Members
heard that youth voice supported the Belonging Framework and the
City Goals by ensuring that young people were heard, were able to
influence decisions, and helped shape
services.
 
Strong engagement
was demonstrated through the participation of 13,796 young people
in Youth Cabinet elections, alongside a range of established
programmes that had delivered
measurable impact.
 
The Committee was
asked to recognise, support and
champion youth voice across the
city.




 


 




13.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the content of this report
b)   
Recognise youth voice as integral to
Sheffield’s strategic priorities
c)   
Support continued embedding of participation across
services
d)   
Encourage Elected Member engagement with youth voice
activity




 


 




13.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




13.3.1


Youth voice was essential to delivering
Sheffield’s strategic priorities and improving outcomes for
children and young people.
 
It was reported that embedding participation
across services led to more effective, inclusive and trusted
decision-making.
 
The recommendations were intended to ensure a
continued commitment to youth voice and to strengthen the role of
Elected Members in championing this work.




 


 




13.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




13.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Reduce or
limit youth voice activity
Reducing or limiting youth voice
activity had been considered. However, this option was not
recommended as it would reduce opportunities for young people to
influence decisions, weaken trust and have a negative impact on the
quality of services.




 


 




13.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Ad-hoc
consultation approach only
Adopting an ad-hoc consultation
approach as the sole method of engagement had been considered. This
option was not recommended as it would result in ineffective and
inconsistent engagement, reduce the inclusion of underrepresented
groups and weaken strategic alignment across
services.
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to recognise and support youth voice as integral to Sheffield's strategic priorities.

content:
12.1


The Committee considered a report
on the Risk Outside the Home (ROTH) Strategy and considered
its implementation across partner organisations.
It was noted that
children could be exposed to harm in community contexts outside the
family home.
 
The Committee's
oversight was recognised as being
essential to ensuring a shared understanding of the risks,
alignment of policy and practice, and the provision of appropriate
resources. The presentation of the strategy supported the
development of coordinated multi-agency responses and strengthened
the local approach to identifying, preventing and disrupting
extra-familial harm.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Notes and supports the implementation of the
strategy.




 


 




12.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




12.3.1


This report is for noting not a
decision.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


The main alternative considered
had been to continue responding to risks outside the home through
existing single-agency or case-by-case arrangements, rather than
through a shared citywide strategy. However, this option was not
preferred as it could lead to inconsistency, missed opportunities
to identify patterns of harm, and less coordinated responses across
services.
 
A further alternative considered
had been to delay implementation until additional local
arrangements were developed. This was not considered appropriate
given the need for a clearer and more consistent multi-agency
approach to preventing, identifying and responding to
extra-familial harm.
It was therefore concluded that
the proposed strategy represented the strongest option for
improving partnership working, clarifying responsibilities and
supporting earlier intervention
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to support the implementation of the Risk Outside the Home (ROTH) Strategy to protect children from harm in community contexts.

content:
9.1


The committee considered a report
which provided an update on Alternative Education Provision
services in Sheffield and the council’s strategic direction
for developing commissioned services that delivers support to
children permanently excluded from
school.
 
The report sought
approval to vary the commissioning decision dated 31 January 2023
for Alternative Education Provision to allow an additional
commission of two years and three months from July 2026 at an
estimated additional cost of up to £7million which would
allow procurement of those services for a further two years
commencing September 2026.
 
The
Strategic Lead for Alternative Provision also gave a presentation
which included a city overview, current position for the AEP
through the framework, purpose of the Policy Committee decision,
rising demand, current challenges and AEP
data.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Notes the strategy for Alternative Education Provision described in
this report.
b)   
Notes the scope of Sheffield City Council’s Alternative
provision and the allocation approved by the Director of
Children’s Services to manage this
service.
c)   
Approve the variation of the commissioning decision dated 31
January 2023 for Alternative Education Provision to allow an
additional commission of two years and three months from July 2026
at an estimated cost of up to £7 million. This will allow
procurement of these services for a further two years commencing
September 2026.
d)   
Notes that the £7 million spend includes the delivery of
Alternative Education Provision for pupils in the city where the
local authority statutory duty arises.




 


 




9.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




9.3.1


It was recommended that the Local Authority
support the further development of a citywide Alternative Education
Provision model, as this would create a clear strategy delivering
consistent, high-quality provision over which the Local Authority
would have oversight. The approach would enable the Local Authority
to develop the quality of provision and ensure that it was
integrated with wider practice to support inclusion and SEND across
the city. It would ensure that the Local Authority was able to meet
its statutory duties to arrange alternative education provision in
school or elsewhere under Section 19 of the Education Act 1996. It
was further recommended that the framework be procured as part of
the Authority's work to ensure that sufficient suitable provision
was developed within the city.
 




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Alternative Option
1
 
 
It was noted that, if no action
was taken and the current framework was not extended, all existing
contracts with providers would cease on 31 July 2026. This would
result in a lack of alternative provision from September 2026.
Consequently, the network of providers would cease to function,
affecting approximately 350 to 450 students across the city who
would be unable to access provision.
 
Members heard that this situation
would have implications for schools and internal partners,
including Inclusion and SEND services. The consequences for schools
could include an increase in exclusions and additional pressure on
the Local Authority to deliver full-time educational packages,
particularly given the current capacity limitations at the
Sheffield Inclusion Centre.
 
It was further noted that, that
scenario would adversely affect families and communities and could
contribute to a decline in school attendance. In addition, it would
negatively impact both the provision available and the
relationships maintained with providers, increasing the likelihood
of losing high-quality provision.




 


 




9.4.2


Alternative Option
2
 
Consideration has been given to
removing the AP framework, allowing schools to individually develop
any offer they wish to utilise directly with providers. This has
been rejected as it creates greater risk of poor practice. This

content:
10.1


The Committee considered a report
which reported the SEND reforms, including the Experts at
Hand model which formed part of a nationally led programme of
transformation and change aimed at improving outcomes for children
and young people with SEND.
 
Members were
advised that funding for the programme would be provided to local
authorities through a grant from the Department for Education. The
grant was required to be spent in accordance with its terms and
conditions and for the purpose of developing the Experts at
Hand model as described by the Department for Education. Local authorities, together with
Integrated Care Boards (ICBs), would act as the lead accountable
partners for local planning and implementation, working closely
with partners across health, care and
education.
 
The report outlined
the development of the programme and progress made to date.
Approval was sought for the delegation of authority to the
Strategic Director of Children's Services to approve expenditure
and commissioning arrangements within the parameters of the
guidance, enabling implementation of the programme plans to
commence.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Acknowledge the £4,304,713 Department of Education Grant
allocation awarded to Sheffield City Council for the purpose of
implementing the Experts at Hand
programme.
b)   
Delegate authority to the Strategic Director of Children’s
Services, in consultation with the relevant portfolio holder and
Section 151 Officer, to take all necessary actions to implement the
programme and allocate funding in accordance with the DFE terms and
conditions, and approved programme
objectives.
c)   
Approve the commencement of commissioning activity for delivery of
the programme, in alignment with grant criteria with an estimated
contract value of up to £1.7 million, and delegate authority
to the Strategic Director of Children’s Services to award and
enter into the resulting contract(s) following completion of the
procurement process, ensuring that we comply with the general
principle of open and transparent decision making and the Openness
of Local Government Bodies Regulations
2014




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The paper outlined the development and plans to
date for implementation of Experts at Hand as part of the SEND
reforms, and requests delegated authority to approve funding and
commissioning plans within the parameters of the guidance to the
Strategic Director of Children’s Services.




 


 




10.3.2


It was noted that Sheffield City
Council was expected to develop SEND services in line with the
national policy direction for which the
grant had been allocated.




 


 




10.3.3


Members heard that the programme
aligned with the ambitions already agreed within the SEND Strategy
and provided Sheffield with an opportunity to implement
improvements at pace.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


It was noted that the Council
could decide not to accept the grant and not to proceed with the
reforms. However, this option was not recommended, as the programme
represented a significant opportunity to build on existing
provision and deliver improvements to the SEND system in
Sheffield.
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to approve the implementation of the Experts at Hand model for SEND reforms in Sheffield.

content:
To provide authority to commission a framework
agreement for the provision of vehicle body shop repairs to the
Council to be undertaken.

Approve the commissioning decision for the
future Bodyshop Repairs Framework with an
estimated contract value of £900k and a contract term
of 4 years.

a)   
The Council requires a bodyshop repair
service to maintain its vehicle fleet.
b)   
The Council does not have the ability to deliver the service
in-house.
c)   
A competitive procurement process is required to ensure compliance
with the Procurement Act 2023 legislation.
 

Option 1: Do nothing
and allow the current framework agreement to expire.
This option has been excluded as there is a
requirement for the provision of body shop repairs and we have a
legal duty to compliantly procure a contract for its supply.
 
Option 2: Further
extend existing framework agreement
The current contract has ended, and we have no
options to extend under procurement law (value and duration). As
ever, the Council must adhere to procurement law, this includes the
legislation that was in place when the original contract agreement
was procured (the Public Contracts Regulations 2015) and the
Procurement Act 2023 (PA23). It is not possible to procure a single
supplier due to the size and complexity of the fleet. A large
proportion of the fleet are specialist vehicles.
 
Option 3:
Self-deliver
This is not an option; the Council has neither
the capacity or the skills to undertake
body shop repairs
topline: The Director of Customer Experience and Communities has decided to commission a framework agreement for vehicle body shop repairs for the Council.

The Executive Director City Futures submitted
a report that sought authority for Sheffield City Council to
purchase the freehold of 517 Manchester Road, Stocksbridge,
Sheffield, S36 1DH (the Property) at the request of the
Stocksbridge Towns Deal Board (the Board) using grant monies paid
to the Town Fund.
 
The report also sought approval for Sheffield
City Council to retain legal ownership and responsibility for the
Property until it could be transferred to a new charity which the
Board intend to set up (Proposed New Charity) for nil consideration
or, in the event of this not being possible, sold on the open
market. 




 


 




5.2


RESOLVED: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 

(a) 
notes that liability will be retained by the Council for the
running and other associated costs in respect of the Property after
completion of the purchase until it is transferred to the Proposed
New Charity or sold on the open market;
 

(b) 
notes that the first £20,000.00 of running costs only is
guaranteed to be reimbursed by the Towns Fund, with any additional
amounts being subject to further Board and Committee approval, with
the Council retaining liability if such approval is not obtained;
and
 

(c) 
grants authority for the Council to purchase the Property at the
request of the Stocksbridge Towns Fund Board using monies from the
Towns Fund.
 
(NOTE: The result of the vote was FOR –
4 Members; AGAINST – 1 Member (Councillor Douglas Johnson);
ABSTENTIONS – 2 Members (Councillor Angela Argenzio and
Councillor Jack Byrom).




 


 




5.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




5.3.1


The Council will have preserved the
opportunity for the Board to ultimately own the Property and fulfil
its wider objectives to the Stocksbridge area as set out above. If
the Council does not purchase the Property, there is the risk that
the Property will be left empty to deteriorate or redeveloped and
used for other, less favourable purposes.




 


 




5.3.2


By acquiring the Property, the Council will
also have provided the Board with further time to formally
establish and register the Proposed New Charity with the Charity
Commission and to submit a detailed delivery plan and business case
to the Council for the refurbishment of the Property and its long
term operation in conjunction with the adjacent new 519 Community
Hub Building. It will also potentially enable them to become the
owner of the Property by way of freehold transfer or lease.




 


 




5.3.3


The Council have also considered the long-term
strategy to deal with circumstances where the New Proposed Charity
cannot be established and the resulting implications.




 


 




5.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




5.4.1


Do Nothing – Not to step in and acquire
the Property within the deadline set by the owner.
 
If the Council do not step in acquire the
Property, then there is the risk that the owner will take the
Property off the market and the opportunity will be lost.
 
The Property could then potentially either sit
vacant and decaying and/or be used for inappropriate or
underperforming uses that will negatively affect the Board’s
wider strategic, economic and financial aspirations for this
prominent shopping area in Stocksbridge.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to purchase a property in Stocksbridge using grant money from the Town Fund.

11.1


Members of the committee
considered a report of the Executive Director Neighbourhood
Services seeking approval from the Environmental Services and
Regulation Committee to Initiate a tender process to procure and
award a contract for the installation, maintenance, and removal of
festive lighting displays over a four-year period.




 


 




11.2



RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY:
That the Environmental Services and Regulation
Policy Committee;

 

(a) Approve the commissioning of a competitive
tender process to let a 4 year

contract for the city centre Christmas Illuminations
contract through a

procurement process.

 

(b) Agree to maintain the set budget of
£87,600 per year over the course of the

4-year contract period. This budget may increase
with the rate of service cost

increases and inflation (This does not include the
budget for Local Area

Committees or District Centres)




 


 




11.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The decision is required to
ensure the continued delivery of a high-quality
Christmas lights programme
across Sheffield, which plays an important role in
supporting the city centre
economy, enhancing the visitor experience, and
contributing to the
city’s festive offer.




 


 




11.3.2


Entering into a 4-year contract
provides value for money, stability of delivery, and the ability to
plan and adapt the scheme in line with city centre regeneration and
stakeholder expectations, while ensuring appropriate maintenance,
safety, and operational standards are met.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
nothing
 
This option would involve
discontinuing the provision of a coordinated
Christmas lights scheme across
the city centre and associated locations.
This option has been rejected
due to the significant negative impact it would
have on the city centre’s
attractiveness, footfall, and economic activity during
the festive period. The
Christmas lights programme forms a key part of
Sheffield’s seasonal
offer, supporting local businesses and enhancing the
overall visitor
experience.
 
Removing the scheme would also
negatively impact public perception of the
city and reduce opportunities
to support wider cultural and community events,
including the annual switch-on.
Therefore, this option is not considered viable.




11.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Deliver
the service in-house
 
This option would involve the
Council directly procuring, installing, maintaining, and storing
the Christmas lights using internal resources. This option has been
rejected due to the specialist nature of festive illuminations,
including design, testing, installation at height, and ongoing
maintenance requirements. Delivering the service in-house would
require significant investment in equipment, infrastructure, and
skilled personnel, as well as introduce additional health and
safety risks and operational liabilities. It is also likely to
result in increased costs and reduced flexibility compared to using
an experienced external supplier with a proven track record in
delivering similar city-scale schemes.




11.4.3


Alternative Option 3:
Short-term or annual procurement
This option would involve
procuring the Christmas lights service on a yearly or
short-term basis rather than
entering into a 4-year contract.
This option has been rejected
as it would reduce the Council’s ability to
secure best value for money,
limit opportunities for strategic planning and
design continuity, and increase
procurement costs and administrative burden.
A longer-term contract enables
the supplier to invest in higher quality assets,
plan effectively around city
centre regeneration, and provide continuity of
service while still allowing
flexibility to refresh elements of the scheme in later
years.
topline: The Environmental Services and Regulation Policy Committee has decided to approve a competitive tender process for a 4-year contract for city centre Christmas Illuminations in Sheffield.

content:
9.1


Hackney Carriage trade
representatives and licence holders requested a review of Hackney
Carriage fares, together with the introduction of a temporary fuel
surcharge, in response to rising fuel costs.
 
Members received a report of
the Executive Director Neighbourhood Services  considering those requests, including the
supporting evidence and rationale, and seeking approval to proceed
with the implementation of a surcharge and to delay a full review
of fares until later in the year, subject to the outcome of the
statutory consultation and provided no objections were
received.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Environmental
Services and Regulation Policy Committee;

a)   
Notes the request made by trade representatives and
amend Hackney Carriage Fares.

b)   
Introduces a temporary fuel surcharge to Hackney
Carriage fares, as set out in the table at paragraph 2.1 of the
report, to end on 29th November 2026 unless extended following the
review described at Recommendation 3.

c)   
Notes that a full review of Hackney Carriage fares
will be undertaken in late 2026.




 


 




9.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The proposed decision ensures
that Hackney Carriage fares remain fair, reasonable and
evidence-based, reflecting increased operating costs while
following the statutory consultation process. It supports the
continued viability of the Hackney Carriage sector, helps maintain
service provision for residents, and aligns with the
Council’s regulatory and public protection
responsibilities.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Alternative Option
1:
 
Retain Current Fares
 
Under this option, no changes
would be made to the current Hackney Carriage fare structure, and
no fuel surcharge would be introduced.
 
While this option avoids any
increase in costs to passengers in the short term, it does not
account for the significant increases in operating costs faced by
licence holders. This could risk undermining the financial
viability of the Hackney Carriage trade and may result in reduced
service availability.
 
This option is therefore not
recommended.




 


 




9.4.2


Alternative Option
2:
 
Permanent Fare Increase
Only
 
This option would involve an
amendment to fares without the introduction of a temporary fuel
surcharge.
 
While this approach would
provide greater long-term certainty, it is not recommended as it
does not allow for flexibility in responding to fluctuations in
fuel prices and may result in fares being set higher than necessary
should fuel costs decrease.
 
The Council has committed to
undertaking a full review of Hackney Carriage fares later in the
year, in consultation with the trade. However, officers consider it
necessary to respond to the immediate financial pressures currently
being experienced, particularly in relation to rising fuel costs.
In this context, the introduction of a temporary, variable
surcharge is considered a more proportionate and responsive
approach, ensuring fares more accurately reflect prevailing
operating costs over time.
topline: The council has decided to approve the introduction of a temporary fuel surcharge to Hackney Carriage fares in response to rising fuel costs.

content:
13.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director, Neighbourhood Services that sought approval to
extend two supported housing services for 12 months and to
commission a range of new services for single adults who are at
risk of or are experiencing homelessness. The new contracts would
run for between six and eight years and the total value of the
contracts is £11,225,785. Together, the extensions and new
services would support a transition to a new delivery model of
supported housing without creating gaps in provision. The new
services would help the Council meet its statutory homelessness
duties by providing a suitable alternative to temporary
accommodation, supporting people to build independent living
skills, and helping prevent rough sleeping.




 


 




13.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Housing Policy Committee:-
 

(a) 
approves the extension of the two existing men’s hostel
contracts for 12 months (1 November 2026 to 31 October 2027) with a
total contract value of £752,000, to allow a planned
transition to a new model of provision;
 

(b) 
approves the commissioning of the following new supported housing
services each for a period of 8 years:
 
                       
i.        
a male-specific service (minimum 70 units), combining scheme-based
and dispersed provision, providing an average of 3.5 hours support
per week, commencing 1 November 2027, with a total contract value
of £3,779,240;
                      
ii.        
a dispersed service for single people (minimum 17 units), providing
an average of 3 hours support per week, commencing 1 October 2027,
with a total contract value of £799,300;
                     
iii.        
a female-specific dispersed service (minimum 14 units), providing
an average of 6 hours support per week for women, commencing 1
January 2027, with a total contract value of £1,111,542;
and
                    
iv.        
a dispersed service for single people (minimum 45 units), providing
an average of 8 hours support per week, commencing 1 June 2027,
with a total contract value of £3,952,643; and

 

(c) 
approves the commissioning of a new supported housing service to
replace the Rough Sleeping Accommodation Programme (RSAP) for a
period of 6 years. This would consist of dispersed supported
housing for people experiencing rough sleeping (minimum 30 units),
commencing 1 October 2026, with a total contract value of
£831,060.




 


 




13.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




13.3.1


The proposed commissioning approach is
recommended as it delivers a structured transition from existing
provision to a more effective, prevention focused supported housing
system for single people, aligned with National and Local Strategy.
It responds to evidence from the Housing Related Support review and
stakeholder engagement by reducing reliance on large hostels,
increasing dispersed and specialist provision, and improving equity
of access particularly for women. The proposals maintain service
continuity while enabling service transformation, ensure better
targeting of support to those most likely to benefit, and
strengthen outcomes such as sustainable move-on and reduced
homelessness. Alternative options, including ending or maintaining
existing services unchanged, would either increase homelessness and
system pressures or fail to address identified gaps and
inequalities.




 


 




13.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




13.4.1


Keep things as they are – This would not
address the recommendations of the Housing Related Support Review,
reflect best practice or be an equitable way to address the overall
needs of single people at risk of or experiencing homelessness.




 


 




13.4.2


Reducing the budget has been ruled out, as
this would have a negative impact on single people and increase
homelessness and/or rough sleeping. Any immediate budget savings
are likely to lead to financial pressures elsewhere by increasing
the use of bed and breakfast accommodation. Ending services goes
against our agreed strategy to stop the use of bed and breakfast
accommodation and reduce the numbers of people in temporary
accommodation.




 


 




13.4.3


Bringing the service in-house has been ruled
out because individuals need a diverse range of provision. The
Council does not have enough suitable housing stock, and partner
organisations offer specialist expertise that supports better
outcomes.
topline: The Housing Policy Committee has decided to approve extensions to existing supported housing services and commission new services for single adults at risk of homelessness.

content:
11.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director, Neighbourhood Services which provided an
overview of the Government’s National Strategy: A Plan to End
Homelessness, the expectations for local authorities, and the
proposed review of the Sheffield Action Plan to align with the
National Strategy. The report sought approval for the proposed
external spending plan, which explained how the Homelessness, Rough

(a)

Homelessness, and the proposed approach to develop a long-term

(b)

(c) 
approves the new investment and extensions set out in the external

i.        
short-term extensions and new initiatives to test approaches and

the table at Section 2.3.8 of the report), totalling
£152,280; and

                      
ii.        
longer-term investment in supported housing commissioning proposals
(as detailed in items 4-6 of the table at Section 2.3.8 of the

(d) 
approves the external distribution of £164,136 from a one-off
Grant awarded to the Council in 2025 to support children in
temporary accommodation, which has been approved as committed
ringfenced spend for 2026 and meets the conditions of the

11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


While considerable progress has been made to
date, homelessness remains a persistent challenge in Sheffield in
the context of a national increase and the cost-of-living crisis.
This places increased demand on Temporary Accommodation and
subsequently increases financial pressures to the Council.
Furthermore, the individual impact of homelessness can be
substantial, often resulting in long-term consequences such as
diminished opportunities and greater inequalities. Efforts to
prevent homelessness are showing positive results through effective
implementation of the Homeless Prevention Strategy. It is essential
to build upon these achievements by undertaking a review of the
action plan and progressing with distribution of the grant.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option
1: Not making amendments to the current Action Plan
 
If the approach to reviewing the Action Plan
is not approved, it would affect the Council’s ability to
meet the requirements set out in the National Strategy, alongside
the Council statutory duties and responsibilities, and limit
delivery of effective actions to relieve and prevent
homelessness.




 


 




11.4.2


Alternative Option
2: Not approving recommendations to externally distribute Grant
Income.
 
If the proposed external spending plan is not
approved, the Council may be unable to deliver the actions and
priorities needed to prevent and relieve homelessness, which could
affect its ability to meet statutory duties and retain
accommodation. Although Local Authorities have flexibility in how
the Grant is used, it is ringfenced for initiatives that prevent
homelessness and address rough sleeping. If the funding is not used
in line with the grant conditions, it may be clawed back, creating
additional financial pressure for the Council and damaging its
reputation with MHCLG and partners.
topline: The Housing Policy Committee has decided to approve a new investment plan of over £24 million to address homelessness and rough sleeping in Sheffield.

content:
12.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director, Neighbourhood Services which sought approval to
commission a Family Supported Housing service for up to 6 years.
The contracts for the two services for families who are homeless or
at risk of homelessness would end on the 30 November 2026 and a new
service was required to avoid a gap in provision. The service would
contribute to meeting statutory homelessness duties by providing a
suitable alternative to Temporary Accommodation and support to
develop independent living skills to minimise the risk of recurrent
homelessness.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Housing Policy Committee approves the commissioning of a service to
support families with housing support needs who are at risk of
homelessness or are homeless. The service would provide a minimum
of 70 units under a contract for a term of six years, with a break
clause at four years, with a proposed total value of
£1,659,963.




 


 




12.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




12.3.1


Two contracts end on the 30 November 2026. The
service helps to meet statutory homelessness duties and contributes
to meeting key national and local objectives to prevent homeless.
Not to commission a new service would make it harder to support
families at risk of or experiencing homelessness and increase the
use of bed and breakfast accommodation. This would mean worse
outcomes for families, alongside being a more expensive option for
the Council.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Ending the service – This would have a
negative impact on vulnerable families and any immediate budget
savings are likely to lead to financial pressures elsewhere by
increasing the use of bed and breakfast accommodation. Ending
services would be counter to the Council’s agreed strategy to
end the use of bed and breakfast accommodation for families in the
coming year, and to comply with the regulatory requirement to limit
any placements to no more than 42 days.




 


 




12.4.2


Not increasing the budget –
Recommissioning but not uplifting the budget would bring risks that
include: not being able to commission a service; commissioning a
service that supports fewer families; the provider giving notice
part way through the contract.




 


 




12.4.3


Bringing the service in-house has been ruled
out because families need a diverse range of provision, the Council
does not have enough suitable housing stock, and partner
organisations offer specialist expertise that have been
demonstrated to support good outcomes.
topline: The Housing Policy Committee has decided to approve the commissioning of a Family Supported Housing service to support families at risk of homelessness or experiencing homelessness.

content:
To review the charges for parking permits, bay
suspensions, parking dispensations and parking tariffs. The
proposed changes will help to better manage parking demand and
contribute to wider traffic management and environmental
objectives.





a)   
Approve an increase in Pay and Display
tariffs in the parking zones outside the city, as detailed in
Appendix A & C, and that these are implemented as soon as
practicable while noting that certain changes will also need to be
subject to the approval of the Charity Trustee Sub Committee before
they can be implemented in the charitable parks.
 




b)   
Approve an increase to City Centre Zone
Pay and Display tariffs, as detailed in Appendix A & C, and
that these are implemented as soon as practicable.
 




c)   
Approve an increase in Permit prices, as
detailed in Appendix B of this report be approved and be
implemented from 15th of June 2026.
 
d)   
Approve changes to the dispensation and
bay suspension charges, as detailed in this report, and those said
changes be implemented from 15th of June 2026.
 
e)   
The chair of the Charity Trustee Sub
Committee to approve price increases proposed in this report before
they can be implemented in the charitable parks
 
 




 

It is anticipated that the proposed parking
tariff and fee revisions set out in this report will support the
effective management of parking demand across the authority’s
parking estate. The proposed changes are intended to encourage the
more efficient use of available parking provision, particularly in
locations and during periods where demand consistently and
demonstrably exceeds capacity. By better aligning parking charges
with observed levels of demand, the authority aims to improve space
turnover, enhance accessibility for residents, visitors and
businesses, and ensure that limited parking resources are managed
in a fair, sustainable and effective manner.

Alternative Option 1:
The Council could maintain its current
tariffs
 

This option was rejected as this would not address
the excess demand parking issues outlined in this report, nor
enable other positive outcomes that may arise, such as better air
quality. Continuing with the current tariffs and not aligning with
the inflation will result in cheaper permits increases the kerbside
space would be likely to start to negatively impact the efficient
use of space and uptake of more active modes such as walking,
cycling and use of public transport.

 
Alternative Option 2:
The Council could make higher and more widespread
increases in tariffs
 
This
option was rejected with the information available; these are not
thought to be appropriate or proportionate to achieve the aims of
the proposed increases.
topline: The Executive Director of Neighbourhood Services has decided to approve changes to parking permits, bay suspensions, dispensations, and tariffs to better manage parking demand and contribute to wider traffic management and environmental objectives.

That the Property declared as surplus to the
service delivery needs of Children & Families Services be
reversed as an operational asset within Sheffield City Council
Asset Register to allow a forward transfer to the incoming Academy
Trust under the Academies Act 2010.

The incoming Academy Trust have applied for
the Property to be transferred for use as a nursery and there are
safeguarding and health and safety concerns associated with a
disposal.
 

The alternative to
reversing the decision to declare the Property surplus would be to
leave the surplus declaration in place. However, as already set
out, the Trust have applied for the Property to be transferred for
use as a nursery and there are safeguarding and health and safety
concerns associated with a disposal.

 
The Property has been
considered for alternative service use within the Council and as a
possible addition to the social housing stock. However, this has
been discounted due to the poor condition of the property and
amount of capital investment required.

 
Portfolio services have been
consulted on identifying an alternative use for the Property but
none has been identified. Continuing to leave the Property vacant
will mean the Council having to commit funding on a regular basis
for securing and basic maintenance.
