content:
To seek a decision on payment of Clean Air
Plan (CAP) grant funds to South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined
Authority (SYMCA) for the delivery of a local Zero Emission Bus
(ZEB) project:
The project will utilise the CAP funds awarded
to SCC and RMBC by HM Government, the funds are ring fenced
specifically for ZEB upgrade and cannot be used for other purposes
without Department
for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (DEFRA) change
approval.
The local ZEB project is to reduce
NO2 from bus emissions to bring concentrations to
within legal limits within the shortest possible time in line with
our Ministerial Directive.
The project to bring forward the
electrification of Holbrook depot from 2029 to 2026/27 and the
purchase of 66 electric vehicle (EV) buses to operate on key routes
in Sheffield from mid-2027.
The project will be delivered by SYMCA as part
of their Tranche 1 bus franchising programme





a)


Approve the payment
of £8,074,337 Clean Air Plan grant funds awarded to Sheffield
City Council by HM Government and approved for the purpose of
implementing ZEB upgrade to accelerate NO2 reduction as
quickly as possible, to South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority
(SYMCA) to deliver the ZEB project as agreed with Department for
Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (DEFRA) as outlined in this
report.
 




b)


Approve upfront
payment of the CAP grant funds noting that SYMCA intend to use the
funds to secure purchase of 66 electric buses to be ordered in May
2026 for deliver in / by May 2027. Advance payment will:
 
-      
Secure delivery of the buses in the
shortest possible time to realise a reduction in roadside
NO2 form bus emissions in Sheffield as quickly as
possible.
 
-      
Secure a purchase price in a volatile
market.
 




 

Timely transfer of the funds to SYMCA will
enable the delivery of the local CAP ZEB scheme to bring forward a
reduction in NO2 from bus emissions to bring
concentrations to within legal limits within the shortest possible
time in line with our Ministerial Directive.

Sheffield City Council (SCC) and Rotherham
Metropolitan Borough Council (RMBC) remain under a joint
Ministerial Direction to achieve legal annual average Nitrogen
Dioxide (NO2) limits at all CAP valid air quality monitoring
locations within in the ‘shortest possible
time’.  There are remaining
exceedances in Sheffield where further NO2 reduction is required
and where bus emissions are a contributing source.
 
Bus emission issues are delaying achieving
compliance and a solution to bring forward NO2 reduction
as quickly as possible at locations significantly impacted by buses
needed to be found. As such, do nothing was not an option and
available options were limited.
Alternative Option 1:
The option to seek bids from operators early
in 2025 utilising the £8.8m available at that point was
tested:
 
·      
The available funding was insufficient to deliver the scale of
change needed to have a material impact on NO2
reduction.
 
·      
The approach proved un-deliverable as the uncertainty associated
with bus franchising limited the scope of future commercial
investment commitments that operators could offer.
topline: The Executive Director, City Futures has decided to approve the payment of Clean Air Plan grant funds for a local Zero Emission Bus project.

Complaint Reference-

Sheffield City

14th May

Breach of Code -


No










 




 
I write to inform you of the
decision of the Hearing Sub-Committee that considered the
Investigators report dated March 2026 into complaint reference,
SC.2026.08 regarding a potential breach of the Members Code of
Conduct by the subject member.
 
The meeting followed the
Hearing Sub-Committee Procedure that was provided with the agenda
and report. 
 
Sub-Committee Members
 
Councillors Simon Clement-Jones
(Chair), Maroof Raouf, Matthew Dwyer and Fatima Adesanya
(Non-Voting independent Co-opted Member)
 
Officers in attendance
 
David Hollis, General Counsel
and Monitoring Officer.
Sherrie Grant, Deputy
Monitoring Officer
Sarah Hyde, Democratic Services
Team Manager.
 
Others
 
Investigator – VWV
Solicitors
Subject Member –
Councillor X
 
 




As per the Hearing
Sub-Committee procedure, the Subject Member and the complainant Mr
B were invited to attend the meeting. 
The complainant did not attend the meeting.
 
The investigator outlined his
findings of the investigation.  The
subject member and Sub-Committee Members were given the opportunity
to ask questions of the investigator.
 
Following consideration of the
report presented by the Monitoring Officer and the Investigator,
the Sub-Committee determined on the basis set out in the
investigation report, that the Subject Member was acting in an
official capacity at the time the complaint occurred and therefore
the Members’ Code of Conduct does apply.
 
The Sub-Committee can make any
of the following recommendations: -
 

·      
Recommend to Council or to Committees that he/she be
removed from any or all Committees or Sub-Committees of the Council
and from any external appointments made by the Council.


·      
Instruct the Monitoring Officer to arrange training
for the member.
 

·      
In a case where the breach relates to use of the
Council’s IT systems, that the Member’s access to those
systems is withdrawn.


·      
That policies/procedures are amended.


·      
That a briefing/information note be
issued.


·      
That an apology be given.


·      
That the Member is censured in writing and a copy of
the letter is published on the Council’s website.

 
·      
Take no action where
it is not considered appropriate in the circumstances to impose a
sanction.




Decision
 
The Sub-Committee decided there
was no breach of the Councillor Code of Conduct and therefore take
no further action.
 




Reasons
 
The Committee agreed with the
investigator’s findings.   The Committee
found that the conduct complained of arose in the context of
political debate on a matter of public interest. In reaching its
decision, the Committee recognised that councillors are entitled to
enhanced protection for freedom of expression under Article 10 of
the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly where they
are communicating political views to members of the public.
 




Appeal
 
There is no right of appeal to
the Council against this decision. However, if the complainant
feels that we have not dealt with the complaint properly then they
can refer it to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman
at 
http://www.lgo.org.uk/make-a-complaint/how-to-complainor

purpose:
To seek approval that the Draft Ecclesfield
Parish Neighbourhood Plan can proceed to the next stages of the
neighbourhood plan process, which is consultation and subsequently
examination.
content:
To seek approval that the Draft Ecclesfield
Parish Neighbourhood Plan can proceed to the next stages of the
neighbourhood plan process, which is consultation and subsequently
examination.

1. The Draft Neighbourhood Plan is publicised
on the Council’s website for a period of at least 6 weeks in
accordance with Regulation 16 of the Neighbourhood Planning
(General) Regulations 2012 ("the Regulations");
 
2. Consultation bodies are notified of receipt
of the Draft Neighbourhood Plan in accordance with Regulation 16(b)
of the Regulations;
 
3. An examiner is appointed with the consent
of Ecclesfield Parish Council in accordance with paragraphs 7(4)
and 7(6) of Schedule 4B of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990
("the 1990 Act") (as applied to Neighbourhood Plans by section 38A
of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004)
 
4. The Draft Neighbourhood Plan is submitted
to the appointed examiner for independent examination after expiry
of the abovementioned publicity period, in accordance with
paragraph 7(2) of Schedule 4B of the 1990 Act and Regulation 17 of
the Regulations.

The submission of a neighbourhood plan to the
Local Planning Authority is strictly guided by legislation and
regulations, as set out in the report above. A local planning
authority must accept the submission of a neighbourhood plan and
proceed to the next stage in the process if it has met all the
necessary statutory rules.
 
Evaluation of the submission has revealed no
issues that would warrant rejection of the submitted plan and
supporting documents. Furthermore, the City Council also recognises
the importance of developing Neighbourhood Plans and welcomes the
next stages of the process with respect to the Ecclesfield
Neighbourhood Plan.

The submission of a neighbourhood plan to the
Local Planning Authority is a statutory process. As documents have
been submitted in accordance with Regulation 15 of the
Neighbourhood Planning Regulations 2012, no alternative options are
considered appropriate.
topline: The Head of Planning has decided to approve the Draft Ecclesfield Parish Neighbourhood Plan for consultation and examination.

To approve that the Council becomes
accountable body for £134,963 of Gambling Harms Prevention
Grant for 2026/27 awarded through the Office for Health Improvement
and Disparities and approve that the Council enters into the Memorandum of Understanding for this
grant.
 





Gambling harms are a
growing public health concern. Funded by the statutory gambling
levy, and awarded through the Office of
Health Improvement and Disparities, Sheffield City Council has been
allocated a Gambling Harms Prevention Grant of up to £134,963
for 2026/27. The Council’s grant allocation for 2027/28 will
be announced towards the end of this financial year.
 




Becoming accountable
body for this grant will support the continued implementation of
Gambling Harms Prevention Strategy for Sheffield 2024-2034. The
grant must be used exclusively to fund gambling harms prevention
activity in accordance with expectations set out in the Memorandum
of Understanding (MoU) between the Secretary of State for Health
and Social Care, acting through the Office for Health Improvement
and Disparities, and Sheffield City Council for this grant. This
MoU covers the the period 2026/27 with
an allocation to be agreed towards the end of this financial year
for 2027/28.
 




 

The only alternative option considered is for
the Council to decline this new grant funding. This option has been
rejected as there are currently limited financial resources in the
Council for gambling harms prevention activity and this new grant
will support the continued implementation of the Gambling Harms
Prevention Strategy for Sheffield 2024-2034.

purpose:
To continue to allocate a portion of the
ring-fenced government funding for stop smoking services and
support, to the South Yorkshire Tobacco Control Alliance (SYTCA)
for the next three years, up to the end of 2028/29. The total
contribution over the three-year period will be £504,354. In
the initial year of the alliance, SCC contributed £168,118,
bringing the total for four years to £672,472.
SYTCA, which began operating in October 2025,
has already begun to realise many benefits for tobacco control in
Sheffield, including preventing duplication of local work
programmes across the four local authorities, reducing costs
through economies of scale, and coordination of regional
communications campaigns which removes the need for local
development and the associated costs.
The recommendations will contribute to the
achievement of the vision of the 2022-2027 Tobacco Control Strategy
in Sheffield which aims for people to live longer and healthier
lives, smokefree. The vision includes that Sheffield children grow
up in a city where smoking is unusual; and that Sheffield is a
smokefree city in which to live, work and play. Our ambition is to
make smoking obsolete by 2030 or to get to 5% prevalence in adults
across all social groups. This strategy was signed off at
Council Cabinet in April 2022.
content:
To continue to allocate a portion of the
ring-fenced government funding for stop smoking services and
support, to the South Yorkshire Tobacco Control Alliance (SYTCA)
for the next three years, up to the end of 2028/29. The total
contribution over the three-year period will be £504,354. In
the initial year of the alliance, SCC contributed £168,118,
bringing the total for four years to £672,472.
SYTCA, which began operating in October 2025,
has already begun to realise many benefits for tobacco control in
Sheffield, including preventing duplication of local work
programmes across the four local authorities, reducing costs
through economies of scale, and coordination of regional
communications campaigns which removes the need for local
development and the associated costs.
The recommendations will contribute to the
achievement of the vision of the 2022-2027 Tobacco Control Strategy
in Sheffield which aims for people to live longer and healthier
lives, smokefree. The vision includes that Sheffield children grow
up in a city where smoking is unusual; and that Sheffield is a
smokefree city in which to live, work and play. Our ambition is to
make smoking obsolete by 2030 or to get to 5% prevalence in adults
across all social groups. This strategy was signed off at
Council Cabinet in April 2022.
 






a)   
To approve funding the South Yorkshire Tobacco Control Alliance
(SYTCA) from our Local Stop Smoking Services and Support Grant
(LSSSG) at 25% for the next three years. The total contribution
over the three-year period will be £504,354.





b)   
To approve officers to work with SYTCA to ensure local
accessibility of, and engagement with, stop smoking support.





c)   
To approve officers working collaboratively with regional partners
in the alliance by attending board meetings and engaging with
subsequent actions. 




 

Approving the recommendations will ensure Sheffield City Council
continues to use ring-fenced government funding for stop smoking
services and support in a way that maximises impact, value for
money and system-wide reach, while supporting delivery of
Sheffield’s Tobacco Control Strategy 2022–2027 and the
ambition to achieve a smokefree city/5% adult smoking prevalence by
2030.
Smoking remains a leading cause of preventable ill health and a
major driver of health inequalities, and regional smoking
prevalence remains higher than the national average. By
contributing 25% of Sheffield’s Local Stop Smoking Services
and Support Grant (LSSSG) for 2026/27-2028/29 (total
£504,354), the Council will sustain SYTCA, enabling shared
delivery across South Yorkshire that reduces duplication, achieves
economies of scale, and strengthens collective capacity and
influence. SYTCA has already demonstrated benefits since operating
from October 2025, including coordinating regional communications
campaigns and helping reduce local campaign development costs,
notably enabling a reduction in Sheffield communications
spend.
The
funding is an accepted use of the ring-fenced grant, is accounted
for in planned expenditure, and supports continuation of
time-sensitive regional work programmes requiring partner
commitment.
Officer involvement will ensure SYTCA’s regional
programmes translate into accessible, locally relevant support in
Sheffield, strengthening referral pathways, promoting
evidence-based messaging, and improving engagement with stop
smoking services, particularly for populations with higher smoking
prevalence and more complex needs.
Active participation in SYTCA governance,
including board meetings and follow-up actions, will help ensure
accountability, alignment with Sheffield priorities, and effective
joint delivery. This will support a consistent regional approach,
shared learning, and a stronger collective voice on policy and
system change.
 

·      
Choosing not to fund SYTCA and allocating the
funding to local stop smoking service initiatives.
·      
Funding SYTCA on an annual basis with a review
annually.
topline: The Strategic Director of Public Health and Integrated Commissioning has decided to allocate £504,354 over three years to the South Yorkshire Tobacco Control Alliance for stop smoking services and support.

sex” only. The Equality and Human Rights Commission's (EHRC)
statutory Code Of Practice For Services, Public Functions, And
Associations, has subsequently been revised and comes into force on
5 August 2026. The revised Code reflects the legal position
following the Supreme Court judgment.

Supreme Court judgment and reflects the EHRC guidance that was in
place at that time.

response to legislative, regulatory and other relevant legal
developments.

made to ensure that the policy reflects the current legal framework
and statutory guidance which will apply from 5 August 2026.

purpose:
Bristol Operations Centre (BOC) provides
security alarm monitoring for Bristol City Council (BCC) premises
and a range of external customers. As a critical service, BOC must
support customers in upgrading their alarm equipment to meet
nationally mandated deadlines associated with the UK's migration
from analogue to digital telecommunications networks and the
planned decommissioning of 2G and 3G mobile networks. In parallel,
BOC is transitioning all security alarm monitoring services to the
Skyresponse platform as part of the BOC Technology Upgrade
Programme, which received Committee approval in July 2025.
This is a revenue generating contract on a cost recovery basis,
which will recuperate money that is spent and be
supported by other revenue Bristol Operations Centre (BOC)
generates. The contract is funded by BOC's revenue
account and the cost of alarms is included on the invoice to the
customer. There is no further funding needed to award this
contract. The value remaining on the now expired contract will be
used as the baseline value (£92,755), with the option of a
£50,000 extension should it be needed down the line. Though
it’s worth noting, the previous contract was in place for 5
years and had a total spend of £147,245, which included a
very high number of upgraded alarms due to the national switch from
analogue to digital networks, so spend is unlikely to be as high
going forward.
Our previous contract with CSL expired on 6 July 2026. A swift
renewal of the contract with CSL is vital in being able meet
deadlines ensure all BCC premises have digital alarms and can have
resilient monitoring ahead of the national switch to digital
telecoms. Without this contract, BCC buildings not already upgraded
will be forced
to seek alternative monitoring providers outside Bristol City
Council in order to have alarms compatible with the
national removal of PSTN lines installed, leading to a direct loss
of revenue for the organisation and undermining
the Council's investment in its alarm monitoring service. In
addition, BOC would be unable to onboard new
customers requiring digital alarm monitoring solutions, restricting
future revenue growth and limiting the service's
ability to expand and having a negative financial impact on the
service and its reputation.

some changes to existing contractual documents relating to Bristol
City Leap in order to enable the purchase of BHNL to proceed.
Decisions relating to those changes to the contractual document
were delegated to the “Chief Executive in consultation with
Cabinet Member for Climate, Ecology, Waste and Energy, Deputy Mayor
for Finance, Governance and Performance, Director of Legal and
Democratic Services and Director of Finance” pursuant to the
6 December 2022 Cabinet Report. To reflect the change to the
committee system, the decision will be taken in consultation with
the Chair of Strategy and Resources in place of the Cabinet Member
for Climate, Ecology, Waste and Energy.
The changes requested to be made by the proposed new owner
are:
-Introduction of a sub-cap relating specifically to heat network
liability within the parent company guarantee given to the Council
by Ameresco Inc. (the “Ameresco PCG”);
-The issue of a comfort letter (the “Comfort Letter”)
confirming the BCC will not call upon the Ameresco PCG to the
extent that there has been any breach of or will be an expected
breach of the key performance indicators set out int the City Leap
Concession Agreement (the “Concession KPIs”). The
comfort letter will fall away at the point in time that a remedial
plan relating to performance of the Concession KPIs has been
agreed.
-The release of Vattenfall AB from a parent company guarantee
provided to the Council in connection with the share sale and
purchase agreement for the sale of the shares in BHNL to Vattenfall
Heat UK Limited (the “SPA PCG”).

essential highways civil engineering design resource to assist with
the design work required to deliver the A4 Portway Strategic
Corridor.
Bristol City Council wishes to procure the services of AtkinsRealis
Highways Design Team through a direct award contract to address
deficiencies and constructability issues within the existing scheme
design. These issues span multiple design disciplines and require
coordinated technical input to correct, complete, and de-risk the
design prior to and during construction. AtkinsRealis will revise
construction drawings which will be approved by Bristol City
Council before being issued to the Principal Contractor for
build.
The additional support is necessary to ensure the design is fit for
purpose and aligned with the construction objectives for the
Portway scheme. The design work could not be completed internally
due to resource levels and other project commitments. Owing to the
need to address the design issues promptly, reducing risk of delay
to construction activities, it is recommended that these works are
direct awarded to AtkinsRealis.
The spend is necessary to increase resource available to address
issues with the existing scheme design to ensure its fit for
purpose before construction. The spend will also include a
comprehensive review of the road resurfacing and reconstruction
proposals, with the aim of identifying savings where
possible.
This decision follows previous decisions taken by Transport and
Connectivity Committee on the A4 Portway Project at the Committee
on 6 February 2025, approving the Full Business Case and
progression to the construction stage.

That Strategy and Resources committee:

Sustainable Transport Settlement (CRSTS) funding and, subject to
MCA approval, approves the acceptance and investment of the funding
to make the East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood scheme
permanent.

Approved the acceptance and investment of match funding in relation
to this project (noting that this may include use of a greater
amount of Section 106 funding if this becomes available during the
project’s lifecycle; or use of alternative match funding, in
the event that S106 contributions reduce and/or other sources
become available), subject to the overall approved budget
envelope.

3.     
Authorised the Executive Director for Growth and Regeneration in
consultation with Chair of the Transport and Connectivity Committee
to approve a greater amount of Section 106 funding should this
become available or alternative match funding if appropriate.

4.     
Authorised the Executive Director for Growth and Regeneration in
consultation with Chair of the Transport and Connectivity Committee
to take all steps required to submit the full business case to the
MCA and to deliver the permanent scheme (subject to further
detailed design work, internal quality assurance processes and
applicable statutory consultation).

5.     
Instructed transport officers to work with the finance and capital
officers as part of the capital budget setting development, to
include for the emerging capital programme prioritisation work a
capital budget bid of £500,000 (this will then be subject to
programme funding sufficiency, prioritisation and approval via the
budget setting process for the relevant financial year) to deliver
mitigations to surrounding roads and areas demonstrably impacted by
changes to traffic patterns following completion of the scheme.
This will include roads such as Crews Hole Rd and Troopers Hill Rd
that have been shown to have increased traffic volumes and other
impacted roads will also be considered.

purpose:
Bristol Operations Centre (BOC) offers a Lone
Working service as a means of protecting staff carrying out work
duties by themselves, in line with BCC’s corporate Health and
Safety and Lone Worker policy. As a critical area in the BOC Tech
Upgrade, which attained committee approval in July 2025, BOC is
required to upgrade its provision of Lone Worker solutions to meet
nationally imposed mandatory deadlines for the UK’s switch
from analogue to digital networks, as well as the decommissioning
of 2G and 3G mobile network towers.
As well as complying with corporate Health and Safety and Lone
Worker policy, the Access Oysta IntelliCare solution offers a fully
digital Lone Working product and has been identified by many
teams’ risk assessment as their preferred method of
protection. As such, the uptake on products provided by Oysta
IntelliCare has outstripped original forecasts, meaning a 50%
uplift on the contract value is imperative in fulfilling the volume
of orders received and ensuring BCC staff have support while
working alone. The cost of this contract uplift is expected to be
recouped by BOC service via recharges to services opting to use
these products, therefore whilst this is expected to be cost
neutral in the BOC service area the additional uplift on this
contract will present a further cost to be managed by wider council
services using the products and solutions. Services have options
around use of these products and the attached solutions, they are
required to manage any costs agreed to within their existing budget
envelopes, including for increased product numbers required.

decision_maker: Public Health and Communities Policy Committee
purpose:
To seek approval for Bristol City
Council’s long-term commitment to fund the major capital
lifecycle replacement works required to maintain the Whitehall
Athletics Track surface, including the respray due in 2028 and the
full surface replacement expected within 15 years. This includes a
forecast contribution of 58%, with potential exposure up to 100%
subject to the delivery of projected operator surpluses, to
safeguard accreditation, safety and continued community use of the
facility.
content:
The Committee for
Public Health and Communities RESOLVED to:
 

1.     
Approve the proposal that Bristol City Council commits to fund
the major lifecycle replacement costs associated with the Whitehall
Athletics Track surface, including the respray required by 2028 and
the full track replacement required within 15 years, as identified
through specialist surveys.
 

2.     
Authorise the Executive Director for Adults and Communities, in
consultation with the Chair of the Public Health and Communities
Committee to take all steps required to finalise and enter into
necessary legal agreements to reflect roles, responsibilities, and
financial arrangements relating to the athletics track lifecycle
and operational model.
 

3.     
Note the financial forecast, including that estimated operator
contributions of £238,594 (42%) will offset the lifecycle
costs over 15 years, and that the Council’s net liability is
forecast to be £334,137 (58%), equating to approximately
£22,276 per year but this could increase to full track
surface lifecycle liability (£572,731 over 15 years,
equivalent to approximately £38,182 per year) if sufficient
surpluses are not generated.
 

4.     
Note that failure to undertake the required lifecycle works will
lead to loss of TrackMark
accreditation, reduced usage by schools and clubs, and
deterioration of important citywide community sports
infrastructure.
topline: The Public Health and Communities Policy Committee has decided to fund the replacement costs for the Whitehall Athletics Track surface in Bristol.

purpose:
The introduction of the Renters’ Rights
Act 2025 is part of a government agenda to improve renters’
rights and standards of homes in the private rented sector. From
the 23 June 2026, the main assessment tool used for housing
enforcement known as the Housing Health and Safety Rating System
(HHSRS), will change.
New powers for Councils to issue financial penalties for the
presence of a high-risk hazards, will come into force on the 22
June 2026. These legal changes are supported by Statutory Guidance,
which the Council is required to have regard to when exercising its
powers under the Act.
As a result, the Council’s current Private Housing
Enforcement Policy will be revised to ensure it reflects the
updated legislative framework and statutory guidance. At the same
time, ‘Bristol City Council Enforcement Policy for the
Housing Health and Safety Hazard Rating System – Housing Act
2004’ will be withdrawn.

purpose:
African and Caribbean Heritage communities
continue to experience structural inequalities and barriers to HIV
prevention, testing and care, including stigma, racism and gendered
barriers. Locally, African and Caribbean Heritage women are
particularly under-represented in HIV testing data. CAB’s
work has created safe, culturally competent spaces that can reach
communities who may not engage with mainstream services.
CAB has been recognised nationally for effective co-production and
has built a delivery model that combines a small staff team with a
wider network of volunteers and community members. CAB has two
dedicated salaried posts: a Project Co-ordinator (funded via wider
sexual health contract arrangements) and a Community Engagement
Facilitator (currently funded via non-recurrent partner
funding).
The Community Engagement Facilitator role is essential for
sustained community health promotion—especially for
women—and for coordinating, supporting and safeguarding
volunteers who are central to CAB’s delivery model. This
grant is predominantly intended to stabilise the Community
Engagement Facilitator role and protect the capacity that enables
community reach, volunteer coordination and women’s
engagement.
As an HIV Fast Track City, Bristol is committed to accelerating
progress towards zero new HIV transmissions. The new HIV Action
Plan for England, 2025 to 2030 sets a national ambition to end new
HIV transmissions through a framework of five priorities: Prevent,
Test, Treat, Thrive and Collaborate. The plan emphasises the need
to ensure equitable progress across five populations where
inequalities persist, including ethnic minority gay, bisexual and
other men who have sex with men, Black African heterosexual men,
and Black African heterosexual women.
Under the ‘Collaborate’ priority, the national plan
requires local partners to carry out a comprehensive HIV needs
assessment using existing data tools and engaging with communities
to identify service gaps and priorities. The findings will inform
the development and publication of local HIV plans across the
country during the 2026/27 financial year.
This grant enables Bristol to meet the local HIV Action Plan
requirement to carry out an HIV needs assessment by funding
Brigstowe to deliver community engagement and focus groups that
capture lived experience and community insight, and support the
development and dissemination of a survey for the general public,
service users, people living with HIV and other
professionals.
This report provides transparency in the decision making of the
Director of Communities

purpose:

programme. The project is to relocate Elmfield Secondary school to
the current site of E-Act Badock’s Wood Primary school on
Doncaster Road. The existing school site will be broadly divided
equally between both schools with construction works to refurbish

In addition to the contract works, whilst construction progresses,

Academy. The additional work is being fully funded by E-Act to
provide enhancement and mitigate potential risks of future
disruption should works be required once the school is occupied. As
the works are deliverable within the programme there is no impact
to Elmfield Secondary school.

the committee authorised the Executive Director for Children and
Education in consultation with Chair of the Children and Young
People Committee to approve the final business case for the
relocation of Elmfield Secondary School for Deaf Children from

spend the funding, including to procure and award contracts (which
may be over the key decision threshold) for the design and
construction works to support the delivery of Elmfield Secondary
school, in-line with the procurement routes and maximum budget
envelopes outlined in the committee report.

purpose:
- On 14 March 2025 the Public Health and
Communities Committee approved an £8.8m BIF3 budget over four
years (£2.2m per annum) from 1 April 2026 to the 31 March
2030 to build city resilience by growing the power of communities
experiencing the greatest inequity.
- The committee approved: £8,136,000 for medium and large
grant funding, £400,000 for small grant funding,
£264,000 for evaluation.
- This report recommends the investment of £200,000 in a
strategic programme of small grants.
- Empowered, inclusive and resilient communities are the
foundations for city resilience. BIF3 provides long-term investment
in vital community infrastructure in communities experiencing
growing inequity and poverty exacerbated by the cost of living,
COVID pandemic, climate crisis and reduced public services.
- Inequity and poverty harms people, fractures communities and
undermines cohesion. This investment recognises the importance of
community and voluntary organisations in addressing these pressing
issues and supports the council to deliver its corporate priorities
and statutory responsibilities.
- In November 2025, the Public Health and Communities committee
approved the investment of £8.136m in a strategic programme
of Bristol Impact Fund 3 medium and large grants. This funded 27
projects which are being delivered by 36 organisations.
- Consultation responses about the future of the BIF3 small grants
programme highlighted the importance of small grants, particularly
for equalities communities.
- The council received £1.8 million of applications for BIF 3
small grants.
- This report recommends a strategic programme of 14 projects for
small grants to deliver the goal of BIF and improve wellbeing,
equity and community wealth.
- The strategic programme: prioritises communities working in the
most deprived parts of the city and communities who face systemic
inequity, supports the development of community infrastructure,
prioritises community cohesion and groups that are led by LGBTQIA+
people, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities and young
people.
- The processes for carefully considering all the applications and
developing the recommended strategic programme.
- A second round of BIF 3 small grants will be allocated, with
projects due to commence between 01 April 2028 and 31 March
2030.
- This grant investment should be seen as one part of a suite of
measures alongside changing systems and structures and reimagining
the way the City Council works to grow the power of
communities.
- Successful applicants will need to meet baseline standards,
complete monitoring and show impact. A budget of £264,000
will support evaluation and create a forum for groups to learn from
each other and develop their practice.
- There are many organisations doing excellent work which BIF 3
cannot fund. We will continue to work to connect VCSE organisations
to opportunities through council colleagues and city partners where
appropriate.

purpose:
Children’s Services have commissioned a
refurbished ten-bedroom property, to provide supported
accommodation for young people aged 16+ who are in care under
Section 20 of the Children Act 1989. The service is designed for
young people with low to medium support needs, delivered within a
structured and high-quality support model. The purpose of the
provision is to support young people to develop the skills,
resilience, and independence required to enable planned move-on
into permanent accommodation within a 12-month period.
This approach aims to:
• Provide safe, stable, and supportive accommodation for young
people
• Equip young people with the life skills and resilience
required for independent living
• Enable planned progression into permanent accommodation
through Home Choice Bristol or the Housing Support Register
Bristol City Council currently has limited availability of 16+
supported accommodation. Consequently, young people under Section
20 are often placed in high-support External Supported
Accommodation (ESA), which is both costly and not always the most
appropriate provision for the needs of this cohort. This provision
addresses this gap by offering an appropriate and Ofsted-compliant
service, staffed by a trained workforce that are able to meet the
identified needs of these young people.

purpose:
Note: This decision is subject to call in. The
deadline for escalation is Friday 12 June 2026.
The Homes and Housing Delivery committee on 19 December 2025
considered the report ‘Responding to people living in
vehicles 2026 – 2031.
The committee:
1.Approved the policy for Responding to people living in vehicles
2026 – 2031 at appendix A1.
2.Authorised the Executive Director Growth and Regeneration and the
Executive Director Housing in consultation with the Chair of the
Homes and Housing Delivery Committee to take all steps required to
implement the policy including any transitional arrangements and
(subject to full council approval of the budget in February 2026),
spend up to the budget envelope set out in the report including
procuring and awarding contracts which may be over the key decision
threshold.
3.Noted that the policy will be applied from 1 January 2026;
however, full implementation of the policy will apply from 1 April
2026 in line with the action plan set out in the report and
appendix A2.
4.Noted the consultation report at Appendix F.
The Albatross Road site at the former Whitchurch Sports Centre,
Bamfield, Bristol BS14 0ZZ is owned by Goram Homes. The land will
be used on a meanwhile use basis to accommodate up to 60 vehicle
dwellers. The creation of new meanwhile sites supports the delivery
of Bristol City Council’s Vehicle Dweller Policy
(2026–2031). The policy prioritises support first, followed
by enforcement where necessary. The use of meanwhile sites
underpins this approach by providing designated, managed spaces
where people living in vehicles can move to, giving them access to
basic services and greater stability while reducing unauthorised
parking on streets and public land.

purpose:
Bristol City Council is a founding partner and
core delivery body within the Bristol Temple Quarter regeneration
programme. The Bristol Temple Quarter Charter sets out shared
principles for inclusive and sustainable growth across the
regeneration area and is being adopted by key partners, including
the University of Bristol and the West of England Combined
Authority.
The purpose of this decision is to approve the signing of the
Bristol Temple Quarter Charter Pledge on behalf of the Council. The
Pledge sets out how the Council will contribute to the Charter
through its existing statutory, strategic and enabling roles,
including planning, transport, regeneration, public realm,
sustainability, community wellbeing and culture.
The Pledge reflects activity that is already in train or resourced
and does not create any new financial or staffing commitments.
Signing the Pledge demonstrates the Council’s leadership role
at Temple Quarter and ensures alignment with delivery partners and
agreed governance arrangements.

purpose:
The Future of Prevention (FoP) project is
Bristol City Council’s participation in the national Local
Government
Association (LGA) and ADASS programme designed to help adult social
care shift from reactive crisis response to
earlier, proactive support.
Bristol will use this pilot to test the feasibility and value of
predictive analytics within Adult Social Care as part of a
structured, nationally supported test-and-learn model. Using
predictive analytics (via Xantura’s OneView platform)
and a nationally developed delivery framework, the programme
identifies residents who may be at risk of
deterioration earlier and supports councils to engage them before
their needs escalate.
To be able to use the predictive analytics a contract is needed
between Bristol City Council and Newton. Newton is
an established consultancy that has provided expertise to many
local authorities nationally. They will be providing
specialist project management and data analytics support to support
Bristol City Council implement and measure the
success of the Future of Prevention project.

content:
At the conclusion of

That the Committee
for Adult Social Care

Bishop Manor Road to deliver a specialised supported living home
for adults with Learning Disabilities and/or Autism.
 
2. To approve progression of the project to Full Business Case development,
including the completion of detailed design, surveys, procurement
preparation, and further feasibility refinement, in accordance with
the scope and approach set out in this report.

consultation with the Chair of the Adult Social Care Committee, to
incur expenditure within the approved Invest to Save capital
envelope to support Full Business Case development.

Business Case, including market engagement and procurement
planning, subject to compliance with the Council’s Contract
Standing Orders and governance arrangements.

consultation with the Chair of the Adult Social Care Committee, to
incur expenditure on the construction and operational delivery
phase of the project in line with the council’s procurement
rules and the maximum budget envelope outlined in this
report.

approval of the Outline Business Case does not commit the Council
to delivery of the scheme, and that any decision to proceed to

Under Council Standing Order 9.1.2 a vote was
taken to re-order the business on the agenda to move Motions 12.6
(Local Decision-Making and Access to Services) and 12.7 (Cohesion,
Division and the Flag Protocol) to be considered immediately after
Motion 1 (The Future of Bingley Pool).
 
Resolved –
 
That under Council
Standing Order 9.1.2 the business on the agenda be reordered to
move Motions 12.6 (Local Decision-Making and Access to Services)
and 12.7 (Cohesion, Division and the Flag Protocol) to be
considered immediately after Motion 1 (The Future of Bingley
Pool).
 
 
12.1    THE FUTURE OF BINGLEY POOL
 
As set out in the published agenda Motion 12.1
was moved by Councillor Wheatley and seconded by Councillor
Fricker.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional published papers Amendment
A) was moved by Councillor Judson and seconded by Councillor
Walker.
 
Following a number
of speakers in accordance with Council Standing Order 18.12
Amendment A was put to the vote and lost. The Motion as set out
below was then put to the vote and was carried.
 
Resolved –

Bradford Council
notes:
This motion
represents the shared collective ambition of all the Councillors of the Bingley East and West to work
together to secure the future of Bingley Pool.

That Bingley Pool has
remained closed since 2020 and was marked for disposal by the
Council's Corporate Landlord Board in October 2025, despite
retaining Asset of Community Value status and strong community
support for its retention.

For more than a decade local
residents, community organisations,
local District Councillors and Bingley
Town Council have campaigned to preserve affordable swimming
provision in Bingley, with the Friends of Bingley Pool leading on
this work.

That the Council has twice
previously supported the principle of retaining swimming provision
in Bingley: first through the Community Asset Transfer process,
which progressed to an approved business plan and agreed transfer
in 2020, and second through the successful £14.4 million
Levelling Up Fund bid, which proposed a major redevelopment of the
site before the funding was subsequently withdrawn by central
government.

That evidence presented by
the Friends of Bingley Pool demonstrates substantial public demand
for a local swimming facility, including a petition supported by
more than 10,000 people, consultation showing overwhelming support
for reopening the pool, and continued backing from schools,
swimming clubs, health professionals, businesses and community
organisations.

The Council's own policy
documents identify Bingley as a Principal Town and a key location
for leisure, health and wellbeing facilities, while Sport England's
Facilities Planning Model highlights continuing shortages in
swimming water space across the district. These documents also
align with the emerging Bingley Neighbourhood Plan, which identifies swimming in
Bingley as a protected service.

Bradford Council
believes:

The improved three year
local authority funding settlement (including the local authority
deprivation funding) and the £2 billion in flexible
devolution funding to WYCA through the Integrated Settlement,
represents an improved financial backdrop for new capital funding
project support to be considered.

That access to affordable
swimming and leisure facilities delivers significant health,
wellbeing, educational and social benefits for residents of all
ages, helping tackle inactivity, improve physical and mental
health, and support community cohesion.

Bingley should continue to
play its role as a Principal Town serving the wider district, with
access to leisure facilities comparable to those available in other
principal towns.

That the principal barrier
to reopening Bingley Pool is the challenge of securing capital
investment rather than any lack of demand, community support or
operational potential.

That a refurbished and
financially sustainable Bingley Pool, whether operated directly by
the Council or through a community partnership model, could make a
valuable contribution to the health, wellbeing and regeneration
objectives of both Bingley and the wider Bradford
District.

 

Bradford Council
resolves:

To request
Executive:
1.   
To pause any disposal or
sale of Bingley Pool and remove the site from active disposal
consideration whilst future options are examined.
2.   
To request that officers
prepare a report setting out viable options for restoring swimming
provision at the site, including a Council-led
refurbishment/redevelopment and operation model, together with
community-led alternatives.
3.   
To request officers to
establish a Bingley Pool Project Board comprising representatives
of Bradford Council, Bingley Town Council, the Friends of Bingley
Pool and other relevant stakeholders to oversee the development of
future proposals.
 

Through its
Executive:

To support the preparation of updated surveys, feasibility
studies, business planning and funding assessments required to
establish the most cost-effective route to deliver an affordable
swimming provision.
To work proactively with local, regional and national partners
to identify potential sources of capital investment and external
grant funding, with the objective of securing the long-term future
of affordable swimming provision in Bingley.

 
To be actioned by: Strategic Director, Growth / Interim
Strategic Director of Corporate Resources / S151
Officer
 
 
12.6    LOCAL DECISION-MAKING AND ACCESS TO
SERVICES
 
As set out in the published agenda Motion 12.6
was moved by Councillor Loy and seconded by Councillor Poulsen.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional published papers Amendment
F) was moved by Councillor Wheatley and seconded by Councillor
Salam.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 a second amendment (additional published papers
Amendment G) was moved by Councillor Place and seconded by
Councillor Birch.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 a third amendment (additional published papers
Amendment H) was moved by Councillor Imran Khan and seconded by
Councillor Jabar.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 a fourth amendment (additional published papers
Amendment I) was moved by Councillor Griffiths and seconded by
Councillor Sunderland.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Order
18.10 Councillor Loy as the mover of the Motion with the consent of
Councillor Griffiths as the mover of Amendment I and Councillor
Wheatley as the mover of Amendment F agreed to incorporate
Amendments I and F into the Motion.
 
Following a number
of speakers in accordance with Council Standing Order 18.12
Amendment H was put to the vote and lost. Amendment G as set out below was then put to the vote, was
carried and became the substantive motion, was then voted on and
was carried.
 
Resolved –
 
That with the
addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion be
amended to read as follows:
 
Council notes:

That
Bradford District is one of the largest and most diverse
metropolitan districts in England, comprising towns and communities
with distinct characteristics and needs.
That
residents frequently express frustration that decisions affecting
their local areas are overly centralised and insufficiently
responsive to local circumstances, for example decisions about
parking charges, planning applications, and household waste
recycling centres (HWRCs).
That Area
Committees already play an important role in community engagement
and local decision-making, but currently exercise limited
meaningful control over local spending, assets, and
policy.
That town
and parish councils can, where they wish to do so, play an enhanced
role in the stewardship of valued local assets and
services.

 
Council believes:

That
decisions should be taken at the lowest level consistent with
effective governance.
That
stronger local accountability can improve public confidence,
increase responsiveness to local concerns, and encourage more
effective stewardship of public resources.
That local
decision-making and service provision is particularly important in
a geographically large and diverse district such as
Bradford.
That
outlying towns and rural communities have been disproportionately
impacted by the removal of local facilities and services, including
HWRCs.
That where
greater local responsibility is considered appropriate, any
devolution of powers, budgets or responsibilities must be supported
by robust governance arrangements, financial sustainability and
clear accountability to residents.

 
Council therefore resolves:
To request officers to undertake a review of
opportunities to strengthen local decision-making across the
Bradford district, including through Area Committees, and, where
appropriate, town and parish councils, ensuring that any
proposals:

Improve
local accountability and responsiveness to residents;
Represent
value for money and are financially sustainable;
Maintain
appropriate governance, transparency and democratic
oversight;
Support
effective delivery of local services across the district;
and
Are
developed following appropriate consultation with ward members,
Area Committees, town and parish councils and other relevant
stakeholders.

The review should consider opportunities including,
but not limited to:

Greater
involvement of Area Committees in local services
priorities;
Opportunities for appropriate local management of community
assets;
Strengthened engagement in highways, parking, public realm and
neighbourhood priorities; and
The future
role of Area Committees and town and parish councils in supporting
local regeneration and community development.

 
To be
actioned by: Interim
Strategic Director, Environment / Strategic Director, Growth /
Director of Legal and Governance
 
 
12.7   
COHESION, DIVISION AND THE FLAG PROTOCOL
 
As set out in the published agenda Motion 12.7
was moved by Councillor Sullivan and seconded by Councillor
Winnard.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional published papers Amendment
J) was moved by Councillor Eglin and seconded by Councillor
Place.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 a second amendment (additional published papers
Amendment K) was moved by Councillor Hickson and seconded by
Councillor McInnes.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 a third amendment (additional published papers
Amendment L) was moved by Councillor Choudhry and seconded by
Councillor Imran Khan.
 
Following a number
of speakers in accordance with Council Standing Order 18.12
Amendments L and K were put to the vote and lost. Amendment J as
set out below was then put to the vote, was carried and became the
substantive motion.
 
In accordance with
Council Standing Order 25.3 Councillor Judson requested that a
recorded vote be taken on the substantive motion which was
supported.
 
A recorded vote was
taken on the substantive motion (Amendment J) and was carried.
 
Resolved –
 
That with the
addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion be
amended to read as follows:
 
Council notes:       

That
Bradford Council’s current Protocol on the Flying of Flags,
whilst intended to be inclusive, at times is perceived by some as
unnecessarily stoking division.
That the
number of flags on the list of those which may be flown on
different occasions is seen as excessive and residents may
reasonably wonder why some national and campaign flags are included
whilst others are not.   
Some local
authorities appear to use their flag protocols to signal their own
“foreign policies” to express support for certain sides
in selective overseas armed conflicts or disputes.
Flying of
flags on Bradford Council buildings and flag poles should be
unifying communities and not be used to support politically
contentious causes or campaigns.
That the
Union Flag is the national flag of the United Kingdom and
represents the shared citizenship, values and traditions that unite
all British people, regardless of their background, faith or
heritage.

 
Council resolves to ask the Executive to
consider:
The introduction of a new flag protocol
that:

Reaffirms
that the Union Flag is the principal civic flag of the United
Kingdom and should be displayed with pride on Bradford’s
civic buildings as a symbol of our shared national identity and
civic unity.
Follows
any special instructions from the Sovereign about flag
flying.
Revises
the criteria for flag flying on specific days to include only those
representing the United Kingdom’s constituent countries, its
Armed Forces, nationally recognised civic commemorations including
Remembrance events, the emergency services, Yorkshire, the
Commonwealth, the memory of the victims of the Bradford City fire,
and other civic occasions of significant importance to the Bradford
District as determined by the protocol.
Allows for
relevant constituent countries flags to be flown in celebration of
successes in major sporting events, such as a World Cup, European
Championships, or the Olympics etc.
That
requests for any other flags to be flown will only be agreed
following a positive vote of the Full Council.

 
To be
actioned by: Director
of Legal and Governance

without delay since there is a real risk that the offer could be
withdrawn or reduced if delayed until the July forward plan
publication. Consequently, the risk to the Council is that it will
be unable to realise an offer at the same level should this sale
fail to proceed.

has been included in the published Forward Plan in July as to do so
would mean the earliest the decision could be taken is August

content:
BRADFORD DISTRICT
AND THE STATUTORY INDEPENDENT INQUIRY INTO GROOMING GANGS
 
The Motion as published was moved by
Councillor Poulsen and seconded by Councillor Sullivan.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional published papers
Amendment A) was moved by Councillor Birch and
seconded by Councillor Morgan.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 a second amendment (additional published papers
Amendment B) was moved by Councillor Imran Khan and
seconded by Councillor Fricker.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Order
18.10 Councillor Poulsen as the mover of the Motion with the
consent of Councillor Birch as the mover of Amendment A agreed to
incorporate Amendment A into the Motion.
 
Following a number
of speakers. Councillor Poulsen in accordance with Council Standing
Order 9.1.7 sought the meeting’s permission to include the
last bullet point of the resolution of the original Motion in the
amended Motion. This was seconded by Cllr Wheatley. This was voted
on and was carried.
 
Resolved:
 
That the last bullet
point of the resolution of the original Motion “To ensure
victims and survivors receive all the necessary support they need
to help re-build their lives.” be included in the Amended
Motion.
 
Cllr Khan proposed that the meeting be
adjourned for further discussions with the Leaders of the Council
Groups. This was seconded by Cllr Salam. This was put to the vote
and was lost.  
 
In accordance with Council Standing Order
18.12 Amendment B was put to the vote and lost. 
 
In accordance with
Council Standing Order 25.3 Councillor Bolton-Williams requested a
recorded vote which was supported.
 
In accordance with
Council Standing Order 18.12 the Motion as amended by Amendment A
with the inclusion of the last bullet point of the resolution of
the original Motion was put to a recorded vote and was carried.
 
Resolved-
 
That with the
addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion be
amended to read as follows:
 
Council notes:
 
·      
Child Sexual Exploitation (CSE) by Grooming Gangs are abhorrent
crimes that target the most vulnerable in our communities and
should be condemned in the strongest possible terms by all members
of this Council.
 
·      
It was over a year ago, on 14 June 2025 that the Labour Government
announced a full statutory Independent Inquiry into “Grooming
Gangs”, with Baroness Anne Longfield CBE appointed to chair
the Inquiry on 9 December 2025. The Inquiry officially commenced on
13 April, and the criteria used to select local areas will be
published by the Inquiry within three months of the formal start
date and will be informed by a combination of factors including the
experiences of victims and survivors, and evidence of prevalence,
harm and risk.
 
·      
The final terms of reference make clear that the Inquiry will
examine what role ethnicity, religion and culture played in both
the offending and the response of institutions such as Bradford
Council.
 
·      
CSE, including organised group-based exploitation and grooming, is
not solely a historical issue but remains an active concern
nationally and locally across the Bradford District.
 
·      
For years, survivors and victims have called for a statutory
inquiry, and have consistently stated that being heard, believed
and seeing meaningful change in the response of authorities and
their systems is as important as any formal finding of blame.
 
·      
For many years, the previous Labour Leadership of the Council
refused calls for a national inquiry and even said it would be not
of additional value.
 
·      
The correspondence sent by the new Leader of the Council,
Councillor Place, to Baroness Longfield on 21 May 2026 formally
requesting that Bradford District be included as a local area
within the Independent Inquiry.
 
·      
It is crucial that we send a strong united message as a Council to
victims, survivors and the Independent Inquiry that Bradford
District must be a selected local area.
 
·      
Irrespective of whether Bradford District is selected as a local
case study by the Independent Inquiry, the council and its partners
have an ongoing duty and moral obligation to identify risk and
prevent exploitation and to learn from historic failures to ensure
robust protections for children today.
 
Council
resolves:
 
·      
For the Council to send a strong unified message to victims,
survivors and the Independent Inquiry that Bradford District must
be selected as a local area.
 
·      
To commission a publicly reported review of the implementation of
recommendations arising from previous local and national reviews
and inspections affecting Bradford District, including identifying
outstanding actions, reporting progress to Full Council, and
setting out what further improvements are required to strengthen
safeguarding arrangements.
 
·      
To establish a cross-party mechanism, such as through the
Children’s Services Scrutiny Committee, for regular oversight
of the implementation of those actions, as well as inviting
survivors and their representatives to help shape the
council’s response to the Independent Inquiry and future
safeguarding arrangements, ensuring that those with lived
experience have a meaningful voice in the council’s future
decision-making.
 
·      
To confirm the Council’s commitment to ensuring that all
public servants and elected members who were complicit in
concealing the mass sexual abuse of children within the district
and beyond, be identified and brought to justice, alongside those
who they aided and abetted.
 
·      
To request that the Leader of the Council write to Baroness
Longfield reaffirming Bradford Council’s request for Bradford
District’s inclusion in the Independent Inquiry with the
support of Council.
 
·      
To ensure victims and survivors receive all the necessary support
they need to help re-build their lives.
 
To be actioned
by:  Chief Executive/Acting Strategic
Director Children’s Services/Director of Legal and
Governance
topline: The Council has decided to support victims and survivors of child sexual exploitation by grooming gangs in the Bradford District and push for inclusion in a statutory Independent Inquiry.

Resolved-
 
Having considered all
valid representations made by the parties at the hearing, the
written representations received during the review process, the
Council’s published Statement of Licensing Policy, the
Licensing Act 2003 (in particular sections 4 and 52 concerning the
promotion of the licensing objectives and the determination of a
review of a premises licence), and the relevant statutory guidance
issued under section 182 of the Licensing Act 2003, the Panel is
satisfied that the operation of the premises licence has undermined
the licensing objectives.
 
In light of the evidence heard, the Panel
do not believe that the premises licence holder would be able to
meet and uphold one or more of the Licensing Objectives, in
particular Prevention of Crime and Disorder, Public Safety, and
Protection of Children from Harm. The available evidence provided
insufficient assurance that criminal offending would not be
repeated. For the above reasons, the Panel has determined that the
licences in respect of Lynxes, 42 Sunbridge Road, Bradford, BD1 2AB, and Lynxes
Spirits, 61 Kirkgate, Bradford, BD1 1PZ, be revoked.
 
To be actioned by:
Assistant Director Stronger Communities and Regulatory Services
topline: The Council has decided to revoke the premises licences for Lynxes establishments in Bradford, citing concerns about undermining of licensing objectives

25A      Voting on Appointments
 
If more than one
person is nominated for a vacant position the Lord Mayor will call
a vote, at which time each member present and entitled will have
one vote for one candidate.  If no candidate receives a
majority of the votes cast the candidate receiving the least number
of votes is eliminated and a further vote taken.  The process
will continue until there is a majority for one candidate.

purpose:
Proposed decision -
Approval to extend the Domestic Abuse Act (DA Act)
Framework to March 2029, in line with confirmed multi-year
financial settlements from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and
Local Government (MHCLG).
 
Approval to extend the well
performing Kent Integrated Domestic Abuse Service (KIDAS) and Safe
Accommodation Support Service (SASS) up to 31 January 2028 to
ensure continuity of statutory service provision, support system
stability, and enable a robust and compliant recommissioning
process, including sufficient time for procurement, mobilisation,
and co-commissioning.
 
Reason for the decision
Extension
of Domestic Abuse Act (DA Act) Framework  - The Domestic Abuse
Framework (originally approved under Key Decision 23/00060 and
extended under Key Decision 25/00033) is currently in place until
March 2027. It provides the governance structure for determining
the allocation and use of Domestic Abuse Duty Safe Accommodation
grant funding, as well as supporting strategic and operational
decision-making. MHCLG has now confirmed multi-year settlements
through the Homelessness, Rough Sleeping and Domestic Abuse Grant
which is consolidating multiple funding streams including what was
the Domestic Abuse Safe Accommodation Grant.
 
Extending the
Framework to align with the duration of the Grant (to March 2029),
and updating it to reflect the consolidated funding requirements,
will:

·        
Ensure continued compliance with the Grant
conditions and statutory duties under Part 4 of the Domestic Abuse
Act 2021,

·        
Enable longer-term strategic planning and
commissioning,

·        
Support delivery of the Kent & Medway Domestic
Abuse Strategy 2024–2029,

·        
Provide flexibility to respond to changing need
within the parameters set by MHCLG.
Extension
of Kent Integrated Domestic Abuse Service (KIDAS) and Safe
Accommodation Support Service (SASS) - KCC have services delivering support to survivors of domestic
abuse which are due to end 31 March 2027:

1.   
Kent Integrated Domestic Abuse Service (KIDAS)
including:

o  
 Referral, Assessment and
Triage (RAT) service, delivered countywide by a partnership
arrangement, through a contract held by the Office of the Police
and Crime Commissioner. The cost of this element is
met in full by the OPCC as their financial contribution to the
integrated service model.

o  
Contract SS16041, delivered countywide by Oasis
Domestic Abuse Service, Clarion Housing group and Look Ahead Care
and Support Ltd.

2.   
Safe Accommodation Support Service (SASS)
SC220255
 
Commissioners are
progressing the recommissioning of domestic abuse support services
and the development of the new Kent Integrated Family Domestic
Abuse Service (KIFDAS), which will bring together multiple funding
streams, services, and activities (including KIDAS and SASS) into a
single, coordinated service, aligned under one contractual
framework. The transition from existing service arrangements to the
KIFDAS model is complex and critical to get right. A well-managed
transition is essential to ensure continuity of support for victims
and their children, minimise operational disruption, and maintain
safeguarding arrangements.
 
Given
the complexity and in response to feedback from partner agencies
during engagement activities, the extension of existing contracts,
until 31 January 2028, is necessary to ensure successful
procurement and mobilisation of the new contractual arrangements,
without creating any disruption to service delivery. The additional
time will also support multiple partners (up to 15) to
collaboratively shape a strong, sustainable funding model that
reflects shared responsibilities and long?term system priorities
for KIFDAS.
 
Background
Domestic abuse is a cross-cutting issue. KCC has statutory
duties under Part 4 of the Domestic Abuse (DA) Act 2021 to assess
need, publish a strategy, and commission support for victims and
their children residing in safe accommodation. Since 2021, these
duties have been supported through grant funding from central
government. The established Domestic Abuse Framework 2025-27
provides the governance mechanism to ensure funding is allocated in
line with statutory requirements, local need, and strategic
priorities set out in the Multi Agency Domestic Abuse Strategy
2024-29.
 
Key
services to support survivors of domestic abuse are the Kent
Integrated Domestic Abuse Service (KIDAS) and Safe Accommodation
Support Service (SASS). Both are due to end 31 March 2027.
Commissioners are progressing recommissioning activity and
development of a new service to replace both and the procurement
will aim to launch in Autumn 2026.
 
Options (other options considered but discarded)

·        
Option 1: Do Nothing - Allow
Framework and contracts to end without extension. This option has
been rejected as it risks a failure to meet statutory duties under
the Domestic Abuse Act and service disruption to victims of
domestic abuse, including adults and children.

·        
Option 2: Immediate Recommissioning – Extend
Framework and proceed with immediate procurement of KIFDAS prior to
full financial and organisational stability.This option has been rejected as it risks the codesigned KIFDAS
model not being achievable within the funding envelope, further
risking a poor market response, reduced value for money and service
disruption caused by insufficient mobilisation period.

·        
Option 3: Extend Framework, KIDAS and SASS services
- This is the proposed option to be progressed
as it maintains continuity and compliance, supports
strategic alignment and co-production and enables robust
procurement and mobilisation.
 
How
the proposed decision supports the Council’s Strategic
Statement
The
extension of the DA Framework and proposed extension of the KIDAS
and SASS contracts supports the delivery of a safer, more resilient
Kent and contributes directly to the council’s ambitions for
prevention, partnership working, financial sustainability, and
system reform as set out in Reforming Kent 2025 – 2028, Our
Council Strategy.

 

Financial Implications
The
total cost for the proposed extension of the Domestic Abuse Act
Framework across 2027-28 and services for the period 1 April 2027
to 31 January 2028 is £6,469,853.39, broken down as
follows:

Extension of Domestic Abuse Framework - The cost of implementing the Domestic Abuse Framework across
2027-29 will be met in full by Homelessness, Rough Sleeping and
Domestic Abuse Grant funding, including unspent grant funding from
previous years (held in reserves). A draft budget forecast for
2027-28 indicates that expenditure will be £5,197,005.52.
This figure includes funding for key service delivery,
including:

£2,110,879.98 for services delivered by the Kent
Integrated Domestic Abuse Service (KIDAS) until 31 January 2028;
and
£572,090.95 for the Safe Accommodation Support Service
(SASS), until 31 January 2028.




 

Extension of KIDAS –

The
countywide KIDAS Referral, Assessment and Triage Service is
provided through the OPCC’s Kent and Medway victim support
contract, and the cost of this element is met in full by the OPCC
as their financial contribution to the integrated service model.
The OPCC has confirmed that this arrangement can continue for the
duration of the proposed KIDAS extension.
The
full cost to extend the KIDAS contract (SS16 041) for 10 months
from 1 April 2027 to 31 January 2028 is £3,383,727.85. Of
this total, £2,110,879.98 is funded from within the Domestic
Abuse Framework allocation set out above. The remaining balance is
met through existing KIDAS funding partner contributions, including
Public Health Grant funding*,the Office of the Police and Crime
Commissioner, Kent Fire and Rescue, the Integrated Care Board, and
district and borough councils (Ashford, Canterbury, Dartford,
Dover, Folkestone and Hythe, Gravesham, Maidstone, Swale and
Thanet). This blended funding arrangement ensures that the full
cost of the extension is met without creating any additional
pressure on KCC’s base budget.




 

* This Public Health contribution is fully supported
by the relevant Director and Cabinet Member
 

Extension of SASS - The
costs to extend the SASS contract (SC220 255) for 10 months from 1
April 2027 until 31 January 2028, is £572,090.95. This amount
is included within the overall Domestic Abuse Framework allocation
set out above and will be met in full by the Homelessness, Rough
Sleeping and Domestic Abuse Act Grant.

purpose:
Proposed decision – To approve
the implementation of the Families First Partnership Programme, in
line with the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill, the
Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 and The Families First
Partnership (FFP) Programme Guide.
 
Following
the Key Decision 
25/00047 in August
2025 to approve the acceptance of grant funding for the Families
First Programme for the period 2026/27, 2027/2028 and 2028/29, and
to permit preparatory, mobilisation and design activity for the
development of the Families First model, under delegated authority,
the Interim Corporate Director for Children, Young People and
Education formally accepted the Children, Families and Youth Grant
through Officer Decision OD/26/00006, which enabled the continued
use of grant funding for preparatory and design activity and the
funding of existing services, but did not authorise implementation
of the new model.
 
This
proposed decision is intended to approve and subsequently implement
the new Families First Partnership Programme model in
children’s services, moving from design into full delivery in
line with statutory requirements.
 
Central
government is investing over £800m between 2025 and 2029 into
the  Families First Partnership (FFP)
programme to support local authorities and their partners to
deliver system wide reform of children’s services focused on
the implementation of Family Help, Multi-Agency Child Protection
Teams and Family Group Decision Making, in response to
recommendations from: The Independent Review
of Children’s Social Care, and The Child Safeguarding
Practice Review Panel’s report on Child Protection in
England. These reforms bring a significant shift and refocus how we
help, protect and support children and families. 
 
The aim of
the Families First Programme is to deliver a fully integrated,
family-centred system of support underpinned by strong multi-agency
collaboration and shared accountability. The aim is for families to
access and receive the right help at the right time from trusted
practitioners who understand their story, coordinating support and
providing consistent presence throughout their journey. The
programme also seeks to deliver financial sustainability, ensuring
that resources are used efficiently to deliver long-term value and
improved outcomes.
 
The
Families First Partnership programme aligns with the
government’s vision for transformation across
children’s social care (CSC) and is expected to realise the
four outcomes of the Children’s Social Care National
Framework:
Outcome 1:
children, young people and families stay together and get the help
they need
Outcome 2:
children and young people are supported by their family
network
Outcome 3:
children and young people are safe in and outside of their
homes
Outcome 4:
children in care and care leavers have stable, loving
homes
 
 
Background
 
The Council
has progressed the transformation journey through initiation and
co-design and a Target Operating Model for Families First for
Children has been developed. The model was designed in
collaboration with statutory partners and colleagues from voluntary
services, frontline practitioners, children, young people and
families, in line with the current timeline.
 
The reforms
set out in 
Working Together to Safeguard
Children 2026, combined with the 
Families First Partnership
Programme Guide underpin the key reforms of Early Help, Child in
Need, and Child Protection service delivery:
 

·  
Family Help (Integrated Early Help and
Child in Need): A single, integrated Family Help system replaces
separate Targeted Early Help and Section 17 pathways, providing
earlier, coordinated, relationship?based support through
multi?disciplinary teams. In Kent, Family Help Teams will bring
together Early Help, Children’s Social Care and Adolescent
Services, led by social work managers, with specialist adolescent
safeguarding roles for extra?familial risks.

·  
Family Help Lead Practitioner (FHLP): A
designated practitioner (social worker or alternatively qualified
professional) responsible for assessing needs, coordinating the
family plan and ensuring the right support is in place at the right
time.

·  
Single Family Help Assessment: One
assessment framework within Liquid Logic (Liberi) enabling
consistent recording and decision?making across Early Help, Child
in Need and Child Protection, reducing duplication.

·  
Multi?Agency Child Protection Teams
(MACPTs): Virtual multi?agency teams holding strategy meetings and
child protection decision?making, improving timeliness,
information?sharing and consistency.

·  
Lead Child Protection Practitioner
(LCPP): A specialist Qualified Social Work leadership role
providing oversight of risk assessment and decision?making across
Section 47 activity, without holding cases.

·  
Family Group Decision?Making (FGDM):
Strengthened expectations that families are actively involved in
decision?making and planning from the earliest point, building on
family networks and resources.
 
These
reforms aim to provide earlier, more coordinated intervention;
strengthen professional decision?making through supervision and
multi?agency challenge; ensure specialist oversight in all child
protection work; and embed a more relational, family?centred
approach across all levels of need, so that families are supported
early and consistently.
 
Given the
statutory nature of the reforms which are underpinned by the
Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, and the statutory
guidance Working Together to Safeguard
Children 2026, a full public consultation
is not required. The Act and the statutory guidance direct Kent
County Council and all the other Local Authorities to implement
these reforms in Children Services.
