invest £500m for the national roll out of Best Start Family
Hubs; a 3-year Programme starting on 1 April 2026.
 
On 7 November 2025,
the Department for Education (DfE) and Department of Health and
Social Care (DHSC) announced that the provisional allocation for
the Best Start in Life Programme for Kent County Council is
£15,354,500, for financial years 2026-29. The DfE and DHSC
will share guidance on the service and delivery expectations ahead
of April 2026.
 
A series of Key
Decisions by the Cabinet Member for
Integrated Children’s Services accepted the original
transformation grant funding for Family Hubs and adopted our new
Family Hub service model. A new Key Decision is required to
adopt the Best Start Family Hub Model and to accept funding for the
3-year programme. 
 
Background – Provide brief additional context
 
In October 2022 the
Cabinet Member for  Integrated Children’s Services
took decision
22/00094 and Kent County
Council (KCC) signed the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the
Department for Education (DfE) which accepted the initial 3-year
transformation grant funding. This decision set out the requirement
for the development of detailed proposals, public consultation and
appropriate governance ahead of a further Key Decision on the
Family Hub model. 
 
In November 2023, after the development of detailed proposals,
public consultation and appropriate governance, KCC Cabinet
took decision
23/00092 to implement the
Family Hub model across the county.  
 
In March 2025, the
Cabinet Member for  Integrated Children’s Services
took 
Decision 24/00124 and Kent
County Council (KCC) signed the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)
with the Department for Education (DfE) which accepted the Year 4
Family Hub grant. This grant funding will end on 31 March
2026.
 
 
Options (other options considered but discarded)
 
The option to not
adopt the Best Start Family Hub Model and not accept the grant
money has been considered. If the announcement related to the
conditions on how the grant is to be used is made in quarter 4 of
financial year 2025/26 (i.e. in February 2026) it will likely
impact on the Local Authority’s ability to mobilise resources
to implement additional service requirements or procure services.
This in turn, will pose a risk to the delivery of services and
cause a reputational risk for Kent County Council.
 
While understanding
the risks associated with a late announcement, we have discounted
the option of not accepting the additional funding in recognition
that children, families and communities in Kent will benefit from
additional support.
 
Final determination of
whether the Best Start Family Hub model can and should be accepted,
and whether the funding can and should be accepted would be
dependent on the terms and conditions associated with the model and
funding – these will be reviewed at the point of
decision.
 
How the
proposed decision supports the Councils Strategic Statement
 
AIM 3: Supporting
residents that need help - The Family Hub
model, supported through Best Start funding, supports Aim 3, by
embedding prevention and early intervention within service
delivery. Family Hubs provide accessible, integrated support for
parents/carers and children, helping families address challenges
before they escalate and empowering them to make informed choices
that improve health and wellbeing. By investing in services that
promote parenting skills, parent-infant relationships and home
learning environment, Family Hubs help to reduce dependency on
crisis interventions and ensure every child has the opportunity to
grow up safe, secure, and supported, and help families stay
together.
 
 

Financial Implications
 
The DfE and DHSC have announced
that the provisional funding allocation for the Best Start in Life
Programme for Kent County Council is £15,354,500, for
financial years 2026-29. The distribution of Kent’s funding
allocation by Programme Strand is set out in the table
below.
 
While the delivery expectations
of the grant are not yet known, the Programme Strands are a
continuation of the current Strands, with the exception of
‘Healthy Babies Offer’, which has changed from
‘Start for Life Offer’.
 
It is expected that the funding
will support the ongoing delivery of Family Hubs in a way that
complements and enhances existing services. Based on current
understanding, the grant is not expected to place additional
pressure on the Council’s revenue or capital budgets.
Additionally, DfE has confirmed that Best Start funding may be used
for delivery of existing services which could support a reduction
in the base budget for Family Hubs. Therefore, a portion of this
funding could be allocated to staff costs associated with
delivering these services.


Decision:
 
As Cabinet Member for Integrated
Children’s Services, in consultation with the Cabinet Member
for Adult Social Care and Public Health (subject to receiving
confirmation from Department for Education (DfE) and Department for
Health and Social Care (DHSC) I agree to:
 
a) APPROVE, the acceptance of the
Best Start Family Hub Grant Award and the deployment of the grant
funding in accordance with the grant conditions and the
adopted service model;  
  
(b) DELEGATE authority to the
Director of Operational Integrated Children’s Services and
Director of Public Health, in consultation with the Cabinet Member
for Integrated Children’s Services and the Cabinet Member for
Adult Social Care and Public Health to agree the terms and
conditions to enter into the necessary grant
agreements;   
  
(c) DELEGATE authority to the
Director of Operational Integrated Children’s Services and
Director of Public Health to deliver the requirements of the
grant;   
  
(d) DELEGATE authority of
required expenditure to the Director of Operational Integrated
Children’s Services and Director of Public Health, in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Integrated
Children’s Services and the Cabinet Member for Adult Social
Care and Public Health, to be managed in line with Council
procurement rules;   
  
(e) DELEGATE authority to the
Director of Operational Integrated Children’s Services and
Director of Public Health, to take other necessary actions,
including but not limited to entering into contracts or other legal
agreements, as required to implement the
decision.
topline: The Cabinet Member for Integrated Children's Services has decided to adopt the Best Start Family Hub Model and accept grant funding for a 3-year program starting in April 2026.

decision_maker: Cabinet Member for Education and Skills
purpose:
Proposed
decision
 
To permanently remove the
specialist resourced provision for pupils with speech and language
needs at River Primary School, following statutory consultation and
representation.
 
Reason for the decision
The specialist resource
provision (SRP) at River Primary School is designated to meet
speech and language needs (S&LN). The number of pupils for whom
the SRP at River Primary School has been deemed appropriate has
fallen significantly. Currently there are only 4 pupils accessing
the SRP and all will move on to secondary school within the next
two years.
 
Background – Provide brief additional context
 
In order to meet the changing
needs of pupils, SRPs now need to provide for pupils who may have
wider communication needs in addition to purely speech and
language. This may include Speech Language and Communication Needs
(SLCN) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).
Whilst the number of pupils
supported by River’s SRP has fallen, the number supported by
the SRP at Whitfield Aspen School has grown significantly (by over
100 places since 2015). This is because it has the existing
resources and expertise to support pupils with multiple need types
including SLCN and ASD.
 
Additionally, as there is no
primary SRP provision in Deal and Walmer, we are looking to address
this by supporting a proposal to create a 14 place primary SRP at
The Downs CE Primary School in Walmer. This is expected to open in
September 2026, supporting pupils with ASD and SLCN. The proposal
to open this new provision in Walmer is part of Kent’s wider
SEND strategy and is linked to Key Decision
25/00085.
 
An SRP in Deal/Walmer would
reduce the distances that residents in Deal, Walmer, Sandwich and
the surrounding villages have to travel to secure specialist
provision. 
 
Kent’s Strategic Statement
 
The proposed decision supports
KCC’s strategic statement as it is necessary for KCC to
continue to deliver the statutory duty, in a cost-effective
way.  It will help to maintain
KCC’s strategic role in supporting schools in Kent to deliver
accessible, high quality education provision for all families,
particularly those with SEND.
 
Options (other options considered but discarded)

 
Option 1: to keep the SRP open for purely speech and language needs was
not viable as insufficient pupils with this need are being
identified to keep the provision viable.  The changing needs of pupils mean that SRPs now
need to provide for pupils who may have wider communication needs
in addition to purely speech and language.
 
Option 2: broadening the need type that the SRP can support, was
considered and discarded as the accommodation and site constraints
at River Primary School mean the premises do not lend themselves to
supporting other need types.

process.

reduce the in-year overspend.

decision_maker: Cabinet Member for Highways and Transport
purpose:
Proposed decision
 
To approve and adopt a
new enforcement policy enabling Kent County Council (KCC) to take
enforcement action against land owners to ensure highways users are
not put at risk from non-compliance under relevant statutory
provisions.
 
To approve and adopt a
new street works enforcement policy enabling KCC to take relevant
enforcement action up to and including prosecution against utility
companies and other entities for non-compliance failures under
relevant statutory provisions.
 
Reason for the decision
As the local Highway
Authority, KCC has a statutory to ensure that the public can use
and enjoy any highway for which they are responsible including any
roadside waste which forms part of it.
 
KCC also has a
statutory duty to coordinate the works of statutory utility
companies.
 
Background
To meet these
obligations, KCC needs to know about all the work happening on the
road network. The work must be done in timely fashion with the
safety and convenience of all road users in mind. The proposed
polices will enable KCC to take enforcement action against
landowners and utility companies when they break the law or act in
a way that is non-compliant to the works orders. This is especially
important when such violations affect the council's ability to
manage and coordinate road works or when the work is done unsafely
or disruptively.
 
How
the proposed decision supports the KCC Strategic
Statement
This proposal is
aligned with the strategic statement and direction of the emerging
'Reforming Kent' agenda
 

·  
to improve the quality the highways network and to
reduce the delays caused by road works.

Decision process
The portfolio was
transferred in January 2026. The decision was taken by the Cabinet
Member who held responsibility for the portfolio at the relevant
time. At the point the Forthcoming Executive Decision was
published, the responsible Cabinet Member was Mr Paul King, Cabinet
Member for Economic Development and Coastal Regeneration. Following
the portfolio transfer, responsibility moved to Mr David Wimble,
formerly Cabinet Member for Environment and now Cabinet Member for
Economic Development and Special Projects.
 
 
 
Proposed Decision: That the
Cabinet Member for Economic Development and Coastal
Regeneration:
 

(a) 
AGREE to end the current DPTIF Partnership and
transfer the existing shares into the beneficial ownership of Kent
County Council
 

(b) 
DELEGATE authority to the Director of Growth and
Communities to take relevant actions to transfer the shares and
cease the operation of the DPTIF, including but not limited to
entering into contracts or other legal agreements, as necessary to
implement this decision. 
 
Reason for the decision
Kent
County Council is proposing to end the current Partnership for the
management of the Discovery Park Technology Investment Fund
(DPTIF), an equity scheme established in 2015 using Regional Growth
Fund monies. 
 
The end of this
Partnership will allow KCC to transfer the shares of the six
remaining companies within the DPTIF investment portfolio into
KCC’s beneficial ownership. The purpose of this action is to
ensure financial savings to KCC and allow KCC to retain the shares
for future growth potential or exit strategy
 
Background
DPTIF
focused on innovative early stage, high-growth companies initially
based in Discovery Park. Managed by NCL under a 10-year partnership
arrangement, this ends on the 14 December 2025.

 
The DPTIF to date has invested
£5,202,500 of equity investment into nine companies within
the DPTIF portfolio. DPTIF provided equity investments to companies
predominantly in the life science sector to support those
companies’ growth, five of the companies are still active
(see Table 1):

(DPTIF) Companies (Table 1)




Companies



Original Investment £

£734,000




Coomtech Ltd


£1,452,500




Emoquo Limited


£350,000




Revolo Biotherapeutics Limited


£500,000




Viramal Limited


£500,000





TOTAL


£3,536,500





 
All proceeds from the
future sale of shares from companies currently within the former
DPTIF portfolio will be returned to KCC, ring fenced as per RGF
requirements and re-invested in local companies via the
KMBF.

recommended):

were considered:

·        
Continue the DPTIF Partnership (not recommended
because the sums expended on the Partnership management fees would
not result in a significant increase in the value of KCC’s
investment portfolio)

·        
Closing the DPTIF Partnership and selling the shares
held by the Partnership (not recommended as the prevailing economic
conditions selling the shares at this time could result in a
significant reduction in the value of KCC’s investment
portfolio).
 
How
the proposed decision meets the challenges in the Interim Strategic
Plan
 
This
proposed decision is consistent with the current strategic plan
priority; Levelling Up and is aligned with the strategic direction
of travel in the planned new Strategic Statement; particularly the
ambition to ‘support local businesses to attract
investment’. Decision making will continue to progress in
line with the new Strategic Statement once enacted

Taking on an Accountable Body role for the
£815,000 Gainshare funding ensures:
 
i)              
The Funding is made available to Onboard Skatepark Sheffield Ltd to
support their development work that enables their relocation to
Royds Mill and the continuation of their services to support
vulnerable young people within the City.
ii)             
That funding is made in the form of a repayable grant meaning that
there is the potential for some grant being repaid to the Council
over a 10-year period to reinvest into other economic and
regeneration projects.
 

Alternative Option 1: Do not act as
Accountable Body
 
The Council could choose not to act as
Accountable Body for the funding and rely on SYMCA to enter a Grant
Agreement with Onboard.
 
This option would enable Onboard to access
funding, but SYMCA would not build in any provisions to recoup
grant should Onboard exceed agreed financial performance measures.
The opportunity to reinvest Gainshare into other Sheffield based
projects would be lost.
 
Alternative Option 2: Provide funding as a
Loan
 
The Council could provide the funding as a
loan rather than a repayable grant.
 
The provision of a loan would require Onboard
to repay the funding on a prescribed date irrespective of their
financial performance and ability to pay. Given the nature of
activity the Council does not consider a commercial arrangement is
suitable to maximise the positive impacts for young people in the
City.
topline: The Executive Director of City Futures has decided to enter into a Funding Agreement with the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority to support Onboard Skatepark Sheffield Ltd's relocation project with £815,000 in funding.

Members of the committee
considered a report of the Executive Director, City Futures
presenting objections received, together with officers’
responses to an Experimental Traffic Order, and seeking approval to
make the Order permanent as currently implemented.




 


 




5.1.2


The Experimental Traffic Order
(ETO) was introduced on parts of Garter Street, Carlisle Street and
Petre Street to prevent obstructive parking and to maintain safe
and unobstructed access for large goods vehicles serving local
businesses.




 


 




5.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Transport, Regeneration and Climate Policy Committee –
 

a)   
Considers the objections to the ETO.

b)   
Approves that the ETO be made permanent, as currently implemented,
by making a Traffic Regulation Order (TRO) in accordance with the
Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984. All objectors will then
subsequently be informed.




 


 




5.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




5.3.1


The Experimental Traffic Order (ETO) on Garter
Street, Carlisle Street and Petre Street has been introduced to
maintain safe and unobstructed access for HGVs and other delivery
vehicles serving local businesses, while minimising the impact on
available parking. The benefits of improved safety, traffic flow,
and business access are considered, on balance, to outweigh the
outstanding objections.




 


 




5.3.2


The Order is required to make permanent the
measures already implemented under the experimental scheme.




 


 




5.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




5.4.1


Given the industrial nature of the area and
the high volume of HGV traffic, the introduction of double yellow
lines along the full length of Garter Street was considered.
However, it was deemed expedient to opt for a scheme which
minimised loss of on-street parking while still delivering its main
objectives.




 


 




5.4.2


A ‘do nothing’ option was also
considered; however, this would likely have resulted in the
continuation of commuter parking, further impeding HGV access to
local businesses.
topline: The Transport, Regeneration and Climate Policy Committee has decided to make the Experimental Traffic Order permanent to maintain safe access for large goods vehicles serving local businesses.

Committee:-

(b)

operation is in the best interests of the Hillsborough Park
Charity, considering the updated evaluation and is satisfied that

the best outcome for the Charity;

visitor experience, and supporting the charity’s purpose of
improving conditions of life for those accessing the
park.




 


 




5.3.2


Income generated through the proposed licence
will be retained by the charity and used to support the ongoing
management and maintenance of the park. This provides a clear
financial benefit to the charity and contributes to the continued
delivery of facilities for public enjoyment, consistent with the
charity’s objects.




 


 




5.3.3


Following the originally preferred
operator’s withdrawn offer, officers have reassessed all
bids. The operator now recommended is considered to provide the
most advantageous proposal when evaluated against the agreed
criteria and the best interests of the charity. Their offer
represents the best value available and based on officers’
knowledge of the operator and their payment history, there are no
concerns over their ability to meet the level of fees proposed or
the terms of the licence.




 


 




5.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




5.4.1


Alternative Option 1 – Do
nothing:
Reason for rejection- there is the option to not
offer a licence to any of the operators who have bid. This would
mean there would be no provision for this type of offer within the
park and would impact on the rental income for the charity which
contributes directly to the management and maintenance of the park.
This would have a detrimental impact on the quality of the visitor
experience. This option has therefore been
rejected.

support the development of the IZ is seen as a valuable tool and

reinvestment into the local
economy.

9.1


The Economic Policy
Officer presented the report which showed the finalised Business
and Economy Decarbonisation Routemap for the Economic Development,
Skills and Culture Policy Committee’s approval. The Routemap
was co-developed in partnership with Sheffield businesses, with
significant engagement across Sheffield’s business community.
It was designed to act as both a plan for collective action but
also a guide for individual businesses to understand their options
for reducing their carbon
emissions.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Economic Development, Skills and Culture
Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the significant amount of business engagement that has
contributed to the co-production of the Business and Economy
Decarbonisation Routemap and put on record its thanks to the
businesses involved in the Routemap’s
development
b)   
Approve the Business and Economy Decarbonisation Routemap at
Appendix 1 of this report.
c)   
Endorse the Sheffield Sustainable Business Network as a key partner
in the delivery of the Routemap, particularly relating to business
engagement and peer to peer support on
decarbonisation
d)   
Note the proposed set of indicators designed to measure the impact
of the Routemap and agree for them to be
included




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The Business and Economy Decarbonisation Routemap
will be an important plan for the city as part of its transition
towards a low-carbon economy. The Routemap provides businesses with
clear guidance and targeted support to understand how they can
contribute to these changes and take meaningful action as part of
Sheffield’s transition to a low-carbon economy. Key to the
Routemap’s success is the buy-in and support from the
business community: the significant engagement that has informed
the Routemap’s development creates strong foundations for
future success.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
nothing
 
The 10 Point Plan for Climate
Action committed the Council to developing a Business and Economy
Routemap. Not fulfilling this commitment, as well as the ambitions
set out in the Council Plan, would undermine trust and confidence
in the Council’s commitment to achieving net
zero.




 


 




9.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Develop a
Business and Economy Routemap with minimal business
engagement
 
This option has previously been
considered and was rejected. This was because the plan’s
success hinges on Sheffield businesses supporting the plan and
seeing its relevance to their future. The best way to ensure this
was for businesses to be partners in the development of the plan.
This approach takes longer but will have longer-term benefits when
it comes to the Routemap’s delivery.
topline: The Economic Development, Skills and Culture Policy Committee has decided to approve the Business and Economy Decarbonisation Routemap for Sheffield businesses.

8.1


The Committee received a report of the
Strategic Director of Adult Care and Wellbeing on the DASS overview
of activity in ACW including latest performance data and reports,
statutory adherence and compliance, progress in delivering the
business plan/strategy, summary of key risks and issues including
mitigation, key achievements during the period, ACW Improvement
Plan development and CQC Outcome, including proposed reporting to
Committee.




 


 




8.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee:-




 


 




 



Notes progress in delivering upon
the Adult Care Strategy Living the Life You Want to Live
Notes the performance update and
areas for prioritisation and focus, including performance dashboard
at Appendix A
Notes the strategy delivery updates
and achievements for this period
Notes the progress of our
Improvement Plan development in response to our CQC report and
agreed the proposed reporting schedule to Committee

 




8.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




8.3.1


Asking for regular updates on the Strategy
Delivery, our Performance and CQC will enable the Committee, wider
stakeholders, and the public to hold the Council to account for
progress and impact and will provide an additional mechanism to
input to future development.




 


 




8.3.2


Endorsing the Strategy Delivery Programme and
Assurance Programme enables Committee to continue to undertake
scrutiny of the service and strategy delivery plan in an informed
and meaningful way.




 


 




8.3.3


Asking for regular updates and refreshes of
the CQC self-assessment, including wider assessment preparations
and communications will enable Committee to have oversight and
assurance that Adult Care know themselves and are able to drive
forward service improvements, alongside the assurance that we are
well prepared for the CQC assessment process.?




 


 




8.3.4


Noting the performance update, enables
Committee to undertake scrutiny of Adult Care performance including
strengths and areas for prioritisation, including the development
of our Performance Management framework / cycle of Assurance,
alongside our improvement plans in this area.?




 


 




8.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




8.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do Not Provide an
Update on The Strategy Delivery Plan Progress – When the
Strategy Delivery Plan was approved by Committee in June 2022 the
was a commitment to review the plan regularly and by not reviewing,
we would not be meeting that commitment. Due to the significant
amount that has been delivered on the plan, leaving it as it would
make it harder to identify the priorities going forward.




 


 




8.4.2


Alternative Option 2: A different
delivery plan - The real options for the delivery plan are around
the individual elements, which will be worked through as part of
the constituent pieces of work. These will be worked through in
different ways, with many of them resulting in their own future
reports to the Committee.




 


 




8.4.3


Alternative Option 3: Do not Review Our
Strategy. The strategy for Adult Care and wellbeing is nearly 3
years ago. Although co-produced the portfolio is in a very
different position now compared to the time when the strategy was
originally written. Undertaking a mid-term review enables us to
refresh our strategy and priority outcomes to ensure that it is fit
for purpose and maintains its relevance.




 


 




8.4.4


Alternative Option 4: Do not work in
partnership / collaboratively. It is a statutory requirement to
work in partnership with colleagues across the health, care, and
wellbeing system, as set out in the 2021 White Paper. The Statutory
Duty to Involve also requires us to engage and involve people who
use services, and unpaid carers in the design and delivery of care
and wellbeing. We would not be meeting these requirements if we did
not work in meaningful partnership across, they system, and with
all stakeholders.




 


 




8.4.5


Alternative Option 5: Do not Prepare
for the CQC Assessment. The CQC assessment of Adult Social Care
Services is not optional. The outcomes of the assessment are
published on the CQC website and have ramifications wider than
Adult Care and Wellbeing. A negative Outcome would mean that we are
not delivering our duties under the Care Act. In addition, a
negative outcome would impact on the reputation of the Council, the
confidence of our customers and partners, recruitment and
retention, staff morale, and potential funding opportunities.




 


 




8.4.6


Alternative Option 6. Do not share the
ACW CQC Self-Assessment with partners and in the public domain: To
not share the self-assessment and ask for comment would go against
the approach and principles we are embedding as business as usual
in Adult Care. To have both credibility and relevance, it is vital
that this is a report which provides an honest and transparent
narrative for adult social care informed by the voices and
experiences of staff, partners, commissioned providers, VCSE, and
the people who access our services, their families, carers, and
those with lived experience.

content:
The Sheffield Equality Partnership (SEP) was
established in 2013 and consists of five Voluntary, Community,
Faith, and Social Enterprise (VCFSE) organisations representing six
protected characteristics which support the Council to engage with
those protected characteristics/communities of identity. These
organisations are Together Women, LGBT+ Sheffield, Disability
Sheffield, Age UK and DiverseCity
Development Trust. The current funding arrangement comes to an end
in March 2026. The recommendation is to extend the existing funding
agreements from April 2026 to March 2027 and during this period
conduct a full review of the SEP funding arrangement and develop a
new approach to be implemented in April 2027.
 
 

1.   
Extend the existing funding arrangement from April 2026 –
March 2027 as described in Section 2.1, paragraph 1 of this
report.
2.   
Undertake a review of the SEP funding arrangement and develop a new
approach to be implemented in April 2027.
 
 

We recommend that the current SEP partners
have their grant arrangements extended until March 2027. This will
enable us to provide ongoing financial support for the VCSFE
organisations that we currently fund through the SEP, to adhere to
three month notice that we are required to give current SEP
partners for ending or altering their grant agreements, and to give
ample time to SCC staff to carry out thorough and appropriate
engagement with SEP partners, communities of identity and the wider
city,

Alternative Option
1: End the current external partnership arrangements
 
This option has been rejected at this time as
it would reduce funding to the VCSFE organisations and potentially
lead to closure of smaller organisations within the city. This
would also reduce funding for organisations led by people with
specific underrepresented protected characteristics. This would not
be in line with our commitments as part of the new Communities
strategy or city Goals to devolve power to communities. We need
time to review the effectiveness of the SEP grant programme and how
it can be aligned with the Council’s wider approach to grants
for VCSFE.
topline: The Director of Strategy, Performance and Communications has decided to extend funding for the Sheffield Equality Partnership (SEP) until March 2027, with plans for a new approach in April 2027.

10.1


The Executive Director Neighbourhood Services
submitted a report setting out details of the Community
Infrastructure Levy (CIL) which is a fixed, non-negotiable, charge
on most developments of 100 square metres or more, or a new
dwelling of any size.
 
The report stated that CIL receipts are split
into two funds: Strategic and Neighbourhood. Neighbourhood CIL is
collected in a “pot” and redistributed across the wards
based on Indices of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)in accordance with a
Cabinet decision in 2018. Under that decision, Neighbourhood CIL
may be spent using ward-based criteria but prospective uses that
are not linked to a single part of the city may not be able to be
funded. This means that the Community Infrastructure Levy is
currently therefore unable to effectively support communities of
interest and identify in the same way that it supports communities
of place.
 
The report therefore proposes to create a
specific non-geographical fund for communities of interest and
identity, and to review the Governance and guidance relating to CIL
to support this.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED: That Strategy and Resources Policy
Committee:-




 


 




 


(a) approves in
principle the creation of a Non-Geographical Community
Infrastructure Levy Fund, specifically for delivering outcomes
relating to Communities of Interest and/or Identity, likely to
require the top-slicing of the Neighbourhood Community
Infrastructure Levy;
 
(b) agrees that
further work is required to design this fund and put in place the
right governance arrangements and criteria for
applications;
 
(c) asks that
officers prepare further information to support a decision at a
Strategy and Resources Committee meeting as early as possible in
the 2026/27 municipal year; and
 
(d) note that
the ongoing review of Governance processes for Neighbourhood CIL
will include any changes required to support the above, and that a
further report to the Committee will present the outcomes of the
review and recommend the necessary decisions to support the
changes, including where necessary proposals for changes to the
Constitution to be recommended to Full Council.
 
(NOTE: The
result of the vote on resolution (a) was FOR – 8 Members;
AGAINST – 5 Members; ABSTENTIONS – 0 Members.
 Resolutions (b), (c) and (d) were
agreed unanimously).




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


As it is
currently established, Neighbourhood CIL may be spent using
ward-based criteria but prospective uses that are not linked to a
single part of the city may not be able to be funded. This means
that the Community Infrastructure Levy is currently therefore
unable to effectively support communities of interest and identify
in the same way that it supports communities of
place.




 


 




10.3.2


The decision would address this issue directly, through the
creation of a specific non-geographical fund for communities of
interest and identity. Alongside this the Council will review the
Governance and guidance relating to CIL to address the lack of
clarity around its use and the decision making associated with
it.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1:
Rather than creating a specific non-geographical fund, there is
an option to simply allow organisations representing Communities of
Interest or Identity to bid for Neighbourhood CIL within the Ward
that they are based. This would require a change to the current
criteria whereby an organisation must deliver a service to the
benefit of the specific geographical area, i.e. the
Ward.
 
There are clear demand risks associated with this approach,
especially in those areas where a significant number of
organisations representing Communities of Interest and / or
Identity are based, e.g. the City Centre.
 
This option would require our Governance approach to be reviewed
to ensure bids were assessed appropriately. In that regard we would
still recommend that Equality Impact Assessments should be
undertaken to support bids.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2:
There is an option to do nothing and to continue with the
current approach to Neighbourhood CIL. This approach would not
address the current challenges for organisations representing
communities of Interest or Identity.
It would also not address the current lack of clarity around the
use of Neighbourhood CIL or the current Governance
approach.




 


 




10.4.3


Alternative Option 3:
There is an option to change the way in which the top-slice is
taken, either through only taking the proportion from income
received in future years, i.e. from 1st April 2026 and/or taking a
smaller proportion of past CIL income in the first
year.
 
The average annual level of Neighbourhood CIL income is around
£400k. If 16.7% of this were taken in future years only this
would equate to around £67k for the full year. In the first
year there would be no available budget until the beginning of
2027/28.
 
Should a smaller proportion of past CIL income, for example 1%,
be taken this would equate to around £78k as a one-off and
£27k per year for future years.
These options have been discounted given the very low level of
budget this would yield and the delay of any available budget for
2026/27.
topline: The Executive Director Neighbourhood Services has decided to create a Non-Geographical Community Infrastructure Levy Fund for communities of interest and identity.

11.1


The Executive Director City Futures submitted a
report summaring options for
introducing free travel for children and young people in Sheffield,
including indicative cost drivers, justification and evidence base,
key assumptions, risks and financial sustainability
considerations.
 
The report sets out options for a potential
January–July 2027 pilot and recommends further development
work subject to Committee direction, to include funding parameters,
detailed network analysis and agreement with operators. The report
confirmed that it is an options and scoping report. It does not
commit the Council to implement a scheme or to allocate funding at
this stage.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Strategy and
Resources Policy Committee:-




 


 




 


(a) notes that
the earliest a free travel pilot could commence in Sheffield would
be January 2027 and this will require concerted work from March
2026, with a decision around whether Members wish to proceed sought
at the first Strategy and Resources committee meeting following the
May 2026 local elections. It is recommended that officers prepare
further information to support this decision at that meeting;
 
(b) notes that
costs of a pilot will need to be funded by Sheffield City Council
(SCC) for any period up until South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined
Authority (SYMCA) launch free bus travel (anticipated to be late
Summer 2027);
 
(c) notes that
there is widespread political support for the provision of free bus
travel for children and young people across the council;
and
 
(d) notes as
context for this report that SYMCA is not planning to introduce
free travel for under 22s (U22) in the region. The Mayor's transport vision, launched on 16th March
2026, indicates that the focus for the Mayor is provision for under 18s (U18). Therefore, a
free travel proposal for U22 in Sheffield would result in ongoing
annual costs to SCC, exposing the council to a significant and
unquantifiable financial liability. As such, it is recommended that
officers work with SYMCA to explore a pilot limited to U18 free
travel only, noting that there is currently no identified budget
for such a pilot.




 


 




11.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The options set
out enable the Committee to provide direction on whether to
progress an Under 18 scheme, an Under 22 scheme, or a phased/pilot
approach, taking account of the scale of ongoing revenue costs,
delivery and capacity risks at peak times, and the absence of an
identified sustainable funding source for the more extensive Under
22 option.
 
Committee
direction will enable officers to focus further work on the
preferred approach, including detailed network analysis, operator
engagement and development of a funding strategy.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do nothing
The council avoids the direct financial commitment that a scheme
of this nature requires, and officer time and resource is then
available to be deployed on other projects. The potential benefits
of the scheme outlined in this report are not realised. 




 


 




11.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Implement a means tested
scheme
Learning from the Barnsley under 18s pilot indicates that
simple, universal schemes are more easily understood by families,
schools and operators, and achieve higher and more consistent take
up than targeted alternatives. By contrast, means testing
introduces significant administrative burden, requiring eligibility
checks, ongoing verification and data sharing arrangements that
increase cost, complexity and delivery risk, while potentially
delaying implementation. Such schemes also risk lower take up among
those most in need, as eligibility thresholds can exclude
households experiencing financial pressure but not meeting strict
criteria, and the application process itself can act as a barrier.
In addition, targeted offers can create stigma and confusion,
increasing the risk of inconsistent use and
enforcement.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to approve recommendations for further development work on a potential free travel pilot for children and young people, subject to funding parameters and network analysis.

content:
14.1


The Director of Commissioning and
Commissioning Officer introduced the report which explained that
the Children, Families and Youth grant will bring together five
funding streams into a single consolidated grant and will be worth
£41.9 million to Sheffield over the three years of the
multi-year Settlement. It outlined the overview of the
grants and requested delegated authority
of:
 
·      
the FFPP funding and the Pupil Premium Plus Post-16 Grant to the
Strategic Director of Children’s
Services
·      
the HAF funding to the Director of Integrated
Commissioning.




 


 




14.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children
and Families Policy Committee:-
 

a)   
Note the developments and plans within the programme that are held
in the Children, Families and Youth grant. This includes the
Families First Partnership Programme, the Pupil Premium Plus
Post-16 activity and the Holiday Activities and Food
programme.

b)   
Approve the delegation of the Families First Partnership Programme
Funding and the Pupil Premium Plus Post-16 Grant to the Strategic
Director of Children’s Services.

c)   
Approve the delegation of the Holiday Activities and Food Grant to
the Director of Integrated Commissioning
including:
                                              
i.    
award new grants from any programme
underspend
                                             
ii.    
withdraw funding as necessary and in line with this report and the
conditions of the grant funding
agreements.

d)   
Approve the Holiday Activities and Food delivery approach and model
which has run successfully since 2021.

e)   
Approve the allocation of Holiday Activities and Food grant funding
to delivery partners including schools, VCFSE partners, and
organisations that will provide a vast range of cultural and
sporting activities across Sheffield.




 


 




14.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




14.3.1


FFPP
 
The ambition is
to build on existing good practice in the city to further improve
the network of services, processes and interactions that aim to
help children, young people, and families from the earliest
opportunity through to the highest level of need. If we continue to
develop our system, we will see vulnerable families thrive,
becoming empowered to become resilient over time and build
connections to their local community. Our local services will also
be joined-up, flexible and responsive to new challenges, becoming
sustainable for the long term creating stronger multi-agency
partnerships which work together to understand local trends,
predict emerging need, and respond to those needing additional
help. It is therefore essential that we continue our ambitions with
the full approval of the committee.




 


 




14.3.2


The Pupil Premium Plus Post-16
 
This element of the grant provides a flexible and responsive
funding stream that enables the Virtual School to strengthen
post?16 education, wellbeing and transition outcomes for
looked?after young people and care leavers. Continued approval is
essential to ensure Sheffield can sustain targeted, evidence?based
interventions aligned to statutory Virtual School duties, support
multi?agency practice, and respond quickly to individual needs
identified through the PEP process. The requirement to complete and
submit the annual Pupil Premium plus Post?16 Virtual School Head
Evaluation Survey to the Department for Education also creates an
important accountability mechanism, reinforcing the need for robust
oversight of expenditure, impact, and
delivery.




 


 




14.3.3


HAF
 
This decision will secure the continued delivery of the Holiday
Activities with Food (HAF) Programme, which provides essential
holiday activities and nutritious meals to some of the most
vulnerable children in Sheffield. The programme plays a vital role
in supporting the council’s wider ambitions to improve health
and wellbeing, reduce inequality, and ensure that all children have
access to positive opportunities during school
holidays.




 


 




14.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




14.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Deliver the HAF programme in house by
the Council:
 
While this would provide direct control over delivery, The
Council does not currently fund or deliver holiday or food
provision for children and young people. Establishing this capacity
would require significant investment in infrastructure and
staffing, and therefore would be unable to directly reach or
deliver holiday activities to eligible
cohorts




 


 




14.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Do not accept the DfE HAF
Grant:
 
Declining the grant would mean forfeiting funding to deliver
holiday activities and food for approximately 26,000 children in
our area who are eligible for free school meals. Without this
funding, the Council would be unable to provide high quality
holiday activities and food during the Easter, Summer, October and
Christmas school holidays. This would increase the risk of holiday
hunger and reduce access to enrichment opportunities for vulnerable
children, undermining statutory duties and local priorities around
child wellbeing and inclusion.




 


 




14.4.3


The preferred approach is to continue to deliver HAF through a
partnership model, building on five years of successful delivery
and strong relationships with schools, voluntary and community
sector organisations, and local providers. This approach maximises
reach, leverages existing expertise, and ensures activities are
accessible and culturally appropriate.
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to consolidate funding streams into a single grant worth £41.9 million for children, families, and youth programs in Sheffield.

12.1


The
Assistant Director of Children and Families introduced the report
which recommended introducing annual increases to Skill Level Fees
in line with the National Minimum Allowance for 2027/28 and
2028/29, capped at 4% per year, providing carers with greater
financial certainty.
 
The
report also proposed allocation of funding to relaunch the Foster
Carer Loan Scheme, using £50,000 in 2026/27 to fund small
property adaptations with a target to create at least four
additional fostering spaces.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Agree policy change that foster carer skill level fees will
increase in line with National Minimum Allowance for the financial
years 2027/28 and 2028/29 up to a maximum of
4%.
b)   
Agree that policy will be reviewed at the end of this time period.
c)   
Agree funding of £50k diverted from placement budget and
allocated to Foster Carer Loan Scheme




 


 




12.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




12.3.1


The proposed changes to fostering payments and
the relaunch of the Foster Carer Loan Scheme are essential to
ensuring that Sheffield City Council can meet its statutory
sufficiency duty and provide the right homes for children and young
people in care. Current payment structures have not kept pace with
inflation or regional market rates, and evidence from carers shows
that financial support is the area most urgently requiring
improvement to support recruitment and retention. Without action,
the Council risks further erosion of in?house fostering capacity,
limiting placement choice and increasing reliance on costly
external residential provision.




 


 




12.3.2


Introducing a clear,
inflation?linked mechanism for reviewing Skill Level Fees over the
next two years provides carers with much?needed certainty and helps
stabilise a workforce that plays a critical role in delivering
safe, nurturing homes for children. This aligns directly with the
Placement Sufficiency Strategy (2023 2026), which sets out the
Council’s commitment to expanding family?based care options
as the most effective and sustainable way to meet children's
needs.




 


 




12.3.3


Re?establishing the Foster Carer
Loan Scheme will enable the creation of additional in?house
placements through small?scale property adaptations, helping to
reduce out?of?area placements and improve children’s ability
to remain connected with their families, schools, and
communities.




 


 




12.3.4


Overall, these recommendations are
necessary to strengthen Sheffield’s fostering offer, improve
placement stability and sufficiency, and deliver better outcomes
for children and young people while reducing long?term financial
pressures on the Council.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Do Nothing - continue make
payments in line with current policy.
 
·      
Foster cares feel undervalued by the Local Authority and
resign.
·      
Failure to change would mean that in real terms carers have not
received an enhancement in recognition of the skill and commitment
they offer children in care for 7 years at a time of significant
increase in the cost of living.
·      
Continued annual negotiation regarding fostering allowances leads
to confusion and dissatisfaction.
·      
Our current policy does not champion our strategic commitments to
education and belonging
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to increase Skill Level Fees for foster carers and relaunch the Foster Carer Loan Scheme to create additional fostering spaces.

content:
13.1


The
Service Manager introduced the report which set out Sheffield City
Council’s approach to supporting care leavers by enabling
young people in foster care to remain with their former foster
carers beyond the age of 18, where that is in their best interests
and all parties agree. The policy aimed to provide a more gradual
and supported transition to adulthood, mirroring the experiences of
young people who continue to live at home with their families after
turning 18.




 


 




13.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Agree to the Policy for Staying Put Providers, with implementation
from 1 April 2026.




 


 




13.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




13.3.1


The recommendation to amend the Staying Put
Policy is driven by the need to ensure that our approach remains
fit for purpose in supporting care leavers as they transition to
adulthood. Since the last policy update in 2019, both practice and
the needs of young people have evolved, particularly in response to
the challenges posed by the Covid-19 pandemic and feedback from
foster carers and stakeholders. The current policy does not fully
reflect the realities of practice, nor does it address the concerns
raised about financial arrangements, parity between local authority
and independent fostering agency carers, and the clarity required
for both carers and young people. Amending the policy will ensure
that it is aligned with statutory guidance, incorporates best
practice, and provides a clear, fair, and sustainable framework for
Staying Put arrangements.
 
Furthermore, updating the policy is essential to
deliver on the Council’s strategic priorities of promoting
stability, belonging, and successful futures for care leavers. The
revised policy will strengthen our ability to recruit and retain
high-quality carers, ensure financial arrangements are transparent
and equitable, and support the sufficiency of placements within
Sheffield. By clarifying roles, responsibilities, and funding
mechanisms, the amended policy will help maximise positive outcomes
for young people, reduce the risk of placement breakdowns, and
ensure that Sheffield City Council continues to meet its legal and
moral obligations to care-experienced young people as they move
towards independence.




 


 




13.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




13.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Not
taking any action
 
If no action is taken, the policy
will remain outdated, and unclear wording will continue to create
confusion. As a result, staying put providers who were formerly
Independent Fostering Agency carers would still receive higher
payments than our in-house foster carers. The 2019 policy also
lacks sufficient detail regarding the Staying Put process, which
has led to inconsistent interpretation and poor practice over time.
By updating the policy, we can ensure clarity and set clear
expectations for all involved—social workers, staying put
providers, and the staying put coordinator—by defining roles,
responsibilities, and processes.




 


 




13.4.2


Alternative Option 2:
Resubmitting the proposed 2024 policy
 
The 2024 policy introduced
significant financial changes and highlighted that the 2019 Staying
Put policy does not clearly distinguish between a young person in
care and an adult living at home. It noted that continuing to pay
skills payments at the full rate does not reflect the shift in the
young person’s status to adulthood, nor the evolving role of
the Staying Put Provider in supporting the young person’s
journey towards independence and home ownership. Resubmitting this
and implementing such substantial financial changes could cause
further concern among foster carers, as many feel that reducing
Staying Put allowances would discourage participation in these
arrangements. This, in turn, could lead to instability for young
people at a particularly vulnerable stage, forcing them to seek
alternative housing options. The proposed policy aims to clarify
financial arrangements for Staying Put carers and addresses
previously undefined sections. The only major financial impact
relates to Independent Fostering Agency carers, whose payments
would be aligned with those of Local Authority carers. This is
considered reasonable, and the payment is deemed sufficient to
support the young person.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to approve a policy to support care leavers by allowing young people in foster care to stay with their former foster carers beyond the age of 18.

Director of belonging introduced the report which informed the

UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy

Reasons for
Decision

The decision is recommended in response to
concerns raised by local parents about the impact of early
smartphone and social media use on children’s wellbeing,
online safety and development. The establishment of a Task &
Finish Group provides a structured and transparent way for members
to examine the evidence, engage with partners and families, and
consider how the Council can best offer support within its role.
The Group will enable informed and proportionate recommendations to
be brought back to Committee for future decision
making




 


 




8.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




8.4.1


Do
nothing

online safety, and doing nothing would not respond to the clear

Refer the issue solely to the
Sheffield Safeguarding Children
Partnership

rejected as it would not give elected members a clear role in
shaping policy or responding to the wider educational and community
aspects identified

A two year commission that continues and expands the
Medical Needs Education Service will allow the Council to meet its
statutory duties in regard to providing
education for children and young people with medical
needs.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Do nothing when the existing contract expires. This
option was rejected because it would leave the Council unable to
meet its statutory duties relating to pupils with medical needs
that make them unable to attend school.




 


 




11.4.2


Providing the service in-house. This option was rejected
as the Council does not have the expertise or staffing required for
this delivery and could not mobilise this in time for the start of
the commission. As above, this would leave the Council unable to
meet its statutory duties.

10.1


The
Assistant Director of Children and Families introduced the report
which sought approval to expand Sheffield’s children’s
residential care provision through the creation of a new two?bed
home designed specifically for children under the age of 12 who
require safe, stable, and nurturing accommodation within the city.
The proposal responded to rising demand, increasing placement
costs, and a shortage of suitable local homes, particularly for
younger children, while supporting the Council’s statutory
sufficiency duty and its Placement Sufficiency Strategy for
Children Looked After and Care Leavers
2023–2026.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Approve the expansion of Sheffield’s children’s homes
provision through the establishment of two new two?bed residential
home for children under 12.
b)   
Approve the diversion of funding from the existing placement
revenue budget to meet the ongoing operational costs of the new
home.




 


 




10.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




10.3.1


Sheffield City Council, as a corporate parent,
has a statutory duty to ensure, as far as reasonably practicable,
that there is sufficient, appropriate accommodation within the
local area to meet the needs of looked?after children. Rising
demand, increasing placement costs, and a shortage of specialist
local provision for younger children mean that the current
sufficiency duty cannot be met without creating additional in?city
residential capacity. Establishing a new two?bed home specifically
for children under 12 will address a clear gap in provision and
support the delivery of the Placement Sufficiency Strategy for
Children Looked After and Care Leavers
2023–2026.




 


 




10.3.2


Expanding local children’s
homes will enable more young people to remain in Sheffield,
maintain family, school, and community connections, and benefit
from trauma?informed, developmentally appropriate care designed to
improve long?term outcomes. The proposal also supports longer?term
financial sustainability by reducing dependence on high?cost
external placements and increasing opportunities for children to
step down into foster care, contributing to both improved outcomes
and more efficient use of resources.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
Nothing Rejected
 
Young people continue to live in
high cost out of city placements away from local connections. There
are insufficient placements in the market that meet the specific
needs of the cohort.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Local
Market Commissioning
 
Expansion of local in-house
children’s homes forms part of the portfolio’s wider
sufficiency. Engagement with private providers to ensure that the
right homes are developed for our children and young people
continues. This option is not ruled out and works alongside
development of in-house provision.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to expand children's residential care provision by creating a new two-bed home for children under 12.

content:
To seek approval for the contract award to
Newton Consulting
Limited as the transformation programme delivery partner for
Adult Care and Wellbeing.





a)


Approval of a 2-year
and £9.1m contract award to Newton Consulting Limited as
delivery partner for the medium-term transformation programme for
Adult Care & Wellbeing.
 




b)


Noting the required
mobilisation of internal resources to support the transformation
programme as referred to this report.




 

The award of this contract will introduce and
develop key skills and best practice across Adult Care and
Wellbeing services.  This will enable
the service to align resource management with the strategic
priority to improve outcomes for the people of Sheffield.
 
The contract award will enable the Adult Care
and Wellbeing directorate to commission and deliver quality
services sustainably as part of a long-term financial strategy.
 
The selection of Newton Consulting Limited as
the transformation partner will accelerate the directorate’s
ability to meet financial targets, establishing a foundation for
manageable growth in the 2026/27 financial year.

Alternative Option 1: Do nothing
·      
The Council could choose not to implement a transformation
programme through a delivery partner and continue to deliver
savings and improvements on an annual cycle. While planned savings
have been delivered over the last five years, this has not been at
the pace required to be financially sustainable.
Alternative Option 2: Deliver internally
·      
Recruiting a specific workforce to design and implement the
transformation programme may cost less than the recommended
option.  However, the recruitment would
be labour and time intensive, and there is not the range of
specific skills and experience required within the Council to
deliver the programme successfully and at pace.  This option would also commit to longer-term
resources for change management, whereas the preferred approach is
to transfer to business as usual and self-management from year
2.
Alternative Option 3: Service by Service
improvement
·      
The Council could choose to enable individual service areas to
develop and implement specific changes associated with agreed aims
and ambition. This has been rejected because it would not achieve
the ‘one council’ approach and the holistic outcomes
and financial benefits envisaged in the Council Plan and the Future
Sheffield Programme.
topline: The Strategic Director, Adults' Care and Wellbeing has decided to approve a £9.1m contract award to Newton Consulting Limited for the transformation programme delivery partner for Adult Care and Wellbeing in Sheffield.

content:
The Bereavement & Coronial Service is
undertaking a comprehensive review of its service offer for
Sheffield’s Muslim community The review aims to ensure the
city’s bereavement and burial services meet the specific
religious and cultural requirements of residents of the Muslim
faith.

 




9.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood
Services which provided an update on progress on the city-wide
review of its burial and cremation provision, since the review
began in January 2026.  The report
sought Committee endorsement of the proposed approach for the next
phase of the review (including wider public consultation), and
confirmed the process for bringing back the final recommendations
for decision later in
2026




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy
Committee Policy Committee:-

(a) 
Notes the progress made to date on the review of Sheffield City
Council’s bereavement and burial service offer for Muslim
residents;

(b) 
Approves the proposed next phase of work, including continued
engagement, benchmarking and operational
analysis;

(c) 
Endorses the approach for developing final recommendations,
including stakeholder workshops, wider public consultation and
operational insight gathering;
and

(d) 
Requests a further report later in 2026 setting out the final
evidence-based recommendations and proposed implementation
plan.




 


 




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The proposed approach enables the Council to
respond appropriately to the concerns raised by residents and
community partners regarding whether the current burial offer fully
meets the religious and cultural requirements of the Muslim
community. Questions raised at Full Council, correspondence with
community representatives and recent engagement activity all
demonstrate a clear expectation that these matters should be
examined in a structured and meaningful way. Proceeding with the
review allows the Council to consider these issues thoroughly and
draw on a broad range of insight.




 


 




9.3.2


This decision will also support the development
of robust, evidence based recommendations that reflect both the
experiences of bereaved families and the operational realities of
delivering faith sensitive services. A comprehensive review will
help ensure that future planning is informed, sustainable and
aligned with the needs of Sheffield’s communities, while
strengthening partnership working and supporting the continued
delivery of inclusive, high quality bereavement
services.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
Nothing
An alternative option would have been to take no
action and retain current arrangements without conducting any form
of review. This, however, was rejected due to the significant risks
outlined below.
 
Choosing to do nothing would have left existing
issues unaddressed, despite the concerns raised by residents and
community partners, through public forums and direct correspondence
with the Council, that more can be done to ensure burial service
provision meets the religious and cultural requirements of the
Muslim community. Furthermore, this issue has been brought to the
Council’s attention both at Communities, Parks and Leisure
Committee and Full Council, highlighting the need for proactive and
meaningful action to be taken.
 
In addition, choosing not to proceed with a
formal review would have risked undermining confidence in the
service at a time when both Elected Members and community partners
have anticipated that this work would be taken forward. Questions
raised publicly, alongside continued engagement with community
partners such as SMBPF, demonstrate that residents are looking to
the Council to respond constructively to the issues they have
raised. Failing to act would have risked giving the impression that
these concerns were not being taken seriously, while also limiting
the service’s ability to plan effectively for the future in
light of demographic change and increasing pressure on burial
provision.
 
Moreover, choosing to do nothing would fail to
acknowledge the feedback gathered from the 2024 consultation and
cross-party Task & Finish group, which recommended this
review.




 


 




9.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Taking an alternative,
expedited approach:
 
Another option would have been to take forward
the review using a different approach, drawing primarily on the
information already available through earlier consultation,
correspondence from residents and discussions with community
partners. While this may have allowed recommendations to be
developed more quickly, it was not recommended. Proceeding in this
way would have limited the opportunity to hear from a wider range
of voices across the Muslim community and would not have enabled
the deeper engagement required to fully understand the issues
raised and the lived experience of those
affected.
 
Moreover, this approach would have reduced the
scope for further benchmarking and operational analysis, which are
important in ensuring that future recommendations are thorough,
evidence based and sustainable. Given the significance of this
work, it is essential to ensure perspectives from across the Muslim
community are integrated fully, and that sufficient time is taken
to complete the review comprehensively. For these reasons, this
option was not considered suitable.
topline: The Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to approve the next phase of a review to ensure burial services meet the religious and cultural requirements of Sheffield's Muslim community.

content:
Sheffield City Council to enter into a formal
grant agreement with Sheffield Hallam University and provide
operational management of two work programmes within the Sheffield
‘Place’ Investment, delivering against agreed outcomes
for the ‘Community Development’ and ‘Move
Well’ work areas. The investment period is two years (April
2026- March 2028). Investment into Sheffield City Council will
cover staff salaries (Sport, Leisure & Events team) plus allow
for investment into VCSE community organisations to deliver
community-based health and wellbeing services

 




11.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood
Services which provided an overview of the Sport England
‘Place’ Investment secured by Sheffield from April 2026
to March 2028.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Communities, Parks, and Leisure Policy
Committee  Policy
Committee:-

(a) 
Approves the Council becoming the accountable body for the grant
funding of £1,018,094.34 from Sheffield Hallam University
Services Limited, subject to the terms of the funding not being
materially different to those outlined in this
report.

(b) 
Approves the Council entering into a formal grant agreement with
Sheffield Hallam University Services Limited for grant funding of
£1,018,094.34, subject to the terms of the grant agreement
not being materially different to those outlined in this
report.




 


 




 


 




11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The recommendation to approve the Council
becoming accountable body for and entering into a formal grant
agreement for grant funding of £1,018,094.34 from Sheffield
Hallam University Services Limited ensures a continued strong
reputational position with national, regional, and local sport and
physical activity partners.




 


 




11.3.2


By accepting investment, SCC can invest in
community services across the five focus communities, ensuring
increased opportunities for residents to improve their health and
wellbeing, and ensuring capacity growth of the VCSE
sector.




 


 




11.3.3


The expansion of the Move Well, will ensure more
residents with long term health conditions can feel support and
motivated to improve their health, and benefit from more connected
and systematic healthcare pathways.




 


 




11.3.4


Whilst there is a small risk in entering into an
agreement and adhering to Sport England terms and conditions, it is
felt that benefits of delivering on this project, both to residents
and reputationally, significantly outweigh these
risks.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Do not accept the £1,018,094.34 investment
and do not enter into a grant agreement with Sheffield Hallam
University Services Limited.
 
Advantages

·      
The Council would avoid any financial, operational or delivery risk
associated with managing the grant and meeting Sport
England’s
compliance, monitoring, and reporting
requirements.

·      
No additional management or governance burden would fall to the
Council.
 
Disadvantages

·      
SCC was identified by NCSEM and partner organisations as the
preferred delivery body for the Community Development &
Services and Move Well work programmes due to its impartiality,
established governance arrangements, and proven experience in
delivering and overseeing high quality physical activity, health,
and wellbeing services. Declining this role would create a
reputational risk with national, regional, and local
partners.

·      
It is unlikely that an alternative organisation would be able to
assume delivery of these elements at short notice, creating a
significant risk that the funding could not be deployed as intended
and may need to be returned to Sport
England.

·      
Failure to accept the funding would result in missed opportunities
to invest in priority neighbourhoods, expand the Move Well service,
and strengthen community led delivery and VCSE capacity, limiting
the Council’s
ability to address physical inactivity and health
inequalities.

·      
Declining the investment would weaken
SCC’s
strategic position within the city’s physical activity and
health system and could reduce future opportunities to secure
external funding and influence programme
design.
topline: The Communities, Parks, and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to approve a grant agreement with Sheffield Hallam University for community development and health programs.

The Library Collection Management Framework
sets out the principles and practices for the selection, purchase,
management, promotion and disposal of stock (also called
Collections) within Sheffield Libraries. The proposed Collection
Management Framework for Non-Lending Material outlines our approach
to managing the material currently stored in the basement of the
Central Library, which includes approximately six miles of
shelving. The proposal sets out an approach to evaluating the non
-lending material and subsequently defines a clear process for
retaining, rehoming, donating or selling items that do not meet the
retention criteria.





10.1


The
Committee considered a report of the Executive Director of
Neighbourhood Services which sought approval for a framework for
non-lending material in the library service, particularly in the
Central Library
Stack.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY:
That the Communities, Parks and
Leisure Committee Policy
Committee:-

(a) 
Approves the Collection Management Framework for
Non-Lending Material;
and

(b) 
Notes that a costed proposal to deliver this
framework will be developed to form part of Council business
planning for the 2027/28 financial
year.




 


 




 


 




10.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The Non-Lending Framework is
designed to complement the Library Collection Management Framework
for the Council’s lending stock. It will ensure a consistent
approach when managing library
material.




 


 




10.3.2


The Committee’s approval of
this framework and its subsequent implementation will make
non-lending material more accessible to the public through
digitisation, exhibitions and other promotions; to better reflect
Sheffield’s communities and reach new audiences and
customers.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Work on
Non-Lending Material without a
framework
This alternative has been rejected
because without a framework work on non-lending material will lack
structure and consistency. This risks making important material
less accessible and lacks transparency about how decisions will be
made.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Do no work
on Non-Lending Material
To care for our material and make
it more accessible we need to assess and curate it so that we can
prioritise material for promotion and digitisation. If we do no
work on non-lending material some of Sheffield’s cultural
treasures will remain inaccessible. This option also has risks
that:

·      
Material that might be more accessible with our
partners remains inaccessible in the
library

·      
Potential discovery of important items does not take
place

·      
Material cannot be valued
accurately

·      
The material risks degradation if not
assessed.

·      
The Library, Archive and Information Service holds
more material than it needs, incurring operational costs for
storage.
topline: The Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to approve a Collection Management Framework for Non-Lending Material in Sheffield Libraries.
