The
Senior Land and Property Surveyor introduced the report which
proposed to sell the Sheffield City Council’s freehold
interest in the land at Blonk Street to the current leaseholder to
enable further investment in the property. The report sought
approval of the Finance and Performance Policy Committee to dispose
of the land.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Approve the freehold sale of land at Blonk Street on the terms set
out in Appendix 1.
b)   
Authorise the Chief Property Officer to finalise the terms of the
sale.




 


 




9.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The
recommended disposal of the Council’s freehold interest
offers a clear and balanced set of benefits for the Council and the
City, as follows:
 
·      
The disposal will facilitate private sector investment in the
property, improving its condition and long-term sustainability, and
supporting regeneration and economic activity in the surrounding
area.
·      
It enables the Council to secure a capital receipt from a
non-operational asset, contributing directly to the Council’s
capital programme and supporting delivery of wider corporate
priorities.
·      
The transaction will remove ongoing management responsibilities
associated with holding the freehold interest, allowing the Council
to focus resources on assets that directly support service
delivery.
·      
The proposed private treaty sale to the existing leaseholder
represents best consideration reasonably obtainable, as confirmed
by specialist valuation advice, and provides the best possible
chance of completion within this financial year. Completion within
this financial year is essential to secure the anticipated capital
receipt, support budgetary targets, and enable timely reinvestment
in priority regeneration projects.
·      
The recommendation aligns with the Council’s Asset Management
Strategy, City Goals, and triple policy drivers (People,
Prosperity, and Planet) by promoting sustainable growth, inclusive
prosperity, and environmental responsibility.




 


 




9.3.2


For
these reasons, the proposed disposal is considered to represent the
most advantageous option for the Council in financial, operational,
and strategic terms.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Do
Nothing
 
The
Council could retain the freehold interest and continue to manage
it alongside the existing long lease. This would maintain the
status quo but would not generate any capital receipt, remove
ongoing management responsibilities, or enable the leaseholder to
invest in the property. Retaining the asset in its current form
represents a missed opportunity to facilitate regeneration and
private sector investment and secure a capital receipt.




 


 




9.4.2



Extend or renegotiate the existing lease.
 
Another option would
be to negotiate an extension of the current lease or revise the
lease terms to capture additional income or secure greater
investment obligations from the leaseholder. While this could
provide some additional revenue, it would not deliver the same
certainty of a substantial capital receipt and would leave the
Council responsible for ongoing management of the lease. It would
not provide the leaseholder with full control to justify
significant investment in the building.




 


 




9.4.3



Open market sale
 
The Council could seek
to sell the freehold interest on the open market to third parties.
While this may have the potential to test market value, it could
lead to uncertainty, delays, or sale to a purchaser with no
intention of investing in the building or contributing to the
regeneration of the area. A competitive process could also disrupt
the existing tenant’s operation and reduce the overall
attractiveness of the opportunity to the leaseholder, potentially
reducing the capital receipt.
topline: The Finance and Performance Policy Committee has decided to approve the freehold sale of land at Blonk Street for further investment in the property.

content:
10.1


The
Assistant Director of Property and Chief Property Officer
introduced the report which proposed to dispose of a parcel of open
space land at Ardmore Street, Attercliffe for the delivery of
Affordable Housing. A written objection to the proposed disposal of
the land had been received. Finance & Performance Policy
Committee was asked to consider the objection and agree to the
disposal of the land.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Consider the objection to the proposed disposal of open space land
at Ardmore Street, Attercliffe and the response to that objection
as set out in the report and Appendix B; and
b)   
Approve the disposal of the land to the Purchaser and for the
purpose set out in the report.




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The
disposal will contribute towards the Councils wider objective to
deliver more affordable housing for the people of Sheffield. The
disposal will ensure delivery of 59 units for social rent and the
Council will also have nomination rights for the new homes ensure
housing need is met.




 


 




10.3.2


A
contaminated site will be remediated and will contribute to
regeneration of a deprived area in Attercliffe.




 


 




10.3.3


The
disposal will raise capital and revenue for the Council.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Withdraw from the sale and do nothing
 
This is
not considered appropriate because:
 
·      
The site would remain in the Councils ownership, and an on-going
maintenance liability would remain with the authority.
·      
The grant to remediate the site would potentially be lost so that
the contaminated site would not be remediated and could not be
brought forward for future residential development for the delivery
of Affordable Housing.
·      
The site has been identified in the Housing Growth Delivery Plan
2025- 2030 as a location for new affordable housing.
·      
Planning considers the merits of the allocation of the sites for
open space purposes when allocating land for housing. The severe
shortage of housing land in the city is a known issue.
·      
By doing nothing, the Council may establish a precedent for future
land disposals and thus prevent them from coming forward as housing
sites in the future.




 


 
 




10.4.2


The
Council to deliver the site itself for new affordable
housing
 
This
option has been rejected because:
 
·      
The Council does not currently have sufficient resources to deliver
all the affordable homes that are required to meet the growing
housing need within the city.
·      
Investment in new homes needs to be balanced against resources
required for repairs and improvements to existing stock whilst
remaining financially prudent.
·      
As a result, and in line with the approved Housing Growth delivery
plan 2025-30, a programme of land disposals to increase the supply
of affordable homes is also being progressed. This still supports
the increased delivery of affordable homes but at less capital cost
to the Council.
topline: The Assistant Director of Property has decided to dispose of open space land at Ardmore Street, Attercliffe for the delivery of Affordable Housing.

content:
12.1


The
Director of Finance and Commercial Services and Assistant Director
of Finance Business Partnering introduced the report which provided
an update on how the Council plans to set a balanced budget for
2026/27. The report set out the budget position, provided an update
on the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement and set out
the associated assumptions, risks and opportunities to be
considered in setting a balanced budget.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the impact of the Local Government Provisional Finance
Settlement (LGFS) on the MTFS period to the end of
2029/30.
b)   
Note the balanced budget position for 2026/27.
c)   
Note the approach taken to budget setting has changed from previous
years, with 2025/26 overspends being built into the 2026/27 budget
and updated MTFS position.
d)   
Note the assumption that Council Tax will increase by 4.99%
(inclusive of a 2% Adult Social Care precept) each year throughout
the MTFS period to support the financial sustainability of the
council.
e)   
Note that the Recovery Grant is only confirmed for the next 3 years
and therefore the council should avoid significant ongoing
financial commitments in order to
sustain the benefit from the improved funding through the
LGFS.
f)     
Note the impact of the Future Sheffield programme and the
pressures, savings and investment proposals set out in the closed
Appendix 1 of this report.




 


 




12.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




12.3.1


N/A




 


 




12.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


The
Council is required by law to deliver a balance budget and
therefore each Committee needs to delivery savings to achieve this.
No alternatives have been considered at this stage.

content:
30.1


The Committee
considered a report of David Luck, Community Services Manager, on
the proposed allocation of fund to address local priorities for the
South East Local Area Committee (LAC)
for 2025-26.




 


 




30.2


The Community Services
Manager explained that due to underspend and return funds from
previous projects and years, it was recommended to allocated
£27,0000 towards the Environmental Stewardship
Project.




 


 




30.3


Councillor Gail Smith,
commented that the project had done an amazing job and had
completed jobs that otherwise would not had been completed such as refurbishing four benches
in Waterthorpe on Thorpe
Green.




 


 




30.4


Councillor Mick
Roobey, explained that the project did not only including work but
also part of an education was involved in the project.




 


 




30.5


RESOLVED: 
That the South East LAC:

Notes
the expenditure under delegated powers against the £100,000
budget for 2025/26 to address local priorities in the South East LAC as detailed in the
report.
Agrees
the award of further grant funding of £27,000 to continue to
fund the environmental stewardship team up to December 2026,
subject to the request to carry forward this amount to the 2026/27
LAC budget being approved by the Director of Finance and Commercial
Services.





 


 




30.6


Reasons for Decision




 


 




30.6.1


Spending decisions
made by the Community Services Manager under the authority
delegated by the LAC in September 2024 are required to be reported
to the next LAC meeting so that the LAC can monitor its delegated
budget and delivery of the Community Plan.




 


 




30.6.2


The further
expenditure under delegated authority outlined in the report
addresses the identified local priorities within the South East LAC Community Plan.




 


 




30.6.3


The proposed use of
funding of £27 000 to extend the Environmental Stewardship
Team will enable environmental work to be carried out across all
four wards within the South East Area to
support the priority themes of the Community Plan.




 


 




30.7


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




30.7.1


Decisions on all
expenditure could be reserved to the LAC
but this would inevitably delay delivery of priority actions to
address specific issues identified in the Community
Plan.
 




 


 




30.7.2


All decisions on
expenditure to support Community Plan priorities could be delegated
to officers. However, this would restrict and undermine the
LAC’s ability to monitor its delegated budget and delivery of
the Community Plan.

Sheffield based charity Endeavour, have submitted
a funding application through the wraparound childcare programme to
set up a new wraparound childcare provision providing after school
childcare from their newly refurbished community building. The
wraparound provision will add to the provider’s AP and youth
provision to serve families of 5 primary schools including one
Specialist School as well as children attending its own AP
provision. Sheffield City Council has received wraparound programme
funding to allocate to schools and providers to increase the
amount of wraparound care. This new provision will deliver 50
afterschool club places commencing February 2026.

That a grant payment of £150,000 be made
to Endeavour Sheffield (registered charity 275061) as a one-off
payment to deliver a new wraparound childcare services for families
of several schools in locality B (Firvale/Firth Park and
surrounding areas). The grant will be subject to a legally binding
funding agreement.

Sheffield City Council is delivering the
Government’s Wraparound programme, to increase the amount of
wraparound childcare for parents of primary aged children. Plans
for delivery of the wraparound programme were approved at Education
Children and Families Policy Committee on 8 February 2024. There is
currently no wraparound provision in Schools across this area of
the city. The demand from parents is insufficient for the schools
to establish their own provision but a small number of parents at
each school need the service to help them work. Endeavour have
ascertained following consultation with the schools and parents
that there will be sufficient combined demand to develop a viable
provision for families across this area. This provision has a robust business plan to develop
quality wraparound childcare provision offering 50 after school
places and could expand further if demand grows. It supports SCC in
its Wraparound Childcare Delivery Plan which has been endorsed by
the DfE.

Refusal of application or approval with
reduced funding allocation

Childcare provider JPAC, have submitted 2 x
funding applications through the wraparound childcare programme to
set up new wraparound childcare provision providing after school
childcare at Coit and St. Mary’s primary schools.  Each school is to host a 60
place breakfast and afterschool club run by JPAC. The
provision at St Mary’s will also be opened up to other primary schools in the High Green
area and children will be transported by walking bus. Sheffield
City Council has received wraparound programme funding to
allocate to schools and providers to increase the amount of
wraparound care. These new provisions will commence delivery by
April 2026 or sooner dependant on when Ofsted registration and
staff arrangements are complete.

That a 2 x grant
payments of £90,000 each be made to Wraparound
Childcare provider JPAC Ltd as a one-off payment to deliver:
• a new 60 place wraparound childcare
service on site at Coit Primary School (£90,000).
• A new 60 place wraparound provision at
St Mary’s school High Green (£90,000).
The grant will be subject to a legally binding
funding agreement.

Sheffield City Council is delivering the
Government’s Wraparound programme, to increase the amount of
wraparound childcare for parents of primary aged children. Plans
for delivery of the wraparound programme were approved at Education
Children and Families Policy Committee on 8 February 2024. There is
currently no wraparound provision at the schools but surveys have established that there is a
high level of demand from parents. The schools have both determined
that they would like to work with an on-site provider and selected
JPAC to deliver. The provision at St Mary’s will be open to
families attending 2 other High Green primary schools where there
is not sufficient demand to set up their own provision. This
reputable provider has long standing experience in delivering good
quality wraparound care for several schools in Sheffield. The grant
funding will help with set up and delivery costs until the
provision becomes financially sustainable.

Options were: a)
Allocation of full funding request (£2000 per place-
£120,000 per provision), b) Refusal of application or c)
Approval with reduced funding allocation.
Option C reduced allocation based on average
costs of £1500 per place was selected. Option A was rejected
in order to ensure sufficient funding to
establish more wraparound places for other schools, option C was
rejected as the provision is needed.

decision_maker: Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee
purpose: Update from police on framework
content:
The
Committee received a verbal briefing on the Right Care, Right
Person (RCRP) policy from Martin Story - Lancashire Police. It was
reported that the policy was introduced locally in 2022 and has
since been rolled out nationally across the
majority of police forces in the UK.
The
briefing outlined that Right Care, Right
Person provided a clear framework to support
decision?making on the
most appropriate agency response to concern for safety reports. The
approach aimed to ensure that individuals were supported by the
agency best placed to provide care, while confirming that the
police would always attend where there was an immediate risk to
life, serious harm, or where engagement was required under Articles
2 or 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It was
emphasised that decisions on attendance were
risk?led rather than
resource?led.
Members
were informed of the police call?handling and response model, including
emergency, priority, routine, standard and telephone resolution
responses, and the use of the nationally adopted THRIVE+ assessment
process to evaluate threat, harm, risk, vulnerability and
engagement needs. Over the past 12 months, approximately 35,000
concern for safety incidents were
received, with police attendance deployed to around 63% of cases
following risk assessment. Where non?deployment decisions are made, call
handlers had the option to escalate to a supervisory review, and
callers are advised to re?contact police should risk levels change. It was noted that no
coroner’s notices have been issued in relation to the
application of Right Care, Right Person since its
implementation.
The
Committee also heard about partnership working to support
vulnerable people, including the use of Street Triage Teams, which
paired trained police officers with mental health professionals
from Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust. These teams
operated extended hours and supported both crisis response and
preventative work, enabling shared decision?making, diversion where appropriate, and
safeguarding. While detention under section 136 of the Mental
Health Act was used where necessary to protect life, it was
stressed that this is a last resort and that the overall approach
seeks to provide timely, appropriate and compassionate support
through multi?agency
collaboration.
The
role of the police and criminal justice system was discussed,
particularly in relation to individuals who fall through service
gaps. Lancashire Police described the use of diversionary panels,
liaison and diversion services, and specialist teams working
alongside forensic mental health services and adult social care to
support vulnerable individuals and reduce repeat contact with the
criminal justice system. It was confirmed that police attendance
remains risk?based, and that where no immediate threat to life is
identified, individuals may be signposted to the most appropriate
service.
Members
also sought reassurance that specialist police officers and street
triage teams operated county?wide, including in more rural and
peripheral areas, and that responses are determined by risk rather
than geography.
See
Item 4 for recommendations.
topline: The Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the implementation of the Right Care, Right Person policy.

to introduce a prohibition of waiting to prevent obstructive
parking behaviour, allowing for the safe access of the premises

The proposals are being pursued
as part of a s278 Agreement under the Highways Act 1980 as part of
a new retail development.
 
Consultations
 
Formal consultation was carried

purpose:
Church Street, Church
View, Carr Head, Lane House Lane, Bank Street, Slack Booth, Hollin
Hall & Floats Mill, Trawden 

The purpose of this proposal is to address
issues of access and safety throughout the village of Trawden by
introducing No Waiting At Any Time
restrictions.
The proposed restrictions have been designed
to mirror the existing on-street parking patterns and to prevent
pavement parking and double parking where it would cause the most
significant obstruction to pedestrian movement and vehicular access
through the village.
 
The proposal also introduces No Waiting Monday
to Friday 8am-6pm restrictions on the corner of Church Street and
Church View to address concerns of visibility for drivers and
pedestrians, particularly during peak times, by preventing parking
during the busiest periods.
 
REASONS UNDER
Section 1 of the RTRA
(a) 
for avoiding danger to persons or other traffic using the road or
any other road or for preventing the likelihood of any such danger
arising
 
(c) 
for facilitating the passage on the road or any other road of any
class of traffic (including pedestrians)
 

Church Street &
Lupton Drive, Barrowford 

The purpose of this proposal is to introduce
No Waiting At Any Time restrictions on
Church Street to address issues with parking and access along this
section of road.
The proposal introduces new No Waiting
At Any Time restrictions on the south
side of Church Street, from outside no. 11 to the eastern extent of
the parking area outside the Corn Mill building. This is to keep
the pinch point outside no. 11 clear of parked vehicles and to
ensure the parking area of the Corn Mill building, which had a
dropped kerb for vehicle access, is not obstructed by parked
vehicles.
 
The proposal also extends the existing No
Waiting At Any Time restrictions on the
north side of Church Street, to prevent parking from migrating to
this area.
No Waiting At Any
Time restrictions are proposed on the south-east side of Church
Street for a length of 15 metres outside the pedestrian access
point to the Ingham Street flats in order
to improve vehicular access by creating a passing place.
 
The proposal also amends the Traffic
Regulation Order to match the existing road markings which have
been present on site for many years, allowing for effective
enforcement.
 
REASONS UNDER
Section 1 of the RTRA
 
(a) 
for avoiding danger to persons or other traffic using the road or
any other road or for preventing the likelihood of any such danger
arising
 
(c) 
for facilitating the passage on the road or any other road of any
class of traffic (including pedestrians)
 

Wellington Street,
Nelson 

It is proposed to increase the potential
parking availability for residents by amending the existing limited
waiting bay on the north-east side of Wellington Street.
 
The purpose of this proposal is to allow
residents, who are part of the existing permit zone, to park in the
bay for an unlimited time at any time on all days.
This proposal also retains the potential for
visitors to the area to park on street by retaining the existing
limited waiting restriction for its existing days and times.
This proposal also introduces a legal order
for the permit holders parking bay which has been marked and signed
on the south-east side of Wellington Street outside nos. 3 to 21
since pre-2009 to ensure effective enforcement can take place.
 
REASONS UNDER
Section 1 of the RTRA
(f) 
for preserving or improving the amenities of the area through which
the road runs
 

Keighley Road,
Colne 

The purpose of this proposal is to address
concerns of visibility issues for vehicles turning out of Craven
Street onto Keighley Road due to vehicles parking on the widened
footway by introducing No Waiting At Any
Time restrictions.
 
REASONS UNDER
Section 1 of the RTRA
(a) 
for avoiding danger to persons or other traffic using the road or
any other road or for preventing the likelihood of any such danger
arising
 
(c) 
for facilitating the passage on the road or any other road of any
class of traffic (including pedestrians)
 

Albert Square,
Barnoldswick 

The purpose of this proposal is to address
access issues along Albert Square by introducing No Loading
At Any Time restrictions alongside the
existing No Waiting At Any Time
restrictions.
The proposals aim to prevent goods vehicles
from loading and unloading which, due to the narrow nature of the
carriageway, can result in vehicular traffic being unable to
pass.
 
REASONS UNDER
Section 1 of the RTRA
 
(c) 
for facilitating the passage on the road or any other road of any
class of traffic (including pedestrians)
 
Consultations
 
Formal consultation was carried out between 06
February 2026 and 06 March 2026 which included advertising in the
local press and notices being displayed on site.  Divisional county councillors were consulted along
with the council's usual consultees and the consultation documents
posted on the council's website.
 
Following formal consultation 4 Objections
were received.
 
Following formal consultation ? responses were received.  The main points raised in the responses along with
Officer comments are outlines in Appendix D.

content:
Becky
Clough and Sophia Chivandire from the
Scheme Advisory Board (SAB) gave a presentation on the Peer Support
project, which was aimed at helping pension funds review current
achievements and identify areas for development and
improvement.
 
When
considering the presentation Board members discussed the
following:
 
· 
That Funds be active participants in any Peer
Support review and that any final report produced should be
constructive, open and transparent.
 
· 
Training should be available for members of Peer
Support Groups which would be comprised predominantly of active
members of Pension Fund Committees/Local Pension Boards and
Officers, though where appropriate, could include experienced
individuals who may have retired. 
 
· 
Effective communications would be necessary to
clarify that Peer Support was not an audit and was different from
the Independent Governance Review required as part of new pensions
legislation, in order to encourage active engagement in the
process.
 
· 
That Peer Support could be a useful tool in
assisting Councils/Funds respond to the statutory requirements of
the Independent Governance Review.
 
Resolved:
That the feedback from the Board on the Scheme
Advisory Board Peer Support project
is noted and the SAB representatives thanked for
their attendance.

content:
The Chairs of the three
Advisory Boards, the Transport Advisory Board, the Economy Advisory
Board, and the Skills Advisory Board, were invited to provide an
update to the meeting on the work their advisory boards had been
undertaken.
 
Councillor Phil Riley provided
an update on the work being undertaken by the Transport Advisory
Board. It was noted that the next meeting of the Board was
scheduled to take place on 22 April 2026, and as such, there were
no new formal updates to report to the meeting. However, progress
had continued to be made in strengthening the Authority’s
transport capacity, including the recent recruitment process for
the Director of Transport, which had attracted a strong field of
applicants.
 
It was also noted that
dedicated transport officers directly employed by the Authority
were now in place, supporting the development and delivery of
transport priorities, which was highlighted as an important step in
moving from strategy into implementation.
 
Matthew Sidgreaves, Interim
Chief Operating Officer of the Lancashire Combined County Authority
provided an update on the work being undertaken by the Economy
Advisory Board, on behalf of Councillor Lynn Williams. It was noted
that the Board had last met on 27 March 2026, and received an
update on the draft Transport Implementation Plan, with discussion
focusing on the importance of ensuring that transport investment
supported economic growth and responded to business needs across
Lancashire.
 
The Board also considered
updates on the North West Business Fund, a loan and equity fund for
SMEs, which was in the process of being brought back under public
control. It was noted that Lancashire would be a stakeholder in the
fund and would benefit from future investment opportunities. The
Lancashire Investment Fund (formerly the Growing Places Fund) had
also been discussed, including new management arrangements under
the Combined County Authority and recent interest in the fund. The
Board had considered how the fund could be better promoted to
support local economic development.
 
County Councillor Simon Evans
provided an update on the work being undertaken by the Skills
Advisory Board. It was noted that the Board had met on 26 March
2026, with key items including the Local Skills Improvement Plan
(LSIP), post?16 capital funding devolution, and the closure of the
UK Shared Prosperity Fund.
 
It was also noted the refresh
of Lancashire’s LSIP aimed to identify current and future
skills needs through employer engagement led by the local Chambers
of Commerce and the Skills Hub and the refreshed plan was expected
to align more closely with the industrial strategy and local growth
priorities, with further work planned before a final draft was
brought forward. The Board also considered the proposed devolution
of post?16 capital funding to the Combined County Authority, with
an indicative allocation of just over £11 million to support
further education and sixth?form college capacity in response to
demographic growth.
 
The Board also discussed the UK
Shared Prosperity Fund, including the challenges arising from the
programme ending in September 2026 and the potential impact on
skills provision, particularly for young people. Lastly, an update
was provided on the Skills Hub activity, including the Lancashire
Cyber Festival Education Week, which had engaged over 10,000 pupils
and students and had been highlighted as a unique and successful
example of talent pipeline development linked to Lancashire’s
defence and digital sectors.
 
Resolved: That the
updates be noted.
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority has decided to note the updates provided by the Transport Advisory Board, Economy Advisory Board, and Skills Advisory Board.

content:
Matthew Sidgreaves, Interim
Chief Operating Officer of the Lancashire Combined County
Authority, provided a verbal update on the progress made following
the completion of the governance review.
 
It was noted that, since the
last meeting of the Board, Leaders had received a formal written
response from the Minister for Devolution, Faith and Communities,
following the submission of correspondence from the Authority
confirming that the review of governance models had been
completed.
 
The Minister’s response
acknowledged receipt of the Authority’s conclusions, welcomed
the work undertaken in reviewing governance arrangements, and
confirmed the Government’s willingness to engage further with
Leaders to discuss both the outcome of the review and the matters
raised in the Authority’s correspondence.
 
It was further noted that a
meeting between Leaders of the Combined County Authority and the
Minister had originally been scheduled for March 2026 but had been
postponed at short notice due to parliamentary business. A revised
date of 12 May 2026 was now proposed for this meeting and subject
to the meeting taking place as planned, it was anticipated that
discussions would include the conclusions arising from the
governance review, the current and future governance model of the
Combined County Authority, the practical operation of the Authority
as a non?mayoral combined authority, and potential next steps and
timescales for further devolution.
 
Resolved: That the
update be noted.
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority has decided to progress with recommendations following a governance review.

board chairs from across the North. They had had also highlighted
Lancashire’s strong base of mid?market businesses, as key
drivers of high?value employment and productivity growth and it was
noted that targeted support for these businesses, including access
to finance, skills and international markets, was being explored,
with discussions ongoing with institutions such as the NatWest
backed Mid Market Growth Council.
 
The Authority’s
unsuccessful bid to the Innovation Business Support Fund was also
discussed by the Business Board and that future funding
opportunities may require more collaborative approaches with
neighbouring areas. The Business Board had also agreed that greater
partnership working would strengthen Lancashire’s position in
future bids.
 
The Business Board also
discussed the potential engagement with the Lancashire County
Pension Fund on opportunities for long?term investment in local
infrastructure and economic growth. The importance of presenting a
confident and proactive outward narrative to government and
investors had been emphasised, including alignment with future
trade missions and international engagement in sectors aligned to
Lancashire’s strategic strengths.
 
Resolved: That the
update be noted.
topline: The Lancashire Business Board's concerns about the lack of reference to Lancashire in the Northern Growth Strategy were noted by the council.

decision_maker: Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
Call-in request report to the Secretary of
State for committee's consideration.
content:
The Chair confirmed
that the meeting was convened in accordance with the
organisation’s governance procedures to determine whether the
threshold for a call-in request submission to the Secretary of
State had been met.
The two key grounds
for consideration were:

Concerns regarding the process followed by the NHS commissioning
body or NHS provider, including:

adequacy and content of the consultation.
whether sufficient time for consultation had been
provided.
how
options had been developed.
whether statutory duties around public involvement had been
satisfied.


Concerns that the decision or proposal is not in the best
interests of the health service in the area, taking into account
patient impact, service access, quality, and long?term
sustainability.

Members noted that
they had been provided with a report within the agenda pack, which
set out detailed information on the Shaping Care Together programme
and the decision taken at the Shaping Care Together Joint Committee
meeting held on 13 March 2026. This report was considered as part
of the Committee’s deliberations.
From the information
provided with the agenda pack, the Committee proceeded directly to
a vote on whether to submit a call?in request to the Secretary of State. It
was unanimously agreed that a call?in request should be made. Members then
discussed the grounds upon which the call?in would be submitted.
The Chair invited
Members to share their comments and observations.
Members raised a
number of significant concerns relating to the process followed by
the NHS Shaping Care Together Joint Committee:

Members felt that the questions raised by the Joint Scrutiny
Committee prior to the ICB’s decision were not appropriately
answered.

 

Members noted that the timing of scrutiny meetings did not allow
proper scrutiny, and that the original schedule would have allowed
only one meeting before the decision was taken. It was also stated
that the meeting on 13 March 2026 provided little opportunity for
effective scrutiny.

 

Members highlighted insufficient evidence of engagement with
deprived and disabled residents, especially in the Skelmersdale
area, despite these groups being potentially disproportionately
affected.

 

Concerns were expressed that the consultation offered a limited
range of options, giving rise to a perception of
pre?determination, with
a preferred option seemingly identified before consultation began.
Members felt that some of the public disengaged from the
consultation for this reason.

 

The
programme was explicitly limited to urgent and emergency care,
despite national guidance highlighting interdependencies with
maternity services. Members also indicated ongoing uncertainty
regarding the future of maternity services at Ormskirk.

 

While
online information was well presented, Members found the
documentation difficult to navigate. Further concerns were raised
that feedback received indicated that some residents reported late
or missing consultation materials.

 
Members also expressed
significant concerns that the decision itself was not in the best
interests of the public, including:

Increased travel
times were identified as a significant risk, particularly for
vulnerable groups, including children requiring urgent assessment,
with potential adverse impacts on health outcomes.

 

Although the report acknowledged increased travel distances,
Members felt there was little evidence of detailed or funded
mitigations. The only mitigation referenced (a shuttle bus) was not
funded.

 

Members felt there was a lack of detailed information on
staffing, including how clinical skills would be distributed across
sites to meet demand. Concerns were raised regarding the capacity
of Southport A&E to absorb increased attendances.
Members discussed concerns about the potential
knock?on effect of
changes to children’s urgent care on maternity services at
Ormskirk, noting the interdependency between the two services. It
was also noted by another Member that maternity services were
currently functioning well and that no formal issues had been
raised.

 

Members felt that ambulance modelling had not been sufficiently
addressed, raising concerns about the assumptions used.

 

It was
noted that the modelling appeared heavily focused on Southport,
Ormskirk and Formby, with limited consideration of other affected
areas, particularly the population in Skelmersdale.

 

Members highlighted that the current split?site model had been identified as a core
problem, yet there was little evidence that stabilising or
improving the split?site arrangement had been fully explored.

 

Concerns were raised about whether the characteristics of
respondents had been sufficiently analysed, with some Members
noting that certain groups may not have been able to participate
effectively.

 
Resolved: That;

A
letter be drafted outlining all concerns raised requesting
Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) Secretary of State
exercise their powers under the National Health Service Act 2006
(as amended) to call in and review the recent decision of the joint
Cheshire and Merseyside, and Lancashire and South Cumbria
Integrated Care Boards (ICB) on the NHS Shaping Care Together
Programme for Members approval.

 

The
agreed letter be submitted to the DHSC Reconfiguration Service
along with completion of the online request form for
consideration.
topline: The Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee has decided to submit a call-in request to the Secretary of State regarding the recent decision on the NHS Shaping Care Together Programme.

purpose:

Early Years settings in Lancashire.

announced by 28 February 2026 and are not altered by this decision,
the proposal only concerns internal allocations and
ring-fencing.

purpose:
It is proposed to make a Traffic Regulation
Order for the reasons as set out in Appendix 'C', which include
measures to address the following:

Safety concerns in relation to both
vehicles that are parked causing serious problems with regards to
the safe movement of traffic and parking that obstructs driver's
sightlines, impeding access and egress at junctions and access to
some businesses. These measures will improve visibility at the
locations and assist with the general movement of
traffic along the roads.
Some of the measures are proposed to
ensure access for refuse vehicles and residential
properties.
Some of the measures are proposed to
allow buses to safely pull in and out of traffic without blocking
the road and for Heavy Goods Vehicles to manoeuvre in a safe manner
with minimal obstruction by parked vehicles.
The order further removes
restrictions that are no longer required to provide additional
unrestricted parking availability for local residents and
businesses improving the amenities of the area
The proposal also formalises
restrictions that are currently on site and corrects
inconsistencies that have been identified within current Orders.
These proposals will not make any changes to the restrictions or
their extents on site, therefore drivers will not be subject to any
changes as a result of these proposals

 
Consultations
 
Formal consultation was carried out between
30th January 2026 until 27th February 2026
included advertising in the local press and notices being displayed
on site.  Divisional county councillors
were consulted along with the county council's usual consultees and
the consultation documents posted on the council's website.
 
Following formal consultation 1 response was
received. The main points raised in the responses along with
Officer comments are outlines in Appendix C.

non-motorised means and this will improve health and air quality

local press and notices being displayed on site.  Divisional county councillors were consulted along
with the county council's usual consultees and the consultation
documents posted on the county council's website.
 
Following formal consultation No Objections
were received.

purpose:
This proposal is to support the implementation of accessibility
improvements at bus stops within the East Lancashire area. These
improvements form part of a wider initiative to provide safe and
suitable boarding and alighting facilities for all passengers,
including wheelchair users, pushchair users, and individuals with
restricted mobility who rely on public transport services.
 
The introduction and alteration of
'Bus Stop Clearway' markings are necessary to ensure that stopping
areas remain free of parked vehicles. Vehicles parking within or
adjacent to bus stops can obstruct bus manoeuvring space and limit
forward visibility, creating additional difficulties for drivers
and for visually impaired passengers. The proposed clearways will
therefore provide unobstructed access for buses and support safe
and efficient passenger movement.
 
Where required, additional
infrastructure such as bus shelters and raised boarding platforms
will be installed to enhance safety, comfort, and accessibility at
the stops.
 
Bus Stop
Clearway
ALTHAM, Simon Jersey
(by) Stop ID 2500LA00207
 
This proposal
will: upgrade the existing bus stop to a Quality Bus Stop Clearway,
ensuring buses can pull in and out safely and consistently.
The implementation of the Bus Stop
Clearway will ensure that appropriate enforcement measures can be
undertaken, thereby improving compliance and delivering benefits
for all road users, including pedestrians.
 
Consultations
Formal consultation took place between 20
February 2026 and 20 March 2026 (Appendix A). This included the
display of site notices and copies of the notice provided to those
affected properties.
 
County Councillors for
the affected divisions were consulted, alongside standard
consultees, and all consultation documentation was published on
Lancashire County Council’s website.
 
Following formal consultation No
Objections were received.

purpose:
Application to record Whitley Road, Upholland
as Byway not Footpath
content:
A report was presented on an application for
the upgrade to byway, the way known as Whitley Road and recorded as
Upholland 6, on the Definitive Map and Statement of Public Rights
of Way.
 
The route under investigation was shown on the
Committee Plan attached to the agenda papers between points
A-B-C-D-X-E-F-G.
 
Committee noted that the applicant had applied
to upgrade the route from point A through to the point X to a
restricted byway, and then from point X through to point G to
upgrade the route to a byway open to all traffic. However, as the
full length of the application route was currently recorded as a
public footpath, then the whole of the route should, if the
evidence supported public carriageway rights, be upgraded to a
restricted byway.
 
Various maps, plans and other documents had
been examined to build up a picture of the history, status, precise
line, width and other particulars.
 
Taking all the evidence into account, it was
considered that there was insufficient map and documentary evidence
for a public vehicular route, with no obvious reason why the public
would use it in vehicles as opposed to using Lafford Lane. In
addition, the fact that parts of the route were shown in private
ownership in the Tithe Award, the lack of any references to it in
the Upholland Urban District Council Highway Minute Books and
current ownership records also weighed against the existence of a
public vehicular through route.
 
It was reported that whilst investigating this
application, it had become apparent that at the northern end of the
route between point G and point Z, a short section of Walthew Green was recorded as a publicly
maintainable vehicular highway on the List of Streets but was also
recorded as part of FP0821006. An inspection of the Draft,
Provisional and First Definitive Map together with the county
council highway records, suggested that part of the footpath G-Z
had been included due to a drafting error and part had since been
recorded as maintainable carriageway. Therefore, it was considered
that particulars on the Definitive Map and Statement should be
amended to remove the footpath recorded on that section G-Z of
Walthew Green as it was no longer of a
category recordable on the Definitive Map and Statement.
 
Committee were reminded that
removal of a section from the Definitive record was only to be done
on sufficient evidence of error. The Trevelyan case (Trevelyan v
Secretary of State for Environment, Transport and the Regions
[2001] EWCA Civ 266) indicated that
although the relevant test was on the balance of probabilities,
evidence of some substance was required to displace the initial
presumption that the way shown on the Definitive Map existed.
Committee were advised that the extent of the vehicular highway
included public rights on foot but the public footpath depiction
should be removed from the Definitive Map and Statement where they
were so subsumed.
 
Resolved: That:
 
(i) 
The application be accepted in part (subject to bridleway not
carriageway status).
 
(ii) 
A Definitive Map Modification Order(s) be made under s 53(2)(b) and
S53(3)(c)(ii) and (iii) to record a bridleway between A and G, and
to modify the particulars in the Definitive Statement to remove the
record of  footpath between Z and G.
 
(iii) 
The said Order(s) be promoted to confirmation, if necessary at
public inquiry.
topline: The Regulatory Committee has decided to approve the recommendations for the upgrade of Whitley Road to a restricted byway and a byway open to all traffic.

point on Monks Gate, Tatham to FP0117012 at Park House,
Hornby.
content:
A report was presented on an application for
the addition of a footpath from a point on Monks Gate, Tatham to
Park House, Hornby at a junction with FP0117012,  to the Definitive Map and Statement of Public
Rights of Way.
 
The application route was shown on the
Committee Plan attached to the agenda papers between points
A-B-C-D-E-F.
 
Various maps, plans and other documents had
been examined to build up a picture of the history, status, precise
line, width and other particulars.
 
Committee were informed that the route through
points A-E was currently not recorded as any highway on the
Definitive Map and Statement.
 
Based on the evidence in the report, it was
suggested that Committee had sufficient evidence, on balance, that
the route was a historical public route available not only for use
on foot or horseback but also as a vehicular highway. There was no
evidence of a legal stopping up of those rights and so it was
advised that the legal maxim "once a highway always a highway"
applied. 
 
Committee were advised if they considered
there was sufficient evidence of an old vehicular highway, officers
had considered whether any of the exemptions or exceptions under
the Natural Environment and Rural Communities Act 2006 applied and
concluded they did not and that the Act would have extinguished any
mechanically propelled vehicular rights, leaving the route to be
appropriately recorded as a restricted byway.
 
The Public Rights of Way Manager answered
questions from Committee.
 
Resolved: That:
 
(i) 
The application with modification to recognise carriageway rights
be accepted.
 
(ii) 
A Definitive Map Modification Order be made under S53(2)(b) of the
Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 to record a restricted byway from
Monks Gate, Tatham to Park House, Hornby as set out in the
report.
 
(iii) 
That the Order be promoted to confirmation, if necessary by
submitting it to the Planning Inspectorate.
topline: The Regulatory Committee has decided to approve the addition of a footpath to the Definitive Map and Statement of Public Rights of Way.

purpose:
There is a clear business need
to procure a provider to deliver Motivational Interviewing training
for Children's Social Care and in accordance with the procurement
regulations, a three-quote process was completed that identified a
new provider who will commence delivery from 1 April
2026. 
 
Two providers submitted
quotes.  Both providers were assessed
against the same requirements and service specification, with
scores awarded in line with the published evaluation
criteria.
 
Provider 1 demonstrated strong
Motivational Interviewing (MI) expertise and a positive delivery
track record. However, several aspects of their submission lacked
the level of operational detail required and did not fully evidence
compliance across key areas such as communication processes, risk
management, structured reporting, and data governance. As a result,
Provider 1 did not achieve the highest score overall.
 
Provider 2 (awarded provider)
scored higher against the service specification. Their submission
provided more comprehensive and fully evidenced responses across
all criterion areas, including communication and issue management,
continuity and contingency planning, data handling, reporting, and
impact measurement. They demonstrated clear organisational
structures, named responsibilities, stronger governance
arrangements, and explicit alignment with the Council’s
operational requirements. This provided a higher level of assurance
that they could deliver the service consistently, reliably and in
full compliance with the specification.
 
In addition to achieving the
highest quality score, Provider 2 also submitted the lowest priced
bid. As price carried a 40% weighting, this further increased their
overall score and positioned them as the most economically
advantageous tender.
 
For these reasons, Provider 2
was selected for contract award. A decision
to start a three-quote procurement tender for Motivational
Interviewing training.

purpose:
Background and
Advice
A waiver is required to make an immediate
appointment of Newtrality Ltd to support on the County Council's
internal Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) programme, with a
particular focus on planning for the disaggregation of the County
Council.
 
Five separate proposals for reorganisation in
Lancashire were submitted to Government in November 2025, ranging
from two to five unitary councils. Government is currently
conducting a statutory consultation to understand the views of
residents and stakeholders, ahead of making a 'minded to' decision
on its preferred solution, which is expected in July 2026.
 
In the period up to the Government's 'minded
to' decision, Lancashire County Council are working on a
preparation programme to establish a detailed baseline, service
taxonomy, Day 1 implementation plan and undertake scenario
planning.
 
Aligned to the cross-council programme, the
County Council has established an internal programme, which is
focused on understanding how the County Council could be
disaggregated under all five unitary configurations currently on
the table.
This work will involve establishing a common
set of disaggregation principles, a detailed disaggregation
methodology, application of that methodology to the data, and
identification of key issues and interdependencies to feed into the
cross-council programme.
 
External support is required to provide
capacity, expertise and knowhow to the internal programme, and
particularly the disaggregation work. It is imperative that the
internal programme is closely aligned to the timescales of the
cross-council programme. To feed into the scenario and
implementation planning being undertaken in the cross-council
programme, initial outputs from the disaggregation modelling are
required by May. A fast appointment of Newtrality is therefore
critical, and timescales don't allow for a three quote process to
be conducted.
 
As a waiver to the quotation process is being
sought, value will be monitored as the commission will work on a
time and materials basis which will be regularly reviewed. This
will enable full flexibility in terms of only seeking support when
and where it is required.
 
During the preparation phase leading up to
Government decision, the team will be assessing the requirement for
longer-term support to enable appropriate time to consider
procurement routes, if further external support is required.
 
 
Implications
 
This item has the following
implications, as indicated.
 
 
Legal
 
The Procurement Act ("PA") apply to
procurement activity where the total contract value exceeds a
certain financial threshold. Above threshold contracts are subject
to the rules laid down within the PA and are to be procured in
accordance with the treaty principles of proportionality, mutual
recognition, transparency, non-discrimination and equal
treatment.  This should be achieved
through competition. 
 
This report seeks a single quote award for up
to £170,000 for the reasons detailed in this waiver, with a
maximum total contract value of £170,000 which is below the
relevant threshold for the Procurement Act 2023 to apply.
 
 
Contractual Terms
and Conditions
 
The service provider will be appointed using
the Council's standard terms and conditions as the framework for
the contract. The Council's Legal Services have been involved in
adapting the standard terms specifically to this piece of work and
the supporting proposal.
 
 
 
 
Procurement:
 
Whilst this contract is anticipated to be
below any regulatory thresholds where open tenders are required to
be called, the County Council's Procurement Rules require a minimum
of three written quotations to be obtained. Approval of a waiver is
requested based on the justification included in this report.
 
Finance
 
The costs of this appointment will be met from
within the allocated LGR budget.  Rates
have been compared against market standards for similar work and
deemed to be comparative.
 
 
Risk management
 
The primary risk associated with this
procurement waiver is the potential for challenge due to the
absence of a competitive tender process, however, this risk is
considered low. The contract value is below the threshold required
under the Procurement Act 2023, and the rationale for the direct
award is clearly documented, including the collaboration with the
other Lancashire councils and significant time constraints. To
further mitigate this risk, the County Council will publish an
award notice on Contracts Finder, ensuring openness and
accountability.
 
The risks are manageable and proportionate to
the value and strategic importance of the service, and appropriate
controls are in place to ensure compliance and continuity.

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
The purpose of the report, in the form of the
presentation slides attached at Appendix 'A', is to provide the
committee with key updates relating to the Lancashire Combined
County Authority.
content:
Matthew Sidgreaves, LCCA Chief Operating
Officer, presented an update on recent activity across the Combined
County Authority.
 
Several key developments since the previous
meeting were highlighted:
 
The authority had recently marked the first
anniversary of its establishment, with communications issued to
stakeholders reflecting on progress and outlining priorities for
the forthcoming year. It was also noted that a scheduled meeting
between the council leaders and the Minister for Devolution, Faith
and Communities was being rearranged, due to the original date no
longer being possible for the Minister.
 
It was noted that the Government had invited
new devolution proposals from councils not currently part of an
existing arrangement, aimed at expanding the number of foundation
strategic authorities.
 
It was reported that the authority had
received confirmation of £250,000 in core capacity funding
for the next financial year. It was noted that there were
disparities between capacity funding levels for foundation
strategic authorities and mayoral strategic authorities, and it was
noted that the council leaders intended to raise these concerns
with the Minister once a new meeting date had been secured.
 
It was reported that the Combined County
Authority Overview and Scrutiny Committee had met recently and that
it had been agreed that the committee would also receive this
committee's work programme for information. Likewise, it was
suggested that this committee should receive a copy of the overview
and scrutiny committee's work programme for information.
 
Regarding the transition into “Phase
Two” of the authority’s development, shifting from
mobilisation to delivery, it was noted that key milestones included
the transfer of transport responsibilities from the upper tier
authorities to the combined county authority from 1 April 2026, and
the devolution of the adult skills budget later in the year. The
first cohort of staff to be directly employed by the authority was
due to join from 1 April, and recruitment to the post of Director
of Transport was well underway, with interviews scheduled for early
April. Work would also continue to strengthen the leadership team
and review statutory officer arrangements.
 
It was reported that the authority had
responded to the Government’s consultation on overnight
visitor levies, expressing support for extending the relevant
powers to all strategic authorities, while stressing the challenges
faced by the tourism sector. The consultation on Local Government
Reorganisation was due to close on 26 March, and the authority had
submitted a neutral response owing to differing preferences
submitted by the constituent councils. Another consultation
concerned the geography of future spatial development strategies,
also due to close on 26 March. The authority had indicated support
for recognising its area as the appropriate footprint.
 
Work was also underway to respond to the
consultation on the licensing of taxis and private hire vehicles,
including consideration of the most practical roles for existing
licensing authorities and strategic authorities. This consultation
was due to close on 1 April.
 
Thematic progress updates for transport,
skills and the economy were set out in the final section of the
report.
 
Clarification was sought on the indicative
timeline for the appointment to the  new
Director of Transport post and the composition of the interview
panel. It was confirmed that the application window had closed,
shortlisted candidates had been identified, and interviews were
scheduled, with an officer-led panel undertaking the process.
 
Clarification was sought on capacity funding
and how this related to the development of in?house functions
referenced in the Phase Two plan. It was reported that limited
capacity funding currently underpinned existing support service
arrangements delivered by constituent councils, and discussions
about potential future increases in funding would influence the
speed at which functions could transition in?house. It was noted
that similar staged transitions had taken place over time in other
combined authorities also.
 
In response to a question about the planned
number of staff transferring to the authority from April and how
these arrangements were being managed and funded, it was confirmed
that fewer than ten posts would initially transfer within the
transport function, with project plans in place across each
thematic area to support operational readiness. Because these posts
were transferring from constituent councils, it was expected that
the budget for those posts would also transfer.
 
It was queried how the
LCCA’s response to the Taxi licensing consultation was being
coordinated with local authorities in Lancashire, other than
the constituent authorities. It was clarified that district council
representation was embedded within the authority's governance
structure and that engagement had already taken place with chief
executives, with further discussions planned with elected members.
The committee was assured that a collaborative and inclusive
approach would continue.
 
Resolved: That the updates be
noted.
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority has decided to approve recommendations and note updates on recent developments and progress in their first year of establishment.

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
Update on 2025/2026 Internal Audit
Plan
content:
Laura Rix, Audit Manager, Lancashire County
Council, presented the Internal Audit Progress Update.
 
It was reported that 39 audit days had been
delivered to date, noting that when the plan was originally
approved at the beginning of the year, it had not been possible to
accurately estimate the number of days that would be required due
to the early developmental stage of the authority. As a result,
some of the allocated time was not expected to be used.
 
It was noted that three pieces of audit work
were currently underway: an assurance framework review for support
services provided by constituent authorities; a review of financial
management and governance; and a review of governance and
decision?making frameworks. These audits were progressing well at
the time of reporting.
 
A query was raised on the outstanding
medium?priority action arising from the earlier audit of risk
management, around how and when the committee would be able to
consider the action as completed. It was clarified that from
2026/27 onwards, progress reports would incorporate updates on
outstanding actions, with formal follow?up work typically
undertaken one year after the original audit. Once the follow?up
review had been completed, a follow?up report would be presented to
the committee. In the interim, any updates on progress or concerns
regarding implementation would be included in the regular progress
tracking tables.
 
A question was raised regarding oversight of
audit work and who would be responsible for scrutinising the
overall delivery of the programme. It was confirmed that all work
was undertaken internally by members of the audit team. The audit
process included early engagement with the client, detailed
scoping, continuous communication throughout testing, and
collaborative agreement of draft actions to ensure they were
meaningful and achievable. Once the actions had been agreed,
finalised reports would be submitted to the committee for
consideration.
 
Resolved: That the report be noted.
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee has decided to review the Internal Audit Progress Update.

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
Approval of LCCA 2026/27 Internal Audit
Plan
content:
Laura Rix, Audit Manager, Lancashire County
Council, presented the Internal Audit Annual Plan and Strategy for
2026/2027.
 
It was noted that the plan had been developed
through discussions with senior officers, including the Chief
Operating Officer and finance colleagues from the constituent
authorities, and it was noted that the authority’s risk and
opportunity register had been used to identify gaps where assurance
work would be required during the forthcoming year.
 
It was reported that the proposed plan
totalled 85 audit days. Priority areas for 2026/27 were identified
within the plan, with particular emphasis on transport transition
arrangements and the adult skills workstreams, which were
considered the highest?risk and highest?priority areas for
assurance activity. It was noted that the scope of individual
audits would be finalised at the point each audit commenced,
although operational circumstances may require adjustments. It was
highlighted that the internal audit plan was intentionally designed
to be flexible and responsive to changes in organisational
priorities and emerging risks, and that any required amendments to
the plan would be brought back to the committee for consideration
and approval.
 
The committee sought assurance regarding the
internal audit service’s capacity to deliver the full
programme, in light of the number of audits scheduled and the early
stage of development of the authority. It was confirmed that
internal audit services operated through three audit teams,
supported by a workforce of 17 auditors. Work was delivered through
a matrix approach, which allowed auditors to collaborate across
teams and allocate resources in line with demand. Two auditors were
currently assigned to the authority's workstreams, supported as
needed by other team members. It was also clarified that much of
the audit activity for the current year had been intentionally
scheduled towards year?end due to the authority’s infancy, as
earlier audit work would have been of limited value before key
systems and processes had matured.
 
Resolved: That the Internal Audit Plan
and Strategy 2026/2027 be approved.
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee has approved the Internal Audit Annual Plan and Strategy for 2026/2027.

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
This report outlines KPMG's indicative
assessment of the audit risks for the LCCA. The planning activities
are ongoing, and the completed risk assessment and planned audit
approach will be presented at the next Audit and Governance
Committee.
content:
Debra Chamberlain, Director, KPMG, the
authority's external auditor, presented an indicative risk briefing
to the committee. It was noted that the full external audit plan
was not yet ready for presentation as planning and risk?assessment
work was still underway, however given the approaching financial
year?end, the external auditor wished to provide early visibility
of the areas likely to feature in the final audit plan.
 
The proposed materiality levels for the first
set of financial statements were outlined to the committee.
Materiality had initially been set at £1 million, based on
the forecast total annual expenditure at month nine. Performance
materiality had been set at £650,000, representing 65% of
overall materiality; it was noted that the percentage had been
deliberately set at the lower end of the acceptable range due to
this being the first?year audit. A misstatement reporting threshold
of £50,000 had also been proposed, and it was confirmed that
any errors above this level would be reported to the committee,
alongside any significant qualitative concerns.
 
Regarding emerging significant audit risks, it
was confirmed that management override of controls would be
included as a mandatory risk in line with auditing standards,
though no entity?specific concerns had been identified at this
stage. The report at Appendix 'A' set out the planned procedures
for testing this risk and it was confirmed that full findings would
be reported to the committee in the ISA 260 report later in the
cycle. A further significant risk had been identified in relation
to grant recognition. The auditors noted that, as a newly
established authority receiving and distributing multiple grants,
it was essential to ensure that revenue and expenditure relating to
grant funding were recognised correctly, supported by sufficient
internal controls. It was confirmed that the controls would be
tested and substantive testing undertaken on a selection of
grants.
 
In addition, an area of audit interest
relating to services provided in kind by the constituent
authorities was highlighted. It was noted that such support should
be appropriately valued and recognised within the financial
statements to avoid understating the cost of running the
authority.
 
The audit cycle and timetable were
highlighted, including the forthcoming value?for?money risk
assessment, which could identify risks of significant weakness
which, if identified, would be reported.
 
The audit fee and confirmation of independence
were set out in Appendix 'A'.
 
It was queried whether the external auditor
was satisfied that no key risks had been overlooked, whether
operational or strategic. It was noted that the full risk profile
could not be confirmed until both the planning work and a review of
the first draft financial statements had been completed. However,
based on material reviewed to date, no obvious omissions had been
identified from the authority’s strategic risk and
opportunity register, and it was confirmed that further analysis
would take place during the value?for?money assessment.
 
In response to a question around the
likelihood of any delay to the audit timetable due to pressures on
staff or delays in information being made available, it was
acknowledged that, as a new entity with a small resource base,
there had been some delays in receiving information but not to a
level that caused concern. It was confirmed that KPMG was working
closely with senior officers to ensure a more efficient flow of
information and that any issues would be escalated where
appropriate.
 
It was queried whether any deviations from the
proposed fees were expected. The committee was advised that no
variation was anticipated at this stage, unless significant delays
or additional resource requirements arose during the audit. It was
noted that the financial statements were unlikely to be complex in
the first year, which reduced the likelihood of any delay or
additional resources and consequential impact on fee changes.
 
A query was raised regarding the
underutilisation of resource for grant recognition schemes, and the
heightened risk allocation in this area. It was reported that many
grants continued to be administered by constituent councils and an
exercise was being undertaken to determine where those grants would
sit. The committee was advised that risk classification was based
on the potential for material misstatement within the accounts,
given the scale of grant flows, and would be reassessed once the
control framework had been reviewed.
 
Resolved: That the report be noted.
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee has decided to discuss proposed materiality levels for financial statements and significant audit risks.

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
To provide Members with an update on the
current position regarding VAT recovery under Section 33 of the VAT
Act 1994 and the interim arrangements in place pending Royal
Assent.
content:
Mark Golden, Head of Accountancy, Blackpool
Council, presented an update on the arrangements for VAT recovery,
as set out in the report, and as requested following consideration
of the issue at the previous meeting of the committee.
 
The report summarised the interim arrangements
in place while awaiting Royal Assent for the Finance (No. 2) Bill
2025-26. The committee was informed that the bill had received
Royal Assent on 18 March, and was now the Finance Act 2026,
confirming that the authority was now eligible to recover VAT on
its activities.
 
It was reported that the LCCA would be
utilising the TechnologyOne finance system, procured by Blackpool
Council, for use by the LCCA. The system had been configured to
record tax invoices accurately without allowing VAT entries to
appear on the VAT return prior to the legislation coming into
effect. Now that the Finance Act was in place, the authority would
be able to submit its first VAT return, and work was underway to
prepare a VAT return for March, ensuring that the authority would
reclaim VAT within the current financial year.
 
Clarification was sought regarding potential
financial loss relating to VAT incurred before 1 December 2025. It
was reported that constituent councils had been incurring
expenditure on behalf of the authority during the early stages of
establishment. Those councils had subsequently invoiced the
authority after 1 December, meaning the VAT was recoverable because
VAT recovery was determined based on the tax point of the invoice.
As a result, the authority was not expected to bear a VAT loss for
the period prior to direct VAT recovery eligibility.
 
In response to a question, it was confirmed
that the authority had purchased the TechnologyOne system for full
organisational use and that it would be used to produce the
statement of accounts and support all financial processing going
forward.
 
Resolved: That:
 
(i) 
The update be noted.
(ii) 
A further VAT recovery update be added to the committee’s
work programme for a future meeting.
