decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
A report explaining current levels of school
attendance and how we're supporting schools to improve.
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head
of Education Improvement to the meeting.
 
The report detailed the current levels of
school attendance across Lancashire and how the county council was
supporting schools to improve school attendance. It was explained
that every Lancashire school had a dedicated Attendance Support
Worker who provided termly visits and advice. An attendance toolkit
for schools was launched in 2025 and offered resources for
graduated, support first approaches, a further toolkit was being
drafted to support parents with a range of tools and advice to help
support good attendance in school. New staff recruited from April
2026 would also enhance attendance service capacity and review
frequency. 
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

The committee enquired about penalty
notices issued to parents when their child missed school, whether
the income was retained by the council, and whether it was felt
prosecution was a proportionate penalty. Officers advised that
approximately £1m was raised last year, which was retained
and was used to fund Attendance Staff and Children Missing
Education Staff. Decisions to issue penalty notices were made by
schools, in line with DfE guidance, with the council acting as the
issuing authority; most notices related to term?time holidays.
Members were advised that enforcement was considered as a last
resort but formed part of the wider approach to supporting
consistent attendance, with prosecutions undertaken in accordance
with national guidance.

 

Members queried the level of control
or influence the council had over school absence penalty notices
and whether advise was issued schools. Officers confirmed that the
council did provide advice to schools, but this was aligned with
Department for Education (DfE) statutory guidance.

 

The committee raised concern that
attendance discussions often focused on returning children to
school, even where mainstream provision may not be suitable.
Officers confirmed that Section 19 arrangements were used when
school was not the right place for a child at that time. This
arrangement allowed schools to work with the local authority to
access alternative education options, including individual or
small?group tuition, provision in community settings such as
libraries or placement in alternative provision or a different
educational setting. Officers explained that Section 19 provides
access to local authority funding, encouraging schools to consider
flexible solutions rather than relying solely on attendance
enforcement. The committee requested, where possible figures on the
number of children accessing alternative provision, due to
difficulties attending school and a list of alternative provision
providers.

 

The Committee discussed attendance
data which showed patterns contrary to expectations, with Preston
performing strongly while Lancaster and Ribble Valley recorded
lower attendance rates. Members queried the underlying factors,
including school type, levels of academisation, deprivation,
rurality, transport challenges, and the measurement of attendance.
Officers noted that performance in Lancaster and Ribble Valley had
improved in the autumn term but highlighted possible complexities
could include long travel distances, particularly to grammar
schools, and weaker engagement mechanisms with academies. The
Committee requested further analysis focused on Lancaster and
Ribble Valley and for a briefing note / report to come back to the
committee to look at this issue in more depth, in particular the
following areas to be considered:

Autumn?term data,
factors driving persistent
absence,
the significant increase in absence
between primary and secondary, in particular
in Ribble Valley and;
the distance children need to travel
to get to school, and if this could be a factor.



 
Resolved: That the following
recommendations be shared with the Cabinet Member for Education and
Skills:
 

That where available,
date be provided on the number of children accessing Alternative
Provision, due to attendance difficulties.

 

That a list of
Alternative Provision providers to be provided to the
committee.

 

That a report / briefing note come
back to the committee providing deeper analysis of attendance
issues in Lancaster and Ribble Valley. Consideration be given to:

Autumn?term data,
factors driving persistent
absence,
the significant increase in absence
between primary and secondary, in particular
in Ribble Valley and;
the distance children need to travel
to get to school, and if this could be a factor.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improving school attendance levels in Lancashire

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
This report discusses all cohorts of children
not in school including discussion around exclusion
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head
of Education Improvement to the meeting.
The Cabinet Member noted the increasing trends
in children missing education, elective home education and
education otherwise than at school. While acknowledging that
elective home education can be positive where provision is of good
quality, it was noted that rising numbers may possibly reflect
wider issues, including SEND challenges and disengagement with the
education system, and there was a need to strengthen support to
re?engage families and enable children to return to school, where
appropriate.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

Members queried whether statutory
School Attendance Orders had increased and the associated
timescales. It was confirmed that orders have risen in line with
increased Children Missing Education (CME) referrals, but capacity
had remained the same, although this was now being addressed, and
the process remained lengthy, often taking several months due to
appeals and complexities, including challenges in securing suitable
school placements and cases where families provide further evidence
to continue home education.

 

Members expressed concern about the
high number of CME in Preston and other areas and requested further
detail on the length of time children were waiting for school
places, the reasons behind cases, and a breakdown by district,
primary and secondary places and distance travelled. Officers
advised that CME numbers were broadly split between primary and
secondary pupils, with higher numbers in Years 10–11, largely
linked to Elective Home Education (EHE) returns, often associated
with exam pressures. It was noted that some cases also reflected
new arrivals into the area, and other key factors for high EHE
numbers included mental health needs and perceptions that schools
cannot meet pupils’ needs, rather than relationship
breakdowns with the school. It was noted that most EHE families
reported positive engagement with the authority, capacity
challenges have existed; improvements were being made through
increased staffing from three to five team members and earlier
intervention. A dedicated phone line for the EHE Team has been
introduced to support both schools and parents in making informed
decisions.

 

Members questioned what actions were
being taken to reduce the numbers of CME, particularly in areas
such as Preston, Hyndburn and Ribble Valley. Officers advised that
further analysis was being undertaken to better understand the
specific drivers in high?demand areas, noting that population
movement in places like Preston could be a significant factor.
Operationally, capacity had been increased within the CME Team,
with additional staffing and a revised approach whereby officers
now retained cases throughout, supporting families until school
places were secured. Additional work was ongoing through Fair
Access Protocols to reduce delays, improve school responsiveness,
and promote a more inclusive culture, including the use of powers
to direct placements where necessary.

 

Further to the above discussion, it
was agreed that the committee would be provided with a breakdown of
figures for Children Missing Education (179 in Preston and 101 in
Hyndburn/Ribble Valley) to provide further detailed
analysis including the length of time out of education, primary and
secondary breakdown, contributing factors, and the possible impact
of travel, distance and transport accessibility. Where possible,
details would be provided about what was being done to specifically
bring down these numbers.

 

The committee queried how it was
determined whether EHE was effective for individual families, and
whether further information was sought from schools to better
understand the reasons behind a family’s decision,
particularly where the school’s account may differ. Officers
advised that suitability was assessed against guidance, including
the expectation of a full-time education (around 25 hours),
provision of literacy and numeracy, and evidence that the child was
making appropriate progress, taking account of any special
educational needs. Alongside working directly with families, the
council analysed patterns in referrals and engaged termly with
schools that have higher numbers of EHE cases to better understand
underlying causes, recognising that accounts from families and
schools can differ and are explored further where needed.

 

It was queried what plans were being
considered to provide additional support for home educated families
and to address issues arising from unmet SEND needs. Officers
advised that work was underway to improve inclusive practice across
schools through the SEND improvement programme, focusing on earlier
identification and support to prevent escalation. Increased
capacity within the EHE Team would also enable more direct support,
including the development of support groups, alongside closer
working with Family Hubs to offer localised support, improve access
to services, and strengthen engagement with families.

 

Members highlighted the role of
colleges in supporting young people, particularly those
transitioning from home education or at risk of becoming NEET, and
raised concerns about funding constraints affecting provision,
especially for 14–15-year-olds. It was noted that while some
colleges offer early access programmes, these are often limited due
to funding arrangements, with variation across areas. It was
suggested by Members that a visit be arranged to one of the
colleges to better understand current provision, including
progression pathways for 14-15 year olds.

 

Members raised concerns about the
potential criminalisation of families where children are not
attending school due to mental health needs, and whether this could
influence decisions to electively home educate. Officers clarified
that families who elect to home educate and provide suitable
education are not subject to fines or prosecution. Enforcement
action in relation to non-attendance followed a graduated response,
with fines or prosecutions used only as a last resort where there
has been persistent non-engagement with support. It was
acknowledged that messaging around enforcement may sometimes be
misinterpreted, and this would be reviewed if specific concerns are
identified.

 

Members requested further analysis
of the increase in CME, including clearer data on trends over time,
inflow and outflow of cases, and whether this reflected local or
national patterns. Officers advised that post-COVID increases, and
greater population movement had contributed nationally and agreed
to provide more detailed breakdowns. Members suggested the
establishment of a forum for home educating families to better
understand their needs, which officers confirmed was being
explored. Concerns were also raised about the potential for
off-rolling; officers reiterated this was unlawful and challenged
where identified, noting that most cases of pupils leaving in Years
10–11 were linked to exam pressures and mental health rather
than school practices.

 

Members queried how the council
fulfilled its statutory duty to ensure suitable education for
home-educated children, given that contact may only occur annually.
Officers explained that current guidance only required families to
provide annual updates, which the council must accept unless there
were safeguarding concerns or other known issues, in which case
more proactive engagement may take place. Assessment of progress
was undertaken where appropriate by reviewing evidence of a
child’s development over time; however, for most families,
the council relied on parental assurance due to limited legal
powers to intervene.

 
Resolved: That the following recommendations be shared with the
Cabinet Member for Education and Skills:
 

That a breakdown of figures for
Children Missing Education (179 in Preston and 101 in
Hyndburn/Ribble Valley) be provided to the committee to provide
further detailed analysis including the length of
time out of education, primary and secondary breakdown,
contributing factors, and the possible impact of travel, distance
and transport accessibility. Where possible, details to be provided
about what is being done to specifically bring down these
numbers.

 

That consideration be given for a
member visit to be arranged to Burnley College or possibly
Lancaster and Morecambe College, to enhance members’
understanding of NEET provision, including progression pathways for
14–15-year-olds.

 

That regarding Data
for Children not in School (CME Referrals and EHE numbers), further
contextual (graphical and numerical) data be provided to
illustrate trends over time, to allow for consideration of
both pre and post COVID trends. Analysis could include:

Flow data showing the number of
children entering and leaving CME over time.
Possible RAG-rated analysis breaking
down the figures.
Comparison with
national trends, including analysis of how local patterns align
with or diverge from post-COVID national data.



 

That officers explore
the establishment of a Home Education Forum or engagement mechanism
to improve communication and understanding with children who are
home educated and their parents, to support partnership working and
early identification of emerging issues and provide progress
updates to the committee when possible.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to address the increasing trends in children missing education and elective home education by approving recommendations for further analysis and support initiatives.

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
This report explains how we calculate need for
school places and the current forecasts
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head
of Education Improvement to the meeting.
 
The report explained how the service
calculated need for school places and the current forecasts. The
committee were informed that the council had a legal duty to ensure
that every child had school place. Officers highlighted that in
some areas there was now surplus school places across Lancashire,
reflecting a national decline in birth rates and reduced pupil
numbers. Work was underway to develop a Surplus Places Strategy in
collaboration with partners, with proposals for it to come back to
scrutiny in the future.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, a summary is outlined below:
 

A Member queried the prioritisation
of out-of-area and SEND applications. Officers advised that
admissions follow the Council’s policy agreed in February,
with priority generally given to children living within the local
area and to looked-after children, while SEND is not consistently
included within all schools’ criteria.

 

Members raised concerns about the
impact of new housing developments on access to school places and
the need for planning to better reflect community needs, including
travel and family considerations such as siblings attending the
same school. Officers advised that school place planning involved
balancing multiple factors, including demand, available capacity
and site constraints, and suggested that concerns regarding
admissions arrangements and local pressures should be reviewed
outside of the meeting.

 

Members queried the potential
implications of increased federation of schools, including whether
shared teaching models could result in additional transport costs
for pupils. Officers advised that current practice typically
involved sharing leadership rather than teaching staff, and where
joint teaching arrangements existed, it was teachers that would
travel between sites rather than pupils, with such models not
commonly in place, but possibly to be considered as part of future
planning in line with the Surplus Place Strategy.

 
Resolved: That the following recommendations be shared with the
Cabinet Member for Education and Skills:
 
i. 
That the draft Surplus Place Strategy come back to the scrutiny
committee once ready in the coming months, as suggested by
officers.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to develop a Surplus Place Strategy to address the need for school places in Lancashire.

purpose:
As set out in Appendix C of the 2025/26
Maintenance of Highways Assets approved by Cabinet on 7 March, a
budget allocation of £500,000 was approved for Coring and
Surveying (PPMS16461) to support pavement design development for
the 2026/27 Highways Maintenance Programme.
We are now forecasting an underspend against this allocation. This
is due to several factors, most notably a reduction in activity
associated with the Local Deterioration Fund (LDF), which has
correspondingly reduced the level of coring and survey work
required during the current financial year.
Conversely, there has been an increased demand for Geotechnical
Investigation and Design (PPMS16464). This pressure is driven by an
extensive programme of Special Schemes, many of which involve full
pavement reconstruction and require more complex ground
investigation work. Several of these schemes have also attracted
significant public and political attention, increasing the need for
robust geotechnical assessment and design.
The originally approved budget provision for PPMS16464 was
£200,000. To support delivery of the 2025/26 programme, this
now needs to be increased by £50,000 to £250,000.
It is recommended therefore that the transfer of £50,000 from
the coring budget to the Geotechnical Investigation budget is
approved.

purpose:
Seeking support from Pensions Committee before
Full Council approve the admission of new Partner Funds to Local
Pensions Partnership Investment.
content:
The Head of Fund presented a
detailed report on the proposed process for Local Pensions
Partnership Investments Ltd (LPPI) to demerge from Local Pensions
Partnership Limited (LPPL) and become the subsidiary of a new
holding company (currently referred to as "TopCo") with Lancashire County Council, the London
Pension Fund Authority (LPFA) and 7 new Partner Funds as equal
shareholders.
 
It was also reported that the
County Council and LPFA would continue as shareholders for LPPL and
its remaining subsidiary Local Pensions Partnership Administration
Ltd which would continue to provide pension administration services
to its existing clients.
 
The Committee considered the
various stages set out in the report required for the demerger and
the establishment of the new holding company to oversee the
expanded pool and the Head of Fund and the Chief Legal and
Compliance Officer from LPPl answered
questions from Committee members. The Committee was also informed
that external legal and tax advice had been sought in relation to
the proposed demerger and admission of new Partner
Funds.
 
Resolved:
 
1.  That the
Committee:
 
a)  note the activity
undertaken to date and the next stages in the process
of demerging Local Pensions Partnership Investments Limited (LPPI)
from Local Pensions Partnership Limited (LPPL) and admitting new
Partner Funds into the LPPI pool.
 
b)  approve a dividend
in specie as set out in the report to facilitate the
demerger of LPPI from LPPL to a new holding company, ("TopCo") subject to the agreement of Full Council on
12 March 2026 to amend the Articles of Association of LPPL to
permit the payment of such a dividend.
 
c)  delegate authority
to the Director of Finance and Commerce (S151
Officer), in consultation with the Monitoring Officer and the Head
of the Pension Fund, to take all necessary steps to implement the
dividend in specie referred to in b) above.
 
d)  note the future
developments arising from the admission of new Partner
Funds into the expanded LPPI pool, as set out in the report
presented, including in relation to internal governance.
 
2.  That the Committee
recommend Full Council be asked to:
 
a)  approve the demerger
of Local Pensions Partnership Investments
Limited (LPPI) from Local Pensions Partnership Limited (LPPL), with
Lancashire County Council becoming a shareholder in a new holding
company (TopCo), and the admission of 7
new Partner Funds into the LPPI pool as equal shareholders in
TopCo.
 
b) 
delegate authority to the Director of Finance and Commerce
(S151
Officer), in consultation with the Monitoring Officer and the Head
of the Pension Fund, to take all necessary steps to give effect to
such approvals, including:
 
i.  the capital
reduction of shares within LPPL 
as set out in the report to create distributable
reserves.

ii.  the amendment
of LPPL's Articles of Association to permit a
dividend in specie from LPPL to TopCo,
as set out in the report.
 
iii. 
subscription to the amounts of "A" share (voting share) and
"B"
shares in TopCo set out in the report
as contribution to the regulatory capital for the
company.
 
iv. 
the cancellation of an amount of shares
in TopCo, leading to a
return of capital to the Lancashire County Pension Fund and London
Pensions Fund Authority (LPFA) as set out in the report.
 
v.  the
capital reduction of shares within TopCo from a nominal
value to a lower value to be confirmed to create distributable
reserves should dividends be determined to be paid in the future;
and
 
vi. 
entering into the various resolutions and agreements
(including
the Shareholders' Agreement) required to implement the transition
to TopCo.
 
c) 
Note that a review of the internal governance arrangements
regarding
certain shareholder matters is currently underway and a further
report on the outcome of the review will be presented to Full
Council in due course.
topline: The Pension Fund Committee has decided to approve the demerger of Local Pensions Partnership Investments Ltd and the establishment of a new holding company with multiple shareholders.

decision_maker: Community, Cultural, and Corporate Services Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
HR update on workforce planning to the
committee
content:
Jacquie McGeachie,
Interim Director of People Service, Deborah Barrow, Head of People
Strategy and CC Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for Resources, HR, and
Property were welcomed to the meeting.
 
Members were provided with an outline of
the report provided as part of the agenda pack through a
presentation drawing out key points. Context was set on the
concurrent change pressures, the efficiency plan, the improvement
plan, and the Local Government Reorganisation.
 
With regard to the Local Government
Reorganisation, members were informed that market volatility had
been anticipated, given multiple councils undergoing Local
Government Reorganisation.
 
Members were provided with some key
workforce metrics:

 

· 
On staffing, it was
reported that the establishment stood at 15,552, whilst headcount
was at 13,620, leaving approximately 1,500 vacancies.

· 
Turnover of staff
remained slightly high.

· 
Absence was
increasing, with additional support being planned.

· 
On length of service,
it was highlighted that around 5,000 colleagues had over 10
years’ service.

· 
Significant investment
was underway for apprenticeships and early careers.

 
Regarding key priorities, members were
advised that these included TUPE compliance, disaggregation
modelling, cultural considerations, wellbeing, Local Government
Reorganisation, and ensuring 'day one' readiness for all
staff.
 
Members were invited
to ask questions and a summary of discussion outlined below:
 
Members raised concerns relating to the
significant proportion of staff who had served fewer than five
years, noting the risk of losing institutional knowledge during the
transition to new unitary structures. It was explained that
modelling work had already commenced to identify which roles would
be required in successor authorities and that clarity would be
provided as early as possible. Senior level roles were expected to
face the greatest challenge, and principles relating to workforce
stability and TUPE regulations would guide future decisions.

Further discussion took place on succession planning and
opportunities for staff to progress within the new structures. It
was confirmed that workforce planning was a key priority and that
the extended lead-in period provided a valuable opportunity to
identify and support emerging talent across the organisation.

Members expressed concerns regarding the capacity required to
manage the significant workload associated with Local Government
Reorganisation. It was stated that resources would be allocated
appropriately, and additional support would therefore be required
across several council services.

The committee also discussed risks relating to specialist roles,
including social care teams and statutory positions. It was
emphasised to members the importance of preserving continuity for
vulnerable service users and acknowledged the complexity of
creating new structures without disrupting long-standing
relationships between practitioners and clients.

Members queried variations in team manager numbers and the
distinction between positions and employees. Members were advised
that the figures reflected increasing workforce demands and the
expansion of specialist roles within the organisation. Temporary
senior arrangements were highlighted as an area requiring
stabilisation prior to Local Government Reorganisation.

The committee received an update on staff survey results, noting a
decline in response rate. This was attributed partly to unusually
high participation in the previous year and indicated that levels
remained consistent with sector norms. Survey responses continued
to highlight concerns relating to change management and
communication, and officers outlined ongoing work to improve
engagement, including staff panels and leadership visibility across
services.

Members explored issues relating to hybrid working policies, staff
confidence in the reorganisation process, and the risk of councils
competing for talent. These concerns were acknowledged and
confirmed that principles for engagement with the 14 other affected
authorities would be developed. They also noted that concerns among
the workforce were linked to uncertainty rather than confirmed
outcomes, and that future updates would be provided as more
information became available.
 
Resolved: That;
 

A future report be provided detailing the
actions following item be brought forward containing a detailed
analysis of the staff survey results, including key themes,
strengths, and challenges.

 

A future report be provided to a future
meeting of the committee on the council’s hybrid working
arrangements and home working policy and its impact on retention,
morale, and service delivery.

 

A future report on the workforce matters
of Local Government Reorganisation be presented to a future meeting
of the committee, anticipated to be in Autumn 2026.  Regular
updates from the People Service to then be scheduled following key
milestones in the Local Government Review process, including a
report following the Government’s decision on the final
model.  The report to set out the planning and key milestones
of the implementation process.
topline: The Community, Cultural, and Corporate Services Scrutiny Committee has approved recommendations for workforce matters in preparation for Local Government Reorganisation.

purpose:
In November 2024, the county council was
notified of structural defects in schools constructed under the
Government’s Building Schools for the Future (BSF) Programme.
Structural engineers advised that further investigation was
required, and until these investigations and any subsequent
remedial works were completed, exclusion zones must remain in place
to ensure the continued safe operation of the schools.

Due to the failure on the part of the PFI Project Companies to take
the required action within an acceptable timeframe, pursuant to a
decision of the Interim Director of Finance and Commercialisation,
the council exercised its contractual step-in rights and arranged
for the installation of Heras fencing around all identified risk
areas, supported by on site security to ensure that no unauthorised
access occurred behind the exclusion zones.

In accordance with the Project Agreements, the associated costs are
being recovered from the PFI Contractors by way of an adjustment to
the Monthly Unitary Payments.

While a definitive timeframe for removing the exclusion zones and
security cannot yet be confirmed, the PFI Contractors have made
progress on the required remedial works, and a phased removal of
fencing and security is anticipated throughout 2026.

Additional funding is now required to secure the ongoing provision
of these arrangements until such time as time as the issues with
the masonry walls are satisfactorily remediated or satisfactory
evidence is provided that they are no longer required.

promenade and St Annes town centre by widening the footway on the
north side of St Annes Road West.
The proposed one-way provision will reduce carriageway usage,
creating an inviting and pedestrian-friendly environment with
integrated planting and a seating area between the Promenade and
Clifton Drive North.
The direction of traffic flows is derived from a study based on the
availability of adjacent roads and vehicle volumes.

purpose:
The committee is asked to consider the 2025/26
Quarter 3 Financial Monitoring Report and make any recommendations
to Cabinet.
content:
At the invitation of the Chair, County
Councillor Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for Resources, HR and
Property, gave an overview of some of the key points of the 2025/26
revenue and capital position at the end of the Quarter 3 budget
monitoring period.
 
Particular
reference was made to:
 
- 
The projected overspend figure had been reduced from some
£28m to just over £6m for the financial year which was
around average for a Quarter 3 position.
- 
£22.5m of savings had been identified by the county council's
Efficiency Review.
- 
The background of rapidly increasing costs, particularly in SEND
and in adults and children's social care, which was being addressed
to reduce the pressure.
- 
The position had improved by £4.208m since Quarter 2.
- 
£60m of planned savings had been identified.
- 
An underspend of £96m in the capital programme due to
re-phasing.
- 
The Dedicated Schools Grant overspend was £73m, largely due
to SEND pressures.
 
At the invitation of the Chair, Brendan
Arnold, Interim Director of Finance and Commerce (Section 151
Officer), made the following comments:
 
- 
Additional progress was expected to be made in reducing the
projected Quarter 3 overspend of £6m further by the end of
the financial year.
- 
The report set out the various risks and pressures and a slight
increase in the projected overspend for home to school transport
was expected during Quarter 4, but this reflected the recovery plan
for SEND.
- 
The pressures around the SEND recovery plan had been built into the
draft budget for 2026/27 which would be discussed by Cabinet later
that day.
- 
There had been a beneficial movement in the Adult Social Care
budget position since Quarter 2, reflecting progress on the
mitigations and management action in place to address the
overspend.
- 
There was a good budget and financial monitoring system in place,
and the county council was in a strong position, particularly when
compared to other, similar, local authorities across the
country.
 
The following points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
It was noted that the report would be considered by Cabinet that
afternoon.
- 
In the Key Variances section, and the references to the use of the
Public Health Grant, and other grants, to offset expenditure,
Members requested further detail on the actual spend and how
successful the use of grants being used in such a way was.
- 
Information was requested on what the eligible expenditure was not
originally budgeted for, and the use of the Public Health Grant,
which was referred to in terms of the £3.676m underspend in
Children, Family and Wellbeing.
- 
In addition, Members asked what level of confidence was attached to
the savings and income generation, for example in schools catering
given that this had been a challenge in previous years, and in
adult social care.
 
In response, officers would circulate
additional information specifically about the Public Health Grant
expenditure following the meeting. It was noted that the forecast
attainment of savings at 82% was based on period 8 numbers, i.e.
two thirds of the way through the financial year, that, as already
reported, mitigation and management action was progressing well and
that, going forward, budget monitoring reports would include more
detail on savings delivery.
 
The following further points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Members requested more detail on the actual percentage of grants
being used to meet savings targets, e.g. Home to School Transport
and the take up of grants to parents.
- 
Assurances were sought that the £2.9m underspend in the use
of the Public Health Grant as regards the prevention agenda in
health would be fully utilised.
- 
The importance of the Public Health Grant not being seen as an
option to subsidise expenditure on other services or
initiatives.
- 
A suggestion that the committee should receive a report at a future
meeting setting out how the Public Health Grant is being used.
- 
The ongoing Social Care Support Officers dispute and the resultant
cost to the county council and the impact on waiting times for
assessments for care packages.
 
In response, officers would circulate
additional information, including a schedule of Public Health Grant
expenditure, following the meeting. It was also reported that
Public Health Grant expenditure was subject to stringent conditions
and that both the Director of Public Health and the Section 151
Officer were required to be satisfied, and to sign off, proposed
expenditure was in line with those grant conditions. It was also
noted that an underspend was sometimes related to timing, and not
necessarily to not utilising the funding available.
 
The following further points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
In terms of the Capital Programme, Members questioned why there was
a significant reduction in the planned delivery for schools and the
Bus Service Improvement Plan, together with a smaller reduction in
highway maintenance.
- 
The committee requested a breakdown of all the capital programme
underspend figures set out in red in the 'Changes to Planned
Delivery' column in Table 4 of the report (page 21 refers).
- 
It was asked how the £2m figure for the winter gritting risk
area had been determined.
 
In response, officers would circulate
additional information following the meeting, some background
information about the East Lancashire Levelling Up Fund was
provided, reference was made to more detailed information on the
capital programme underspend being set out later in the report, and
the winter gritting being a case of erring on the side of caution
and a less harsh winter, to date, than might otherwise have been
the case.
 
The following further points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Schools Basic Needs Sub-block variance and the impact of the school
year.
- 
In terms of highway patching, what was the £5.4m spent on and
what is the detail of the up to £8m overspend.
- 
Further detail was requested on the £1.1m reduction in
spending on highway lighting and maintenance.
- 
Pressures in care around mental health and the projected
overspend.
- 
Areas of risk, in particular the Treasury Management and the
Dedicated Schools Grant deficit.
 
In response, officers would circulate
additional information following the meeting and, in terms of the
Schools Basic Needs Sub-block, more detailed monitoring reports
will be provided going forward. It was also reported that annual
spend on mental health services was currently around
£20m.
 
The following further points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Corporate Property Operational Planned Maintenance and the forecast
variance of £12.469m and the impact on the quality of
customer service and staff working environments.
- 
Possible delays to the 77 Road Safety, Active Travel, Sustainable
Transport Programmes, Cycling and Travel Schemes.
- 
How both spending and delivery is audited.
 
In response, officers would circulate
additional information following the meeting, delays were often due
to the nature of phasing and delivery of programmes, and Levelling
Up funding, in particular, was very
closely monitored by Government against detailed
specifications.
The following further points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Workforce and Agency costs and the impact on the budget of
recruitment challenges and sickness absence.
- 
Expected works of two new schools and whether a new school at
Whittingham would still be going ahead or if there would be
expansion of schools in the East of Preston.
- 
Minimum Revenue Provision and the visibility of interest
charges.
 
In response, officers would circulate
additional information following the meeting. It was also
referenced that the Community, Cultural and Community Services
Scrutiny Committee would be considering a report on Workforce
matters on 12 February, that the potential impact of local
government re-organisation would be having an effect, and that
there always remained the challenges of competing with the private
sector.
 
The following further points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
The overlap between the county council, NHS and Integrated Care
Board, particularly in relation to mental health and a suggestion
that the Director of Public Health and an appropriate
representative from the Integrated Care Board attended a future
meeting of the committee to discuss this issue.
- 
The previous practice that proposed highways capital schemes were
shared with divisional councillors on a district-by-district basis
by District Highways Leads to allow councillors to comment and make
suggestions, together with a similar draft list of proposed works
in schools.
- 
Guidelines had previously been requested on any overlap between the
remit of the committee and that of the Audit, Risk and Governance
Committee, for example in respect of scrutinising Treasury
Management.
 
In response, officers would consider these
aspects following the meeting. 
 
Resolved: - That:
 
(i) 
The committee gives future consideration of the Public Health Grant
expenditure, and particularly expenditure on mental health
promotion in Lancashire.
(ii) 
The committee notes that the Health and Adult Services Scrutiny
Committee would be considering a report on mental health services
at its meeting on 12 April 2026.

purpose:
This
report provides an update to Cabinet on the Council's 2025/26
revenue and capital financial position, as at the end of Quarter 3.
Securing sound and robust finances is the number one priority for
the Administration as financial security enables the delivery of
the Council's ambition for providing efficient and effective county
services to the residents of Lancashire.
 
The
forecast position at the year-end at Quarter 3 is based on several
assumptions relating to current expenditure, expected demand, cost
pressures and service knowledge and a risk assessment of savings
delivery trends and service knowledge.
 
Lancashire County Council is not unique in facing spending
pressures and challenges in delivering council services and demands
upon services. Lobbying by the local government sector of
government for increased resources continued ahead of the outcome
of the Fair Funding Review 2.0 which was published following the
publication of the Local Government Provisional Finance Settlement
in December 2025.  The resulting outcome
of this is reflected elsewhere on this agenda to
Cabinet.  Nonetheless, constraining
expenditure streams within agreed budget totals is central to the
Council’s mission to attain financial control in its
operations generally.
 
The
forecast revenue outturn position for 2025/26 at the end of Quarter
3 is an overspend of £6.117m, which represents 0.49% of the
approved budget.  Services have prepared
and continue to develop mitigation strategies with the aim of
eliminating or reducing to the maximum extent possible all these
adverse variances.  The end of the
financial year position will set out the results of these
endeavours and in the meantime the position will be closely
monitored. 
 
The
2025/26 Capital Programme agreed by Full Council in February 2025
of £299.635m was the highest value programme agreed in recent
years (in financial year 2024/25 Capital Programme delivery of
£199.152m was achieved). 
 
The
Programme has been revised to take account of the roll forward from
the last financial year, additional grants received and a review of
the profiling of likely spend at the year-end for those projects
that will be delivered over a longer period than expected in
February, which is established practice for a programme of this
size and complexity. The value of the Revised Programme has
therefore been adjusted to the sum of £299.106m. Approval of
this Revised Programme is detailed in the recommendations of the
report and details by service blocks are shown in Appendix
'B'.
 
The
forecast outturn against the Revised Capital Programme in the
current year is £203.257m resulting in a forecast underspend
of £95.849m (32.05%). This forecast delivery of
£203.257m represents 103% of the delivery achieved in
2024/25.  As is usual with the delivery
of large and complex programming it is not unlikely that this
underspend will increase as the financial year
progresses.
 
The
forecast Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) revenue outturn position at
the end of Quarter 3 is an overspend of £73.08m forecast due
to the growing demand and placement costs for pupils with Special
Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND). Consistent with many
councils nationally, the DSG funding allocation for many years has
not increased in line with the growing demand. The Council
continues to face major challenges with the increasing numbers of
pupils with SEND, bringing significant financial and service
pressures in this context. The position is being closely monitored,
with mitigation strategies developed with the aim of reducing the
variances. The draft Budget for 2026/27 contains sufficient
resources to sustain delivery of the SEND service and to finance
the associated DSG Deficit.

increasing the number of SEND units across the county. This report
outlines the wider informal engagement that has taken place and
feedback received. Approval is requested to proceed with formal
consultation for the 11 project proposals outlined within this
report.

purpose: Update on progress of the committee
content:
The Committee received an update on the progress and
ongoing work of the Joint Health Scrutiny Committee on the Shaping
Care Together Programme.
 
Concerns were expressed regarding the suitability of the
venue used for the preliminary meeting and requested whether
meetings ought to be recorded for the public. Members were advised
that while meetings were held in public, recording was dependent on
local facilities. Nevertheless, the concerns were
acknowledged.
 
Members discussed the possibility of using an alternative
venue capable of broadcasting or recording meetings. Officers
confirmed that the request could be referred to the Joint
Committee. It was suggested that venues such as West Lancashire
Borough Council facilities could provide Teams-enabled rooms and
improved accessibility while remaining reasonably local for Sefton
residents.
 
Resolved: That;
 
 
i. 
The report be
received.
 
ii. 
Further options be
explored with Sefton Council and West Lancashire Borough Council on
the use of Microsoft Teams?enabled rooms and other technical
options to support hybrid attendance and public accessibility to
joint committee meetings.

decision_maker: Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
Update on work programmes and
recommendations
content:
The Committee considered the
Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee and Steering Group
Work Programmes for 2025/26, including in-year requests.
 
Members
discussed ongoing consultations relating to vascular and
orthodontic service changes. Concern was expressed at the lack of
visible progress in launching public consultations, noting that the
Committee had previously agreed that these matters required
consultation. It was confirmed that the Committee was awaiting
necessary information from the relevant health bodies and would be
brought back to the Committee once received.

The in-year request was introduced concerning 'NHS Never Events',
which was described as serious but entirely preventable clinical
incidents occurring due to failures to follow established
procedures. It was outlined that scrutiny of data, trends, and
corrective actions could support improvements across services.
Members were advised that these were reported through Trust Quality
Accounts, which the Steering Group reviews on an annual basis. It
was suggested that this could provide an initial evidence base
before determining whether a more detailed report should come to a
full committee meeting.

Resolved: That;
 

 
i. 
The current position
regarding consultations on vascular and orthodontic services be
noted and that updates be requested.

 
ii. 
An item on 'NHS Never
Events' would first be considered by the Steering Group as part of
its review of Trust Quality Accounts in May with an invitation
extended to CC De Freitas to attend.

 
iii. 
The in-year request on
mental health integration be incorporated into the agenda for the
22 April meeting, aligning with the scheduled discussion on adult
mental health.
topline: The Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations on work programs for 2025/26, including consultations on services and 'NHS Never Events'.

decision_maker: Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
Report of the Morecambe Bay Hospital
Trust
content:
The Chair welcomed
Louise Jones, Director of Communications and Engagement and Dr
Helen Skinner, Chief Medical Officer to the meeting to discuss the
proposed bed reductions at Royal Lancaster Infirmary.

The Committee were provided with a summary of the report provided
with the agenda pack received on the proposed closure of 24 beds at
the Royal Lancaster Infirmary. In addition to providing assurances
that no services would be stopped or reduced as part of this
proposal, the following key areas were highlighted:
 

· 
Expansion of the virtual ward capacity from 46 to a planned 73
beds.

· 
Significant operational improvements over the last six months,
including enhanced board round processes, improved discharge
coordination, and reductions in patients not meeting criteria to
reside.

· 
Increased utilisation of same?day emergency care.

· 
Partnership work with local authorities to reduce
delays in discharge pathways.

· 
Alternative community?based admission pathways.

Committee members raised a series of detailed
questions concerning the safety, timing, and impact of the proposed
bed closures which included:
 

· 
Whether patients not meeting criteria to reside
continued to require care, and whether reduced bed capacity would
add pressure to social care services. The Trust stated that around
two-thirds of delays were within the Trust’s control, with
improvements already reducing the number of patients waiting, and
that community capacity had not been negatively
impacted.

· 
The difference in quality of care between hospital
beds and virtual wards. It was explained that virtual wards deliver
hospital-level interventions such as IV antibiotics and diuretics
within a patient’s home environment.

· 
Financial implications if bed closures were delayed.
The Trust noted that failure to deliver planned savings would risk
a deficit but emphasised that clinical safety would always override
financial considerations.

· 
Whether the scale and permanence of the bed
reduction constituted a significant service change. Members
expressed concerns given the proportion of beds affected, the
Trust’s OPEL 4 status, pressures on the ageing population,
and the need for clear evidence that community services could
safely absorb displaced activity.

 
Further
concerns raised included the suitability of patients’ homes
for virtual ward care and the need for tangible evidence and
supporting documents to demonstrate safety and service
continuity.
 
Resolved: That;
 

 
i. 
The proposal represented a 'significant service change' which would
inform the need for a period of public consultation before
implementation.

 
ii. 
Further documentation be provided demonstrating the
safety, capacity, and operational readiness of community
alternatives, including virtual wards and discharge
pathways.
topline: The Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the closure of 24 beds at the Royal Lancaster Infirmary, pending further documentation and public consultation.

decision_maker: Environment, Economic Growth and Transport Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
Overview of Get Lancashire Working Plan and
background, and establishment of Connect to Work.
content:
The Chair welcomed County
Councillor Brian Moore, Cabinet Member for Economic Development and
Growth, Dan Dixon, Programme Manager (Supported Employment), and
Lydia Ferguson, Enablement and Employment Team Manager, to the
meeting. The report outlined the development of Get Lancashire
Working, the strength of partnership working in Lancashire, and the
development and mobilisation of Connect to Work, a large scale
supported employment programme which went live in the summer of
2025. A presentation to complement the report was provided at the
meeting and a copy is set out in the minute book.
 
It was explained that Connect
to Work was one programme within the wider context of employability
and employment creation work carried out by the economic
development function at the council. The aim of the programme was
to help people with long term health problems access employment
opportunities.
 
A summary of the discussion at
the meeting is set out below.
 
· 
On how the Connect to Work programme was expected to
scale up over the next five years and whether this was on track, it
was reported that based on modelling and agreed profile numbers
with the Department for Work and Pensions, it was hoped to achieve
3500 participants by year 3. Currently the programme was on track
with the number of participants joining. Funding for this work was
dependent on spending reviews with funding reducing for years 4 and
5.
· 
It was emphasised that there was a risk with
recruitment of employment specialists and the number needed across
Lancashire. Integration with the local NHS was also key to the
success of the programme.
· 
The Get Lancashire Working Plan highlighted the
other target groups that the Lancashire Skills Hub was working on
in addition to the aims of the Connect to Work
programme.
· 
Current employment rate for Lancashire was 75.2%
with approximately 43,000 people needed to reach the national
target set by Government of 80% through the Connect to Work
programme and other programmes and target group work.
· 
The county council was not contributing any money to
the Connect to Work programme as it was fully funded by the
Government.
· 
On whether small and medium sized enterprises were a
targeted audience for marketing the programme, it was confirmed
that officers were working with the Federation of Small Businesses
and continued to identify marketing opportunities both online and
face to face. It was acknowledged that small and medium sized
enterprises in Lancashire were a key part to the success of the
programme.
· 
It was suggested that the county council should
establish an introduction to work or voluntary scheme with
flexibility to set the number of hours worked per week as a way of
assisting people back into work.
· 
A question was asked about the consistency of
getting to know people and whether a personal approach to
understand their circumstances was being applied. The committee was
informed that the first appointment for a participant involved
meeting with an Employment Specialist to carry out a vocational
profile and determine an individual's needs. Employment Specialists
also had access to Better Off Calculators which helped to assess
financial impact and facilitate conversations with people on
potential options. Lived experience was embedded in the design and
delivery of the programme.
· 
On whether there was a link for young people between
access to affordable and suitable accommodation, and whether
securing and sustaining work could support them in achieving a
greater level of independent living than they currently
experienced, it was highlighted that the challenge for the council
was to overcome the barrier of whether someone could earn more in
employment than what they received through receipt of benefits. The
council was also working in partnership with the Lancashire and
South Cumbria Integrated Care Board to deliver its WorkWell
programme that aimed to help disabled people and people with health
conditions to start and stay in work.
· 
A mechanism for quality assurance across the network
of providers had been established in the form of a Fidelity
Assessment system. Monthly reviews were held with service providers
and participant feedback on the customer journey was also
sought.
· 
With regard to participants' aspirations, it was
explained that the vocational profile appointments would also take
into account what a person enjoyed doing, their interests, what
skills they had at home, what they aspired to be, career
progression and identifying appropriate training needs.
· 
One councillor highlighted that a training company
based in the Fylde Coast area had already delivered the maximum
number of courses allocated in the Blackpool area and that funding
provided for this purpose had been used up. It was not clear if
this matter related to a service commissioned by the county
council. The Cabinet Member requested further information on this
matter in order to determine whether or not it related to the
Connect to Work programme and whether or not it would be possible
to vire money between providers in the area to strengthen
performance in any areas where it might be needed. It was suggested
that this matter form a recommendation to the Cabinet
Member.
 
It was also suggested that a
progress report outlining key performance indicators on retention
rates for different group successes such as veterans, disabled,
long-term unemployed, youth unemployed and the different areas of
Lancashire be provided to the committee within 6 to 12 months'
time.
 
Resolved: That,
 
(i) 
The Cabinet Member for Economic Development and
Growth be asked to consider the possibility of virementing money
between procured providers of the Connect to Work programme to
enable any underperforming areas to benefit.
 
(ii) 
A progress report outlining key performance
indicators on retention rates for different group successes
(veterans, disabled, long-term unemployed, youth unemployed) and
the different areas of Lancashire be provided to the committee
within 6 to 12 months' time.
topline: The Environment, Economic Growth and Transport Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the development and mobilisation of the Connect to Work program.

decision_maker: Environment, Economic Growth and Transport Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
This report provides members of the
Environment, Economic Growth and Transport
Scrutiny Committee with the work programme for 2025/26. The work
programme is a work in progress document and topics can be moved or
added to the programme to respond to any emerging
priorities
content:
The committee received the work
programme for the 2025/26 municipal year. A copy of the formal
written response from County Councillor Warren Goldsworthy, Cabinet
Member for Highways and Transport to the Committee's
recommendations on its Review of the TAMP made at its meeting held
on 23 October 2025, was presented at Appendix 'B'.
 
A briefing note on the
allocation of Local Transport Grants for 2025/26 was included with
the agenda set out at Appendix 'C'. In determining how to proceed
with this request, it was reported that the topic could not be
included as part of the Delivery of Major Transport and
Infrastructure Schemes – Electric Vehicle Infrastructure
report scheduled for the March meeting, as they were two separate
issues.
 
It was highlighted that
£15,009,946 pounds of capital grant funding was remaining
since approval was given by Cabinet in September 2025. Information
on how the unallocated funds would be spent remained unclear as
plans were currently in development. In considering how to proceed
with the request, it was one member's understanding that the
council was not intending to allocate the remaining funds and felt
that this represented a missed opportunity to complete improvements
needed. It was requested that written clarification be sought from
the Cabinet Member on what the intention was and to determine if
the money would be used to compensate for an overspend in other
areas. It was suggested that the reply be provided by email at the
earliest opportunity rather than wait until the next scheduled
meeting on 19 March 2026. There was a consensus from the committee
that its views should be reported to the Cabinet Member and that an
answer be provided at the earliest opportunity to enable the
committee to proceed with a potential review of the decision made
if the funding was still available before the end of the current
financial year.
 
On the Cultural and Tourism
Strategy request, it was reported that the county council did not
have a joint Culture and Tourism Strategy, but that the two areas
were separate entities covered by three separate
strategies:
 

Cultural Services
Strategy 2024-2028.
Remade: A Cultural
Investment Strategy for Lancashire which was currently being
revised.
Marketing Lancashire
Tourism Growth Strategy.

 
It was noted that the Cultural
Services Strategy would come under the remit of the Community,
Cultural, and Corporate Services Scrutiny Committee. In addition,
the committee was informed that the Cultural Investment Strategy
for Lancashire 2025-2035 would be presented to the Lancashire
Combined County Authority in the near future as cultural investment
would come under the Lancashire Combined County Authority from
April 2026.
 
On the tourism element of the
request, it was reported that work on producing a new Tourism
Growth Strategy was due to commence in the first quarter of 2026/27
with an anticipated completion date by the end of Quarter 3. It was
suggested that the tourism element of the in-year request be moved
to the 2026/27 work programme. In considering how to proceed with
the request, it was felt that whilst the new Tourism Growth
Strategy would be reviewed by the Lancashire Combined County
Authority Overview and Scrutiny Committee, the Environment,
Economic Growth and Transport Scrutiny Committee could still review
the strategy in terms of its relevance for the county council's
area. It was further suggested that the committee reviews the
strategy in quarter 3 or quarter 4 of 2026/27, once the strategy
had been written.
 
Resolved: That;
 
(i) 
The work programme for 2025/26 at Appendix 'A', be
noted.
 
(ii) 
The formal written response from County Councillor
Warren Goldsworthy, Cabinet Member for Highways and Transport to
the Committee's recommendations on its Review of the TAMP at
Appendix 'B', be noted.
 
(iii)Clarification from the Cabinet
Member for Highways and Transport on how the remaining
£15,009,946 was to be allocated or whether this money was to
be used to compensate for any overspend in other areas, be sought
at the earliest opportunity and prior to the next scheduled meeting
of the committee taking place.
 
(iv)Tourism Growth Strategy be
added to the Environment, Economic Growth and Transport Scrutiny
Committee Work Programme for 2026/27.
topline: The Environment, Economic Growth and Transport Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations on the allocation of remaining capital grant funding and add the Tourism Growth Strategy to the work programme for 2026/27.

purpose:
Application for 7-7-FP9 and 7-7-FP6 (part of
Hall Lane, Longton) to be upgraded from footpath to bridleway on
the Definitive Map and Statement of Public Rights of Way between
Hall Carr Lane and the vehicular section of Hall Lane (U8231) at
the junction with Footpaths 7-7-FP9a and 7-7-FP10.
content:
A report was presented on an application for
7-7-FP9 and 7-7-FP6 (on part of Hall Lane, Longton) to be upgraded
on the Definitive Map and Statement of Public Rights of Way from
footpath to bridleway, between Hall Carr Lane and the vehicular
section of Hall Lane (U8231) at the junction with 7-7-FP9a and
7-7-FP10.
 
The application route was shown on the
Committee plans attached to the agenda papers between points
A-B-C-D-E-F-G-H.
 
Various maps, plans and other documents had
been examined to build up a picture of the history, status, precise
line, width and other particulars.
 
It was reported that ownership of the
application route was not registered between point A and point F
and that ownership was not known. From point F through to point H,
the land crossed by the application route was all in the registered
ownership of Marsh Farm (LAN197980).
 
Based on the evidence in the report, it was
suggested that Committee had insufficient evidence, on balance,
from which to infer that the application route was a historical
public route carrying intended dedication of public rights on
horseback or cart. It was suggested that there was particular
difficulty in inferring dedication of higher rights at the Marsh
Farm location.  Without the route
passing through Marsh Farm and connecting with Hall Carr Lane, it
would leave the remainder of the route as having to be sufficiently
evidenced as dedicated as a dead end cul de sac highway and it was advised there was
insufficient evidence from which to infer, on balance, such a
dedication.
 
The recommendation was that the application be
refused and that no Order be made to alter the Definitive Map and
Statement.
 
Committee were informed if they considered
there was sufficient evidence of an old vehicular highway, Officers
had considered whether any of the exemptions under the Natural
Environment and Rural Communities Act 2006 applied and considered
that they did not and that the Act would have extinguished
mechanically propelled vehicular rights, leaving the old vehicular
route to be appropriately recorded as a restricted
byway. 
 
Resolved: That:
 
(i) 
The application be rejected.
 
(ii) 
A Definitive Map Modification Order not
be made.
topline: The Regulatory Committee has decided to reject the application to upgrade a footpath to a bridleway in Longton.

content:
A report was presented on an application for
the addition of a bridleway from Wennington Road to Old Moor Road,
Wennington in the Parish of Tatham to the Definitive Map and
Statement of Public Rights of Way.
 
The application route was shown on the
Committee plan attached to the agenda papers between points
A-B-C-D-E-F-G.
 
Various maps, plans and other documents had
been examined to build up a picture of the history, status, precise
line, width and other particulars.
 
Committee were informed that the route through
Points A-G was currently not recorded as any highway on the
Definitive Map and Statement.
 
Based on the evidence in the report, it was
suggested that Committee had sufficient evidence, on balance, that
the route was a historical public route available not only for use
on foot or horseback but also as a vehicular highway. There had
been no legal stopping up of those rights and so it was advised
that the legal maxim "once a highway always a highway" applied.
 
Committee were informed if they considered
there was sufficient evidence of an old vehicular highway, Officers
had considered whether any of the exemptions or exceptions under
the Natural Environment and Rural Communities Act 2006 applied and
considered they did not and that the Act would have extinguished
any mechanically propelled vehicular rights leaving the route to be
appropriately recorded as a restricted byway.
 
Resolved: That:
 
(i) 
The application with modification to recognise carriageway rights
be accepted.
 
(ii) 
A Definitive Map Modification Order be made under S53(2)(b) of the
Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 to record a
restricted byway from Wennington Road to Old Moor Road, Wennington
as set out in this report.
 
(iii)That the Order be promoted to confirmation,
if necessary by submitting it to the Planning Inspectorate.
topline: The Regulatory Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the addition of a bridleway from Wennington Road to Old Moor Road.

purpose:
Application for the diversion of part of
Footpath FP0205027 at Bramblewood, Barnacre-with-Bonds,
Wyre.
content:
A report was presented on an application for
the diversion of part of Footpath FP0205027 at Bramblewood, Barnacre-with-Bonds, Wyre.
 
The length of existing path to be diverted was
shown on the Committee plan attached to the agenda papers by a bold
continuous line and marked as A-B. The proposed alternative was
shown by a broken line marked A-C-D.
 
Consultations with the statutory undertakers
had been carried out and no objections or adverse comments on the
proposal had been received.
 
Committee were advised that the proposed
diversion was considered expedient in the interests of the owners
of the land for reasons of privacy and security. Bramblewood was a private residential dwelling and,
currently, the public footpath passed close to the house and
divided the garden.
 
Diverting the path from the middle of
Bramblewood would significantly
increase the privacy and security of the residents, whilst
providing a route that was safe and convenient for public use.
 
Resolved:
 
(i) 
That an Order be made under Section 119 of the Highways Act 1980 to
divert part of Footpath FP0205027 shown by a bold continuous line
and marked A-B on the Committee plan to a bold broken line marked
A-C-D.
 
(ii) 
That in the event of no objections being received, the Order be
confirmed and in the event of objections being received and not
withdrawn, the Order be sent to the Secretary of State for the
Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Authority take a
neutral stance with respect to its confirmation.
 
(iii) 
That provision be included in the Order such that it is also made
under Section 53A of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, to
amend the Definitive Map and Statement of Public Rights of Way in
consequence of the effect of the Order.
topline: The Regulatory Committee has decided to approve the diversion of part of Footpath FP0205027 at Bramblewood for the privacy and security of residents.

purpose:
This report updates Lancashire Pension Board
members on the Fund's progress in reviewing its Communications
Strategy.
content:
Ms Brown, Pensions Governance
Lead, presented a report on the progress of review of the
Lancashire County Pension Fund (LCPF) Communications Strategy which
included a proposed exercise to engage with those scheme members
for whom LPP had a postal address but no email and provide them
with contact details regarding pension benefits.
 
When considering the proposed
exercise Board members made the following comments:
 
· 
Whilst acknowledging that the preference was for
'digital first' approach the proposed paper based exercised was
welcomed as a way of engaging with scheme members, most notably
deferred members within 10 years of retirement.
 
· 
Care needed to be taken about the style and content
of any paper-based mail drop so that recipients did not dismiss it
as junk mail or a scam.
 
· 
It was suggested that the mail drop include a
dedicated telephone contact number at LPPA with specific staff who
were briefed on the purpose of the exercise answering
calls.

· 
That where possible feedback should be sought from
deferred members to assess the effectiveness of the paper-based
exercise.
 
· 
Consideration should be given to the timing of the
paper-based exercise, for example linking it to the circulation of
Annual Benefit Statements.
 
· 
It was noted that the Fund would pay the cost of the
exercise. 
 
Resolved:
 
1.  That the findings
and conclusions to date of the review of the LCPF
Communications Strategy, as set out in the report presented, are
noted.
 
2.  That the Head of
Fund note the views of Board Members and explore
with the Chief Executive of LPPA how to undertake a paper-based
communications exercise to engage with deferred scheme members, for
whom the administration service does not have an email address, and
encourage them to register with Pension Point.
topline: The Lancashire Local Pension Board has decided to engage with deferred scheme members through a paper-based communications exercise.

purpose:
This report provides an update on various
regulatory issues and industry news to assist the Local Pension
Board members in their role.
content:
Ms Hunt, Technical &
Administration Pension Lead, from the Pensions Team, presented a
report on pension related regulatory issues and Board members
discussed the following:
 
· 
The LGPS shared cost AVC arrangement, and the
legislation to bring unused pensions funds/death benefits payable
from a person into a person's estate for Inheritance Tax purposes
with effect from 6 April 2027.
· 
Draft statutory instruments which relate to pooling
and local investment proposals in the LGPS, though the term 'local'
was not clearly defined. The Board was informed that in Lancashire
the Combined County Authority had developed a Growth Plan to help
identify propositions for small/large scale investments within
Lancashire.
· 
The proposed abolition of admission agreements and
their replacement with a 'deemed employer' approach where new
employers would be responsible for tasks like enrolment, ill health
retirement decisions, and payment of pension strain
costs.
· 
A proposal to enable Academies to consolidate their
participation in the LGPS into a single pension fund rather than
being spread across multiple funds, but with measures in place to
prevent employers from choosing a Fund based solely on lower
contribution rates.

In response to a query
regarding the increase in workload for the Local Pensions
Partnership Administration Ltd (LPPA) associated with various
regulatory matters in the report the Head of Fund suggested that
the matter be addressed in a future report to the Board.
 
Resolved:
 
1.  That the updates on
various regulatory matters, as set out in the report
presented and given at the meeting, are noted.
 
2.  That a report be
presented to a future meeting on the specific work areas
of the Local Pensions Partnership Administration Ltd impacted by
various regulatory issues and the Company strategy to address any
increase in workload.
topline: The Lancashire Local Pension Board has decided to approve recommendations on various regulatory matters related to pensions.

purpose: Statement of accounts - 2024/25
content:
Khadija Saeed, Head of Corporate Finance, and
Brendan Arnold, Interim Director of Finance and Commerce, presented
the Statement of Accounts 2024/25.
 
It was noted that members received a briefing
on 30 June 2025, with the draft accounts published by that date as
required. The external audit was largely completed, with only a few
items outstanding, and an unmodified opinion was expected. Some
amendments had been made since the June publication, with the main
ones set out in the report.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

Officers would provide requested
redundancy figures from April 2025 to date, a breakdown of the
declared interests held by councillors and committee members in
relevant companies, and additional detail on the figures relating
to children who have missed education, after the meeting.

 

Grant Thornton representatives
confirmed that the increase in external audit fee levels covered
additional work, notably on investment properties. Members were
referred to the reconciliation included in the report pack which
reconciled the financial statements to the fee, which included work
relating teachers’ pensions, LCDL and prior?year items.

 

Council Tax short?term debt had
reduced, as relating to the amounts reported in the council's
balance. Officers would provide a breakdown of Council Tax debt per
district after the meeting.

 

Under IFRS 16, the Private Finance
Initiative liabilities were recognised and as they were paid down,
the liability value decreased; this flowed through to the reported
amounts.

 

School reserves were monies held on
behalf of schools, arising from prior?year surpluses passported
from the education grant. They belonged to schools.

 

In relation to academisation
disposals, under regulations, assets transferred and were
de?recognised from the Council’s balance sheet when a school
converted to academy status; effectively, the Council would no
longer own those buildings post?conversion.

 
Resolved: That
 
 
i. 
The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts for Lancashire County Council be
approved as set out in the report.
 
 
ii. 
The Chief Financial Officer be authorised to approve any immaterial
further changes to the statement of accounts for 2024/25; and
 
 
iii. 
The management Letters of Representation, as set out, be approved
and signed by the Interim Director of Finance and Commerce and the
Chair of the Audit, Risk and Governance Committee, prior to them
being made available to the external auditor.
topline: The Audit, Risk and Governance Committee has decided to approve the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts for Lancashire County Council.

purpose: Annual report to March 2025
content:
Sarah Ironmonger and Ian Pinches, Grant
Thornton UK, presented theAuditor's Annual Report.
 
It was noted that the report covered value for
money arrangements across financial sustainability, governance, and
economy, efficiency and effectiveness. No significant weaknesses
were reported, though some improvement recommendations were
raised.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

Assurance was provided on the
follow?through of recommendations, the delivery of recurring
savings, and progress on structural transformation. It was
emphasised that ongoing dialogue had taken place and that, although
the Council had adequate reserves, it needed to avoid reliance on
one?off measures.

 

Scrutiny of the 2026/27 draft budget
had taken place and improved Dedicated Schools Grants forecasts
were confirmed, which had reduced the projected year?three
deficit.

 

Savings delivery for 2025/26 stood
at around 82%, with new plans identified to support future
savings.

 

Around 460 responses had been
received to the 2026/27 budget consultation, far higher than last
year. More information would be circulated to committee members
after the meeting.

 
Resolved: That the Auditor's Annual
Report be noted.
topline: The Audit, Risk and Governance Committee has decided to approve the recommendations in the Auditor's Annual Report.

content:
Khadija Saeed, Head of Corporate Finance, and
Brendan Arnold, Interim Director of Finance and Commerce, presented
the Treasury Management Activity 2025/26.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

Short?term local authority lending
markets provided favourable rates and readily accessible cash for
sub?12-month needs. Counterparties depended on availability and
prevailing rates, with supply/demand pushing rates higher later in
the year.

 

The quoted borrowing rates were
per?annum, with costs time?apportioned for the exact number of days
borrowed.

 

Regarding the Dedicated Schools
Grant (DSG) deficit position, officers explained pressures within
the special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) block,
alongside the statutory override that permitted DSG deficits to be
carried forward and financed through borrowing. It was noted the
special school build programme aimed to reduce costly out of area
placements, and highlighted improvements in forecast budget
provision.

 
Resolved: That the Treasury Management
Activity 2025/26 be noted.
