purpose: Audit findings for LCC to March 2025
content:
Sarah Ironmonger and Ian Pinches, Grant
Thornton UK, presented the Lancashire County Council Audit Findings
Report 2024/25.
 
It was highlighted that the audit had gone
smoothly. The auditors outlined adjusted items and unadjusted items
resulting from the audit. It was noted that the unadjusted impact
was not deemed to be material.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

The Private Finance Initiative and
IFRS 16 lease understatement of approximately £10 million was
a one-off implementation issue during its first year.

 

Headline materiality was used for
the overall conclusion, but lower sampling thresholds and
triviality reporting ensured sensitive items were captured. This
resulted in fewer missed issues. It also allowed management to
adjust items where appropriate.

 
Resolved: That the Lancashire County
Council Audit Findings Report 2024/25 be noted.

content:
Georgia Jones and Stuart Basnett, Grant
Thornton UK, presented the Lancashire County Pension Fund External
Audit Findings Report 2024/25.
 
It was highlighted that the audit had gone
smoothly and the auditors expected to issue an unqualified
opinion.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

In reference to valuation
differences between draft accounts and manager confirmations, it
was confirmed the Pension Fund assets were around £12bn,
making the difference less than 0.5%. Subsequently, this was deemed
immaterial and driven by the December to March valuation timing.
Had it exceeded materiality, management would have made adjusted
changes.

 

Digital Services had mitigated
Oracle Fusion risks via strengthened privileged access reviews,
segregation of duties, generic account evidence, leaver access
windows and formal access requests. Additionally, monthly
monitoring checks were now in place and a dedicated team had been
established. It was confirmed no fraudulent accounts had been set
up.

 

Regarding pooling and management
fees, the sector was undergoing significant change. Cost recovery
would be pursued where appropriate, with arrangements under
review.

 

The Fund held approximately
£150m in direct local property investments within Lancashire,
alongside a diversified global portfolio via Local Pensions
Partnership Investment Limited.

 
Resolved: That the Lancashire County
Pension Fund External Audit Findings Report 2024/25 be noted.

purpose:
This report sets out for the committee the
internal audit work performed following the
13 October 2025 Committee meeting, up to 05 January 2026.
content:
Andrew Dalecki, Head of Internal Audit,
presented the Internal Audit Progress Report.
 
It was noted that 51% of the internal audit
plan was completed or underway, despite staffing pressures, and
most assurance opinions remained positive. Follow?up audits
indicated good implementation progress. Key work included primary
school audits, treasury management advisory work, grant work and
several unplanned assignments responding to emerging risks.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

School attendance audits had focused
on the actual education being received, ensuring a clear
distinction between alternative provision and genuine cases of
children missing education.

Within the recruitment and
onboarding sample, only one employee had fully documented probation
reviews, with others lacking complete records. Internal Audit had
acknowledged this was disappointing and committed to resampling in
the follow?up audit. The recommended use of Oracle Fusion reminders
would create persistent prompts for line managers, and Internal
Audit had undertaken to work with People Services to strengthen
monitoring and compliance reporting, including possible escalation
to Executive Director level, to ensure completion was actively
checked.

The service's approach to
maintaining capacity and quality included active recruitment, a
rebalanced team structure with more trainees and auditors,
succession planning, and matrix working across directorates, whilst
noting that it would take time for newer staff to build
experience.

It was reported to Internal audit
that some historic treasury decision making records had been lost
or corrupted during a device to cloud migration, limiting certain
evidence trails. Digital Services were unable to find any lost
data, and future decisions would be recorded in Mod.Gov to ensure
secure retention. The loss related to officers' notes rather than
high?volume transaction data, though the materiality of the
information was acknowledged.

Regarding historic investments and
compliance, it was explained that although deviations from the
matrix had occurred, such as ratings below AAA and exceeded limits,
policy at the time had permitted exceptions with Director of
Finance approval. Current controls and reporting had since been
strengthened. Further information about the specific non?compliant
areas and the rationale for each exception would be provided after
the meeting.

School fund (unofficial) accounts
were standard practice in almost all schools and were used for
non?DSG income such as fairs and donations. These accounts were
required to be audited annually, managed under terms of reference,
and used solely for pupils’ benefit with appropriate
financial controls in place.

The full Treasury Management
Internal Audit Report would be published, excluding confidential
information, after the meeting.

 
Resolved: That the Internal Audit
Progress Report be noted.
topline: The Audit, Risk and Governance Committee has decided to approve recommendations in the Internal Audit Progress Report.

purpose: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
content:
Khadija Saeed, Head of Corporate Finance, and
Brendan Arnold, Interim Director of Finance and Commerce, presented
the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27.
 
It was noted that the strategy set out the
borrowing requirement to finance capital commitments, proposed
counterparties for short?term deposits, and confirmed the plan for
no new investments greater than 12 months.
 
A commissioned review with Arlingclose Limited
had set out options for the long?term investment portfolio;
officers proposed holding existing investments until a business
case for sale had arisen and a Working Capital Enhancement Reserve
was being established to support cash?flow and any future disposal
opportunities.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

The long?term gilts portfolio had
yielded roughly 2% per annum, generating steady income, although
capital values had remained depressed following BoE interest rate
increases. They highlighted that, unlike pension or insurance
funds, the Council had experienced fluctuating cash flows, and
funds tied up in gilts had reduced liquidity, increasing the need
for short?term borrowing. The budget had contained sufficient
provision for this approach.

 

The strategy avoided selling bonds
at a loss unless there was a clear long?term business case.
Specialist treasury advice had been sought to identify potential
market opportunities. A cash?backed reserve would also been built
through property disposals, underspends, and windfalls to improve
liquidity and support any phased sales if long?term modelling
indicated a net benefit.

 

Further information, setting out
yield calculations, and the execution routes used, including
third-party broker involvement would be provided after the
meeting.

Relating to the internal audit
report on Treasury Management, the use of the term “broadly
compliant” was clarified in relation to historic
decision-making on treasury management, which was the subject of an
internal audit review. It was explained that although certain
lending limits had been exceeded and some documentation gaps had
existed, overall treasury management activity had aligned with the
approved framework in place at the time, including Director of
Finance approval routes for investments below AAA. It was noted
that the current strategy now applied tighter parameters and
strengthened reporting requirements.

It was clarified that any potential
bond sales would need to be supported by a robust long term
business case, assessed in line with the Prudential Code and
treasury management guidance, with the purpose of optimising risk
and liquidity.

The proposed restriction on entering
new investments longer than 12 months had reflected the
Council’s priority to reduce borrowing and maintain strong
liquidity. It was confirmed that any surplus cash would have been
used to reduce debt rather than commit to long dated
investments.

 
Resolved: That the Treasury Management
Strategy 2026/27 as set out, be recommended to Full Council for
approval.
topline: The Audit, Risk and Governance Committee has decided to approve the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, setting out borrowing requirements, investment options, and cash flow management.

purpose:

and Opportunity Register for the
committee to consider and comment on. The register has been
refreshed to reflect

management
arrangements are both robust and effective.
content:
Hannah Race, Head of Governance, presented the
Corporate Risk and Opportunity Register – Quarterly
Update.
 
It was noted that there was continued close
monitoring of the Adult Social Care demand, SEND, the Council
Improvement Plan, and school places. The Financial Sustainability
risk score had reduced from 16 to 8, reflecting the anticipated
adoption of the two?year financial strategy, confirmation of the
multi?year settlement which enabled longer?term planning, and the
progress made in managing the in?year budget.
 
In response to questions, members were
informed that:
 

Risk scoring for financial
sustainability was seasonal and linked to the budget setting cycle.
When a balanced draft budget is in place, and in?year overspend
forecasts are reduced, the associated risks are naturally
de?escalated. More information about historic risk scores would be
provided after the meeting.

 

Systems were confirmed to be
dependable and the Chief Financial Officer's Section 25 assessment
indicated the Council was in a satisfactory position. Quarterly
movement in risk scores should be expected.
A risk deep dive into Adult Social
Care demand, including mental health access and outcomes, would be
provided at a future meeting.

 
Resolved: That the Corporate Risk and
Opportunity Register be approved.

purpose:
A report to provide additional information on
possible alternative key parameters to be used in the funding
strategy and the impact on Scheme Employer contribution
rates
content:
The Chair reminded the
Committee that at the meeting in December 2025 a decision on the
key parameters of the Funding Strategy Statement had been deferred
to allow further information/advice to be provided in relation
to:
 
a) A scale of options
between 110% and 120% in relation to the Funding
  Buffer
(including associated employer contribution rates and relative
risk
 
metrics).
b) Up to date
information regarding the financial markets.
c) Information
regarding the Funding Strategy Statements of other LGPS
 Pension
Funds, where known.
 
He highlighted paragraphs in
the report which related to each of the points above, and referred
to the recommendation that the Committee 'approve the parameters as
detailed in the draft Funding Strategy Statement of the proposed
funding buffer (120%), recovery period (20 years), Future Service
Discount Rate (CPI + 2.25%) and Past Service Discount Rate (CPI +
2.65%) and note that these parameters result in a provisional
average employer contribution rate of 11.0% from April 2026 –
a reduction from the current 17.1%. This recommendation provides a
high likelihood of achieving the Fund’s key long-term
objectives of ensuring the solvency of the Fund and long-term
stability of contributions, while also delivering very significant
contribution reductions'
 
The Chair then invited the
Senior Officers present to comment before the debate, and the
Director of Law and Governance referred to the evidence and
information set out in the report and the procedure for the
Committee for considering the advice presented prior to decision
making. 
 
The Director of Finance and
Commerce (Section 151 officer) referred to the previous discussions
regarding the key parameters and reminded the Committee of its
fiduciary duty to employers and scheme members within the Fund,
which would be readily fulfilled by the recommended funding buffer
of 120% or a buffer of 115% but could be challenging at
110%.
 
The Head of the Pension Fund reported that the
significant increase in the funding level at the valuation
presented an opportunity to return some of surplus back to
employers through reduced contributions, whilst mitigating the risk
of potential future rate increases. He added that the recommended
funding buffer of 120% would reduce employer contributions from
17.1% to around 11% whereas a buffer of 115% would reduce rates to
an average of 9.1% and a lower buffer of 110% would further reduce
rates to an average around 7.4%. He also referred to the assessment
of risks associated with the different employer contribution rates
(as set out in Appendix C to the report) and noted that the single
biggest risk would be that setting contribution rates too low at
this valuation may require them to increase in the future.
 
The Chair opened the debate and
Councillor Whipp thanked the officers and advisers for the
additional information provided in the report and reaffirmed his
view that the current 110% funding buffer and 16?year surplus
repayment period should be retained.
He highlighted the importance
of generational equity between pensioners and active members,
reminded the Committee that the existing parameters had been
established when the Fund was in a weaker position, and stated that
at one?third over?funded the Fund was able to maintain the current
position without jeopardising beneficiaries. He expressed concern
that maintaining contribution rates at higher levels could impose
additional pressure on local authority budgets, potentially
resulting in workforce reductions that would in turn reduce both
employer and employee contributions. Reference was also made to
previous officer advice that any buffer level on a scale between
110% and 120% could be defended, and to actuarial advice regarding
the increased prudence of moving from 110% to 120%.
 
Councillor M Smith spoke in
support of Councillor Whipp's proposal, referring to the current
strong funding position as a result of the performance of the
Fund's investments. He noted the cash surplus and the potential to
reduce employer contributions whilst satisfying the fiduciary duty
of the Committee.
 
The following Motion was
then MOVED and
SECONDED - That the Committee retain
the current 110% buffer and the 16?year repayment period,
consistent with proposals made at previous meetings.
 
The Actuary referred to the
funding level and surplus which was due to the performance of the
Fund's investments over the last three years and cautioned that the
surplus was volatile and the current situation could reverse in the
future. He reminded the Committee that any risk of having to raise
contribution rates in the future would be mitigated by a high
buffer whereas concerns regarding affordability would be addressed
with a lower buffer, though with an associated increased risk of
future contributions being increased.
 
The proposed Motion was
discussed, with the current funding level, pressures on local
authorities, employer contributions, the volatility of investment
markets and the potential mitigation of risks via the funding
buffer all being referred to by Committee members. During the
discussion it was noted that the Motion related to a recovery
period of 16 years and that the modelling set out in the report did
not account for that as it was not included in the resolution
agreed by Committee in December.
 
An amendment to the Motion was
therefore proposed and it was MOVED
and SECONDED that the reference to a 16-year recovery period be deleted and
replaced with the 20-year recovery period as reflected in the
modelling by the Actuary.
 
At this point, the Chair
adjourned the meeting for a short break.
 
The Committee reconvened and
was joined by the Head of Democratic Services who advised Committee
members regarding the Motion for a Funding Buffer of 110% with a
16- year recovery period and the subsequent amendment to change the
recovery period to 20 years in accordance with the modelling and
advice from Officers/Actuary as set out in the report.
 
Councillor Whipp accepted the
proposed amendment and the Head of Democratic Services confirmed
that the amended Motion before the Committee was now to agree a
Funding Buffer of 110% with a 20-year recovery period.
 
On being put to the vote the
Motion was LOST.
 
Councillor Whipp then proposed
a Motion that the Committee approve a Funding Buffer of 115% with a
20-year recovery period.
 
The Committee discussed the
Motion, and in response to a question the Director of Finance
confirmed that a Funding Buffer of 115% would satisfy the required
fiduciary duty of the Committee. The Head of Democratic Services
also clarified for the Committee that the other key parameters in
the recommendation set out in the report would remain the
same.
 
The Motion was then put to the
vote and it was Resolved: That a Funding Strategy Statement with a funding buffer (115%),
recovery period (20 years), Future Service Discount Rate (CPI +
2.25%) and Past Service Discount Rate (CPI + 2.65%) resulting in a
provisional average employer contribution rate of 9.1% from April
2026 (a reduction from the current 17.1%) is approved as it
provides a high likelihood of achieving the Fund’s key
long-term objectives of ensuring the solvency of the Fund and
long-term stability of contributions, while also delivering very
significant contribution reductions.
 
Following the vote
Co-opted members Ms S Roylance and Mr P Crewe, County Councillor S
Rigby and County Councillor M Lavalette all indicated they
wished their opposition to the Committee not
following the recommendation set out in the report, based on the
advice of the Actuary and officers for a 120% funding buffer, to be
recorded in the Minutes.
topline: The Pension Fund Committee has decided to approve a Funding Strategy Statement with a funding buffer of 115% and reduced employer contribution rates, despite opposition from some members.

purpose:
The 
Complaint Handling Code published by the Local Government and
Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO) came into effect on 1 April
2025.  From April 2026, the LGSCO will
commence judging all councils in England on compliance with the
Code.  The Code applies to all
council services under the Corporate Complaints
Procedure (e.g. Highways, Transport, Education, Environment)
but does not affect statutory children's or adult social care
complaints. Many of the stipulations of the Code (such as
Equality Act compliance and a 2-stage officer led procedure)
already form part of the council's current Corporate Complaints
Procedure, although some further updates are required to make it
fully compliant.
 
As a new digital recording system for
Corporate Complaints is being launched in February 2026, it is
therefore proposed that the new system will apply timescales to
fully align with best practice and with the Code. Therefore, the
Corporate Complaints Procedure must also be revised from February
2026. 
A draft revised Corporate Complaints
Procedure, fully compliant with the Code is attached at Appendix
A.
 
The main changes are as follows:  
 
a) 
The differences between a
‘service request’ and
a ‘complaint’ are clearly defined. 
b) 
If we decide not to accept a complaint, an explanation will be
provided, setting out the reasons why the matter is not suitable
for the complaints process and the right to take that decision to
the Ombudsman.
c) 
We have 5 working days to acknowledge a complaint, however the new
complaints system will do this automatically.
d) 
Stage 1 complaints should be responded to within 10 working days
from the acknowledgment but may be extended with reasons
provided.
e) 
Stage 2 remains 20 working days from the acknowledgment (the
same as the current procedure) but may be extended with reasons
provided.
f) 
If we need to extend the timescale, we must provide a reason and
provide details of the Ombudsman.
g) 
A maximum time limit of 3 months to respond is clearly defined.
h) 
A senior officer is responsible for complaint
performance, identification of trends, and driving
service improvements. 
i) 
A 'Member Responsible for Complaints' is referenced (the Cabinet
Member for Data, Technology, Customer and Efficiency already
carries out this function).
j) 
An annual complaints performance and service improvement report on
Corporate Complaints will be produced every financial year for
consideration by county councillors for scrutiny and challenge.
k) 
An annual self-assessment will be published alongside all annual
reports outlining service improvements and learning and made
public.
 
The Executive Leadership Team (ELT) have been
briefed on the proposed changes, and information was shared at a
briefing with Cabinet/ELT alongside consideration of the annual
reports of complaints for 2024/25.
 
Under section 9.52, paragraph 58 of the
council's Scheme of Delegation to Officers, Directors are
authorised to prepare, approve and amend policies relating to the
operation of the services under the officer's management (except
where these are otherwise reserved to members).
 
This is a decision to update a policy which
may impact the public, and therefore it will be recorded and
published in accordance with section 9.49 of the Scheme of
Delegation to Officers.

purpose:
Following a review of Lancashire County
Council's Highway Safety Inspection Policy and associated annexes,
several adjustments are recommended. The proposed changes include
the adjustment of guidance response times in the risk matrices to
better reflect the risk based approach as described in the UK Roads
Liaison Group’s "Well-Managed Highway Infrastructure: A Code
of Practice". This means accounting for highway network hierarchy
and an emphasis on Inspector risk assessment to determine
appropriate response times. An extension of the existing validation
process to include all public reported defects other than
emergencies is also proposed to improve the accuracy of assigned
response times.

purpose:
Consideration of the county council's 2026/27
Budget
content:
At the invitation of the Chair, County
Councillor Stephen Atkinson, Leader of the County Council, and Mark
Wynn, Chief Executive, gave an introduction on the draft budget to
the committee.
 
In doing so, the Leader thanked all those
officers who had been involved in putting together the draft budget
and highlighted that this was a unique opportunity for the
committee to make positive recommendations on the budget as part of
the consultation process which had attracted nearly 500
responses.
 
The Leader set out the challenges that the
county council faced, including the national challenge of
increasing demand on services whilst noting that the county council
was in a good position compared to many other local authorities
across the country. He advised that Cabinet would be proposing the
lowest council tax rise for 12 years and was recommending capital
investment of £290m.
 
The Chief Executive set out some of the
context to the budget process, reflecting that, whilst the budget
was a complex process, scrutiny of the draft budget was something
that good councils did well.
 
The Chief Executive outlined that the budget
process had run alongside the efficiency review which had informed
some of the proposals in the draft budget. The draft budget also
contained proposed ways forward for some of the challenges, for
example SEND and in relation to investments, and also set aside
some funding for Local Government Reform.
 
In concluding the Chief Executive echoed the
Leader's thanks and appreciation to all those officers who had been
involved in the process and highlighted that this meeting of the
committee was one of the most important meetings in the run up to
Full Council setting a budget on 26 February.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Leader and Chief Executive for their introductory comments.
 
At the invitation of the Chair, Brendan
Arnold, Interim Director of Finance and s151 officer, gave the
committee an overview of the draft budget, and the process around
it, and made particular reference to:
 
• 
The Operating Environment
• 
Budget Scrutiny
• 
Key Strategic Issues - Provision.
• 
Very Long-Term Investment Portfolio
• 
Key Statistics
• 
Capital and Debt
• 
The Provisional Settlement
• 
Savings and Efficiency Review
• 
Risks and Issues
• 
Next Steps
 
Subsequently, Kieran Curran, Head of Corporate
Strategy and Policy, gave the committee an overview of the budget
consultation exercise, and a summary of the responses received,
which had run from 3 December 2025 to 13 January 2026. The budget
survey questionnaire and the full budget survey report were also
provided to the committee.
 
Particular reference was made to:
 
• 
How the consultation was undertaken
• 
Information on the feedback received from residents, stakeholders,
and others
• 
How the county council was responding to the issues raised
• 
Next steps
 
The following points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Return on long term investments (bonds) and the cost of specialist
advice.
- 
The core spending increase in relation to the proposed council tax
increase.
- 
Risks to the county council's budget of any delay to the vesting
day for local government re-organisation.
- 
Any future risk of not taking the full council tax rise
available.
- 
Assumptions in the Section 25 report.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Interim Director of Finance and S151 officer, and the Head of
Corporate Strategy and Policy, for their presentations.
 
At the invitation of the Chair, County
Councillor Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for Resources, HR and
Property, made some brief remarks on the draft budget and thanked
all those involved in the Efficiency Review Cabinet Member Working
Group, the work of which had run alongside the budget process and,
as outlined earlier, informed some of the proposals in the draft
budget.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Cabinet Member for Resources, HR and Property for his
remarks.
 
The committee then received a series of
presentations from Cabinet Members and senior officers, covering
each of the county council's directorate areas of work in turn.
 
1. 
Adults, Health and Wellbeing Services
 
At the invitation of the Chair, County
Councillor Graham Dalton, Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care, and
County Councillor Daniel Matchett, Cabinet Member for Health and
Wellbeing, addressed the committee.
 
A presentation was then given by Helen
Coombes, Executive Director, Adults, Health and Wellbeing, together
with Sakthi Karaunanithi, Director of Public Health; Mairead
Gill-Mullarkey, Director of Operations; John Williams, Director of
Operations; and Matthew Emerson, Director of Strategic
Commissioning and Quality.
 
The following points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
The Disabled Facilities Grant, the Better Care Fund, improved
partnership working with districts and improving the pathways for
applicants.
- 
The balance between investment and savings.
- 
Utilising the voluntary, community and faith sector.
- 
Hospital discharge pathways and changes to modelling/working.
- 
Reportable illnesses (TB and Measles).
- 
25 full time equivalent posts would be lost across the whole
directorate over 3 years.
- 
The impact on the budget of the recent consultation on the care
homes and day centres.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Cabinet Members and officers for their attendance.
 
2. 
Education and Children's Services
 
At the invitation of the Chair, County
Councillor Matthew Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills,
and County Councillor Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for Resources, HR
and Property, addressed the committee.
 
A presentation was then given by Dave Carr,
Director of Policy, Commissioning and Children’s Health; and
Paul Turner, Director of Education and Inclusion.
 
The following points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Investment in Children's Care Homes and impact of savings.
- 
Children's Mental Health issues and provision.
- 
Use of the Public Health Grant
- 
SEND Brokerage Team and level of risk.
- 
Early Years top slicing of funding.
- 
Success of income generation modelling.
- 
Whether grant funding is new or existing.
- 
Home to School Transport and potential establishment of council
owned, not for profit, companies.
- 
Continuation of existing planned SEND Units.
- 
Best Start in Life and Family Hubs Grant and the impact on phonics
development.
- 
Implications of any full-time equivalent staffing reductions.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Cabinet Members and officers for their attendance.
 
 
3. 
Place
 
At the invitation of the Chair,
County Councillor Joshua Roberts, Cabinet Member for
Rural Affairs, Environment and Communities; County
Councillor David Dwyer, Cabinet Member for Data, Technology,
Customer and Efficiency; County Councillor Warren
Goldsworthy, Cabinet Member for Highways and
Transport; County Councillor Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for
Resources, HR and Property; County Councillor
Brian Moore, Cabinet Member for Economic Development and Growth;
and County Councillor Matthew Salter, Cabinet Member for Education
and Skills, addressed the
committee.
 
A presentation was then given by Phil Green,
Executive Director of Place, together with Simon Lawrence, Director
of Growth and Property; Matt Townsend, Director of Highways and
Transport; Jonathan Edwards, Director of Environment and
Regulatory; and Clare Coupe, Director of Communities and
Engagement.
 
The following points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
A breakdown of the aggregated savings to be provided.
- 
Use of Public Health Grant to support road safety.
- 
Changes in reserves.
- 
Mobility crossings.
- 
Reduction in operational expenditure and maintenance.
- 
Transport costs of waste in relation to food waste changes.
- 
Opportunities for income generation around Trading and Scientific
Services, country parks and pre-planning application advice.
- 
Provision for upgrading and additional locations for Waste
Recycling Centres.
- 
Anaerobic Digestion and levels of food waste required.
- 
Consultation with all county councillors on the draft Highways
Capital Programme.
- 
Closer working with town and parish councils.
- 
County council investment in the Eden Project, Morecambe.
- 
Highway Development pre-application fees.
- 
Budget provision for repair of historic road surfaces, e.g. cobbled
surfaces.
- 
Visibility of the interest costs of capital programme in the
revenue budget.
- 
Outstanding delivery of decisions relating to highways  taken under the previous administration.
- 
Impact on rural areas of winter gritting reductions.
- 
Opportunities for museum services as a result of local government
re-organisation proposals.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Cabinet Members and officers for their attendance.
 
4. 
Resources
At the invitation of the Chair, County
Councillor Stephen Atkinson, Leader of the County Council; County
Councillor Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for Resources, HR and
Property; and County Councillor David Dwyer, Cabinet Member for
Data, Technology, Customer and Efficiency,
addressed the committee.
 
A presentation was then given by Laurence
Ainsworth, Executive Director of Resources, together with Brendan
Arnold, Interim Director of Finance and Commerce (s151 Officer);
Sarah Reed, Interim Director of Strategy and Innovation; Jacquie
McGeachie, Interim Director of People; and Peter Lloyd, Director of
Digital.
 
The following points were raised and
discussed:
 
- 
Service re-design.
- 
100 full time equivalent posts would be lost across the whole
directorate over 3 years. As the current number of vacancies was
136, this would be managed accordingly to reduce the impact.
- 
Technology savings and any long-term risks, e.g. to security of
systems and the cloud.
- 
Supplies and Services – recycling of the county council's own
goods such as furniture and ICT equipment.
- 
Salary sacrifice and insurance savings equating to £1m.
- 
£11m of redundancy costs and if those were comparable to
previous years or comparable to other local authorities.
- 
Potential of establishing an arms-length purchasing organisation
and collaborating with external organisations established by other
local authorities.
 
The Chair, on behalf of the committee, thanked
the Leader of the County Council, Cabinet Members and officers for
their attendance.
 
Following a brief adjournment, the Interim
Director of Finance and Commerce (s151 Officer) gave the committee
an overview of the guiding principles for reserves and capital
which were set out in the report and how they might be applied as
part of the budget process.
 
It was also noted that cross referencing
between budget headings and information in the efficiency review
report considered previously by the committee, would be introduced
into the budget report to be considered by Cabinet and Full
Council.
 
The committee then discussed the
recommendations that it might wish to make to Cabinet in respect of
the draft budget for 2026/27.
 
Following a period of debate, it was moved by
County Councillor Azhar Ali, and seconded by County Councillor Gina
Dowding, that: -
 
(i) 
Cabinet be urged to consider different, not for profit, models as
to how to upgrade care homes and day centres in Lancashire, having
regard to value for money.
(ii) 
Cabinet be asked to establish a cross-party working group,
reporting to the relevant scrutiny committee, on the modernisation
of care homes and day centres in Lancashire.
(iii) 
Cabinet be asked to put into the budget an indicative sum for
modernisation of care homes and day centres.
 
On being put to the vote, equal votes were
cast, five in favour of the motion and five against the motion,
with no abstentions.
 
The Chair declined to use their casting vote
and, in accordance with Procedural Standing Order D20.5, the motion
was LOST.
 
It was then moved by County Councillor Azhar
Ali, and seconded by County Councillor Gina Dowding, that: -
 
(i) 
Cabinet be urged to consider different, not for profit, models as
to how to upgrade care homes and day centres in Lancashire, having
regard to value for money.
 
On being put to the vote, the motion was
CARRIED.
 
(ii) 
Cabinet be asked to establish a cross-party working group,
reporting to the relevant scrutiny committee, on the modernisation
of care homes and day centres in Lancashire.
 
On being put to the vote, the motion was
CARRIED.
 
Following a further period of debate, it was
moved by County Councillor Mark Jewell, and seconded by County
Councillor Gina Dowding, that: -
 
(i) 
Cabinet be asked to give consideration to concerns related to
Mental Health outcomes both in Adults and Children's and to whether
or not the Council is resourcing this to a level that the
appropriate assessments can be undertaken in a timely manner.
 
On being put to the vote, the motion was
CARRIED.
 
(ii) 
Cabinet be asked to utilise the Public Health Grant first, and
other funding sources, to support those mental health issues that
may be identified.
 
On being put to the vote, the motion was
CARRIED.
 
(iii) 
Cabinet be asked to consider the funding required to implement the
improvement plan for Adult Social Care as a result of the Care
Quality Commission inspection report.
 
On being put to the vote, the motion was
CARRIED.
 
Following a further period of debate, it was
moved by County Councillor Aidy Riggott, and seconded by County
Councillor Azhar Ali, that: -
 
(i) 
The Leader be asked to write to the relevant Secretary of State to
receive assurance that the Council will not be looked on less
favourably by the Government in future funding allocations by
setting a council tax precept below the maximum available.
 
On being put to the vote, the motion was
CARRIED.
 
It was therefore:
 
Resolved: - That:
 
Care Homes and Day Centres in Lancashire:
 
(ii) 
Cabinet be urged to consider different, not for profit, models as
to how to upgrade care homes and day centres in Lancashire, having
regard to value for money.
(iii) 
Cabinet be asked to establish a cross-party working group,
reporting to the relevant scrutiny committee, on the modernisation
of care homes and day centres in Lancashire.
 
Mental Health Outcomes/Adult Social Care
Improvement Plan
 
(iv) 
Cabinet be asked to give consideration to concerns related to
Mental Health outcomes both in Adults and Children's and to whether
or not the Council is resourcing this to a level that the
appropriate assessments can be undertaken in a timely manner.
(v) 
Cabinet be asked to utilise the Public Health Grant first, and
other funding sources, to support those mental health issues that
may be identified.
(vi) 
Cabinet be asked to consider the funding required to implement the
improvement plan for Adult Social Care as a result of the Care
Quality Commission inspection report.
 
Future Funding and Council Tax Precept
 
(vii) 
The Leader be asked to write to the relevant Secretary of State to
receive assurance that the Council will not be looked on less
favourably by the Government in future funding allocations by
setting a council tax precept below the maximum available.
topline: The Budget and Finance Scrutiny Committee has decided on recommendations for the draft budget, including upgrades to care homes, mental health resources, and council tax precepts.

content:
Andreas Feldhaar and Roxanne McAllister gave
the Board a presentation and workshop session on the draft
Corporate Parenting Strategy objectives.
 
The Board received a presentation and workshop
session on the draft Corporate Parenting Strategy 2026-2030
objectives.
 
The following seven Objectives were proposed
to the Board, who were then asked to discuss and comment on the
objectives during the workshop.
 
1. 
Children and young people have a voice in the way we deliver our
services.
2. 
Recognising and championing the individuality of our children and
young people, promoting big dreams and goals and celebrating all
their success.
3. 
Children and young people will have a safe, stable and loving home
to live in and be cared for.
4. 
Children and young people are well prepared, supported and have
lasting relationships when leaving care.
5. 
The health and wellbeing of our children and young people in care
and care leavers will be a priority for everyone.
6. 
Children and young people are safe inside and outside their
homes.
7. 
Children and young people will be supported to achieve their own
goals and be ambitious in education, employment and training.
 
Following discussions, feedback was received
from each group as below:
 
Objective 1
 
In terms of this Objective the group were
supportive with the content however would look to use
"influence/power/impact" instead of "voice" of the children and
young people.  There also needed to more
information regarding localised participation groups.
 
Objective 2
 
The Board was informed that this group
recommended using the term “uniqueness” rather than
“individuality,” as it was more meaningful for young
people. They suggested clearer statements on recognising cultural
identity, lived experience and intersectionality. The group felt
some sections of the draft lacked clarity and required more
specific commitments on what the Council would do in practice.
 
Objective 3
 
The feedback highlighted the value of a
clearer narrative explaining the full care pathway, from early
years to care leavers, including kinship care, foster care,
residential provision, Supported Accommodation, Staying Put and
Staying Close. Members also recommended using more relational
language such as “cared about” rather than “cared
for,” and replacing “professionals” with
“trusted adults”.
 
Objective 4
 
This group provided feedback which emphasised
the need for consistent language linked to the Leaving Well model.
The group reported that clarity was required around who held
responsibility for preparing young people for adulthood, including
district councils and other partners. The group highlighted the
importance of young person?led decision?making, transparency about
how decisions were made, and embedding co?production throughout the
strategy. Members also discussed weaknesses in communication
routes, noting that information often failed to reach young people
through current processes. They stressed that young people should
be supported to be as actively involved as they wished in visits,
meetings, assessments and plans.
 
Objective 5
 
The Board noted the group’s suggestion
to develop a young?person?friendly version of the strategy to
ensure accessibility. Feedback emphasised that the strategy should
refer to developing young people’s skills and confidence in
managing their own health as they move into adulthood. The group
also recommended defining “good health and wellbeing”
from the perspective of young people. Members discussed the need
for flexible service delivery, greater choice for young people in
accessing health services, and future?proofing language in light of
forthcoming changes to corporate parenting duties nationally.
 
Objective 6
 
Members were informed that the group viewed
the term “safe” as too passive and preferred
“protected from harm,” reflecting a stronger
professional responsibility. The group also recommended referencing
psychological safety and the complexities of transition to adult
safeguarding frameworks. Members highlighted the need for clear
commitment to proactive safeguarding at all stages of the care
journey.
 
Objective 7

The Board noted that the content was broadly supported, however,
identified several areas where language and grammar required
strengthening. The group reported that the draft over?emphasised
the role of social workers and personal advisers and did not
sufficiently reference schools as corporate parenting partners. It
was suggested that the objective be reworded to reflect the shared
responsibility held by all stakeholders involved in each
child’s education journey.
 
In general, the recurring themes across all
groups included the need for clearer, more accessible language;
consistency of terminology; strengthened co?production; and
ensuring the strategy directly reflected young people’s
voices.  In terms of the distinction
between the corporate parenting “Objectives” and the
“Promise to Children,” it was clarified that the
Promise described individual practitioner commitments, whereas the
Objectives set out the strategic priorities for corporate parents
as a whole.
 
Resolved:  That the Corporate Parenting
Board:
 
(i) 
Noted the comments provided and requested that officers incorporate
feedback received into the next draft of the Corporate Parenting
Strategy.
(ii) 
A further draft of the Strategy will be presented at the next
meeting in March 2026.
topline: The Corporate Parenting Board has decided to approve recommendations for the draft Corporate Parenting Strategy objectives for 2026-2030.

purpose:
Planning application LCC/2025/0001 Planning
application for a change of use of an area of green space (Use
Class F2(c) into an outdoor area for educational purposes (Use
Class F1(a). Land to the south of Woodnook Primary School; between
Belfield Road and Royds Street, Accrington
content:
A report was presented on an application for a
change of use of an area of greenspace (Use Class F2(c)) into an
outdoor area for educational purposes (Use Class F1(a)) on a parcel
of land to the south of Accrington Woodnook Primary School between Belfield Road and
Royds Street, Accrington.
 
The report included the views of Hyndburn
Borough Council, the Ecology Service and Lancashire County Council
Highways Development Control. Twelve representations objecting to
the application had been received, the details of which were set
out in the Committee report.
 
Committee's attention was drawn to the amended
Update Sheet which included details of 3 further representations
received from residents of Royds Street, and an additional
condition to remove the permitted development rights that would
apply upon the change of use being granted, allowing new school
buildings to be erected on the application site without the need
for a planning application.
 
The Head of Development Control presented a
Powerpoint presentation showing site
location plans and an air photograph of the site, proposed
development layout plan, improvement of wider open space plan and
photographs of the view towards the existing school and the view
across existing open space.
 
It was reported that Paragraph 1 in the
Committee report referred to 'outdoor play area' which should have
stated 'outdoor classroom'. County Councillor Sutton stated that
this error may have resulted in more objections being received.
 
It was confirmed to Committee that the county
council owned the application site and the wider open space
surrounding the site. County Councillor Owens queried why no
improvements had been proposed for the wider open
space.  It was reported that improvement
works were only covering the area behind the houses as this area
was the most affected by the proposed development.  The overall proposal was part of the county
council's levelling up programme so it was necessary to specify to
central government exactly what the money was being spent on with,
taking into account budgetary constraints. However, as the land on
the application site was well-used by residents, better facilities
for residents would be provided on the wider open space, in terms
of properly surfaced footpaths, to improve access.
 
It was reported that the trees to be removed
to create the footpath network were not considered to be
significant species and had therefore not been required to be
included in the arboricultural
assessment.
 
The officers answered questions from
Committee.
 
Resolved: That planning
permission be granted subject
to:
 
(i) 
The conditions set out in Appendix 'A' of the
Committee report.
 
(ii) 
The addition of condition 7 as follows:
 
 
7. The provisions of Part 7 Class M
to Schedule 2 of the Town and County Planning (General Permitted
Development) Order 2015 or any amendment, replacement or
re enactment thereof are excluded and
shall not apply to this development. Any development referred to in
that part shall only be carried out pursuant to a planning
permission granted under part III of the Town and Country Planning
Act 1990 or any amendment, replacement or re-enactment thereof.
 
Reason : To
safeguard the amenity of local residents and to conform with Policy
DM29 of the Hyndburn Local Plan.
topline: The Development Control Committee has decided to grant planning permission for the change of use of greenspace near a primary school, despite objections from residents.

diversion of a Public Right of Way, construction of a water
attenuation pond and landscape and ecological mitigation areas,
including 2 metres high acoustic and ecology fencing, temporary
soil/material/plant storage and compound areas at the
junction.
 
The report included the views
of the Lead Local Flood Authority, County Archaeology Service,
Ecology Service, Environment Agency, United Utilities, Natural
England, Lancashire County Council Highways Development Control and
National Grid.
 
The scheme had been included in
several public consultations as part of wider proposals to improve
the local road network. It had first been consulted on in 2015 and
2019 as part of plans to dual the A582, which involved changes to
multiple junctions including the one subject to this application.
More recently, in summer 2024, the scheme had been presented during
a public engagement exercise focused on traffic calming and
sustainable travel measures in Preston, Penwortham, and Lostock
Hall. The scheme has also featured in consultations for both the
South Ribble Local Plan and the Central Lancashire Local Plan,
though these had only considered the general concept of road
network upgrades without detailed designs. Feedback from these
consultations influenced the scheme’s design, leading to
improvements in accessibility, pedestrian and cycle infrastructure,
and bus stop provision.
 
For the current application,
five letters of objection and one letter expressing neither support
nor objection had been received, the details of which were
set out in the Committee report.
 
Committee's attention was drawn to the Update
Sheet which included details of the consultation response from
South Ribble Borough Council and some amendments to the wording in
the conditions. It was noted that 'Condition 8h' should have read
'Condition 9h'.
 
The Senior Planning Officer
presented a Powerpoint presentation showing site location plans,
site plan as existing (junction site), site plan (separate works
compound), air photograph of the site and proposed new junction
arrangements plan. Also shown were photographs of the view from the
footway between Centurion Way and Fidler Lane showing the most
easterly roundabout, views taken from Model Farm showing the two
roundabouts with the most westerly in the foreground and the view
showing the route the remodelled Centurion Way would
take.
 
In relation to a query about
the objections from United Utilities, it was reported that
Condition 3 covered these concerns.
 
In response to a question about
what the consequences would be if the programme or funding
expectations changed, Committee were informed that this application
was part of a wider programme of works along the A582 and, as part
of the business case of securing considerable funding from the
Department of Transport, planning permission was required to be in
place to demonstrate the project could be delivered. The entire
scope of the work along the whole of the A582 had to be within the
overall budget envelope; if there were any additional costs to this
development, which was a relatively small part of the wider
programme of works, the design for the overall programme would need
to be looked at as this would have an impact on the works required
along the whole route.
 
A short adjournment took place
whilst clarification was sought in relation to tree cover removal
required for this development.
 
Upon reconvening the meeting,
the Head of Development Control presented a Powerpoint slide of a
plan taken from the arboricultural survey, showing the location of
the vegetation to be removed from part of the route, which had been
put in place when the road was first built in 1970. As part of this
particular scheme, the highway was required to be widened on the
approach to the junctions, which was the area of landscaping being
lost. It was reported that these were not veteran or specimen trees
and that, as part of the bio-diversity net gain works, off-site
planting would be carried out to mitigate this loss. The scheme
included new noise reduction fencing to protect those residents
living closest to the junction and a condition relating to
landscaping the site after the junction improvements had been
carried out, which would include new planting where there was space
to do so.
 
It was reported that condition
7 referred to no excavation or ground disturbance works taking
place until a detailed programme of archaeological investigation,
recording, and protection had been submitted to and approved by the
County Planning Authority.
 
Resolved: That planning
permission be granted subject
to:
 
(i) 
The conditions set out in Appendix 'A' of the
Committee report, covering time limits, working programme,
construction environmental management plan, construction matters,
archaeology, drainage, landscaping and habitat and landscape
management.
 
(ii) 
The following changes to the conditions:
 
Condition 3  - Amend wording of condition to say 'No
development of the Croston Road junction improvement shall commence
until…'
 
Condition 4 -  Amend wording of condition to say 'No development
of the Croston Road junction improvement shall commence
until…'
 
Condition 7 - Amend wording of
condition to say 'No development of the Croston Road junction
improvement shall commence until…'
 
Condition 8 - Amend wording of condition
to say 'No development of the Croston Road junction improvement
shall commence until…'
 
Amend management period to 25
years.
 
Condition 9 - Amend wording of
condition to say 'No development of the Croston Road junction
improvement shall commence until…'
 
Condition 9h) – inset
'temporary' before 'protective fences, exclusion barriers and
warning signs'.
 
Condition 10 i) amend management
period to 5 years

purpose:
The purpose of this paper is:

• To introduce the Health and Wellbeing Board on the
development of a 5 Year Strategic Commissioning Plan and the
specific contents within
• Present the proposed Commissioning Intentions for
2026-27
• Outline key milestones, deliverables and assurance
expectations
• Set out progress to date and highlight areas requiring
Health and Wellbeing Board engagement, oversight or decision.
content:
Jane Cass, Director of Partnerships and
Collaboration, presented the report of the Lancashire and South Cumbria Integrated
Care Board (ICB) setting out the development of the NHS Medium-Term
Planning Framework and the emerging 5 Year Strategic Commissioning
Plan. The report also provided an update on the Commissioning
Intentions for 2026/27, key milestones, and areas requiring Health
and Wellbeing Board engagement.
 
Members were informed that the Integrated Care Board has
commenced early development of its Commissioning Intentions for
2026/27, informed by national planning frameworks. The 5 Year
Strategic Commissioning Plan will be supported by the Joint
Strategic Needs Assessment (JSNA), Clinical Strategy, delivery
plans, and organisational development planning.
 
The Board noted that the 5 Year Strategic Commissioning
Plan would be available from April 2026 and it was requested that
it be presented to a future meeting of the Health and Wellbeing
Board.
 
The Board received a presentation outlining Commissioning
Intentions for 2026/27 aligned to the NHS “Three
Shifts” model: Hospital to Community, Sickness to Prevention,
and Analogue to Digital. Key areas include neighbourhood health
model development, prevention and early diagnosis, and digital
transformation.
 
Members emphasised the importance of alignment with Joint
Strategic Needs Assessment (JSNA), financial sustainability, and
equitable service transformation. The Board welcomed early
engagement and noted interdependencies with Neighbourhood Health
Plans.
 
Following the presentation, a Board member raised
concerns regarding the continuing difficulties experienced by
residents in accessing NHS dental care across Lancashire and it was
requested that the Director of Public Health provide, at the next
appropriate opportunity, a clear and comprehensive update on the
current state of NHS dental provision.
 
The update was requested to include:
 
· 
Latest statistics on access to routine and urgent NHS dental
appointments across Lancashire.
· 
Identification of significant gaps in provision, with particular
reference to communities experiencing the greatest health
inequalities.
· 
Assessment of the extent to which these gaps are widening
inequalities and placing avoidable pressure on other parts of the
health system.
 
In light of the scale of unmet need, the
Member further asked that the Director set out practical local
opportunities to expand provision, including:
 
· 
How prevention programmes could be strengthened or better
targeted.
· 
The current availability of skilled dental professionals and
clinical facilities, including any facilities equipped for dental
training and treatment but currently under?utilised due to the
absence of NHS commissioning arrangements.
· 
Opportunities to support recruitment and retention within the local
dental workforce.
· 
How collaboration with the Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB could
be accelerated to unlock additional capacity and improve access to
NHS dental care.
 
The Director of Public Health was also asked
to outline the specific actions Public Health Lancashire is
currently taking, or urging partners to take, to improve NHS dental
provision in the short and medium term, and to identify any support
or decisions required from the Board to drive progress.
 
In view of the Board’s statutory
responsibilities for population health, confirmation was also
requested of how oral health outcomes—including indicators
relating to children’s oral health, adult oral disease
prevalence, and emergency dental attendances—will be
routinely reported to the Health and Wellbeing Board to enable
monitoring of trends, emerging risks, and the impact of local
interventions.
 
Following the requests made to the Director of
Public Health, it was agreed that a report on Oral Health, would be
made to address the issues raised at the next Board meeting in
March 2026.
 
Resolved:  That the Health and Wellbeing Board:
 
(i) 
Received the update
and considered how it can further contribute and get involved, for
example to receive updates and contribute to the development of the
plan, or indeed, a draft.
(ii) 
Agreed that the
Lancashire and South Cumbria Integrated Care Board continues to
attend the Health and Wellbeing Board to provide progress reports
and share drafts of the strategies outlined in the
report.
(iii) 
Agreed that the 5 Year
Strategic Commissioning Plan will be presented at a future meeting
of the Health and Wellbeing Board.
(iv) 
Agreed to receive a report from the Director of Public Health at a
subsequent Board meeting addressing the issues raised on Oral
Health.
topline: The Lancashire Health and Wellbeing Board has decided to address the issue of improving access to NHS dental care in the region by developing a 5 Year Strategic Commissioning Plan.

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
The presentation outlines that Lancashire
Child and Youth Justice Service (CYJS) is a multi-agency
partnership supporting around 500 children annually through
prevention, diversion, and statutory interventions. The service has
strengthened its place-based, partnership-led approach to tackling
anti-social behaviour and exploitation, with notable achievements
in reducing first-time entrants and custodial sentences.

Key strengths include robust multi-agency collaboration, effective
support for accommodation and mental health needs, and innovative
community projects. However, challenges remain with rising
re-offending rates and high numbers of children not in education,
employment, or training (NEET), reflecting broader national
trends.

CYJS is focused on improving data sharing, workforce development,
and multi-agency strategies to address serious youth violence and
NEET rates. Ongoing preparation for inspection and continuous
improvement in governance and service delivery remain priorities
for the year ahead
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew Salter, Cabinet Member for
Education and Skills (on behalf of County Councillor Simon Evans, Cabinet Member for Children
and Families) and Georgine Lee, Head of Service Fostering, Adoption
and Adolescent Services to the
meeting.
 
The report presented that the Lancashire Child and Youth
Justice Service was a multi-agency service supporting approximately
500 children annually through prevention, diversion and statutory
interventions. A detailed presentation was also provided to members
of the committee.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from the
committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

Members queried the timeliness of
KPI data, noting that the service was often required to work with
information that was slightly out of date. Officers acknowledged
the challenge regarding published data which provided national
comparison and advised that work was ongoing to improve the
currency and availability of performance data via the development
of an internal dashboard which would provide month by month data.
The service also now conducted a monthly data meeting to track
trends, allowing officers to identify emerging increases or
decreases allowing them to respond proactively.

 

In relation to reoffending data, the
committee noted that the chart presented contained information
approximately two and a half years old. Officers clarified that
this was inherent to the methodology, as reoffending rates were
measured over an 18?month period following a young person’s
last recorded offence, resulting in inherent reporting lags.
Officers further advised that although the rate of reoffending had
increased for the period April 2024 to March 2025, this could not
be compared with national benchmarks yet due to that data not being
published yet.

 

Members raised concerns that
different teams across the service were independently tackling NEET
issues and queried whether more shared approaches or data
integration could streamline this work. Officers confirmed that
although multiple teams were involved such as the Children in Care
Team, School Improvement and Virtual School, the committee could be
reassured that the service was aligned and teams worked
collaboratively, ensuring consistent approaches across the system
to ensure there was no duplication of service.

 

The committee sought clarity on the
recommendation in the report to support service priorities for the
coming year, asking for greater detail on what those priorities
specifically entailed. It was confirmed that the service priorities
for the upcoming year were focused on the Areas for Development for
2025 / 26. It was recommended that further information be provided
on the service priorities.

 

The committee asked what progress
had been made in reducing the criminalisation of looked after
children and how trauma?informed practice was being embedded across
the system. Members expressed concern that some residential care
staff, who are often underqualified and may not fully understand
the complex needs of young people, could be more likely to contact
the police rather than using deescalation and trauma?informed
approaches, potentially leading to unnecessary criminalisation.
Officers advised that, while specific figures could be provided if
required, the service was absolutely working actively with
children's homes to support children at risk of criminal or sexual
exploitation and to ensure that appropriate, trauma?informed
responses were used. This was a joint piece of work between
Children's Social Care and Youth Justice and wider partnerships. A
strategic data initiative had been developed and was being led by
Safer Neighbourhoods which was identifying hot spots, key schools
and children's homes that may require support and a restorative
approach was being used in those areas with staff and children.
Officers emphasised that the impact on victims is fully considered
and that this approach is embedded within current practice as well
as a trauma informed approach.

 

The committee noted that reoffending
rates in South Ribble were the highest in the county and queried
how many of the young people who reoffended had previously engaged
with the Prevention and Diversion Programme, given the scale of the
issue. Officers explained this was something the team were now
considering in depth. It was noted that a significant proportion of
children who did engage with the programme did not go on to
reoffend, and that checks were routinely carried out to establish
whether a young person was known to the service, and if so, the
level of engagement they had. Officers highlighted that while
engagement was mandatory for those subject to a statutory order,
the Prevention and Diversion Programme itself was voluntary and
dependent on consent, which presented challenges in securing
consistent participation. Work was also underway to analyse the
types of offences involved such as anti?social behaviour or more
serious criminal activity, to build a clearer picture of patterns
and contributing factors. Officers confirmed that this analysis was
ongoing and would be supported by a detailed action plan.

 

In discussing the identified Areas
of Development, Members sought clarification on the proposed
community and faith mapping activity, noting that such information
was not routinely monitored at a national level and questioned its
purpose. Officers explained that the exercise would be to focus on
understanding the demographics of young people involved in serious
youth violence, where local data currently showed a
disproportionate representation of certain groups. The intention
was to gather a fuller picture of community needs in Lancashire and
determine whether targeted work was required to address imbalance
or vulnerability. Members queried how a young person’s faith
would be identified, and officers confirmed that this information
was requested at the point a child is booked into police custody.
Officers also acknowledged the distinction between faith and
ethnicity, noting that both factors required sensitive and accurate
consideration as part of the wider mapping exercise.

 

Members noted that none of the
current Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) included financial
measures and asked whether there was comparative information on the
cost of delivering the service, particularly in relation to
reoffending in comparison to other authorities. Officers confirmed
that such data was available, including budget information from
other local authorities and their expenditure on children who were
remanded, although this information was not presented as part of
the KPI set. It was emphasised that the financial impact of not
engaging with young people at an early stage would likely be far
greater, as the cost of subsequent interventions increases
significantly when reoffending is not effectively addressed.

 
Resolved: That the following
recommendations be shared with the Cabinet Member for Children and
Families:
 
i. 
That in the 2026 / 2027 scrutiny work programme, the Child and
Youth Justice Service item be considered earlier in the cycle,
along with the Child Justice Plan which will go through Cabinet and
Full Council in May 2026. A provisional date of October 2026 is
recommended. 
 
ii. 
Details of the key service priorities over the coming 12-month
period to be shared with the committee.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improving the Lancashire Child and Youth Justice Service's performance and priorities.

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
The report will share the attainment data for
2025 from Lancashire schools, an Annual Report of the work
completed by the Education Improvement service to support this and
the draft Education Strategy The Lancashire Way 2026 -
2028.
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew Salter, Cabinet Member for
Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head of Education Improvement to the meeting.
 
A
report and presentation were provided to the committee and
included Attainment Data for Lancashire schools, the Annual
Report on the work of the Education Improvement Service and the
draft Education Strategy "The Lancashire Way" for 2025 –
2028.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from the
committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

Members queried whether lower early
years outcomes in Burnley, Hyndburn and Pendle were linked to
weaker uptake of early education places for two? and
three?year?olds. Officers confirmed that uptake was indeed lower in
those districts, however, overall Lancashire’s participation
rates for two? and three?year?olds were high and remained around 8%
higher than national figures. Officers highlighted the extensive
work taking place to improve engagement, including sharing of
information in multiple languages and strengthening outreach.
Immediate actions included making all early year's services and
training free of charge, which was expected to remove cost barriers
and support greater take?up, particularly in areas of concern.
Officers added that the Education Strategy would enable more
targeted district?level work, bringing together early years
providers to focus collectively on local needs, priorities and
development.

 

Members noted the persistent
4–5% attainment gap between boys and girls in secondary
school and asked whether data for September 2025 showed any
improvement. Officers confirmed that the gap remained unchanged. It
was highlighted that there was significant work ongoing to address
boys’ outcomes, including participation in a national Boys
Impact Conference, promoting International Men's Day and
celebrating positive male role models, and focusing on improving
boys’ attendance which was a concern and was known to
significantly influence attainment. Members welcomed these
initiatives but emphasised the need for continued action to
accelerate progress. In response to questions about whether the
same disparity existed amongst disadvantaged pupils, officers
confirmed that the attainment gap between boys and girls was also
the same across disadvantaged cohorts.

 

Regarding early years performance
specifically in Preston, officers advised that it was confirmed
that district?level data could be provided to the committee
following the meeting.

 

Members queried the comparative
performance data for maintained schools and academies. Officers
confirmed that this data was available and, overall, maintained
schools performed better. However, it was noted that many academies
inherited schools that were already underperforming, which meant
direct comparisons were challenging. It was noted some previously
inadequate maintained schools had transferred into academy trusts,
while maintained schools that remained with the authority had
largely sustained their performance. Officers also highlighted that
the service held data on which schools bought into services; it was
noted that those that did buy in, tended to perform more strongly
than those that did not.

 

The committee queried whether early
years issues, such as parents not engaging in early learning
activities including reading and phonics, particularly where
children did not attend nursery may be contributing to challenges
including speech delay and reduced school readiness skills such as
potty training. Officers agreed that these factors could have an
impact and explained that the Family Hubs provided key support to
families and new investment was being directed into Family Hubs to
strengthen support for early years and the home learning
environment. Officers also noted that work was underway to ensure
that as many families as possible were able to access the Hubs and
benefit from the support available.

 

The committee raised concerns that,
for disadvantaged pupils in the GCSE years, barriers as simple as
not being able to afford transport to school could impact
attendance and attainment. Officers confirmed that support for
these issues is provided at school level, with schools able to use
Pupil Premium funding to address such barriers. Pupil Premium plans
are in place to ensure that this funding is targeted effectively to
support disadvantaged pupils, including helping to remove practical
obstacles to learning.

 

Members queried the extent to which
early years outcomes are affected when English is not the first
language spoken at home, and whether additional teaching at an
earlier stage is required for these children. It was explained that
the service provided an English as an Additional Language (EAL)
service, which supported schools in meeting the needs of children
who are new to English. In early years, children often acquired
language skills more quickly, though a slight initial delay can be
observed as younger children tend to spend more time listening and
observing before actively using the language.

 

Members raised questions regarding
support for NEET young people, particularly those with an
Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP). It was noted that previous
NEET funding for both enrolled and unenrolled students was no
longer available, creating a potential gap in provision for some
young people. Officers explained that while Education and Skills
Funding Agency (ESFA) funding had previously supported this work,
elements of this funding had been redirected into the wider schools
funding pot. As a result, some districts continued to fund NEET
support while others did not, leading to variation across the
county. It was noted that how this may evolve under the future
Combined Authority arrangements would be interesting to
consider.

 

In relation to alternative
provision, officers confirmed that the council continued to work
closely with schools through Section 19 processes, supported by a
funding panel and resources dedicated to young people who required
alternative education pathways. The committee noted that some
colleges did offer provision for 14–16-year-olds; however,
others had withdrawn due to increased safeguarding requirements and
staffing costs. Despite this, several colleges such as Blackpool
and Fylde College continued to deliver a strong offer. Officers
noted that opportunities remained to strengthen collaboration with
colleges so they could play a wider role in alternative provision
where appropriate.

 

Members queried whether the draft
Education Strategy sufficiently reflected the purpose behind
learning, noting that the current vision placed strong emphasis on
academic subjects such as English and Maths, but did not explicitly
reference employability skills or preparation for life beyond
school. In response, the Cabinet Member for Education and Skills
acknowledged the importance of ensuring that the strategy promoted
a broader skills-based approach. It was agreed that revised wording
could be incorporated into the draft to strengthen the focus on
life skills and employability alongside academic learning.

 

Members asked about the role of
locality-based education groups and whether effective local
initiatives such as recent work with a school on vaping could be
shared more widely across Lancashire. An example was provided where
a school conducted an internal pupil survey and worked with local
police to address illegal vape sales and successfully secured the
closure of businesses selling vapes to children. Officers confirmed
that this kind of best practice was already shared across districts
and that the intention was to strengthen approaches like this
further. The vaping initiative was highlighted as a strong example,
with the development of a Lancashire-wide Vaping Charter now agreed
by secondary headteachers, stemming from the work highlighted in
East Lancashire. Officers also stated that wider partners,
including Public Health, Trading Standards, the Police, Health
colleagues and the ICB, were involved in supporting and
disseminating best practice across the county.

 

Members sought clarification on what
the draft strategy meant by “local provision" They noted
concerns that, in some areas, children may not have a school within
walking distance, and that transport was not always available, an
issue that could disproportionately affect disadvantaged families.
Members asked how “local access” was defined within the
strategy. Officers explained that this section related specifically
to early years, and that further detail could be explored at the
next meeting when School Place Planning would be considered.
Officers made reference to DfE guidance,
which defined reasonable travel distances for children as
approximately 2–3 miles. However, officers emphasised that
within the strategy, “local” primarily refered to ensuring that children with SEND were
not travelling long distances away from their communities and
peers, and that wherever possible they could attend schools closer
to home.

 
Resolved: That the following recommendations be shared with
the Cabinet Member for Education and Skills:
 

That the Lancashire Way Education
Strategy 2025 – 2028 be recommended to be presented to
Cabinet in March 2026 for ratification.

 

That emphasis on the skills development element
be highlighted more in the Lancashire Way Education Strategy 2025
– 2028. 

 

That attainment data for Early Years
Education be shared for all districts in Lancashire. 

 

That attainment data for Maintained
School's vs Academies be shared with the committee.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the Lancashire Way Education Strategy 2025-2028, focusing on skills development and sharing attainment data for Early Years Education and between Maintained Schools and Academies.
