decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
To provide Members of the LCCA Audit and
Governance Committee with an overview of the Authority’s
initial financial assurance framework; to invite questions to
officers; and to seek improvements based upon Members’
perceptions and expectations.
content:
Steve Thompson, CCA Finance Lead, presented an overview of
the financial assurance framework and associated documentation
approved in March 2025 at the commencement of the CCA, noting minor
updates would be required, such as aligning statutory budget dates
with meeting schedules. It was noted that some documents, set out
in the appendices, would be updated formally throughout the
year.
 
Operational finance systems had been implemented using a
hosted enterprise platform with feeder systems for accounts
payable/receivable, e-procurement, and contracts registers. Access
arrangements enabled all partner organisations to work effectively
together, and this had worked well to date.
 
The committee was briefed on the pending Section 33 status
for VAT recovery. Although VAT registration had been completed for
the CCA, and it was included in the Finance Bill, this could not be
enacted without Royal Assent which had not yet been given. Until
granted, expenditure continued to be incurred by lead authorities,
although it would be claimed retrospectively.
 
It was noted that the KPMG had been appointed as external
auditor. Audit planning for 2025/26 would encompass the initial
period from February 2025, creating an extended first audit year
and avoiding a separate audit for the partial year.
 
Reported revenue increased from an initial £20m
budget to £40m by Quarter 2, and the capital programme
increased from £3.3m to £70m, although this was largely
due to transport funding passported through the LCCA.
 
In response to a question on social value, it was noted
that the LCCA’s social value approach is still under
development and is expected to form part of a wider procurement
framework to be presented at the February meeting. This framework
would set out the procurement policy, strategy, and a defined
social value policy. It was confirmed that work was underway with
the three constituent councils to understand their existing
approaches to develop a combined, consistent model for the
LCCA.
 
In response to a question, it was reported that current
in-kind support services were covered by service level agreements
(SLAs) amounting to approximately £400,000 for 2025/26 and
would be recognised with contra entries in the three contributing
authorities' year-end accounts. It was confirmed that arrangements
for 2026/27 were under review, with the likelihood of moving to
paid SLAs where appropriate, with the value to be determined,
taking account of recharges against programme funding such as the
administration of the Adult Skills Fund.
 
The committee noted the current short-term investment
stance pending clarity on medium-term commitments, with improved
options to be considered in the forthcoming Treasury Management
Strategy.
 
Resolved: the LCCA Audit
and Governance Committee noted the report, and requested a further
update on the VAT recovery at the next meeting
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority's Audit and Governance Committee has approved recommendations for updates to the financial assurance framework and documentation.

content:
Andrew Dalecki, Head of Internal Audit, presented the

framework.
 
In response to a question on closing off actions, it was

would be reported back to the committee in a timeframe agreed with
the action owner.
 
The 33% delivery against the audit plan was queried. It was
noted that although

scheduled work was intentionally concentrated towards Quarter 4 to
ensure a sufficient volume of transactional activity to
test.
 
In response to a question about the limited
number of audit days allocated to grant work, it was
noted that current activity was focused on preparatory support for
services that will require grant audits. It was noted that

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
The report, supported by the presentation
slides included at Appendix A, is intended to update the Committee
on recent activities undertaken by the Lancashire Combined County
Authority.
content:
The Chief Operating Officer (COO) presented a report
summarising progress since the previous meeting. Recent strategic
documents were highlighted, including the Lancashire Growth Plan,
Get Lancashire Working Plan, and the draft Local Transport
Plan.
 
Transport: Since the previous meeting of this committee and
a subsequent meeting of the LCCA Board in December, the Authority
had prepared for assuming the role of sole Local Transport
Authority for Lancashire from April 2026. For 2026/27, the Board
had approved a commissioning and assurance model to discharge
transport duties, enabling the LCCA to build strategic and
technical capacity gradually while retaining local expertise
through close collaboration with the three constituent councils.
The Department for Transport had confirmed a consolidated funding
settlement that would combine previously separate grants e.g. Bus
Service Improvement Plan and Active Travel, to flow via the LCCA
from April.
 
Skills: The Authority remained on track to assume
responsibility for the Adult Skills Fund (c. £40m) from the
2026/27 academic year commencing August/September 2026, with
mobilisation and preparation activities ongoing.
 
In response to a question, it was confirmed that
foundational arrangements for the LCCA to act as an employer were
in place. Subject to consultation and the application of relevant
transfer regulations, a small number of posts were expected to be
transferred from the three partner authorities to the LCCA from
April 2026. These would largely be strategic roles, with most
operational capacity initially retained by constituent councils
under the commissioning model. Further transfers were expected in
October 2026 and March 2027.
 
Advisory Boards: The committee received a summary of recent
activity across the three Advisory Boards. The next round of
meetings was scheduled in January, with outcomes to be reported to
this committee in due course to maintain information
flow.
 
Governance Review: the committee noted the completion of
the governance review considering non-mayoral versus mayoral
arrangements. A joint letter had been sent by the Leaders of the
three constituent councils to the Minister for Devolution prior to
Christmas, indicating a willingness to explore further devolution
subject to conditions on investment certainty, public and
stakeholder consultation, and formal approvals by each constituent
authority and the LCCA. Further updates would be provided once
ministerial responses were received.
 
In response to a question around challenges and barriers,
capacity constraints inherent in a partnership model where many
officers worked in dual roles were acknowledged, and it was
confirmed that key support services currently provided in-kind by
constituent councils were recorded on the corporate risk register.
It was agreed that the corporate risk register would be used as the
standing mechanism to report on barriers and
mitigations.
 
Resolved: the LCCA Audit
and Governance Committee noted the report
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority's Audit and Governance Committee has approved recommendations for assuming the role of sole Local Transport Authority and responsibility for the Adult Skills Fund.

decision_maker: Lancashire Combined County Authority - Audit and Governance Committee
purpose:
This report sets out the updated LCCA
Corporate Risk and Opportunity Register, which is presented to the
Audit and Governance Committee on a quarterly basis in line with
its
responsibility for the oversight of the LCCA's risk management
arrangements.
content:
The committee received the Quarter 3 update to the
corporate risk register.
 
One risk score, for Transport, had increased at the time of
reporting, but was expected to reduce following the CCA
Board’s approval of the commissioning and assurance
model.
 
A
new risk was added regarding awareness and application of
procurement rules by third-party providers; it was noted that
Blackpool Council, who held oversight of procurement, were
developing templates and standardised procurement to mitigate the
risks.
 
Regarding the improvement recommendation in the internal
audit report on risk management, it was confirmed that training was
planned to take place over the next quarter, and an update would be
provided to the next committee meeting.
 
Clarification was sought on the
process for adding new risks to the risk register and how, from a
committee perspective, risk appetite should be assessed. It was
explained that the Corporate Risk Register captures strategic,
cross?cutting risks that could impact the LCCA’s core
business. Beneath this was a more detailed service?level risk which
recorded operational risks. Operational risks scoring 12 or above
were considered for escalation, while any strategic risks were
escalated directly to the Corporate Risk Register.
The Corporate Risk Register was
reviewed by the lead officers supporting the LCCA, alongside the
three Chief Officers from the constituent authorities and the Chief
Operating Officer. This process informed the register which was
brought to the committee.
Regarding risk appetite, it was
noted that the CCA’s approach is outlined in the Risk
Management Strategy which would be recirculated for information. It
was confirmed that the current approach was intentionally
light?touch, reflecting the early stage of development.
 
In response to a question, it
was agreed that officers should review
whether any partnership arrangements should be recorded at service level or
escalated to the CCA’s corporate risk
register.
 
Following discussion, the committee approved the updated
register.
 
Resolved: the LCCA Audit and Governance Committee:
 
i. 
approved the LCCA's
Corporate Risk and Opportunity Register as set out at Appendix A of
the report
ii. 
requested the Risk
Management Strategy be recirculated for information
iii. 
requested officers to
review whether any partnership arrangements should be recorded at
service level, or escalated to the CCA Corporate Risk
Register
topline: The Lancashire Combined County Authority's Audit and Governance Committee has decided to approve the updated Corporate Risk and Opportunity Register.

purpose:
It is proposed to make a Traffic Regulation
Order relating to various roads within the Hyndburn area to
introduce Prohibition of Waiting restrictions and a No Waiting
Monday to Friday 7am to 7pm restriction , Remove obstructive
parking that blocks sightlines of drivers , Improve access for
large vehicles associated with nearby businesses and Hyndburn
Borough Council depot, thereby improving general road safety for
all highway users.
Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 26 September 2025 and
24 October 2025 which included advertising in the local press and
notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.

During the formal consultation, three objections were received
regarding the proposed introduction of No Loading Monday to Friday
8am – 6pm on Cartmel Avenue, Accrington.

After consideration of the points raised, Officers propose to
review this proposal with the intention of alleviating the concerns
raised during consultation. To allow for full consideration by
Officers, a modification has been carried out to defer the
introduction of the restrictions and remove the original advertised
proposal from the Order.
A modification consultation was undertaken from 05 December 2025 to
02 January 2026. This consultation gave effect to the original
proposals, with the exception of the proposals relating to Cartmel
Avenue, which are proposed to be deferred.

No objections were received during the modification consultation.
Therefore, officers recommend that the Cartmel Avenue proposal be
removed from this Order.

parked vehicles.

required to provide additional unrestricted parking availability

area

purpose:
An Independent Domestic Violence Advisor
(IDVA) is a specialist professional who works with a victim of
domestic abuse to develop a trusting relationship. They can help a
victim with everything they need to become safe and rebuild their
life, and represent their voice at a Multi-agency Risk Assessment
Conference (MARAC), as well as helping them to navigate the
criminal justice process and working with the different statutory
agencies to provide wraparound support.
Safe Lives report that following support from an IDVA service, at
the closure of their cases:
• The majority of survivors reported cessation of abuse
• 84% of survivors reported feeling safer
• 73% of survivors felt their quality of life had
improved
Safe Lives (2022) https://safelives.org.uk/what-is-an-idva
Bristol City Council has been administering the Ministry of Justice
funding for these posts within Next Link on behalf of the Office of
the Police and Crime Commissioner following a decision made by
Cabinet on 24th January 2023. This arrangement enables a holistic
commissioning approach (with benefits for both commissioners and
providers), including oversight of service delivery and supporting
providers to problem solve any issues as they arise.
It has recently been announced that this funding is to be extended
for 2 further years to March 2028. This report seeks approval to
accept and spend this funding extension from the Ministry of
Justice (via the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner for
Avon and Somerset) to enable continued funding of Independent
Domestic Violence Advisors, working as part of the Next Link Plus
service.
The procurement team have confirmed that the delegation of this key
decision is covered in the original contract which states
“This report seeks authorisation from Cabinet for authority
to be delegated to the Executive Director for People in
consultation with Cabinet Member for Public Health to take all
steps necessary to procure and award the contract(s) necessary for
the implementation of Domestic Abuse and Sexual Violence Services,
in-line with the procurement routes and maximum budget envelopes
outlined in this report.” The variations being made are
necessary for the implementation of domestic abuse and sexual
violence services within the timeframe the key decision covers
(01/08/2021 – 31/07/2028).

purpose:
Approval to dispose of land at Gainsborough
Square, Lockleaze to be developed for age restricted Affordable
Housing units for independent retirement living.
07/04/2026 via email.
Most recent decision-making forum was Supported Housing Board
05/08/2025 with approval to proceed with negotiations with Anchor
Hanover Group to bring forward the site for age restricted
Affordable Housing units for independent retirement living under
the Bristol City Council’s Homes For Bristol: Interim
Affordable Housing Delivery Plan 2025-2027.
It has been intended that the land at Gainsborough Square,
Lockleaze, is disposed of for age restricted Affordable Housing
units for independent retirement living since earlier Cabinet
decisions were made. Adult Social Care contributed throughout the
process and supported the move from Extra Care Housing toward age
restricted affordable housing as the preferred and deliverable
model for the site.
In 2019 a Grant Agreement was signed with Homes England for the
investment of Local Authority Accelerated Construction (LAAC)
funding of £577k towards remediation, demolition, site
investigation, ecological and infrastructure works at the site.
This funding was drawn down and the former Lockleaze Adult Day
Centre was demolished and the site cleared, and various surveys
were undertaken.
The LAAC funding originally required that redevelopment was
achieved by hybrid modern methods of construction (MMC). However
the Council was unable to procure a developer to bring the scheme
forward in this way and the Grant Agreement was subsequently varied
to ‘Category 4: Off-Site Manufacturing – Sub-Assemblies
and Components’ and housing unit numbers proposed increased
from 56 to 60. Various other amendments to milestones have been
agreed with Homes England.
To address the viability of more complex and costly age restricted
affordable housing the Council’s Adult Social Care will
provide £900,000 of grant funding towards the cost of
construction subject to usual grant conditions.
A 2024 procurement exercise resulted in only one interested
Registered Provider, Anchor Hanover Housing Association and
officers have since negotiated with Anchor with regard to disposal
of the site at a nominal value of £1, and for Anchor to bring
forward the site for age restricted Affordable Housing units for
independent retirement living, which has been subject to a planning
pre-application process which was generally positive, and is likely
to result in a development with more homes than originally engaged.
A Red Book valuation for the purposes of s.123 Local Government Act
1972 has been undertaken by an external Registered Valuer which has
reported that the unrestricted market value of the site in the
region of £920,000 on the basis of open market housing and
the restricted value for the age restricted affordable housing is
£1, which confirms ‘best consideration’ and that
the undervalue for this transaction for this specific use required
by the Council is £920,000. The Council’s overriding
duty to seek best consideration is subject to certain exceptions,
most notably section 2 of the Local Government Act 2000, providing
the Council with well-being powers to accept a disposal at
undervalue within the £2 million threshold, where the
authority considers the disposal will help it to secure the
promotion or improvement of the economic, social or environmental
well-being of its citizens. Delegated authority was awarded to the
Executive Director for Housing by Homes and Housing Delivery Policy
Committee on 14th February 2025 to make this decision
notwithstanding it would otherwise have been a key decision.
Homes England (LAAC) are supportive of Anchor bringing forward the
development, and further revisions to the LAAC milestones have been
agreed which Anchor has confirmed they can meet. A further Deed of
Variation to the Grant Agreement is expected to allow Anchor not to
use an MMC approach at all, and instead a traditional build,
however still at pace to satisfy the agreed milestones, and Homes
England has confirmed support for this.
The Council will place conditions to the disposal by way of a legal
restriction on the title of the property that will ensure the
delivery of the aged restricted affordable housing. It is
recommended that the Council enter into a contract with Anchor
Hanover Group to dispose of the land and for redevelopment.

Bristol Heat Network Zone, including consultation on the boundary

Heat Network Zone Coordinator Body to manage the zone.
content:
It
was RESOVLED that the Committee for Environment and Sustainability
noted:
 

That the
Government has proposed the creation of Heat Network Zones across
England in the Energy Act 2023 and that these will be managed
locally by Zone Coordination Bodies, which will sit within local
authorities and/or combined authorities.
That
Bristol City Council has been working closely with the government
to define a zone within central Bristol in line with the national
guidance and to co-design an appropriate Zone Coordination Body for
the city and/or region. 
The principle of Heat
Network Zoning as an important part of the transition of the
city’s energy system

 
It
was RESOVLED that the Committee for Environment and Sustainability
(Unanimously FOR):
 
1.     
Approved the principle of the city
council taking on some of the functions of the Zone Coordination
Body and that further work be undertaken to bring detailed
proposals to the relevant committee for decision in due
course.
2.     
Approved consultation on the boundary of
the Central Bristol Heat Network Zone and delegate to the Executive
Director of Growth and Regeneration, in consultation with the Chair
of the Environment and Sustainability Committee, the determination
of the details and timing of the consultation and liaison with the
new Zone Coordination Body to inform their decisions on future
designation of the zone.

purpose:
Bristol City Council’s current Data
Analytics Platform (DAP) is outdated, costly to maintain and
heavily dependent on external proprietary code. Data is stored in
thousands of CSV files, creating inefficiency, operational risk and
slow delivery of insights.
To modernise this, we require a partner to support the
implementation of a new platform based on Microsoft Fabric, a
unified and scalable data environment offering simpler data
ingestion, improved performance and reduced long term costs. This
will replace fragile legacy pipelines and create a more robust
foundation for analytics.

purpose:
A decision was taken at Cabinet on the 7th
March 2023 in relation to the Future of Youth Services in Bristol
which delegated authority to the Executive Director Children and
Education to take all steps required to agree terms and enter into
grant agreements to award grants for youth services across the
following 7 years at a total cost of £6m. This decision
relates to the award of grant funding to providers to deliver
services in South Bristol which aligns with the South Bristol
Locality Youth and Play Development Plan (2026–27). The
funding supports delivery across Priority 1–3 wards and
underpins the successful implementation of the South Bristol Area
Action Plan, ensuring continuity of youth and play services
including open access youth work, play ranger sessions and targeted
provision. This programme is designed to operate in conjunction
with the new Youth Zone (224), aligning local delivery with the
Area Plan’s strategic intention for 224 to act as a major hub
for inclusive, high-quality youth provision, expanding access,
strengthening early-help pathways and reducing inequalities across
neighbouring Priority 1 wards including Knowle West, Hartcliffe,
Bishopsworth and Hengrove.

content:
To seek approval to extend the council’s
current electricity supply contracts
for twelve months to ensure continuity of supply and
cost certainty while the replacement Sleeved Pool contract is
re?tendered and awarded. 

That the Strategy and Resources Committee
(unanimous vote in favour):

Approve the deferral of the
previously approved budget envelope of £33M for the Sleeved
Pool supply to the council sites approved at the July 2024 meeting
of the Environment & Sustainability committee, to apply for a
four year period from the date that the Sleeved Pool arrangement
goes live.
Authorise the Executive Director for
Growth and Regeneration, in consultation with the Chair of the
Environment and Sustainability Committee, to take all steps
required to enter into a new call off contract of 12 months for the
sleeved electricity supply with TotalEnergies via Laser Energy, in
line with the procurement routes and maximum budget envelopes
outlined in this report.
Authorise the Executive Director for
Growth and Regeneration, in consultation with the Chair of the
Environment and Sustainability Committee, to take all steps
required to enter into a new call off contract of 12 months for the
Non-Half-Hourly and Unmetered electricity supply contracts via
Laser Energy, in-line with the procurement routes and maximum
budget envelopes outlined in this report.
Authorise the Executive Director for
Growth and Regeneration to invoke any subsequent
extensions/variations specifically defined in the contract(s) being
awarded, up to the maximum budget envelope outlined in this
report.

 
That the Committee for Strategy and Resources
noted:

The cost envelope requested reflects
the budgets set for the extension period, however the forecast cost
of electricity usage for the duration of the requested extension
currently exceeds the available budget. Council officers will seek
to introduce measures to reduce energy usage and limit overall
spend to within the approved cost envelope.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Policy Committee has decided to extend the council's electricity supply contracts for twelve months to ensure continuity and cost certainty.

purpose:
The council purchases electricity through the
Laser Energy procurement framework. This provides access to a
managed portfolio and allows the Council to benefit from
competitive pricing and risk managed energy purchasing. A tender to
set up an alternative new supply arrangement (the Sleeved Pool) has
run in to technical difficulties, so a continuation of the current
supply arrangements is required in order to maintain continuity of
electricity supply for council sites and to support the export of
renewable electricity from council owned generating assets.

Disposals to Goram Homes to Support Housing Delivery” and 3
March 2022 “Goram Homes – Pipeline of Housing
Development Sites 2022” authorised the Executive Director of
Growth and Regeneration in consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Housing and the Director of Finance to approve the transfer of land

The site benefits from outline planning consent (19/02632) for up

provision of energy centre for communal heat and power. Reserved
Matters Approval (23/02376/M) for phase 1b was granted 10 May 2024.
A reserved matters application for phase 8 is due to be
submitted.
The Council entered an option agreement with Goram Homes on 18
December 2025. Goram recently exercised the option by service of an
option notice to acquire part of the site (phases 1b and 8) in
accordance with the terms of the agreement. The land contract is in
an agreed form and ensures all key contractual terms and safeguards
for the Council including best consideration.

purpose:
The Drug and Alcohol Treatment and Recovery
Improvement Grant (DATRIG) funding decision was taken at the
strategy and resources committee meeting on 17/03/25 as a finance
urgent key decision appended to the period 10 finance outturn
report, appendix A6, as noted in item 124; point 10 of the decision
notice.
As a result of the funding being approved, we now have
£132,000 to be allocated to up to four community led research
projects answering the question ‘How can we best meet the
substance use needs of Bristol’s diverse communities’
Research projects will be undertaken by trusted Voluntary,
Community and Social Enterprise (VCSE) Alliance partners and will
be led by the communities they are working with. The outcomes of
the research will be used to influence service providers and
partners in ensuring the substance use treatment and recovery
services offered in Bristol reflect its diverse communities and are
accessible to all.
The fund would be administered through Quartet Community Foundation
on our behalf.

purpose:
The Bristol Floating Harbour Team manages
harbour water levels to approximately ± 20 cms by
controlling water ingress at Netham Lock and expelling water as
necessary at Underfall Yard. Water from the River Avon carries a
high level of silt that enters the harbour at Netham and is carried
to the lower end of the harbour around Cumberland Basin. Further
silt deposits enter the harbour from the River Frome. Approximately
every three years it is necessary to carry out dredging, to ensure
the navigable channel throughout the harbour remains usable to all
vessels.

purpose:
Demand for Education, Health and Care Needs
Assessments (EHCNAs) has risen sharply. Requests have increased by
approximately 35 percent and the number of children awaiting
assessment has risen by around 31 percent.
The Educational Psychology (EP) service completed 1,418 advices in
2025, representing a 53 percent increase on 2024. The SEND
assessment team finalised 1,069 EHCPs in 2025 (a 37 percent
increase on 2024). Despite maximising recruitment, overtime and use
of associates, the EP service cannot meet the operational target of
170 advices per month (during term time) without additional
commissioned capacity.
This decision provides temporary commissioned capacity to ensure
statutory performance continues to improve and that the backlog is
reduced at pace which will minimise the time families spend waiting
for the outcome of their assessment.
•Stakeholders (health and social care partners, Bristol Parent
Carer Forum) recognise progress in productivity and
collaboration.
•The Department for Education has noted the coherence of the
SEND and Inclusion strategy and the collaborative way agencies
work.
•Statutory performance remains under close scrutiny with a
likely Ofsted SEND inspection within the next 12 months.

purpose:
The council is aiming to lease properties on
the Emergency Accommodation Framework for over 10 years, which
would allow these properties to sit in the General Fund. The
decision to authorise the Executive Director to take all necessary
steps to enter leases of at least 10 years plus one day was taken
at the Homes and Housing Delivery Policy Committee on
18/07/2025.
The council requires expert legal support to enter these long
leases. Browne Jacobson LLP have specialist experience in this
area, having previously advised other Local Authorities on a
similar approach. Given this and the time pressures associated with
the delivery of savings, the council is therefore direct awarding a
contract, via the Agora Framework, to Browne Jacobson LLP to
provide the necessary legal support in drafting, executing and
registering these leases.
The direct award also avoids any potential delays in delivering
savings and additional costs associated with a tender exercise,
thereby providing value for money.
The rates associated with this exercise have been reviewed by the
council’s Legal service and assessed as being
reasonable.

purpose:
Can Do Bristol is a digital volunteering
platform commissioned by Bristol City Council and developed in
partnership with Made Open Communications Ltd, who have served as
the specialist supplier since the platform’s inception in
2016. The platform enables residents, community groups, and
organisations to connect, collaborate, and participate in
volunteering and social action across the city. It operates on Made
Open’s licence model based on active user numbers and is
managed in alignment with the Council’s IT and data
governance frameworks.
The platform plays a key role in advancing civic participation,
community resilience and digital inclusion, aligning with the
Council’s strategic priorities under the One City Plan and
Corporate Strategy 2025–2030. It reflects the Council’s
values of empowerment, equity, and collaboration, and is a
practical tool for delivering the One City Approach. Can Do Bristol
supports community connection and cohesion, particularly important
in the current context of rising social tensions, and has
demonstrated its value during citywide responses to the COVID-19
pandemic and cost-of-living crisis.
With over 13,000 approved members and thousands of monthly
interactions, the platform continues to enable grassroots social
action and inclusive civic engagement. It is supported by a
cross-sector advisory group and partnerships with equalities-led
organisations, helping to embed equity and accessibility into its
ongoing development.
This decision seeks to renew the licence and contract with Made
Open for a further four years to ensure continuity of service,
uphold data governance standards, and support the Council’s
statutory duties under the Localism Act 2011 and Care Act
2014.
Following a review of alternative options, a direct award to Made
Open has been identified as the most viable and cost-effective
solution. Their proprietary platform architecture, deep integration
with Council systems, and proven track record of inclusive civic
tech delivery make them uniquely positioned to continue this work.
Their continued delivery offers best value for money by avoiding
the significant financial, technical, and operational risks
associated with replacing or rebuilding the platform, while
maintaining service continuity and strategic alignment.

purpose:

and 3 Abstained):
 
1. That the Committee for Environment &
Sustainability approves the proposed replacement strategy for
operational vehicle fleet that are utilised by the Council’s
Waste Services provider, Bristol Waste Company (BWC).

paper regarding the potential relocation of the Albert Road depot
to a future meeting of the Environment & Sustainability

purpose:
Due to programme prolongation, the external
works including the compound area adjacent to the Trenchard Street
rear exits achieved Practical Completion in December 2025 extending
the defect liability periods to March 2026 with an agreed formal
project closure of April 2026.
This approval is for the Provision of NEC Project Management, NEC
Supervision, and PMO Services via the Council’s Strategic
Partner including Project Assurance for cost, engineering and
design.
Current Variation Order VO13 scope was based on the following
programme, targeting December 2025:
•Section 1 Main Building: the current approved VO is based
upon an advised completion of Regulatory works within the main
building by end of October 2025, with the certification of
remaining works by end of December 2025. This assumes the Final
Documentation, Legals, Agreements and Financial close by the end of
December 2025 in addition to the completion of Section 2, the
issuing of the final certification at end of defects at the end of
December 2025.
•Willmott Dixon final account and Consultants accounts not
closed until December 2025.
The scope and variation for the programme and rationale are:
•Willmott Dixon’s revised timetable that reflects the
outstanding works and the documentation remaining at the time of
this variation order is now as below:
Section 1 Main Building:
•Regulatory compliance by end of October 2025.
•Outstanding works certification by end of January 2026.
•Three months later than planned, prolonged completion of
regulatory works and protracted issues with completing
documentation and certification, and greater number of disputes by
Willmott Dixon on outstanding defects.
Section 2 - External works:
•The planned completion of these works was end of August 2025
with a three-month defects period completing November 2025. This
would have constituted the final certification of the project
allowing for total project close out in November 2025.
•Due to protracted design approval process increased
complexity due to existing services, equipment, and re-mobilisation
the latest completion date advised by Wilmott Dixon for these works
is now mid-December 2025, giving a final certification date of
mid-March 2026.
Variation Order O14 reflects this three-month delay to the external
works as well as the projected certification dates. It also covers
the additional works that have delayed the closing of the contract.
These include:-
oSecond round of BREEAM correspondence that requires further
action
oDelayed archiving period due to late documentation
oIncrease admin dealing with Willmott Dixon disputed items
oExtended Highways Audit
oExtensive work required by consultants to provide letters of
comfort which has de-risked the ownership of the
building/project
oThe physical works on site have taken longer than initially
anticipated, with many disputes had with Willmott Dixon to complete
works.
oAdditional and extended period of contract administration due to
the compounded impact of the above

The current version of software provided under
this contract by Document Output Solutions UK Ltd will be
de-supported by the supplier in December 2026 meaning that from
then until the contract ends the supplier would not provide
assistance with fault fixing or other support and
maintenance.
The supplier does provide support for the same software but as
Software as a Service (SaaS), i.e., via a browser-based solution,
rather than onsite installation. This means that the council is
required to move to this new support model before the current
version of the software becomes end of life and de-supported.

purpose:
The acquisition is required to construct and
maintain the River Malago Restoration Project. The restoration
works were identified in the Bedminster Green Framework (2019) as
strategic infrastructure required to reduce flood risk to the wider
area and to support the regeneration of Bedminster. The restoration
works will restore historic in-channel heritage features (the
penstock), improve public realm and green spaces, improve habitat
to facilitate biodiversity net gain, and reduce flood risk to the
wider Bedminster area.

purpose:
New social
housing regulations came into effect in April 2024 as part of the
Social Housing Regulations Act 2024, which placed various
requirements on social landlords.

Tower Hamlets Homes was insourced to the council in 2023 and
this meant that the requirements outlined by the Social Housing
Regulations Act 2024 were imposed on the council. When reviewing
the impact of this legislation on the council, it became apparent
that the Anti-Social Behaviour (ASB) Policy for council tenants and
leaseholders was out of date: requiring a review refresh. The
Council has a responsibility as a social landlord to have an up to
date ASB Policy that sets out clear service standards around the
management of ASB.

An ASB improvement programme began in January 2025 and the
development of an ASB Policy was identified as a key
workstream.

The Council does not currently have an ASB policy that
clearly sets out what it considers to be ASB and how instances of
ASB will be managed. As such we are developing an ASB Policy that
reflects how the council (including housing, ASB teams and
Environmental Health) will address ASB locally.

As part of the development process, it has been established
that a number of policies and processes are either out of date or
no-longer effective in terms of meeting the needs of local
people.

At this stage, it is being asked that the newly proposed
‘triage process’ for ASB case allocation and escalation
is reviewed and approved to ensure the resultant ASB Policy can
reflect our local approach to addressing and managing
ASB.

Going forward, it this item will require Cabinet to review
and approve the newly developed ASB Policy.

decision_maker: Portfolio Holder for Adult Care and Health
content:
That the projected
net overspend of £9,348k on controllable expenditure based on
information as of December 2025 be noted.

One of the “Making Bromley Even
Better” ambitions is to manage our resources well, providing
value for money, and efficient and effective services for
Bromley’s residents. To meet this we will need to maintain a
relentless focus on efficiency, outcomes of services and prudent
management of our finances.
 
The “2025/26 Council Tax” report
highlighted the financial pressures facing the Council. It remains
imperative that strict budgetary control continues to be exercised
to minimise the risk of compounding financial pressures in future
years.
 
Chief Officers and Heads of Finance are
continuing to place emphasis on the need for strict compliance with
the Council’s budgetary control and monitoring
arrangements.

liquidity.

points within Bromley, in accordance with the finalised contractual
terms.

scheme to the capital programme be approved at the value of
£900k which would be fully grant funded.

 

Proposed sites are
only considered outside properties with the express permission of
the resident affected.

 

Ward Members are
consulted prior to proposed sites being published.

decision_maker: Portfolio Holder for Transport, Highways and Road Safety
content:
The Portfolio Holder for Transport, Highways
and Road Safety agreed that
the schemes listed in Appendix ‘A’
of the report included in a programme of planned highway
maintenance for 2026/27, should be undertaken by the
Council’s existing highway term maintenance contractor.
 
The Portfolio Holder for Transport, Highways
and Road Safety agreed that the decision to include additional
schemes in the programme be delegated to the Director of
Environment & Public Protection, based on the results of
further condition assessments.
 
The Portfolio Holder agreed that the
additional grant funding received from the Department for Transport
be utilised to improve the condition of the borough’s highway
assets.

A well-maintained highway facilitates safe and
reliable travel for pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists, and
contributes to the vitality of the borough and the local
economy.
 
Maintaining the highway asset through timely
intervention reduces the need for more expensive maintenance
treatments at a later date, along with the demand for reactive
maintenance, such as repairing potholes and broken paving. This
improves value for money and customer satisfaction, reduces
unplanned network disruption, and contributes to reducing third
party claims for damages. There is a strong case for continued
investment in planned maintenance of the highway asset, which would
reduce the demand for more costly reactive repairs.
 
This report recommends a programme of planned
carriageway and footway maintenance projects to be funded from
existing LBB capital budgets and DfT grant funding
topline: The Portfolio Holder for Transport, Highways and Road Safety has decided to approve a programme of planned highway maintenance for 2026/27 and utilize additional grant funding to improve the condition of the borough's highway assets.

purpose:
Consideration and recommendations of feedback
received from the public following a preliminary public
consultation on changes to parking charges proposed for
2026–27, that aim to improve road safety, encourage
sustainable travel, and ensure our parking services cover their
costs.
content:
Consideration and recommendations of feedback
received from the public following a preliminary public
consultation on changes to parking charges proposed for
2026–27, that aim to improve road safety, encourage
sustainable travel, and ensure our parking services cover their
costs.

To progress to statutory public consultation via the
Traffic Regulation Order process of the following:
 
(1) 
Proposal to introduce
an additional resident’s permit charge
based on vehicle size (area) in 2026/27.
 
(2) 
Proposal to increase
visitor permit charges in 2026/27.
 
(3) 
Proposal to increase
the all-day parking charge at all Park and Ride sites in
Bath.

Parking charge proposals have been formulated in accordance
with the requirements of s122 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act
(1984) (RTRA 1984). The aim of these proposals is to address both
pedestrian safety and traffic management considerations, supporting
the council’s Corporate Strategy and local transport policy
whilst also remaining consistent with the council's commitments to
Liveable Neighbourhoods and the Journey to Net
Zero.
 
Vehicle sizes are increasing, driven by consumer demand for
larger models like SUVs, which made up over 60% of new UK car sales
in 2024—up from less than 50% in 2020. Research shows that
bigger vehicles such as SUVs and vans are more likely to cause
serious injuries or fatalities to pedestrians (especially children)
and cyclists because of their height and blind spots. Large
vehicles also block buses, emergency services, and deliveries on
narrow roads, making travel more difficult for everyone.
 
Reviewing visitor permit charges complements a
separate review of base charges in 2025/26 for resident parking
permits to ensure that Resident Parking Schemes are self-financing
so that their operating costs are not covered by other council
funds.
 
A proposed increase to all day parking charges
at out park and ride sites for motorists not using the park and
ride service protects the long- term viability of the service and
ensures that those using these sites for short-stay parking to
heath and recreation, particularly Lansdown Park & Ride to the
North of the city, are not impacted.

None.  Proposals
outlined in the report have been subject to public
consultation.
topline: The Cabinet Member for Sustainable Transport Strategy has decided to progress with proposed changes to parking charges in 2026-27 to improve road safety and encourage sustainable travel.

purpose:
The Chartered Institute of Public Finance and
Accountancy’s Treasury Management in the Public Services:
Code of Practice 2021 Edition (the CIPFA Code) requires the
Authority to approve a treasury management strategy before the
start of each financial year.
This report fulfils the Council’s legal obligation under the
Local Government Act to have regard to the CIPFA Code.
content:
(1) 
To recommend the actions proposed within the Treasury Management
Strategy Statement 2026/27 (Appendix 1 of the
report) to Council.
 
(2) 
To note the Treasury Management Indicators detailed in Appendix 1
of the report.
 

The Local Government Act 2003 requires the
Council to ‘have regard to’ the Prudential Code and to
set Treasury Indicators for the next three years to ensure that the
Council’s capital investment plans are affordable, prudent
and sustainable.
 
The Act therefore requires the Council to set
out its treasury strategy for borrowing and to prepare a Treasury
Management Strategy; this sets out the Council’s policies for
managing its investments and for giving priority to the security
and liquidity of those investments.

The Director of Finance (S151
Officer), having consulted the Cabinet Member for Resources,
believes that the above strategy represents an appropriate balance
between risk management and cost effectiveness. Some alternative
strategies, with their financial and risk management implications,
are the table below.
 




Alternative


Impact on income and
expenditure


Impact on risk
management






Invest in a narrower range of counterparties
and/or for shorter times.


Interest income will be lower.


Lower chance of losses from credit related
defaults, but any such losses may be greater.




Invest in a wider range of counterparties
and/or for longer times.


Interest income will be higher.


Increased risk of losses from credit related
defaults, but any such losses may be smaller.




Borrow additional sums at long-term fixed
interest rates.


Debt interest costs will rise; this is
unlikely to be offset by higher investment income.


Higher investment balance leading to a higher
impact in the event of a default; however long-term interest costs
may be more certain.




Borrow short-term or variable loans instead of
long-term fixed rates.


Debt interest costs will initially be
lower.


Increases in debt interest costs will be
broadly offset by rising investment income in the medium term, but
long-term costs may be less certain.




Reduce level of borrowing.


Saving on debt interest is likely to exceed
lost investment income.


Reduced investment balance leading to a lower
impact in the event of a default; however long-term interest costs
may be less certain.

content:
The local authority is
experiencing a shortage of foster placements, particularly for
sibling groups and children with complex needs. This is resulting
in:

• Children being placed outside the local area.
• Increased costs for independent fostering agencies.
• Increases in children placed in residential settings where
their plan is foster care.
• Disruption of sibling relationships.

A policy has been developed to support foster carers to receive
financial support from the local authority to make alterations /
extensions to their homes which enable them to look after more
children. Foster carers have been surveyed and there is a strong
interest in this scheme from them. Two foster carers have actively
come forward and are requesting support to enable their current
children to remain with them.

(1) 
To agree the proposal to offer housing alterations for foster
carers, and note the draft policy Housing Alterations Policy for
Bath & North East Somerset Foster
Carers. 
 
(2) 
To agree the delegation of final approval for
the policy and associated processes to the Director
of Children’s Services in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services.
 
(3) 
To note  the allocation
of £500,000 of capital funding for the works which is
included in the proposed capital programme as provisionally
approved, delegating responsibility for the full approval of the
funding to the Director of Children’s Services in
consultation with the Director of Finance (S151 Officer), and to
delegate decisions on each individual case to the Director of
Children’s Services.

This policy will help to address the shortage
of foster carers, which is placing considerable pressure on
children’s services and social care.  Currently, at least 11 children remain in
residential care despite their care plan being foster care. To
address this, the Council is developing a policy to fund home
extensions or alterations for existing foster carers whose housing
limitations prevent them from accommodating more children.
 
The policy will enable existing foster carers
to care for more children in care. 
Survey results show that an overwhelming majority of existing
foster carers responded positively to the proposals. 
 
Supporting more children and young
people in local homes, means that travel times to school and other
settings is reduced, and social workers and other have shorter
travel times. This delivers a more sustainable model of social
support that is both environmentally responsible and community
focused.

This project is part of the
wide-ranging Children’s Transformation programme underway in
Children’s Services.  No other
options related to this project have been specifically
reviewed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to address the shortage of foster placements by offering housing alterations for foster carers

purpose:
To continue to support further investment (if
necessary, from the Council) for the delivery of the Somer Valley
Enterprise Zone scheme.
content:
(1) 
To reaffirm the commitment to promoting the Somer Valley Enterprise
Zone (SVEZ) scheme, notwithstanding the Council’s recognition
of potential viability concerns with the project.
 
(2) 
If the SVEZ scheme proceeds, to acknowledge that up to £53m
may need to be secured from various means to ensure the delivery of
the project, including potential further investment from the
Council, other public funding sources, public loans and developer
partnership.

The affirmation of the Council’s
commitment to deliver the scheme is necessary due to current
evolving advice on the viability deficit, which is revisiting the
viability scenarios and assumptions underpinning the
scheme.  The delivery of the SVEZ is
identified as a corporate priority in the B&NES Economic
Strategy (2014-2030).  The SVEZ will
provide economic, environmental and social benefits to the
area.

1) 
Do nothing –
without continued support for further investment and based on the
viability position as currently assessed, there is a considerable
risk to securing the Compulsory Purchase Order (CPO). If the CPO is
not secured, the scheme will not come forward. Support for further
investment is therefore critical to the delivery of the scheme, in
parallel with exploring other options for resolving potential
viability concerns.
 
2) 
Delay – the
Council could delay promoting the CPO until there is more certainty
as to the viability position and other options being available for
resolving viability concerns (for example, appointing a developer
partner). However, the scheme has been in contemplation for many
years and is needed to address existing issues in the area. Further
delay adversely affects landowners affected by the scheme due to
prolonged uncertainty. It could also risk funding sources which are
already committed or expected to be committed. The Council
considers that the scheme should come forward now and has already
committed to progressing the scheme as soon as practically
possible, subject to future approvals prior to implementation, and
with other options pursued in parallel.

purpose:
The Bath City Centre Phase 3 project —
now renamed the Bath Bus Infrastructure Improvements (BBIP) project
— aims to deliver an Outline Business Case (OBC) by March
2027. The project will focus on improving bus infrastructure within
Bath to enhance the reliability and efficiency of bus
services.

Bath’s current bus network is experiencing increasing delays,
longer journey times, and lower than expected customer
satisfaction. These issues are expected to worsen if no action is
taken, particularly in light of forecast housing growth identified
through the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) targets. The
BBIP project will therefore review and shortlist a package of
infrastructure options aimed at improving bus reliability and
addressing these challenges.
